en: Preface to the Annotated Collation of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* The *Annotated Collation of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is a compilation by the śramaṇa Shi Guangmo of Western Wu.
By elucidating the profound mysteries and rectifying errors, it seeks to assist the sūtra and correct the study of the mind. Is he not, indeed, one of those who have received the seal of the mind?
Indeed, it has long been difficult to clarify the study of the mind. Among our Confucian tradition, beginning from the sovereigns of the Tang and Yu eras, it was said:
"The human mind is perilous; the Dao-mind is subtle. Only through refinement and singleness may one truly hold fast to the Mean.
This was the transmission from the Sage of Yu to Great Yu, serving as the constant method for governance and peace. Former scholars have explained that what issues forth from...

That which pertains to form and breath is the human mind (*renxin*); that which issues from principle and righteousness is the mind of the Way (*daoxin*). The human mind easily becomes private and is difficult to make public;
therefore, it is perilous. The mind of the Way is difficult to clarify and easy to obscure; therefore, it is subtle. Only by being refined can one discern them.
Yet, it is not mixed with the private interests of form and breath; it maintains itself as one, being purely the correctness of principle and pattern (*yili*).

The way for the governance and peace of the world and future generations must surely be rooted in this. Now, when the followers of the Śākya (*Zhugan*) discourse on the mind, they speak of the "true mind" and the "deluded mind.
What they call "tranquil illumination" and "mysterious penetration," or "the non-duality of emptiness and existence," [are their doctrines].
That which stands alone and remains is the true mind. As for that which is constructed from the roots and objects, and manifested through deluded thoughts and perceptions, this is the deluded mind.
One must empty all that is deluded and integrate all that is true; only then does one attain correctness.
Thus, although the names differ from those transmitted by our Confucian tradition regarding the "human mind" (*renxin*) and the "mind of the Way" (*daoxin*), their substance is in fact the same.
For the most part, it is the deviation or correctness, the partiality or completeness of this very mind that the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* elucidates in detail.

However, it does not merely point to the private attachments of form and breath, but also concurrently rectifies the errors of consciousness and views; thus, it accords with our Confucian practice of "investigating things" (*gewu*).

This leads to the study [of this work]. Its meaning accords quite well with [the teachings of the sages]. One can truly believe that its merit in exhorting one another toward goodness provides a beneficial contribution to the world’s moral instruction.
Therefore, our Great Ancestor, the August Emperor Taizu, with the vast and profound benevolence of Heaven and Earth, [honored it].
An imperial decree was issued to all monasteries and temples throughout the empire, commanding monks, nuns, Daoists, laypeople, and all others to transmit, study, and expound upon this sutra.
The intent was that every person might rectify their own mind and assist in propagating the sacred transformation. How magnificent!
The mind of the Sage Emperor is profound and far-reaching. However, the phrasing and tone of this scripture are difficult and arduous, and its meanings are buried in the obscure and mysterious;
without an explanation, one cannot enter it. Furthermore, even those who have explained it have not yet fully reached its source.
The Layman Lin Shangqiong of Sanyuan in my province of Min has sent me this commentary from afar and requested a preface from me. I have therefore accepted his service.
In the intervals between the myriad affairs of state, he retired and closed his chambers. He read it several times over;

then, closing the volume, he contemplated the methods for governing and the mind with which he employs them. It appears that the essence of being "without external boundaries" is fully revealed in this memorial.
Tracing the currents back to their source, pruning the ornate to grasp the substantial, its systematic organization and analytical dissection surpass all others.
The preceding explanation has been provided; I have further detailed the introduction at the beginning of this compilation so that it may be transmitted.
Moreover, by placing this sutra alongside the classics bequeathed by our Confucian sages and predecessors upon my seat, I hope that my daily conduct may become no less than half of the *Analects*.
Preface to the Revised Commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, composed by Ye Xianggao,
Grand Secretary of the Imperial Academy, Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince, and Minister of the Ministry of Rites of the Ming Dynasty,
in the fourth month of the summer of the Gui-chou year of the Wanli era.

In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, our Buddha spoke directly of the wondrous nature of this mind, establishing its names and categories so that it would not be confused with the teachings of demons or externalists.
Now, as for this mind: it is truly pure, harmonious, and refined; it is empty, penetrating, and luminous.

It transcends all numerical categories yet is not non-existent; it engages with manifold names yet is not existent. Buddhas and sentient beings are of one essence; things and self share the same root. How could it be... [the four]...?
How could it be fathomed by the phrases of ordinary speech or measured by the minds of the multitudes?

It is because all sentient beings are deluded regarding their own minds and cling to external natures that they give rise to views such as superior and subtle, minute particles, existence and non-existence, oneness and difference, and the self (*ātman*). These are all truly false conceptualizations.

The World-Honored One refuted each of them one by one to reveal the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātmāryajñāna*), stating that it is inherently complete and does not arise from [external conditions].
He attained it. This is identical in meaning to Bodhidharma’s direct pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
It was for this reason that he instructed the Second Patriarch, saying, "The four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* can serve as a seal for the mind. Is not his intention found here?

Some claim that because Bodhidharma’s separate transmission of the mind-seal does not establish written words, it is called "direct pointing," and thus they equate the teachings with Chan; this is likely not correct. They do not understand this.
The Sūtras likewise dispel the finger of verbal expression to reveal the moon of ultimate reality; how could they fail to establish direct pointing? Take, for instance, the Chan practitioners:
their claim that "words are themselves non-words" is merely a pedagogical device of their school, a convoluted manipulation of intellectual understanding.

Their efforts are already misguided; where, then, is the so-called "direct pointing"? Indeed, direct pointing clarifies the ultimate reality, while the manipulation of intellectual understanding reaches toward the provisional; these two have never been at odds.
This contradicts my ears. The pedagogical method of this sutra is likewise so. Thus, Chan and the Teachings (Jiao) are certainly different names for the same essence.
Former scholars such as Jiang Zhiqi and Song Lian regarded the Chan of Bodhidharma as merely meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
This not only shows they failed to understand Bodhidharma’s Chan, but they also lacked knowledge of the meaning of this sutra.
The title of this chapter of the sutra is "The Heart of the Buddha’s Words. This "Heart" refers to the Mind directly pointed out by the Dharma;
the Mind directly pointed out by the Dharma is what the World-Honored One called the "Sublime Mind of Nirvana" when he held up a flower to show Kāśyapa.

To seek its source and unite with its ultimate principle is a tradition that has long existed. However, the text and meaning of this sutra are extraordinary and profound, making it truly difficult to read and understand; many have retreated, seeing it as a precipice too steep to climb.
There are those who possess [this knowledge]. Fortunately, there remain ancient commentaries; scholars rely on them to gain entry.
Yet, they are still unable to penetrate deeply and seek out the ultimate tenets, because the old commentaries are not detailed. As the Sūtra says:

"The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness. Thus, regarding the single category of the eight consciousnesses, it is identical to the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Ghanavyūha*, and other sūtras concerning Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises serve as corroborating evidence for these points; yet, the ancient commentaries often omit them—is this not to be regretted?

(Guangmo), desiring to elucidate the Great Way, I did not hesitate despite my own ignorance. I have thus consulted the sūtras and śāstras, various ancient commentaries, and the two translations from the Wei and Tang dynasties, synthesizing them to compose this sub-commentary (*shu*).
Regarding those parts of the sūtra that are obscure and difficult to understand, I have reconciled the two translations and appended [the relevant passages].
Below that, I have endeavored to enable readers to grasp the meaning through their own insight. I have excerpted what was already clear in the commentary and clarified what was obscure.
I have titled this work the *Chandingshu* (Annotated Revision). This is because I do not prize the alteration of phrasing or the indulgence of one's own whims to confuse the intelligence of others;

my sole aim is to ensure that the original text is free from impediment. Once the commentary was completed, I had it carved into woodblocks to be distributed throughout the regions, with the sincere intention of seeking correction.
Fellow practitioners, as for my offenses and my self-reproach, I shall not take them into account.
Written on the fifteenth day of the eighth month in the thirtieth year of the Great Ming Wanli era by the later scholar-monk Guangmo of Wuxing at the Qinting Mountain Monastery on West Lake.
Preface to the Revised Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra The study of rectifying the mind has a constant principle, whereas the dispositions of false views are manifold. Why is this?

It is because the mind is not something that exists as a substantial entity, yet its wondrous nature is luminously manifest and cannot be said to be non-existent. Nor is the mind nothingness; its profound spirit...
Silent and still. It cannot be said to exist, for existence is not existence; nor can it be said to be non-existent, for non-existence is not non-existence.
Whether both or neither, one reaches the ultimate limit of existence and non-existence, yet the substance of my mind has never lacked even a single drop thereof.
Therefore, when people of old allowed the four propositions to flow crosswise and indulged in a hundred negations, how could they have ever added anything to this mind?
The First Patriarch said: "If you wish to clarify this mind, you should seal it with the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
To 'seal' is to mean the exclusion of heterodoxy. Once all heterodoxies are destroyed, what further need is there for a seal?

When the thickets have been cleared and the Great Way is level and open, then there is nowhere that is not the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Thus, what mind is not the Dharma, and what Dharma is not the mind?"
When both mind and dharmas are empty, and even this emptiness is empty, only then may one speak of the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra*, there have been four translations spanning the Liu Song, Northern Wei, Liang, and Tang dynasties; the four-fascicle version is likely the Song edition.

Based on the words of the First Patriarch regarding its transmission, this particular lineage is uniquely clear. This sutra is characterized by terse phrasing and detailed meaning, and its sentiments are authentic.
The principle is profound; those who understand and enter it are rare indeed. It is a pity that among the ancient masters, those who first provided commentaries no longer remain;
their names have vanished, and we do not behold their complete works. Next, I obtained Master Shou’s Collected Annotations. Upon my initial study, I found its purport to be extremely subtle;
however, it was laborious in its citations while neglecting the fundamental sources. Furthermore, I obtained Master Le... [text continues].
Master Jie’s [commentary] is largely identical to that of Master Shou. As for Master Qing of the present day, he produced the *Lengqie jing guanji* (Record of Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra).

Although his reflections are extensive and profound, he is biased and negligent regarding the nature of literary talent; he indiscriminately gathers speculative opinions and interpolates them into the sacred scripture.
Is this not a case of being skillful at employing the short while being clumsy at employing the long?

When I returned from my duties at court and was released from the worldly net, in my later years, I rested on the shores of West Lake with the venerable Master Ren’an Mo. We once discussed this sutra together;
hearing his transcendent and profound discourse caused my heart to be pierced through and my ears to be startled. It sets forth the essential meaning.
He expounded his subtle purport with elegance and a clear sense of direction. Essentially, he brought to light all those points that previous eminent scholars had failed to explore or savor;
the facts were verified and the principles were lucid, the diction was level and the tone harmonious. He presented me with these tens of thousands of words in brilliant array.
I, therefore, further collated and edited them for publication in woodblocks. This work may serve as a model for the study of rectifying the mind.
In the future, though the empty objects of the sensory realms may vanish at their primordial limit and kalpas may come to an end, his merit shall never be exhausted.
I know this because Master Mo’s faculty of the tongue will not perish.
In the summer of the thirty-fourth year of the Wanli era, the year of Bingwu, on the fourth month, the day of the Buddha’s birth,
[he who was] conferred the degree of Jinshi (Presented Scholar), the rank of Chengzhilang (Chengzhi Lang), and served as... [text continues].
Imperial Edict Appointing [the Author] as a Participant in Military Affairs for Ji, Liao, Bao-ding, Shan-dong, and Other Regions;
Granted the Rank of the Fourth Grade and the Title of *Zhufang Si Zhushi* (Registrar of the Bureau of Military Affairs) of the Ministry of War. Composed by Yuan Huang of Wutang;
Revised with Reference to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Preface to the Memorial.

The Tathāgata appeared in the world; the Dharma came from the West. Holding up a flower to show the assembly, and facing the wall to transmit the lamp—all these were direct pointers to the mind-seal as the ancestral source of the Buddha-way.
Indeed, the Buddha is the mind, and the mind is the Buddha. Are there two things, Buddha and mind? No.
Without the self-awakening of noble wisdom, one is not fit to speak of the Buddha; without a spiritual mirror that encompasses all in its emptiness, one is not fit to speak of the mind.
The mind attains Buddhahood by manifesting the primary truth (*paramārtha*); the Buddha relies on the mind to transform and deliver humans and devas.
Therefore, whenever a Buddha appears in the world, he speaks only of this mind. Outside of the mind, there is no dharma that can be taught. Those who understand this principle may be discussed with.
Lanka! In the past, I heard that in the Western Regions there is the city of Laṅkā, situated upon a mountain bordering the great ocean, with its sides so precipitous as to have no gateways;
it cannot be ascended except by the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), and for this reason it is named Abhyudgata, meaning "Unsurpassed.

The Buddha, through the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), has reached the ultimate state which directly transcends the delusions of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna-vikalpa*); it is not something that can be reached by false knowledge. And...

This sutra points directly to the wondrous mind and cuts off all paths. For the mind is one alone; to depart from this mind is to become an outsider, to hold evil views, or to fall into worldly dharmas.
Roughly speaking, there are five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*).
Various divergent theories such as these constitute the view that slanders cause and effect, uproots the roots of goodness, and destroys the causes of purity. All [who hold such views]...
If such were the case, one would surely fall into hell; what hope then could there be for the noble truth?

Therefore, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, having attained mastery of the Great Vehicle, respectfully inquired of the World-Honored One regarding the great meaning of the one hundred and eight propositions. The World-Honored One answered each question as it was asked, primarily to demolish all heterodox views.
Just as the world is unreal, he demolished [false attachments] by means of illusions, dreams, gandharva cities, and mirages.
Candraprabha, it is like the impossibility of producing phenomena from three conditions when they lack consciousness; this is refuted by the examples of a tortoise growing hair or sand yielding oil.
It is like the verbal expression of various marks of false conceptualization; this is refuted by the four kinds of verbal expression. It is like falsely establishing "is" and "is not";

this is refuted by the categories of "is-phrase" and "is-not-phrase. It is like the two conditions and six causes of beginningless false conceptualization; this is refuted by the examples of clay and a jar, or thread and cloth, or grass and a mat.
Regarding seats, types, sprouts, curd, ghee, lamps, light, form, and so forth—just as the seven kinds of self-nature are refuted by means of the seven kinds of ultimate objects;

just as the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are not different, they are refuted by means of the analogy of a lump of clay, atoms, a fierce wind, the ocean, and waves.
These points are repeatedly exposed and refuted one by one. Once all these doctrines have been refuted, there is self-awakening.
It is fully revealed that self-awakening is itself Buddhahood, and Buddhahood is itself the One Mind. The substance of the mind is fundamentally empty and inherently quiescent;
merely to remain far removed from all marks is called "non-appropriation" and is called "Muni. Thus, the nature of the three periods of time is empty, and one returns to original stillness.
How could a Buddha be obtained from another? This great sutra originally consisted of one hundred thousand verses, later expanded to one million.
It consists of three thousand six hundred thousand words, totaling one hundred and fifty-one chapters.

The present scripture contains only the single chapter "The Buddha’s Heart-Essence" (*Buddhaguhya-citta*), which is the first of those one hundred and fifty-one chapters. Its language is concise yet its principles reach the ultimate;

it shares the same meaning as the Dharma’s direct pointing to the human mind to realize Buddhahood by seeing one's nature. Thus, the Dharma once said to the Second Patriarch: "The four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra*..."
This can serve as a seal for the mind; there is indeed purpose behind it. According to worldly tradition, Bodhidharma did not rely on written texts, and thus he is called "Direct Pointing.

Yet, one might not realize that the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* already fully expounds the Buddha-mind. Was Bodhidharma’s refusal to rely on texts perhaps merely a case of "transmitting what was received without creating anything new"?
I am originally an ordinary fool who has recently escaped the net of worldly entanglements; fortunately, I have encountered...
Dharma Master Ren’an traveled with his staff to Mount Qin, where he found contentment in his poetic compositions. Suddenly, he presented me with a draft of a memorial for review.
Reading it day and night, I observed how he drew upon diverse citations and subtle proofs to reconcile differences and unify them;

he was truly able to intuitively grasp the Buddha’s esoteric words and penetrate the wondrous truth of this sutra. As the six periods of the day and night cycle through, the five branches of knowledge are therein initiated.
On a quiet night, I have reflected deeply and privately concluded that the Buddha’s teachings in four volumes can be summarized by four characters.

What are these four characters? They are: awakening (wu), cultivation (xiu), following (sui), and realization (zheng). For the Way cannot be entered without awakening; it cannot be practiced without cultivation;

there can be no gradual progress without following; and it cannot be fully understood without realization. Why is this so? Because sentient beings within the three realms of existence, due to ignorance (avidyā), rely upon—
The internal mind and external objects create various karmas and undergo various sufferings, like a dream not yet awakened from, or like being intoxicated and not yet sober.

If one can attain great enlightenment upon hearing these words, recognize the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), and realize that objects are illusory manifestations of one's own mind, then the delusive thoughts of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma will be extinguished.
One will then be able to enter through the noble eye of wisdom and discern the truths (*satya*).

In principle, once both subject and object are stilled, the objective realm and contemplation merge as one; essence and function mutually encompass each other, and stillness and illumination silently interpenetrate.
Thus, while not sharing the nature and characteristics of the nihilistic views of external paths, the fundamental tenets remain unimpaired. Having attained awakening, how can one not practice?

Those who enter the samādhi of dhyāna must distance themselves from crowds, stay far from the mundane world, and minimize sleep, so as to devote themselves with single-minded diligence to the work of tranquility.
One must especially distance oneself from the verbal teachings of the sūtras and śāstras that harbor evil views, as well as from the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

one’s efforts should instead be directed toward advancing superior practice. Now, there are four types of dhyāna: the dhyāna of foolish worldlings, the dhyāna of observing meanings, the dhyāna of taking suchness as its object, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.
Among these four dhyānas, one should select the three characteristics of noble wisdom, which are as follows: [the characteristic of] non-existence...
All marks are the marks of the domain of the self-vows of all Buddhas; they are the marks of the ultimate realization of noble self-awakened wisdom.
One should diligently cultivate and study only these. By practicing until this is attained, one can finally cast off the mind of a lame donkey and transcend the views of the non-Buddhists.
However, how could one reach unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment all at once? One must proceed through successive stages. As for these stages, the levels of Buddhahood differ;
only upon reaching the realm of non-existence does one truly attain the ground of Buddhahood. Prior to the seventh stage, one has not yet transcended conditioned activity.
Upon ascending to the eighth stage, one is first designated as "Immovable. Thereupon, one gradually ascends through the various stages, abiding in the realm of samādhi.
One thoroughly realizes that all samādhis are solely one's own mind and attains the "illusion-like concentration" (māyopama-samādhi).

This is what the sutras refer to as "entering accordingly into the signless state," "entering accordingly into the samādhi realms from stage to stage," "entering accordingly into the body of the Tathāgata," and "entering accordingly into the transformations of suchness. All of these...
There is a progressive sequence of continuity through which one enters the primary meaning of ultimate reality, swiftly attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, being fully endowed with the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), one realizes the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma*) and realizes the supreme supramundane dharma;
this is the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. It is designated as such because it responds to and accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

As a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), he recompenses the causes of retribution, and is thus called the retributive Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*). Because his fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) shines forth clearly, he is called the wisdom Buddha (*jñāna-buddha*).
Because the essence of principle is non-dual, he is named the suchness Buddha (*tathatā-buddha*).

At that time, naturally adorned with supreme majesty, having reached the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), he dwells in a subtle and wondrous palace of a great lotus flower, surrounded by a retinue of similar kind.
Circumambulating, he took his seat and received empowerment. He manifested supernatural powers and beheld all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas face-to-face.
Furthermore, by means of two kinds of immeasurable supernatural power, he discerned all dharmas and benefited sentient beings; thus my task was completed.

However, in sum, it was merely the realization of my own numinous mirror-like, vacuous, and inclusive wondrous mind. How could there be any other dharma? Therefore, this sutra is called [the Sutra of the Wondrous Mind].
It may be that the Buddha’s words are validated by the mind; it may be that the Buddha’s words are validated by the Buddha; it may also be that there is neither Buddha nor mind.

For how could the mind be something that can be spoken of? When the Buddha speaks of the mind, these are all transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), not the Dharma-Buddha (*dharma-buddha*). Those who read this sutra should realize this for themselves.
Preface to the General Principles of the Sūtra, composed by Li Dashi of Kuocang in the ninth month of autumn in the year of Jiyou,
the thirty-seventh year of the Wanli era.

According to ancient practice, the general exegesis of a sutra is divided into three major sections: first, the Introduction (nidāna); second, the Main Body (śarīra); and third, the Dissemination (parīndanā).

This classification applies to a complete work as a whole. Since this present scripture has not yet reached its full extent—only one chapter having arrived thus far—it contains an introduction but lacks a section on dissemination.
Consequently, we do not adhere strictly to these three divisions, but simply provide a direct commentary.
Furthermore, in ancient exegeses of the scriptures, the structural divisions were muddled and the categories of meaning proliferated excessively;

this was intended to lead students to seek the source and grasp the fundamental tenets, so that they might understand the origins of the teachings. Yet it is not realized that in these末代 (final ages), among those who study, the ignorant are many while the wise are few.

To trace out every branch and pluck every leaf exhausts the mind; one often sees those who place this scripture on a high shelf and do not read it for years, precisely because they find it so difficult.
However, this present scripture extensively refutes divergent views and reveals only the single mind (*ekacitta*).
It provides answers according to questions without fixed sequence; its major sections and key points are easy to clarify, while the remaining minor details are [left to be understood].
Whether detailed or concise is acceptable; what is included or omitted depends on the person. Why labor over this? Generally, the words of Confucian scholars rarely address this matter.
Now, however, the direct path is pointed out, leading straight to the One Mind without any further entanglements.
This sutra has three translations; the commentary now presented is based on the Song dynasty translation.

Among these three translations, where there are differences in wording but identity in meaning, I have harmonized those two versions and appended them beneath the main text so that one may understand their agreement.
In compiling these various commentaries, where there were errors regarding facts or principles, I did not dare to offer extreme condemnation, but instead clarified them briefly.
Where such matters did not harm the fundamental essence, I omitted them. My sole aim was to open the eye at the crown of people's heads so that they might recognize the correct path.
In these annotations, whenever citations from ancient commentaries or established statements from various sutras and śāstras are introduced, their titles are first indicated;
where there is no mention of "so-and-so says," these are the words of the editor who compiled and verified the text.

Wherever Sanskrit terms appear in the sūtra, they have been translated into Chinese and appended below them, so as not to impede the reading of the text and to ensure that the meaning and intent are fully understood.
Regarding the non-Buddhist teachers mentioned in the sūtra, there are separate treatises on their doctrines; however, were one to cite their details at length, it would cause the student...

Weeping at the crossroads. For this reason, the present commentary does not prize linguistic completeness; its primary concern is the thoroughness of the meaning. It aims merely to clarify the meaning of the sutra. Regarding the format of the commentary:
the main text of the sutra is set in large characters in a single column running straight down, while the annotations are in small characters arranged in two columns side by side. The remainder...
Various examples of meanings. One should comprehend and integrate them through mental insight.

*The Chapter on the Mind of All Buddha-Speech*, Part One of One.

"The Heart of the Buddha’s Speech" (*Sarvabuddhavākcitta*) refers to the ultimate heart-mind (*paramārthacitta*) taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Although this sutra was originally spoken by our Śākyamuni Buddha, why is it called "all"? This is because the one is identical to the all.

Since this single sutra elucidates the meaning of this heart-mind in full detail, it is called the "Heart of the Buddha’s Speech. As for "fascicle" (*pin*), it means a category; because meanings and categories follow one another, they are termed "fascicles. It is traditionally transmitted that this great body of the sutra consists of one hundred thousand verses (*gāthā*), one million phrases, and thirty-six thousand words, totaling one hundred and fifty-one fascicles.

What has been transmitted to this land is merely the single "Fascicle on the Heart of the Buddha’s Speech. According to the opening of the sutra, which contains the phrase "Thus have I heard," etc., one knows that the present fascicle is the [first of the] one hundred and fifty-one.

This is the first chapter of the eleventh [fascicle]. Therefore, the word "First" (第一) appears below the chapter title. Although the fascicle is divided into four parts, the chapters end with the first. There are editions where the numbers "2, 3, and 4" appear below the chapters; these are corruptions. If one were to provisionally use "the first of the first" (第一之一), it would be appropriate.
[This is] the second [section]. Thus have I heard.

At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the Southern Sea, adorned with various precious flowers, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas. From those various and diverse buddhas...

From all the buddha-fields, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—possessing the sovereign power of immeasurable samādhis and sporting with supernatural transformations—arrived, with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati as their leader;
all the Buddhas then poured water upon their heads in the consecration of sovereignty.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that when a Wheel-Turning Sage King takes the waters of the four great oceans in a golden vessel and pours them over the crown of the crown prince’s head, he confers upon him the rank of a Wheel-Turning King. This World-Honored One employs this as a metaphor for Bodhisattvas on the higher stages who are capable of succeeding to the rank of a Buddha; thus, he uses the water of wisdom to pour over their crowns.

This signifies that their minds correspond with the Buddha-wisdom, just as a Buddha undergoes consecration (*abhiṣeka*), thereby manifesting that their rank is adjacent to Great Enlightenment. Now, Mahāmati and the others occupy these higher stages, and their practice is not that of inferior worthies;

therefore, the compiler of the sūtra records this account of consecration. Regarding the phrase "the realm manifested by one's own mind," one should skillfully understand its meaning. (This phrasing is inverted; such is the literary style of India. If it were merely polished according to the conventions of this [Chinese] land...)

One should say: "He has skillfully understood the meaning of the objective realms manifested by one's own mind" (this phrasing accords with the beginning of the text). He universally manifests various forms of sentient beings and various minds through immeasurable gates of liberation according to their respective types.

He has attained ultimate penetration regarding the five dharmas, the [three] self-natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness. (The subsequent sutra states: "As for the five dharmas...")

These are: name (*nāma*), appearance (*nimitta*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*). There are three self-natures (*svabhāva*): the self-nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected self-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). There are eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*): the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, the seventh manas, and the eighth ālaya.

Regarding the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*): they are the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). The various meanings and explanations are found in the following text. The above constitutes the praise of the Bodhisattvas' virtues by the scribe; however, it lacks the praise of the Śrāvakas' virtues. Furthermore, among the listed assembly, the Pratyekabuddhas are missing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati was together with the Bodhisattva Mati (Mati is also called Mati; it is translated as "wisdom") as they traveled along...

Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, they rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha with verses.
The world is free from arising and ceasing; it is like flowers in the sky. Wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet gives rise to the mind of great compassion.

(The five aggregates combine and gather to form the world. The *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "To speak of the five aggregates is to speak of the world. That which the world relies upon is the reliance upon the five aggregates; thus one does not escape the phenomena of the world.

This is because when one observes the world with Buddha-wisdom, it is like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent. Without giving rise to conceptual discrimination, one is free from arising and ceasing. Whether as existent or non-existent, both are unobtainable; hence it is said that "wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence. Nevertheless, sentient beings, due to craving...)

Driven by delusion, they falsely cling to existence and non-existence, giving rise to various evil views. Out of compassion for their ignorance, the Buddha, sustained by the power of his original vows, arouses great compassion to rescue and deliver them.

All phenomena are like illusions and are far removed from mind and consciousness; since wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, he arouses great compassion while remaining free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
The world is ever like a dream; wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence. Thus he gives rise to the mind of great compassion.

Knowing that both persons and phenomena lack self-nature (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), and that afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are eternally pure and signless (*animitta*), he gives rise to the mind of great compassion. (The World-Honored One knows that all phenomena are like illusions.)

He is far removed from mind and consciousness; he gives rise to illusion-like compassion and delivers illusion-like multitudes. Because he does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence, these four preceding verses are as follows: the first verse praises him based on the five aggregates (*skandha*); the second verse praises him based on mind and consciousness; the third verse praises him based on various views;

and the final verse praises him based on the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*). In sum, this means that the World-Honored One has abandoned all deluded thoughts and realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); having himself attained liberation, he is further able to deliver others. The Sanskrit term *jñeya* is translated as "the knowable. Afflictions (*kleśa*) are obstructions regarding phenomena; the knowable (*jñeya*) is the obstruction regarding principle.

It is said that the Buddha is eternally free from these two obstructions, his mind is constantly pure, and it is devoid of the characteristics of subject and object. There is no nirvāṇa in anything; there is no nirvāṇa whatsoever.
There is no Buddha, nor is there the nirvāṇa of a Buddha. It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened; it is entirely free from both existence and non-existence.

"We Buddhas are all free from all outflows (*āsrava*), and are therefore called 'Most Victorious. The above twenty phrases conclude with the final line expressing a request for explanation. What is it that is called...?

And the meaning of non-self? Why is there no sentient being? Why is there conventional discourse?

[How does one] see [reality], and how do the views of permanence and annihilation not arise? (The two characters "non-arising" apply to the preceding phrase to sever the view of annihilation; it asks: how are the two views of permanence and annihilation severed so that they do not arise?
How is it that the Buddha and non-Buddhists are not contradictory in their characteristics? How will there be various different schools in future ages?

(After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the sūtras of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna will differ into twenty schools. What is emptiness, and what is its cause? "Decay" (Sanskrit: *kṣaṇa*; translated as "one instant" in the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, which states that the smallest unit of time is called a *kṣaṇa*; here it means "decay in an instant"; the Wei translation renders it as "the thought does not abide," for while this refers to time, that refers to the thought;
"decay" carries the meaning of "non-abiding"). What is birth from a womb (*garbha*)? (A "womb" refers to the fact that the various internal organs are stored within the womb;

the question’s intent actually encompasses all four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—but here only "womb-birth" is mentioned, implying the others by association). ...is it moving? For what reason are they like a phantom, a dream, and a *gandharvanagara* (the city of the *gandharvas*—in Sanskrit, *gandharva* is translated as "seeking fragrance," the musical deity of Śakra;

This is what the world calls a "sea city" or a "mirage";
what is commonly seen today in the seas off Dengzhou and Laizhou is the city where the *gandharvas* dwell). And the world’s shimmering mirage (*marīci*)...

The moon reflected in water. (Illusions, dreams, the city of Gandharvas, mirages, and the moon in water all serve as metaphors for the unreality of the world; the term "world" (*loka*) applies to both preceding and following phrases.

Who reveals the various natures of sentient beings, the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and the arts and crafts? (The term *vidyāsthāna* is translated in the Wei version as the "five fields of knowledge. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:)

The five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthānāni*) are as follows: first, the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), which explains glosses and defines characters, and clarifies categories and distinctions; second, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), including technical skills, mechanical devices, the principles of Yin and Yang, and calendrical calculations;

third, the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), involving incantations to ward off evil, medicinal herbs, minerals, acupuncture, and moxibustion; fourth, the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*), which examines and determines the correct and the false, and investigates the authentic and the spurious; fifth, the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), which thoroughly elucidates the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*) and the subtle principles of cause and effect.

Regarding *gāthā* (the Sanskrit term for *gāthā* is translated as "verse" or "stanza"): how many types of long verses and short phrases constitute it? What is called "treatise"? How do food and drink arise, and how do various desires arise?
What is meant by "king"—the wheel-turning monarch or the minor king? How does one protect the kingdom? How many kinds of devas are there? What is meant by "earth"?
Regarding the lunar mansions, the sun, and the moon—how many kinds are there for each? For those who practice for liberation, how many kinds are there? As for disciples...

How many kinds are there? What is an ācārya (the Sanskrit term *ācārya* is translated as "Preceptor" or "Model Teacher")? Furthermore, how many kinds of Buddhas are there? (The following verse states:)

The transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), the retribution-born Buddha (*vipākaja-buddha*), the suchness Buddha (*tathatā-buddha*), the wisdom Buddha (*jñāna-buddha*), and so forth—these were questions regarding names and meanings; this [question] concerns their types. Furthermore, how many kinds of births are there?
(This asks about the original births of the Buddhas in the past. As for Māra and the various heterodox teachers, how many kinds are there of each?

How are they established?

[This is] a measure (the Wei translation renders it as "provisionally establishing names"; the Tang translation renders it as "merely a designation"). I only pray that the Most Victorious One will explain [it]. (The above consists of seventy-two lines; the final line concludes with the request for an explanation).

What is the wind and cloud of emptiness? (The Wei translation reads: "By what cause are there winds and clouds? What is mindfulness and intelligence? (Mindfulness and intelligence; the Wei translation reads "wisdom. [Note: *nian*])
This refers to *manasikāra* (attention). It is said that attention is intelligence; it is not a wisdom devoid of attention.

Therefore, it is called "mindfulness-intelligence" (*smṛti-mati*). What are the forest trees? What are the creeping vines? What are the elephants, horses, and deer? How are they captured? What constitutes the base and lowly? By what cause is one base and lowly?

(The former phrase asks about the characteristics of being base and lowly; the latter asks about the causes of such baseness. What is the inclusion of the six joints? (The "six joints" are rendered as "six periods" [of the day] in the Wei and Tang translations.)

According to the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), there were two traditions at that time. One says there are three seasons in a year, namely spring, summer, and autumn. What is an *icchantika*? (The Sanskrit term *icchantika* is translated as "one who lacks faith"). Regarding men, women, and those who are neither male nor female—how are all of these born?

(There are five types of those who are neither male nor female: the congenital, the castrated, the envious, the transformed, and the semi-hermaphrodite). How does one regress from practice? How does one advance in practice?

"Birth" (in the Wei and Tang translations, this is rendered as "advancing"). By what dharma does the Dhyāna Master establish what kind of person? (In the Tang translation, "Dhyāna" is translated as *yoga*.

In Sanskrit it is *dhyāna*, translated as "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*) or "cultivation through reflection. *Yoga* is translated as "correspondence"). When sentient beings are born into the various realms of existence, what are their marks and what are their appearances?
(Marks refer to color; appearances refer to form; categories refer to lineage). What constitutes wealth? By what cause is wealth attained? (The first line asks about wealth).

The marks of wealth (the second line asks about the causes of wealth). What is meant by "Śākya clan"? (In Sanskrit, it is fully called Śākya; translated as "Able One" [Capable Benevolent One]. This is the Buddha's surname. "Clan" [zhòng] refers to lineage or descendants.)

(The causes and conditions for this understanding are explained in the text below). For what reason is there the Śākya clan? (This asks for the cause of establishing the lineage. The *Sūtra of Past Deeds* says: King Ikṣvāku was named Sujāta. His first queen was named Subhadrā; she gave birth to a son named Dīrghāyu.

The second queen gave birth to four sons: first, Jvalanmukha; second, Suvarṇavarṇa; third, Hastikaḷabha; and fourth, Viśvantara. At that time, Queen Subhadrā wished to establish Dīrghāyu [as heir] and petitioned the king to banish the four sons from the kingdom.

They went to the north of the Snowy Mountains and dwelt in a forest of straight trees. He did not return. His father, the King, sighed and said: "My son is a Śākya (the clan name of the Śākyas originated from this). How is it that he is of the Ikṣvāku lineage?

O Unsurpassed Honored One, please explain. (The *Mahāprātihārya-sūtra* states: After King Mahāmuñja had attained the state of an immortal, his lifespan became exceedingly long. When he grew old and could no longer walk, his disciples went outside to beg for food. Fearing the danger of tigers and wolves, they placed him in a grass basket and hung it upon a tree.

A hunter saw him from afar and, suspecting him to be a bird, shot at him. Blood dripped onto the ground, from which two sugarcanes sprouted. Exposed to the sun, they split open; from one emerged a young boy, and from the other, a young girl. When the ministers heard of this, they welcomed them back to the King.)

In the palace, he was raised and brought to maturity. The son was named Sujāta; the daughter was named Sujātā. The son was established as king, and the daughter was established as queen. How does the Long-Suffering Sage [teach]? What is his instruction?

the world-systems of the Lion’s Victorious Mark; those situated sideways or inverted; and those like Indra’s net.

[The Buddha] enters Parinirvāṇa. (Sugata is one of the ten epithets of the Buddha. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 17, states: "Good" (*śubha*) means high; "gone" (*gata*) means not high. "Not high" refers to the mind of the Tathāgata; "high" refers to...)

He would not be called a Tathāgata. For this reason, the Tathāgata is named Sugata. This is in the spirit of what Laozi said regarding "the highest goodness being like water. It means that he does not head toward the other three realms or the two vehicles, but heads only toward Great Bodhi. This is the designation for proceeding directly to Bodhi. The Sanskrit term is *parinirvāṇa*; in full it is *mahāparinirvāṇa*. Translated, it means "Great Extinction" (*dà mièdù*).

"Extinction" (*miè*) refers to quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), meaning that one has attained the bliss of quiescence and crossed over the suffering of birth and death. Extinction. Because all evils are extinguished. "Bhikṣu" (monk) is translated as "Beggar for the Dharma" (*yācanaka*); it is an honorific title for the Saṃgha). Those most excellent sons—the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—by what cause do they undergo a hundred transformations?

(Prior to the seventh stage, one has not yet transcended conditioned activity; only upon ascending to the eighth stage is one termed "Immovable. (In Sanskrit, Kāśyapa is called *Kāśyapa*, translated as "Drinker of Light"; Krakucchanda is translated as "That Which Should Be Severed"; Kanakamuni is fully called *Kanakamuni*, translated as "Golden Silence. equality of letters (*vyañjana*), equality of words (*pada*), equality of dharmas, and equality of bodies (*kāya*). (The detailed explanation is found below). Why does he speak of annihilation and permanence, as well as self and non-self?

(The Wei translation uses the term "one mind," which corresponds to the present meaning of *tattva* [reality]; furthermore, the following two phrases are omitted in the Wei translation). (*Harītakī* is the Sanskrit term; translated as "brought by the Heavenly King" (*devendra-hṛta*). *Āmalaka*—the translation of the term is not yet detailed. The *Fanyi mingyi ji* [Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings] says: "The leaves of the tree...")
It is like a jujube tree; its flowers are small and white, and its fruit is like a walnut, with a sweet and sour taste (suitable for medicinal use).

Mount Kīla, the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), the Diamond Mountains (*Vajra*), and all other such peaks are adorned with immeasurable jewels and filled with sages and *gandharvas*. It is composed of four precious substances and stands within the great ocean upon the Golden Wheel (*Kāñcanamaṇḍala*). Night exists because of this. *Cakravāḍa* is also the name of a mountain; it encircles the world, and because the light of the sun and moon cannot reach it, it is named Iron Enclosure (*Cakravāḍa*). the final phrase lacks a concluding prayer for explanation. Below this, the Buddha summarizes the questions asked. Although the phrasing is complex and interwoven, nothing has been omitted. As for those points that were not reached in the questioning, the Buddha further supplements them.

That which is refuted by this sutra is [the view of] self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), which is precisely what this sutra reveals. May students not be negligent regarding these points of refutation and revelation.

"Excellent, excellent is your question! O Mahāmati, listen attentively. I shall now explain to you in sequence that which you have asked. "Kṣaṇa. It proceeds toward the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). [The terms] "arising and non-arising," "nirvāṇa and emptiness," can be understood through the inquiry. "Absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) has the sense of "perishing. This summarizes the question: "In what way does the kṣaṇa perish? It means that because the kṣaṇa transmits and is not permanent, it perishes.

Regarding the intent of the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) and the ancient commentaries, they both take the single phrase "proceeds toward the absence of intrinsic nature" as the answer, stating: "The dharmas of arising and non-arising, nirvāṇa, space, and the kṣaṇa, which Mahāmati asked about, are all seen through conceptualization; from the beginning, they lack intrinsic nature. This interpretation is erroneous. Why? Because the answer...

The verses are located separately in the subsequent text; this section merely summarizes the questions. How could a single isolated phrase within this summary serve as the actual response? Out of ignorance, I have interpreted the phrasing of the question as a whole, taking the phrase "momentary movement toward the absence of self-nature" as the summary text rather than the answer.

(Asura. In Sanskrit, the full term is *asura*, translated as "non-deva. My Dharma has five aspects: self-nature, perception, that which is perceived, as well as the two views of manifestation (the two views of manifestation being, according to the Wei translation, the seen and the seer), the vehicles, and the various lineages;
gold, silver, and mani-jewels; the icchantika, the great elements, turmoil, and the single Buddha (turmoil refers to the disorder of the land;

the single Buddha refers to those such as Kanakamuni who are "I"); wisdom, suchness, flame, attainment, and the path. (Wisdom and suchness are to be known; attainment and the path refer to realization.)

Regarding the practitioners of liberation: how many kinds of "attainment" (phala) are there? This refers to the meaning of the four fruits (*catur-phala*). How many kinds of "orientation" (*pratipannaka*) are there?

This refers to the meaning of the four orientations (*catur-pratipannaka*). Sentient beings exist or do not exist; elephants, horses, and various birds and beasts—how are they captured? This is an analogy for the establishment of the *siddhānta* through reasoning. (Regarding "analogy through reasoning":

this refers to two of the three members of a syllogism—thesis, reason, and example. Regarding *siddhānta*: *siddha* is a Chinese term and *anta* is a Sanskrit term. *Siddha* means "universal"; *anta* is the full Sanskrit form *dāna*, translated as "giving. It signifies that the Buddha universally bestows upon sentient beings the four dharmas of the ultimate truth as an antidote for worldly people.)

As well as agent and action, these are pervasive within the thicket of delusion (*vana*). (The term "thicket" [*vana*] refers to a dense forest; it is a metaphor for various false views, as many sutras frequently use the "dense forest" to represent false views, implying that false views are as thick as a forest.

The Tang translation renders this as "multitude of forests. Regarding "pervasive within delusion," this refers to the two lines: "Why is there the delusion of views? and "How does delusion increase? "Pervasive" [*tong*] has the meaning of "viewing").

In the measure of mind (*cittamātra*), nothing truly exists, and the various stages (*bhūmi*) do not reach one another. (This refers to the four lines following "Why is the true meaning not expounded at all times?": "nothing truly exists" [*bu xian you*] and "do not reach one another" [*bu xiang zhi*].)

(That is not true reality). A hundred transformations, yet a hundredfold non-appropriation. Medical treatises, arts and crafts, technical skills, and all fields of knowledge (hereafter, the Buddha supplements what Mahāmati failed to ask):
Regarding the various mountains, Sumeru, the earth, the vast oceans, and the dimensions of the sun and moon;

as for sentient beings—low, middle, and high (animals are low, humans are middle, and the various devas are high)—how many atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute each of their bodies? (The final phrase refers to how many atoms compose the dimensions of these various bodies). How many [atoms] are there in each *kṣetra*?

Dust. How many [units] are there in a *dhanus* (bow)? (Four *hasta* make one *dhanus*. One asks: how many particles of dust are there in one *dhanus*?). *Hasta*, *pada*, *krośa*, half-*yojana*, and *yojana*.
(The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: four *hasta* make one *dhanus*; five hundred *dhanus* make one *krośa*; eight *krośa* make one *yojana*. The *Mingyi ji* says:

one *hasta* is one person’s one chi and eight cun; by Buddhist measure, this is three chi and six cun. Thus, four *hasta* equal seven chi and two cun, which constitutes one *dhanus*. It should be understood that the subsequent units increase accordingly. The Sanskrit term is *krośa*, also written as *krośa*; it is translated as "five" [li]).

One hundred *dhanus* (bows). It is also said to be the distance of one "ox-bellow" (*gośabda*), meaning the furthest range at which the sound of a cow's bellow can be heard. One half-*yojana* is twenty *li*; one *yojana* is forty *li*. Thus, the Wei translation states: "From a cubit (*hasta*) and a pace (*krama*) up to ten, twenty, and forty [li]. The Sanskrit term is *yojana*, also transliterated as *youxun* (由旬), translated as "limit" (*pramāṇa*).
[Regarding the sequence of measurements: Seven *paramāṇu* (extreme atoms) make one *anu* (mote); seven *anu* make one copper-dust (*loharajas*); seven copper-dusts make one water-dust (*ab-rajas*);

seven water-dusts make one rabbit-hair-dust (*śaśarajas*); seven rabbit-hair-dusts make one window-dust (*vātāyanacchidrarajas*); seven window-dusts make one louse (*yūkā*); seven lice make one barley-corn (*yava*); seven barley-corns make one finger-joint (*aṅgula*). (The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: seven *paramāṇu* make one *anu*; seven *anu* make one copper-dust; seven copper-dusts make one water-dust; seven water-dusts make one rabbit-hair-dust; seven rabbit-hairs...)

Seven *ūrddhvareṇu* (dust particles on a wool-fiber) make one *vālaraja* (dust particle on a cow-hair). Seven *vālaraja* make one *rajasāśikam* (window-dust mote). Seven *rajasāśikam* make one *likṣā* (nit). Seven *likṣā* make one *yūka* (louse).

Seven *yūka* make one *yava* (barley grain). Seven *yava* make one *aṅgula* (finger-breadth). Twenty-four *aṅgula* make one *hasta* (cubit). Four *hasta* make one *dhanus* (bow-length). Five hundred *dhanus* make one *krośa*.
How many barley grains (*yava*) are there in a *paṭha*? How many barley grains are there in an *aratta*? [How many] *droṇa*, *khāri*, *lakṣa*, and *koṭi*... up to [the higher units]?

"Bimbara. How many [units] are there in each? (The *pata*—translated in the Tang version as one *sheng* [dry measure]; the *āḍhaka* as one *dou*; the *droṇa* as one *hu*; the *nakharī* as ten *hu*; the *lakṣa* as one hundred thousand;

the *koti* as one hundred million; and the *bimbara* as one trillion. This refers to how many atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute one *sheng*, up to how many atoms constitute one trillion; hence it is said, "How many are there in each?").
How many *aṇu* are called a *śarikṣapa*? How many *śarikṣapa* are called one *ratni*?
How many *latīmaṣa* make one *maṣa-dhāna*? Furthermore, how many *dhānā* make one *kāliśana*?
How many *kāliśanas* constitute one *pala*? What is the measure of these accumulated quantities? How many *palas* make one *meru* (in the *Ārya* tradition; translated as "dust" in the Tang version)?

[How many make one] *sarṣapa* (translated as "mustard seed")? [How many make one] *latī* (translated as "grass seed")? [How many make one] *maṣa* (translated as "bean")? Regarding the term *mīlú* (彌樓): The *Mingyi ji* (Collection of Names and Meanings) states that some claim *mīlú* translates as "radiance" (*ābhā*), referring to the seven golden mountain ranges, so called because they possess a golden radiance. However, according to the *Paramārthadharmavijaya-sūtra*, it is called *Sumeru*. Thus, *Sumeru* is the older translation for *mīlú*.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* also renders it as *mīlú*, indicating that there are variations in the Sanskrit pronunciation. Furthermore, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it refers to the "inner and outer *mīlú* mountains," namely Sumeru and the Cakravāḍa mountains.

Thus, there is a discrepancy between the two versions of the text; it is not known which is correct. These details are recorded here in full, awaiting future scholars to collate them. The current text states that they increase in this sequence, up to the point where a certain number of *jin* (catty) constitutes Mount Meru.
The meaning of the final phrase is incomplete, but can be understood by inferring the intended sense. These are the matters that ought to be asked: why is it necessary to ask about other things?

How many [atoms] are there in the bodies of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Buddhas, and the Sons of the Victorious One (*jina-putra*) respectively? Why is this not asked? How many *yojana* are there in a flame?

How many *āruta* are there in a wind? How many *āruta* are there in each root? How many are there in the pores and the eyebrows? (One should ask regarding the three vehicles: how many atoms are there in each body?)

Regarding the flames, the winds, the six sense organs, the pores of the skin, and so forth—how many atoms (*paramāṇu*) compose them? Why was this not asked? From the various mountains and Mount Sumeru down to the earth, there are thirty-eight items; because Mahāmati’s questions did not reach this point, the Buddha supplemented it himself.

Indeed, such numerical quantities can only be known by a Buddha and cannot be fathomed by those of lower stages; therefore, Mahāmati was unable to pose the question. It is like the "Asaṃkhyeya" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the bodhisattvas were unable to speak of them and the Buddha spoke of them himself.

Furthermore, in the world there is a treatise on calculation that lists twenty-three numerical units: starting from one up to ten constitutes the first ten; next there are thirteen units, beginning with ten times ten being a hundred, ten hundreds being a thousand, then ten thousands, ten millions, and ten billion.
*Kiṅ*, *gai*, *zi*, *huài*, *gōu*, *jiàn*, *zhèng*, *zài*—even these worldly numbers are said to be such that heaven and earth cannot contain them, let alone the scope of what the Buddha knows.
How does the Sovereign King of Wealth protect? How does the Holy Wheel-Turning King protect? What constitutes protection? What constitutes liberation? This is explained extensively and in verses.
(Concluding verse, comprising both long and short lines: As you have asked, regarding the various desires of sentient beings and their diverse kinds of food and drink.

What is that which is produced with a cause? (This summarizes the category of "existence"). What is that which is produced both with and without a cause? (This summarizes the category of "both"). And what is that which is neither with nor without a cause?

How is it that these are conventional designations? I pray you, explain these extensively. What are the characteristics of that which is asked about? And regarding that which is asked about as "non-self" (*anātman*), how is it so? What is the embryonic matrix (*garbha*)?
And what are the various different bodies (the term *yishen* refers to the remaining parts of the body, meaning the four limbs)? What are the views of eternalism and nihilism?

(The final phrase [inquires]: how many kinds of establishment are there? What is meant by "treatise"? What are the teacher and the disciple? What about the various types of sentient beings? How do these come to be? What constitutes food and drink?

How many kinds of Māras are there? (This refers to the measure of their designations. What is the tree and the climbing vine? This is what the Son of the Most Victorious One asks (O Son of the Most Victorious One; the Buddha addresses Mahāmati as "the Son of the Most Victorious One").
What are the various realms (*kṣetra*)? How long did the Rishi practice austerities? What constitutes a clan (*gotra*), and from which teacher did he receive his training?
What is meant by ugliness? How does a person practice? Why is there no awakening in the desire realm?

How is the Akaniṣṭha [heaven] (the Sanskrit *Akaniṣṭha* translates as "Ultimate Limit of Obstruction," the name of the highest heaven in the form realm) established? What are mundane supernormal powers? What is a bhikṣu?
What is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*)? What is a reward Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*)? What is a Tathatā Buddha? Equality.

The Buddha of Wisdom. (The *Zongjing Lu*, fascicle 16, states: "Responding to conditions and manifesting according to the capacity of beings is called 'transformation' (*nirmāṇa*); recompensing for past causes is called 'retribution' (*vipāka*); the manifestation of original enlightenment is called 'wisdom' (*prajñā*).
Since the principle and its substance are non-dual, it is called 'suchness' (*tathatā*). How is the Sangha defined? When the Son of the Buddha asks thus, [the answer is:
the lute, the waist-drum, and the flower; the lands are devoid of light. There are seven kinds of "mind-ground"; what has been asked is entirely according to reality. This and many others besides.
"What the Son of the Buddha should ask" (the final two lines conclude the summary of Mahāmati’s questions; the following eight lines are divided into two stanzas that introduce the response).
"Corresponding to each and every characteristic, far removed from the faults of all views, the *siddhānta* is beyond verbal expression—I shall now reveal it.

"Each and every characteristic" refers to the characteristics within Mahāmati’s questions. "Verbal expression" refers to the designations for those characteristics. All characteristics are fundamentally in correspondence with true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). When one is far removed from the faults of views such as existence and non-existence, then even names and words are transcended. Because of this transcendence...

Regarding the statement on the path: because it is universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, it is called the *siddhānta* that transcends verbal expression. Listen well, O Son of the Buddha, to these successively established phrases; these one hundred and eight phrases are as spoken by all Buddhas.

(As for "successively established phrases," this refers to the subsequent answering phrases being established in sequence. The final two phrases mean that one should respond to the preceding questions in accordance with what has been spoken by all Buddhas; this is the formal answer in the text below.

The phrase of non-arising and the phrase of arising (the Tang translation reads "the phrase of arising and the phrase of non-arising"; in the present text the order is inverted; it should read "arising...").

A phrase does not give rise to a phrase. In every response, the first half of each sentence seizes upon the characteristics of the question, while the second half refutes them. Relying on the gate of the True Suchness of the Mind, all characteristics are refuted; therefore, everything is called "not" (*fei*).

In the following text, wherever a character belongs to the sense of refutation, the Tang translation consistently uses "not. In this present scripture, some characters are changed to others that likewise carry the sense of refutation, such as "without," "detached from," and "unequal. Furthermore, "non-arising" and "arising" are the characteristics of the meaning being elucidated.
Phrases and syllables (these refer to the *pada-kāya* that expresses meaning; all subsequent instances follow this pattern): phrases of permanence and phrases of impermanence;

phrases of characteristics and phrases of the absence of characteristics; phrases of abiding-and-changing and phrases of non-abiding-and-changing (*sthity-anyathātva*; these are two of the four marks of conditioned phenomena—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—which were not explicitly mentioned in the question but are supplied here from the answer);

phrases of momentariness and phrases of non-momentariness; phrases of intrinsic nature and phrases of the absence of intrinsic nature; phrases of emptiness and phrases of non-emptiness; phrases of cessation and phrases of non-cessation.

The extreme statement is not an extreme statement; the middle statement is not a middle statement. (Regarding the "extreme-middle statement," it was not included in the previous question; it is now supplemented as a response. Generally, when a question is posed but no answer is forthcoming, [the answer is provided here].)

Regarding the response that "that which emerges does not emerge," this is entirely contained within the phrase "the measure of the mind" (*cittamātra*). According to the ancient commentary, because there are these three types of permanence, the text repeats the phrase.

I, however, suggest that by citing a single instance of "permanence," all three are fully encompassed. If one were to rely on the three types of permanence, they ought to appear three times. To list them as two would leave it unclear to which category each belongs. For now, I shall follow the Wei translation.

The meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is explained as follows: it refers to the process of change, flux, and continuous succession without interruption; this constitutes the "permanence of continuity" among the three types of permanence (whereby the preceding phrase on "permanence" pertains to the other two types of permanence).

The phrase of conditions and the non-condition phrase; the phrase of causes and the non-cause phrase; the phrase of afflictions and the non-affliction phrase; the phrase of craving and the non-craving phrase; the phrase of skillful means and the non-means phrase;

This refers to what is called "the finger pointing at the moon. There are phrases concerning existence and phrases concerning non-existence; phrases concerning both and phrases concerning neither.

(Above, the Tathāgata provides a general response to the meaning of the one hundred and eight phrases from the perspective of the True Suchness of the Mind (*citta-tathatā-mukha*). Therefore, all are said to be “not. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: “The fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind is neither mind nor form,” and so on, up to “neither permanence, bliss, self, nor purity.”)

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "One should know that the self-nature of True Suchness (tathatā) has no marks of existence, no marks of non-existence, and so forth, up to no marks of unity, difference, or both. This meaning of 'non-' is the same as in the present sutra.

Now, while the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are immeasurable, the fixed enumeration of one hundred and eight phrases is intended to correspond to the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings; one should understand that these afflictions themselves are also immeasurable, and this number is merely cited as a general total. Furthermore, regarding the term "one hundred and eight phrases," it is taken in the sense of a complete unit of meaning rather than referring to the literal phrase of speech.

“Mahāmati, these one hundred and eight phrases were spoken by the Buddhas of the past. You and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study them. (Regarding the phrase "spoken by the Buddhas of the past":

this means that with the appearance of Buddha after Buddha in the world, this Dharma of the mind has been taught. Since there is no dharma that can be taught apart from this mind, they are thus exhorted to believe deeply and practice it.

Examining the textual meaning of the preceding and following sections, one knows that the meaning of the one hundred and eight phrases in the previous text constitutes a general inquiry and a general response. Hereafter, Mahāmati again extracts and analyzes these one hundred and eight phrases to pose specific questions, and the World-Honored One answers according to each question; these constitute specific inquiries and specific responses. Nevertheless, none of them transcend the one hundred and eight phrases.)

The meaning of these questions and answers is essentially to refute all heterodox views and reveal the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the mind of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). Therefore, it is titled "The Chapter on the Essence of the Buddha’s Words.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses?

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing; they are not to be known through discursive reasoning. The various consciousnesses have two kinds..."

Arising refers to the arising of the continuous flow (*pravāha*) and the arising of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). There are two kinds of abiding: the abiding of the continuous flow and the abiding of the characteristics.

There are two kinds of cessation: the cessation of the continuous flow and the cessation of the characteristics.
