Because it possesses the characteristic of being caused by an agent, it cannot be established as an eternal inconceivable. (This excludes that contrary characteristic and concludes that it is not eternal.

Mahāmati, my ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is eternal and inconceivable; it is established by the characteristic of the cause of ultimate truth, transcends existence and non-existence, and attains the characteristic of self-realization (*pratyātma-gati*).

Therefore, there is a characteristic; because it is the cause for the wisdom of the ultimate truth, there is a cause. This is because it is free from both existence and non-existence. (When that which relies on the ultimate truth serves as the characteristic of the cause:)

It is devoid of the nature of existence and non-existence. For example, it is like unconditioned space and nirvāṇa; because they are extinguished [of all conditioned phenomena], they are eternal. (The ancient commentary states: "Like the three unconditioned dharmas, they are free from the marks of existence and non-existence.")

Therefore, it is eternal. This is used as an analogy for the causal characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is eternal because it is free from existence and non-existence. Thus, Mahāmati, this is not the same as the heterodox theories of eternalism and the inconceivable.

(Concluding the preceding question: "In this way, Mahāmati, this permanence and inconceivability are that which is attained by the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) of all Tathāgatas.
Because it is thus, one should practice and study that which is attained by the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is permanent and inconceivable.

(The section beginning with "This permanence" clarifies that what the Tathāgata has attained is permanent because it is realized through self-awareness; the section beginning with "Because it is thus" uses the permanence of the Tathāgata to admonish others to practice and study. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the permanence and inconceivability of the non-Buddhists [is different].
It is of the nature of impermanence. Because it arises from the cause of differing characteristics, it is not permanent by virtue of the power of its own causal characteristics.

(This reiterates that what is reckoned as permanent by outsiders is, in fact, impermanent in nature, because it is established through differing causes. This refers to the permanence of the non-Buddhists; since it relies on differing causes and is not produced by the power of its own causal characteristics, they falsely reckon it to be permanent—thus, those who reckon it as permanent are deluded).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, when the various non-Buddhists perceive that the nature and non-nature of created things are impermanent, they engage in conceptualization regarding their so-called "permanent" and "inconceivable."

They calculate permanence. (This explains the origin of the non-Buddhists' calculation of permanence. Regarding "the nature of being produced is non-nature": it means that upon seeing those various phenomena such as form, because they are produced, their nature is non-nature. Having seen impermanence, they falsely engage in self-reflection.)

Those who calculate that which is produced as being permanent do so because, as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* says: "Where one sees change and flux, it is called the nature of impermanence; where one sees continuity, it is called permanence, for the agent is able to continue.

Mahāmati, I too, having perceived through such causes and conditions that the nature of what is produced is neither existence nor non-existence, and having realized the state of self-realized noble wisdom, speak of that permanence as being without cause (this refers to the Tathāgata refuting their calculation:
while the calculation that what is produced is impermanent seems plausible, the state of permanence they contemplate is actually not so; they calculate a different cause to be permanence).

Therefore, the Tathāgata also regards that which is produced as impermanent. Having seen its impermanence, he knows that all productions are like illusions and thus awakens to true permanence. True permanence is the realm of self-realization. Those [who follow other paths] reckon that what is produced is impermanent, and that permanence arises from a creator.

Therefore, it is said that they are eternal and without cause). Mahāmati, if the various non-Buddhists establish their "eternal" and "inconceivable" [nature] based on causal characteristics (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), then because their own characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*)—whether as existence or non-existence—are like the horns of a rabbit, this so-called "eternal" and "inconceivable" is merely a conceptual construction of verbal expression (*vāk-kalpanā*). (This reveals the causal characteristics of the non-Buddhists.)

It does not establish permanence. When one examines the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its cause, because its nature is non-nature, it is identical to a rabbit’s horn. If "emptiness" merely acquires the name of a cause, then that so-called "permanent and inconceivable" is nothing but a conceptual fabrication of speech.
Such is the fault of the various non-Buddhists. Why is this? Because they are mere conceptual fabrications of speech, identical to a rabbit’s horn;

the specific characteristics of their own causes are not their portion (this reiterates the external faults to clarify that the Tathāgata’s own cause is not within their scope). Mahāmati, my permanence and inconceivability are based on...
Because it is realized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is eternal because it is free from the faults of being a conditioned entity or a non-entity.

It is not like the impermanence of external entities or non-entities which is reckoned as eternal through deliberation and calculation. (This further clarifies that the Tathāgata’s true eternity is due to self-realization; it is free from the errors of existence and non-existence. It is not like the heterodox who reckon the impermanence of external entities and non-entities as eternal through arbitrary deliberation and calculation.
Mahāmati, if one were to reckon the impermanence of external entities and non-entities as an inconceivable eternity through deliberation and calculation, [it would be a false view].

Yet they do not know the characteristic of the eternal and inconceivable self-cause; they remain far removed from the characteristic of the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization. They should not speak [of this].

(This clarifies that the non-Buddhists merely know how to discriminate impermanence and speculate upon it as being eternal; they do not know the cause of the eternity they speculate upon, for it is not the characteristic of the self-cause.

Thus, they are far removed from the cause of self-realization. For this reason, they should not speak of eternity. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the various Śrāvakas, fearing the suffering of the conceptual construction of birth and death, and...
They seek nirvāṇa, yet they do not understand that all natures—the distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—are merely false imaginings and lack inherent nature.

(This is intended to refute the heterodox views of the Śrāvakas. It means that while the Śrāvakas merely know to fear the suffering of saṃsāra and seek the bliss of nirvāṇa, they do not realize that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday;

neither possesses inherent nature. They conceive the cessation of future sense faculties and their objects to be nirvāṇa; this is not the transformation of the ālayavijñāna through the noble wisdom of self-realization. (The Tang translation reads: "false...")

They calculate the cessation of future sense-faculties and their objects as *nirvāṇa*, yet they do not know that the realization of the realm of one’s own wisdom—the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—is the Great *Nirvāṇa*.

This clarifies that the Śrāvakas merely conceive of the cessation of faculties and objects as *nirvāṇa*, but it is not the Great *Nirvāṇa* of the transformation of the storehouse consciousness through the noble wisdom of self-realization. Therefore, the ignorant speak of three vehicles and speak of the mind-measure (*cittamātra*) tending toward non-existence.
For this reason, Mahāmati, they do not understand that all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present are [the manifestation of] their own minds.

Manifesting objective realms. Clinging to external objects that are manifestations of one's own mind, the wheel of birth and death constantly turns. (The first "therefore" below concludes the preceding section on the attachments of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles.

This means they do not comprehend the provisional and the ultimate; they cling to the existence of the Three Vehicles, yet claim that the Mind-Only nature leading to nothingness is the ultimate limit. The second "therefore" below clarifies that they do not know the Tathāgata’s own mental realm, but instead cling to objects manifested outside the mind, and are thus turned by the cycle of birth and death).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are unarisen; this applies to the past, the future, and the present.

This is what all Tathāgatas have taught. Why is this? It is because the nature of one's own mind-manifestations is neither existence nor non-existence, for they are free from the arising of both existence and non-existence.

(All phenomena refer to the various dharmas of existence and non-existence; both existence and non-existence are delusions, for they are fundamentally unarisen. This is the common teaching of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. Below, the reason for their non-arising is questioned and explained:

it is because all phenomena of existence and non-existence are manifestations of one's own mind, and thus they are entirely devoid of the characteristics of arising as existence or non-existence. Mahāmati, all natures are unarisen; all dharmas are like the horns of a rabbit or a horse.

"O Mahāmati, all phenomena are non-arising; they are the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization. Because foolish ordinary beings do not realize that their own nature is conceptual construction, they imagine the existence of all natures.

[In truth,] all natures are the very absence of nature, and all phenomena are the substance of the absence of nature. This means that since all natures are unarisen, all phenomena are like the horns of rabbits or horses—they are not truly existent. For it is said that since nature does not arise, phenomena likewise cannot be apprehended. Yet, these various foolish ordinary beings, with their unreal conceptual constructions, calculate that all natures arise;
this is merely what is calculated by their deluded thoughts. "O Mahāmati, all phenomena are unarisen; they are the sphere of the noble wisdom of self-realization."
Regarding "the sphere of experience" (*viṣaya*): the self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena do not arise; they are not the dual spheres of the false imaginings of ignorant fools.

They are established as the body and resources [of the *ālayavijñāna*], proceeding according to the characteristics of their own nature. (The Wei translation states: "O Mahāmati, the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all dharmas do not arise, because they are the sphere of noble wisdom realized within one's own body.

O Mahāmati, they are not the dual spheres of the intrinsic discrimination of ordinary people. O Mahāmati, these are the body, the means of subsistence, and the vessel-world of the *ālayavijñāna*, because they are the intrinsic characteristics of coming and going. All dharmas are non-arising; this is personal realization.

This is the sphere of the noble ones’ wisdom. It is the sphere where all natures and characteristics are non-arising; it is not the sphere of existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing that belongs to those fools. Therefore, that sphere of existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing belonging to those fools is established as the objective domain of the self-nature body and wealth of the eight consciousnesses (because it is the characteristic of the self-nature of consciousness).

Mahāmati, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) evolves through the appearance of the grasped and the grasper. Fools fall into the two views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and they long for the arising of all natures.
They give rise to the false discrimination of existence and non-existence; this is not the case for the wise and noble. Mahāmati...

Wisdom. One should cultivate and train therein. (This follows the preceding discussion on the establishment of the body and resources through the nature of consciousness, clarifying that the two views of the foolish arise from this.

That is to say, because the foolish are subject to the evolving of the marks of the grasper and the grasped within the *ālayavijñāna*, there arise the three views of the marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing. However, by nature these are fundamentally non-arising; yet ordinary fools falsely cling to the arising of all natures, giving rise to a chaotic confusion of perceptions of existence and non-existence.

This is the false conceptualization of ordinary fools and does not belong to the noble ones. Therefore, one must strive to learn. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five lineages of immediate succession (*pañca-anantarya-gotra*). (The five lineages of immediate succession, Wei...)

Translated as *The Dharma for Realizing the Nature of the Five Vehicles*. This text arises because, based on the previously discussed realm of self-realization, various different calculations were made; therefore, it is now clearly indicated that there are five distinct natures (*gotra*). This indicates the number, and the following lists the names. The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "Regarding 'uninterrupted' (*anantara*):

this means that Buddhas and sentient beings share the same *dharmatā*, which from the beginning has been without interruption. Because their capacities and conditions differ, they are divided into five. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: "As for 'nature' (*gotra*): similarity is called 'seed' (*gotra*), while identity of essence is called 'nature' (*gotra*). What are these five? They are:
the uninterrupted nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the uninterrupted nature of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Tathāgata vehicle... [and so forth].

The *anantara-gotra* (uninterrupted lineage), the *aniyata-gotra* (indeterminate lineage), and the *pratyeka-gotra* (individual lineage) [these are the names listed; their meanings are explained below]. How is one to know the *anantara-gotra* of the Śrāvaka-yāna?

If, upon hearing an exposition on the analytical knowledge that severs the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), all the pores of one’s body bristle with joy and delight, and one takes pleasure in cultivating the wisdom of signs (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*) rather than the signs of awakening through the cultivation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this is [the sign of the *anantara-gotra*].

This refers to the lineage of the uninterrupted seed-nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Regarding "the time of knowing through severance": this refers to followers of the Lesser Vehicle who, upon first hearing the Dharma wheel turned in its three revolutions, declare for themselves that they have already known and already severed [the afflictions].

Because they hear the Four Noble Truths and first attain the name of "understanding," their entire bodies experience joy. Regarding "delighting in the cultivation of the wisdom of characteristics" (*xiāngzhì*): Tiantai regards the afflictions of views and thought (*jiàn-sī*) as the delusions of grasping at characteristics; the "wisdom of characteristics" mentioned here is the wisdom that destroys these delusions of grasping at characteristics. This is the wisdom of the Śrāvakas.

There are eight kinds: first, the dharma-knowledge of suffering; second, the subsequent knowledge of suffering; third, the dharma-knowledge of origination; fourth, the subsequent knowledge of origination; fifth, the dharma-knowledge of cessation; sixth, the subsequent knowledge of cessation; seventh, the dharma-knowledge of the path; and eighth, the subsequent knowledge of the path. These are explained in detail in the *Tiantai sijiao yi jizhu* (Collected Annotations on the Tiantai Fourfold Teaching Ritual).

Regarding the phrase "not cultivating the characteristics of awakening through dependent origination": "dependent origination" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). "Awakening" refers to those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, who contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and awaken to the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Now, the Śrāvakas merely cultivate the Four Noble Truths and do not contemplate dependent origination; hence it is said they "do not cultivate" it. The Śrāvaka’s uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) is seen at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where the arising afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)...

The afflictions of the vital breath are not yet severed; one has not transcended the inconceivable death of transformation, but has transcended the death of segmentation. One makes the true lion’s roar:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life is established, and there is no further existence"—knowing this as it truly is.

One cultivates the realization of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons) until attaining the awakening of *parinirvāṇa*. (Regarding the vision of the eighth stage: this refers to the realm of non-existence, which is realized equally by the three vehicles. However, because there are differences in what is perceived, they are distinguished as Great or Small.)

The fourth sutra states: "In the eighth stage, the Bodhisattvas, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, extinguish the conceptual characteristics of mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna). Thus, the point at which these three vehicles sever delusions is the same. It further states: "In the eighth stage, the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas attain nirvāṇa. Thus, the point realized by these three vehicles is the same.

If this is so, how could the Śrāvaka possibly reach the eighth stage of a Bodhisattva? There must be a specific intent here; it is not a case of confusion between the categories. Regarding the *Tiantai sijiao yi* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings of Tiantai), according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), ten common stages for the three vehicles are clarified. First: [text continues].

1. The Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*); 2. The Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*); 3. The Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*); 4. The Stage of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*); 5. The Stage of Thinning (*tanu-bhūmi*); 6. The Stage of Freedom from Desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*); 7. The Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*); 8. The Stage of the Pratyekabuddha; 9. The Stage of the Bodhisattva; 10. The Stage of the Buddha. From the Stage of Dry Wisdom up to the Stage of the Bodhisattva, the bodhisattva practices and studies all of them, yet does not realize [the ultimate fruit].

At the Stage of the Buddha, one both studies and realizes. Therefore, these are called the "common stages" (*sāmānya-sthāna*) for the three vehicles. Furthermore, regarding the use of the distinct stages of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-vidhi*), where the names are distinct but the meaning is common, they correspond to the ten stages of the Common Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-vidhi*). Ten.

Faith corresponds to the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*). The thirty minds correspond to the stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*). The stages of the Eight Persons and the Stage of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*) correspond, respectively, to the first distinct stage, the Joyful Stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). The stage of Thinness (*tanu-bhūmi*) includes both the path and the fruit; the path corresponds to the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), and the fruit corresponds to the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). The path and fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*);

the path corresponds to the Blazing Wisdom Stage (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), and the fruit corresponds to the Difficult to Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*). The path and fruit of the Arhat; the path corresponds to the Presence Stage (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), and the fruit corresponds to the Far-reaching Stage (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*). The stage of the Pratyekabuddha corresponds to the eighth, the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). The Bodhisattva stages correspond to the [tenth] Good Wisdom Stage (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). The Buddha stage corresponds to the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). This is the application.

The names of the stages in the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) serve to distinguish those of the Shared Teaching (Tong-jiao). As for the mention of the "eighth stage" in the present text, it refers specifically to the eighth stage of the *pratyekabuddha* in the Shared Teaching. Since the *śrāvaka* has not yet eroded their residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), they remain inferior when compared to the *pratyekabuddha*; therefore, the text merely says "seeing.

Furthermore, the eighth stage of the *pratyekabuddha* in the Shared Teaching and the eighth stage, the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), in the Separate Teaching are identical in terms of severing delusions and realizing the truths. Thus, does the intent of this sutra belong to the Shared Teaching? Regarding the phrase "arising afflictions are severed, but habit-afflictions are not severed":

"arising" refers to the primary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*). They are called "arising" because they move; this refers to the severance of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Because one cannot erode the habit-energies, they are said to be "not severed. As for "death by transformation" (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*), the explanation is found in the preceding text. Regarding "death by segmentation" (*bhava-cyuti*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "It refers to all impure... [text continues].

Regarding wholesome and unwholesome karma: due to the auxiliary power of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the coarse matured fruits (*vipākaphala*) experienced within the three realms—such as the length of one’s physical life—are subject to fixed limits determined by the force of their respective causes and conditions; therefore, they are called "segmented" (*paricchinna*). This refers to the four lines following "The Master [said]: in the original text.

"Lion's Roar" (*siṃhanāda*) signifies fearless preaching. This refers to those śrāvakas who have already crossed over birth and death and realized *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are able to preach fearlessly amidst the great assembly. The three phrases following "I am born" constitute the meaning of fearless preaching. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that an arhat possesses four knowledges:

"My births are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence. The current text omits the third phrase. In both the Wei and Tang translations, all four phrases are complete; this must be an omission or abbreviation resulting from the translation process.

Furthermore, regarding "my births have been exhausted": the *Daming Fashu* states that this refers to an Arhat who has completely severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa*) and will no longer undergo birth and death within the three realms. Regarding "the holy life has been established": this refers to an Arhat who, through the accomplishment of the practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom, has attained this fruit.

Regarding "what was to be done has been accomplished": this refers to an Arhat who originally sought liberation from the three realms and cultivated various holy lives; since birth and death are now exhausted and the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished. Regarding "no further existence is to be received": [this means that there is no more rebirth].

This refers to the Arhat. Since their afflictions, karma, and birth-and-death have been exhausted, they will no longer receive a body in future lives. "As it truly is" (yathābhūtam) below refers to the Śrāvaka: one who knows as it truly is that the five aggregates are without self, realizes the emptiness of persons, and attains Nirvana.

"Mahāmati, as for 'separate and uninterrupted,' these refer to self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), sentient being (*sattva*), life-span (*jīva*), nourisher (*poṣa*), and individual (*puruṣa*) (the term 'separate' means that various dharmic characteristics such as self, person, sentient being, and life-span are each viewed individually;

'nourisher' and 'individual' are alternative names for the *puruṣa*, which is called 'nourisher' because it gives birth to and sustains all things; 'individual' is also called 'great man' (*mahāpuruṣa*), likewise carrying the sense of generating, nurturing, and establishing.
Although these views are distinct, their wondrous nature is eternally pervasive, and thus they are also termed 'uninterrupted'). Those sentient beings form such a realization and seek parinirvāṇa."

[The Buddha said: "Pāṇḍava. Those sentient beings who hold individualistic views [are as follows]. Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who say that everything arises from a creator; having perceived all phenomena, they declare, 'This is parinirvāṇa.

(This calculation holds that all dharmas arise from a creator, and they perceive this [creator] to be nirvāṇa). They form such a realization, yet the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is not their portion;

they possess no liberation. (The Chinese translation says: "They have no liberation because they have not seen the selflessness of phenomena. [Regarding the phrase "forming such a realization," this refers to the aforementioned Śrāvakas].)

The various individual [śrāvakas] and those of the three types of views among the outsiders conceive such notions; because they do not perceive the meaning of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they are outside the scope [of the path].

Mahāmati, these śrāvakayāna practitioners who are of the lineage of outsiders possess the notion of "emergence" regarding that which is not emerged from [saṃsāra]. In order to overturn those evil views, one should practice and study [the Mahāyāna]. (This summarizes the error of both the individual śrāvakas and the outsiders.

"The notion of emergence regarding that which is not emerged" means that while they have not yet emerged from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), they form the conceptualization of having attained liberation. For those of the Bodhisattvayāna, it is for the purpose of overturning that evil view of the notion of emergence regarding that which is not emerged.)

Therefore, one should practice and study [this]. Mahāmati, as for those of the lineage of the uninterrupted *pratyekabuddha-yāna*, if they hear it said that there is an uninterrupted [realization] through individual conditions, their body hairs stand on end and they weep with flowing tears; they do not associate with others, have no attachment to anything, and [perceive] various kinds of self-bodies.
When various supernatural powers—whether manifesting as separation or union—and various transformations are described, their minds enter into them accordingly.

If it is known that they possess the lineage of the uninterrupted vehicle of the *pratyekabuddhas*, one teaches the vehicle of the *pratyekabuddhas* in accordance with that. This is called the characteristic of the lineage of the uninterrupted vehicle of the *pratyekabuddhas*.

(The phrase "not approaching conditions" [不相近緣] is translated in the Tang version as "separation from the conditions of clamor. The passage beginning with "If it is known... refers to relying on the twelve links of dependent origination.)

They merely provide instruction and transformation, transmitting it to one another and preaching this Dharma-vehicle. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "This refers to those who are Pratyekabuddhas without further training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as those at the initial stage. The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) says:

"It means that if one knows that causes and conditions are distinct and do not combine, and thus does not approach various conditions nor cling to anything; or if, at times, upon hearing the teaching of various bodies, or transforming one body into many, or combining many bodies into one, or regarding supernatural powers and transformations, the mind perceives something attainable—this is the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
"Mahāmati, there are four kinds of the immediate lineage of the Tathāgata vehicle, namely: the immediate [lineage] of self-nature dharma..."
The lineages are: the lineage of uninterruptedness regarding the dharmas of self-nature; the lineage of uninterruptedness regarding the noble self-awakening;

and the lineage of uninterruptedness regarding the excellence of external lands. (The *Jizhu* states: "The wondrous essence, perfectly luminous, is called the 'uninterruptedness of the dharmas of self-nature. Not abiding in self-nature is called the 'uninterruptedness of the dharmas apart from self-nature. Not obtained from without [is the third]. )

It is said: "The uninterruptedness of the noble self-awakened [state], the equality of the dharma-realm, and the superiority of external lands. Mahāmati, if one hears these four matters as they are explained one by one, [one will understand them].

Furthermore, when it is taught that the manifestation of one’s own body and wealth from within one’s own mind establishes an inconceivable realm, those whose minds are not struck with fear or terror possess the characteristic of the lineage of the Tathāgata-vehicle without interruption.

(This means that if sentient beings, upon hearing the teaching of these four matters, and hearing that the body [arises] from the manifestation of their own mind, are not struck with fear or terror, they belong to the Tathāgata-vehicle.

Regarding the establishment of the inconceivable realm of body and wealth: it is like the Buddha manifesting various bodies, various lands, various transformed appearances, and various sublime adornments, wherein the environment and its inhabitants interpenetrate, and principle and phenomena are mutually pervasive.)

They are mutually integrated and do not depart from the one mind; this is called the inconceivable realm of name, body, and wealth. Mahāmati, regarding those of indeterminate lineage, it refers to when those three types are being taught.

They enter according to what is taught and are perfected accordingly—namely, the three types: Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas. The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "These are indeterminate persons; they enter according to what is taught and achieve perfection by following their training.
Because their nature can be shifted, they are called 'indeterminate'. Mahāmati, this refers to those who have first begun to cultivate the stages (*bhūmi*).

It is a formal establishment of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) so that they may transcend and enter the stage of non-existence (*akiṃcanya-bhūmi*). (This concludes the meaning of the aforementioned establishment of the five vehicles, referring to those who have first begun to practice on the stages.)

This is established in order to cause those of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) to transcend and enter the stage of non-existence (*akiṃcanya-bhūmi*); thus, this establishment is made. "Non-existence" directly points to the Tathāgata’s reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and does not merely refer to the eighth stage of non-existence.

Therefore, the following verse says: "The Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is far removed from the two teachings; abiding in non-existence, why establish the three vehicles? (It is incorrect to claim, as the New Translation [Xin Shuo] does, that this passage restricts [the teaching] only to those of indeterminate lineage). That which is the "self-awakened treasury" (*svasaṃvedana-garbha*)...

Having purified the habitual tendencies of their own afflictions and perceived the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), those Śrāvakas who dwell in the bliss of samādhi shall eventually attain the supreme body of a Tathāgata.

(The Tang translation states: "Those Śrāvakas dwelling in the bliss of samādhi, if they can realize and know the *ālayavijñāna* which is their own support, perceive the selflessness of phenomena, and purify the habitual tendencies of the afflictions, will ultimately attain the body of a Tathāgata.

[Regarding] 'the self-awakened store': this refers to the *ālayavijñāna*. It means that one who can realize and know the *ālayavijñāna* from which self-awareness arises, thereby purifies the afflictions of their own nature, perceives the selflessness of phenomena, and is thus a Śrāvaka dwelling in the bliss of that very samādhi, is able to awaken.")
This person shall also attain the most supreme body of a Tathāgata. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The fruit of *srotāpanna*, the *sakṛdāgāmin* and the *anāgāmin*, and the attainment of *arhatship*—these states of mind are deluded.

*Srotāpanna*: According to the *Vajra Commentary*, this is translated as "Entering the Stream. Because one enters the stream of the Eightfold Noble Path, this is the first fruit. The word "fruit" (*phala*) applies generally to the three persons mentioned in the subsequent lines. *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner), also called "One who returns once":

This person dies here, goes once to the heavens, and returns once to the human realm before attaining the end of all suffering and entering *nirvāṇa*. This is the second fruit. *Anāgāmin* (Non-returner), also called "One who does not come": This person dies within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The realms. Having exhausted the outflows (*āsrava*) therein, one does not come to be born again; these are the three fruits. Regarding the Arhat, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Arha" means "thief" and "han" means "to destroy. Because all thieves of affliction (*kleśa*) have been destroyed, it is so called.

Furthermore, it is said to mean "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*), because having exhausted all outflows, one is worthy of receiving offerings from humans and devas. Moreover, "a" means "not" and "rahant" means "birth"; because there is no further birth in future lives, it is so called. Since it encompasses these three meanings, the Sanskrit name is retained. These are the four fruits.

As for those whose minds are deluded by these [fruits], it is said that although their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have been destroyed, ignorance (*avidyā*) remains entirely; thus it is said their minds are deluded. The Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle are not my vehicles.
It is said: "For the foolish who possess little wisdom and for the noble ones who dwell in seclusion" (the *Jizhu* commentary states:

"The Tathāgata, for the sake of the ignorant and those of little wisdom, and for the Śrāvakas who incline toward quiescence, taught the three vehicles and the one vehicle, and further established the 'non-vehicle. Since the three do not exist, the one also does not exist. 'Dwell in seclusion' refers to being free from desire and abiding in nirvāṇa). This is the Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
Far removed from the two teachings, one abides in non-existence. Why then establish three vehicles? (Within the gateway of the ultimate truth, whether three or one, all are utterly transcended;

thus they are not vehicles at all. Yet, in that which is not a vehicle, there is fundamentally nothing existing; how could there be the distinction between three and one? Regarding the various dhyānas, the immeasurables, and so forth, as well as the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*):

sensation and perception are entirely stilled, and even the "mind-only" (*citta-mātra*) does not exist. (The *Jízhù* [Collected Notes] states: "The various dhyānas, immeasurables, and so forth" refers to the four meditative concentrations.)

The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samādhi*)—that is, the four meditative absorptions of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*)—and the complete cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*), which refers to the *śrāvaka*’s attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). When the Tathāgata speaks of various dharmas such as dhyānas and samādhis, these too lack any reality;

he speaks in this way for the sake of deluded people whose minds consist of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-citta-mātra*). Therefore, it is said that "there is also no mind-only" (*na ca citta-mātram asti*).

Mahāmati, those icchantikas are not [truly] icchantikas. Who could turn them away from worldly liberation? (In the Wei translation, following "Mahāmati," there is the phrase "what is the vehicle of no-nature?

This passage is introduced by way of the five natures; therefore, the Wei translation includes the phrase "the vehicle of no-nature. Regarding *icchantika*, the Great Sūtra states: *icchan* means "faith" and *tika* means "lacking. Because they lack faith, they are called *icchantikas*.

Thus, "lack of faith" is the literal meaning of the translation. The intent of the current text contains two aspects: first, that these *icchantikas* are the *icchantikas* of actual practice; second, the phrase "not [truly]... clarifies that Bodhisattvas rely upon *icchantikas* to fulfill their original vows.)

This is because, were it not for those icchantikas, the bodhisattva’s vow could not be fulfilled; from whom, then, would liberation from all worldly realms proceed? Therefore it is said: "Were it not for the icchantikas, from whom would liberation from the world proceed? Mahāmati!
There are two kinds of icchantikas. The first are those who have abandoned all roots of goodness and yet make vows for the sake of sentient beings since beginningless time.
What is meant by "abandoning all roots of goodness"? It refers to slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and uttering evil words, saying:
"This is not a teaching that accords with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or liberation. Because they have abandoned all roots of goodness, they do not attain parinirvāṇa.

(The Wei translation says: "Mahāmati, there are two kinds of icchantikas. What are the two? First, those who burn away all roots of goodness; second, those who, out of compassion for all sentient beings, make the vow to exhaust the entire realm of sentient beings. Mahāmati,")

What is meant by "burning away all roots of goodness"? It refers to slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka by saying, "That is not a teaching that accords with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or liberation. By thus abandoning all roots of goodness, one cannot attain Nirvāṇa. (The phrase "This is not... below is precisely the slanderous speech.
Second, because of the original vows and skillful means of the Bodhisattvas, it is not that they do not enter Parinirvāṇa;

rather, while they themselves enter Parinirvāṇa, [they cause] all sentient beings to do so as well. (The Wei translation says: "Mahāmati, those who out of compassion for sentient beings make the vow to exhaust the realm of sentient beings are Bodhisattvas. Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas employ skillful means to make such vows.")

"If there are sentient beings who do not enter nirvana, I likewise shall not enter nirvana. For this reason, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not enter nirvana. This explains the second [point] regarding the Bodhisattva’s vow. As for the character "two" (er), it should be read as the character "then/how" (yunhe).

Only then does it correspond to the preceding passage; it is not that it does not descend [into the meaning]. That is to say, it is not that the Bodhisattva truly does not enter parinirvāṇa; rather, in order to cause all sentient beings who have abandoned their roots of goodness to enter parinirvāṇa, he manifests the appearance of not entering parinirvāṇa. Mahāmati!
That they enter parinirvāṇa is called the characteristic of not entering parinirvāṇa; this also leads to the state of an icchantika (the Wei translation says:

"This is called the two kinds of icchantikas who lack the nature for nirvāṇa; for this reason, they resolutely adopt the conduct of an icchantika"). Regarding the phrase "they enter parinirvāṇa," "they" refers to all sentient beings mentioned above; it means that those sentient beings enter parinirvāṇa.

This is precisely the characteristic of a bodhisattva not entering parinirvāṇa. This is because the two natures—nirvāṇa and non-nirvāṇa—are equal. Furthermore, regarding the statement that they "reach the state of an icchantika," this means that the bodhisattva manifests in conformity with their affairs, likewise through the nature of equality, as a category similar to the state of an icchantika.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, in this context, what is meant by 'ultimately not entering parinirvāṇa'? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The bodhisattva-icchantika, having known that all dharmas are originally in a state of parinirvāṇa, [remains thus] until the end."

They ultimately do not enter parinirvāṇa, yet they are not icchantikas who have abandoned all roots of goodness. (In this context, two types of icchantikas are indicated. Among these two types, which one ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha replied: "The bodhisattva-icchantika does not enter parinirvāṇa. Why? Because the bodhisattva thoroughly knows that all dharmas are originally of the nature of nirvāṇa;

therefore, there is no nirvāṇa into which they can enter. Nevertheless, they are not actual icchantikas who have abandoned their roots of goodness. Mahāmati, as for those icchantikas who have abandoned all roots of goodness, furthermore...
By virtue of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), roots of goodness may sometimes arise.
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata does not abandon any sentient being. For this reason, even a bodhisattva who is an icchantika does not enter parinirvāṇa.

(This means that although they are utterly evil, the Buddha’s great compassion still employs the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and supernatural powers to guide them through skillful means, causing them to plant roots of goodness. Below, the text interrogates and explains the reason why these roots of goodness arise; the intent is that they cannot arise through their own power, but truly result from the Tathāgata’s non-abandonment.

"For the sake of all sentient beings"—this refers to those such as Aṅgulimāla and others. From "By this" onwards, [the text] concludes by clarifying the Bodhisattva’s intention not to enter *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should be well-versed in the three self-natures (*trisvabhāva*).
(From the previous section where Mahāmati requested the teaching on self-nature until now, the World-Honored One’s first chapter extensively refuted the delusions of existence and non-existence;

the second chapter saw Mahāmati inquire about the manifestation of the flow of one's own mind, to which the World-Honored One replied with eight metaphors. He further clarified the characteristics of the teachings of the three Buddhas, wherein the meaning of the three self-natures was briefly indicated but not yet complete. Consequently, he explained the two types of Śrāvakas, as well as the eternal, inconceivable five natures.)

[etc. Now, in this third chapter, the World-Honored One, having spontaneously explained the meaning of *icchantika* without being questioned, begins here to reveal the names of the three self-natures (*trisvabhāva*) in order to fulfill the intent of the previous request. Nevertheless, although the World-Honored One answers regarding the three natures, their meaning encompasses the five dharmas; therefore, he later concludes by manifesting the names of the five dharmas.

Since the preceding extensive refutation of external doctrines was entirely [a refutation of] the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), what are the three self-natures? They are: the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). (These three natures are largely identical, with minor differences, to those established in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. There, they are termed the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*)).

Now, conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) is the imagined nature; dependent origination (*paratantra*) is the other-dependent nature; and the established nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is the perfected nature. Mahāmati, the self-nature of conceptual construction arises from signs (*nimitta*).
(Signs are the other-dependent nature, for dependent origination is the objective sign; this means that conceptual construction arises from dependent origination. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, how does the self-nature of conceptual construction arise from signs? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The other-dependent nature consists of the characteristics of things and signs, which manifest through activity."

The characteristic of phenomena (vastu-lakṣaṇa). [Regarding] "the characteristic of phenomena": through the conjunction of causes and conditions, that which is capable of grasping and that which is grasped constitute the phenomenon (vastu); their shape, location, length, and brevity constitute the characteristic (lakṣaṇa). The second occurrence of the word "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the characteristic of the phenomenon itself. The characteristic of manifest activity (saṃskāra-prabhāsvara-lakṣaṇa).

"Formations" (saṃskāra) refers to the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha). These two characteristics—the characteristic of manifestation from the aggregate of formations and the characteristic of the arising of false discrimination—are stated as the phrase "from the characteristic of arising. These are the phenomenal aspects of dependent origination and belong to the objective referent (ālambana). The characteristic of the manifestation of formations is precisely the form (rūpa) subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).

The phrase "arising from the characteristics of conceptualization" (yán cóng xiāng shēng) means "to follow" or "to depend upon. The *Exposition of the Holy Teachings* (*Xiǎnyáng shèngjiào lùn*), fascicle six, states: "The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) can perform five kinds of functions; its third function is that it serves as the basis for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The present text first clarifies the meaning of how the nature of false conceptualization arises from conditions and gives rise to characteristics. (The following text will properly clarify the essence of the nature of false conceptualization.

There are two kinds of attachment to the nature of false conceptualization, which were established by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. ("Established" [jiàn lì] is translated as "expounded" [yǎn shuō] in the Tang version. [This refers to the section] above the term "attachment.")

Because the text explains two kinds of characteristics, there are consequently two kinds of imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): namely, the characteristic of attachment to names and signs, and the characteristic of attachment to the characteristics of things.

The characteristic of attachment to names and signs refers to attachment to internal and external phenomena. The characteristic of attachment to the signs of objective entities refers to attachment to the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of those very same internal and external [phenomena].

"Names and signs" refers to the characteristic of names, which belongs to the four non-material aggregates (*skandhas*). This is because attachment arises from the manifestation of characteristics through formative forces (*saṃskāra*);

thus, that which is manifested by the aggregate of formative forces does not transcend the two dharmas of the internal mind and external objects. "Objective entities" refers to the object of cognition (*ālambana*). This is because attachment arises from the signs of entities produced through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); these signs of entities produced through dependent origination do not transcend the internal [mind].

Because external objects consist of both particular and universal characteristics, and because there is no separate phenomenon apart from these particulars and universals, this is called the characteristic of the two kinds of imagined nature (this concludes the naming of the two kinds of imagination).

That which arises depending upon and conditioned by [something] is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). (This follows from the two kinds of false imagination mentioned above to clarify the nature of dependent origination;

that is, the basis and the object of those false imaginings are of the nature of dependent origination. This concludes the preceding section. What constitutes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?

It refers to that which is attained by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), as well as the realm produced by the destination of self-realized noble wisdom, free from the false imaginings of names, marks, and the characteristics of things. This is called the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind of the perfected nature.

(Completion. This refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. That is to say: its intrinsic nature is non-biased, thus it is "perfect" (*pari*); its intrinsic nature is untainted, thus it is "accomplished" (*niṣpanna*); its intrinsic nature is non-delusory, thus it is "real" (*satya*). The meaning of the current text is that if one is free from the two perceptions of name and thing, then there is no delusion. This is what is attained by noble wisdom.)

Thus it is untainted (*anāsrava*). That which is born from the noble path (*ārya-gati*) is without partiality; therefore, it is named the "perfected intrinsic nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The *tathāgatagarbha*-mind is the essence of the fruit, and the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*) is the virtue of the fruit. It is by means of this that its name is established and revealed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Name and appearance (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the two aspects of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*)—these constitute the perfected aspect (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).

(Name and appearance are two of the five dharmas. Conceptualization refers to false discrimination (*parikalpita*). Together with correct wisdom and suchness, these comprise the names of the five dharmas. When these names of the five dharmas are forgotten, that is the perfection of intrinsic nature.

As for the "two aspects," they refer to the two aspects of name-appearance and phenomena. This verse does not merely repeat the prose; it further clarifies the three natures by means of the five dharmas).
“Mahāmati, this is called the Sūtra on Examining the Five Dharmas and the Self-Nature. It is the sphere of activity reached by the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

(‘Sphere’ [gati] refers to a category; it means that those of the Bodhisattva vehicle rely on the cultivation of the noble wisdom of self-realization, and thus Bodhisattvas are designated as the ‘category of self-realization.

The conclusion of the title is thus understood. You and all other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study this. (This exhortation to the Bodhisattvas to study this belongs to the preceding chapter, as the summary of the questions posed occurs only after the verses.)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully contemplates the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*). (The ancient commentary states:

"Having already cultivated and studied the five dharmas and the three natures, one should further examine the two kinds of selflessness, namely, the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. What are the two kinds of selflessness?

They are the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Regarding the entry into selflessness: "person" refers to the conventional designation for the provisional combination of the five aggregates (*skandha*). When one investigates each part within this body, none of them possesses a self; what, then, could constitute a "person"? Therefore, it is called the "selflessness of persons."

"Non-self" (anātman) here refers merely to the breaking down of the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). "Dharma-non-self" (*dharmanairātmya*): "Dharma" refers to the various substantial dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and bases. Previously, the person (*pudgala*) was treated as a conventional designation; now, the substantial dharmas themselves are being clarified.

Because the grasping at a person (*pudgalagrāha*) is narrow, it is easy to sever; because the grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) is broad, it is difficult to eliminate. Thus, the *Commentary on the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas* states: "The self is narrow and dharmas are broad; for one who is deluded about the person must be deluded about dharmas, whereas one who is deluded about dharmas is not necessarily deluded about the person.

However, when one investigates each of these dharmas individually, no essence of a self is found; hence, it is called "dharma-non-self. This refers merely to the breaking down of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates, elements, and bases. The following text will clarify the meaning of non-self based on wisdom (*jñāna*), so the names "person" and "dharma" have not yet been explicitly stated. Now, I shall briefly explain them. (This is the heading; the following is the explanation).
What is the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*)? (Following the text on the selflessness of phenomena, there should be the word "knowledge" [jñāna] here.

It refers to that which is free from "self" and "what belongs to the self," and which gives rise to consciousness through the grasping and attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), as well as the collection of ignorance, karma, and craving, such as the eye and forms.

It is the treasury of all the faculties, the manifestation of one's own mind as the vessel-world and the body, and the appearance of one's own false imaginings, which are established and displayed. (This explains the meaning of the selflessness of persons based on knowledge. Regarding the five aggregates...)

This body is a gathering place for all evils; it is a conceptual construction (*prajñapti*) of false imagination and lacks true reality. To be "free from self and what belongs to self" means that because the body is unreal, one is free from self and what belongs to self; this phrase clarifies the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Below the section on the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), the meaning of their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is correctly explained. It is said that the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and bases assemble to form the body. "Ignorance" refers to nescience (*avidyā*). There are three types of karma: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable. "Craving" refers to sensual craving. Thus, through ignorance, karma, and craving, the eye and other faculties arise.

The six sense organs and the six objects, such as form and so forth, through grasping and attachment, give rise to the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and others. Regarding the phrase "all [the worlds]," this refers to the vessel-world (bhājana-loka), the physical environment. Regarding "the body and its repositories," the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the limbs and members; "repositories" (*kośa*) refers to the internal cavities of the body, including all the viscera, intestines, and stomach.

It is said that the various sense organs, the body, the repositories, and so forth, are merely manifestations of one's own mind, established and displayed through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). They are like a flowing river, like a seed, like a lamp, and like the wind.

"Like clouds, they perish moment by moment in succession. (This follows the preceding section to provide a metaphor that clarifies the momentary disintegration of the aggregate-body (*skandha-kāya*). This means: like a river rushing away, never returning and never lingering; like a seed sprouting, gradually forming and gradually decaying;

like the wick of a lamp burning down, becoming ash and embers flame by flame; like the nature of wind, which is not constant and does not abide for even a moment; and like floating clouds, which shift and transform, arising and ceasing without permanence—so too is the transformation and decay of the aggregate-body. Because it disintegrates, there is no self; thus it is said that "there is no person-self" (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

The five metaphors above collectively manifest the characteristic of the aggregate-body’s successive disintegration. "Successive" (*kṣaṇa-anupūrva*) indicates that it does not disintegrate instantaneously. The five metaphors in the following text individually manifest the different habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the aggregate-body; therefore, each is used as a metaphor.)

[The first] half of the verse clarifies habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); the second half illustrates this through a metaphor (the prose commentary is easily understood). It is restless like a monkey: this means the body is full of agitation and lacks constancy, just as a monkey never rests for even a moment.

It delights in impure places like a fly: this means the body is the root of craving and attachment; it constantly seeks to dwell with defilement, just as flies swarm upon putrid filth. It is insatiable like wind or fire:
this means that because this body greedily pursues objects without satiety, it is like a wind-blown fire consuming a wilderness, which likewise knows no satisfaction. Since beginningless time...

The cause of the habit-energies of falsehood is like a water-drawing wheel; the wheel of existence within the realms of birth and death is likewise. (This means that the body is the cause of the habit-energies of falsehood.

The cycle of birth and death, with its fluctuations between suffering and pleasure and ascent and descent, is like a water-drawing wheel, moving up and down alternately. The phrase "the wheel of existence within the realms of birth and death" corresponds to the metaphor of the water wheel.

Various bodily forms are like illusions produced by spells; when the mechanism is triggered, the image arises. (The Tang translation states: "Various physical bodies and their dignified movements and halts are like a corpse that moves due to the power of incantations, or like a wooden man moved by a mechanical device.")

Movement. ○ This refers to this body, which is originally composed of the combination of the four great elements and is no different from a corpse. It moves due to the operation of the conscious mind; it is like a wooden man who, relying on the power of illusory spells, has his joints activated and the wooden figure rises. Thus, the above ten metaphors—both general and specific—[illustrate this].

Each [of these] clarifies the faults of the aggregate-body (*skandha-kāya*). All arise from the attachment of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*); fundamentally, there is no real self. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Skillfully knowing those characteristics is called the wisdom of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya-jñāna*).

(The definition of the name may be understood from this). What is the wisdom of the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya-jñāna*)? (Previously, when "non-self of persons" was indicated, the word "wisdom" was absent).

This refers to awakening to the self-nature of the characteristics of deluded conceptualization regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—("awakening" being the wisdom that awakens, while the "aggregates," etc., are the phenomena to be awakened to)—just as it is with the aggregates, elements, and bases.
It is free from "I" and "mine. It is the cause of the accumulation of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas).

Bound by the ropes of karma and craving, it arises through mutual conditioning and is without movement (the Chinese translation says "without an agent"). (This uses the person as an analogy for phenomena to clarify the meaning of non-self. Just as below [in the section on the aggregates] the common characteristics of the aggregate-body are cited as an example—meaning that if the person has no self, phenomena are likewise so—the subsequent text concludes:
"All phenomena are also thus. All phenomena are likewise free from the characteristics of unreal false imagination, whether they be specific or general characteristics. False...

The power of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the birth of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), not that of the noble sages (*ārya*). This is because the mind, intellect, consciousness, and the five dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

(This applies the dharma to the person to clarify the meaning of non-self; thus it says, "all dharmas are likewise. From "devoid of self-nature" below: because the dharmas of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth—characterized by specific and general marks (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—are manifested through the false conceptualizations of ordinary worldlings, and due to the power of the perfuming of seeds and manifestations of those false conceptualizations, they continue in an uninterrupted succession.

This is the birth of ordinary worldlings, not that which exists for the noble sages. Regarding "mind, intellect, and... below: this refers to how the noble sages are able to be free from the mind, intellect, consciousness, the five dharmas, and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The meaning of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) has already been illustrated above; here, it is further extensively revealed.

[This is] the characteristic of the benefit of selflessness). Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully discern the selflessness of all phenomena (and, by means of the principle of the selflessness of phenomena, exhort them so that they may come to know it well).
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is skilled in the selflessness of phenomena will, before long, attain the first stage of a bodhisattva.

One contemplates the ground of non-existence (*anupalambha*). One observes and realizes awakening with joy. (The phrase "not long" means that because of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one is adjacent to the stage of the noble ones (*āryabhūmi*);

this reveals the loftiness of one's practice. Regarding the contemplation of non-existence in the first ground, the text of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* on the first ground states: "The equality of all bodhisattvas is non-existent," which is precisely the meaning of equality. As for "realizing awakening with joy": awakening is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.)

"Opening" refers to all sentient beings who were closed off from the Buddha’s knowledge and vision by ignorance; now, having ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*), they begin to open the Buddha’s awakening, and thus give rise to joy. The *Avataṃsaka* explains the causes and characteristics of this joy in detail, stating that it is because they have accomplished manifold joys.

It is named the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Furthermore, Tiantai says: "On this ground, one abides in the stage of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), wherein the hundred realms manifest as Buddhas, achieving the Way through the eight phases (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*) to benefit sentient beings.

The present 'contemplation of non-existence' is precisely that practice of effortlessness. This is because this ground first acquires the name 'effortlessness,' and this name applies throughout the upper and lower grounds). Progressing gradually in this sequence, one transcends the characteristics of the nine grounds and attains the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

(Regarding why the tenth ground is called the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud, the *Huayan shu* quotes the thirteenth fascicle of the *Vyavahāra-śāstra*: "In the tenth ground, by means of the gate of samādhi and the gate of dhāraṇī, one gathers all causes of the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*), which pervade the ālayavijñāna...")

Within consciousness, it is like floating clouds that pervade empty space; by means of these clouds of hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*), at every single moment, at every single mark (*lakṣaṇa*), at every single minor sign (*anuvyañjana*), and at every single pore, they rain down immeasurable and boundless Dharma-rain.
Because it suffices all sentient beings who are to be converted by raining down the rain of Dharma like a cloud, it is called the "Dharmameghā Bhūmi" (Cloud of Dharma Stage).

Upon that [stage], one establishes an image of a great king of jewel lotuses adorned with immeasurable jewels and a great jewel palace, produced through the cultivation of the realm of the illusory nature;

Having accomplished this, he sits upon it. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the section on the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmika*), states: "Once the Bodhisattva has entered the stage of receiving the position of consecration, ten million *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis all manifest before him.

When these samādhis manifest, a great jewel lotus suddenly appears.
