Accomplished through the cultivation of all practices, this is identical to the present sutra (consulting that [text] will clarify it).

Surrounded by a retinue of sons of the Conquerors (*jina-putra*) of the same class (those of the same class refers to bodhisattvas of identical practice), they have come from all Buddha-fields to receive the consecration from the hands of the Buddhas, just as the crown prince of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) receives his consecration.

As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the chapter on the Ten Stages, states: "At that time, all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, knowing that in a certain world a certain bodhisattva was able to perform such vast and expansive practices, arrived to confer upon him..."
At that time, an immeasurable and boundless assembly of Bodhisattvas, up to those of the ninth stage, all came to surround him, paying homage and making offerings.

Then, from the space between the eyebrows of all the Buddhas of the ten directions, there issued forth a pure light called "Augmenting All-Knowledge and Supernatural Powers," with countless rays of light as its retinue. It shone universally upon all worlds in the ten directions, manifesting various kinds of magnificent adornments. Having manifested these things, the light entered the crown of the great Bodhisattva’s head.

At that moment, this Bodhisattva attained one million samādhis previously unattained; he was said to have received the rank of consecration, entered the realm of the Buddhas, became fully endowed with the ten powers, and was reckoned among the number of Buddhas, just like the son born to a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Son, when the mother is the principal queen, in that wheel-turning realm, they cause this crown prince to sit upon a precious golden throne of the white elephant. They take the waters of the four great oceans and place them within a golden vase; the king holds this vase and pours it over the crown of the prince’s head.

At that moment, he is said to have received the royal office and is reckoned among the number of consecrated Kṣatriya kings. It is the same for the Bodhisattva receiving his office: because the water of the Buddhas’ wisdom is poured upon his crown, he is said to have received his position. This present sutra is entirely identical to that meaning; it is merely more concise than that [other text], which is more extensive.
Having transcended the stage of the Buddha-sons and reached the destination of the self-realized noble wisdom, one shall attain the sovereign Dharma-body of a Tathāgata.

Because one perceives the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). (The aforementioned benefits are all attributed to the merit of perceiving the selflessness of phenomena. This is called the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena. (This concludes the definition of the selflessness of phenomena mentioned previously.
You, all you Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, should practice and study this. (This exhorts them to cultivate the meaning of the selflessness of phenomena.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the characteristics of establishing [existence] and slandering [non-existence], we pray that you will explain them."

[The Buddha] said: (The Ancient Commentary states: Because one has observed the two types of selflessness above, one is able to depart from the two views of existence/non-existence and permanence/annihilation; therefore, [the interlocutor] requests an explanation of the characteristics of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*). To assert existence where there is no existence is called superimposition; to assert non-existence where there is no non-existence is called denial.)
May I and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas be free from the two extremes of the evil views of reification and denial, and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having awakened, may we leave behind the reification of permanence and sever the view of denial, so as not to slander the True Dharma.

(The Ancient Commentary states: "Having realized the evil views of existence and non-existence, one is able to leave behind the reification of the view of permanence and the denial of the view of annihilation, ensuring that one does not give rise to disparagement toward the True Dharma; for the True Dharma is free from both existence and non-existence.")
To speak of existence or non-existence is itself to slander the true Dharma. At that time, having received the request of Mahāmati Bodhisattva, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

Establishment and denial—there is no such thing as that "mind-only" (cittamātra). (Establishment and denial are produced by false imagination; since they are from the beginning devoid of reality, it is said that there is no such thing as that "mind-only").
The establishment of the body, its enjoyments, and the mind cannot be known [by them]; the ignorant, lacking wisdom, engage in establishment and denial.

(Regarding the phrase "the establishment of the body and its enjoyments," the Wei and Tang translations render this as "body, requisites for livelihood, and dwelling. In the phrase "the establishment of the body and its enjoyments," the term "establishment" refers to the sense of establishing one's livelihood and occupation, not to attachment.)

Regarding the establishment of permanence: as for those whose minds cannot understand, the two characters "reverse mind" (fǎnxīn) connect with the meaning of the preceding phrase. This means that both body and mind lack substantial reality and do not know one another; this speaks of their delusion.
Due to ignorance and lack of wisdom, they give rise to the characteristics of establishing [existence] and slandering [non-existence] regarding all phenomena.

At that time, the World-Honored One further elucidated the meaning of these verses. (Although the meaning of the verses was clear, it had been presented briefly rather than extensively; therefore, he elucidated it again so that its details might be known.)
He addressed Mahāmati, saying: "There are four kinds of establishing what does not exist as existing. What are the four? They are:

the establishment of non-existent characteristics, the establishment of non-existent views, the establishment of non-existent causes, and the establishment of non-existent natures. These are called the four kinds of establishment.

(Regarding 'establishing what does not exist as existing,' it means that although things are fundamentally non-existent, one arbitrarily establishes them by the name of 'existence'; hence, 'non-existent existence. The explanation of the four kinds of establishment will be seen below. Furthermore, [he] slandered..."
"Denial" (abhyākhyāna) refers to the act of denying that which has been established by another, based on an improper investigation of non-apprehension.

This is called the characteristic of denial regarding an establishment. (That is to say: when one investigates the four kinds [of establishments] mentioned in the preceding text and finds them non-apprehensible, then those establishments are deemed improper. "Improper" means they lack reality; thus, one subsequently gives rise to denial.)
This is called "the lower" (a summary of the meaning of the two preceding sections). Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of establishing a characteristic where none exists?

It refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), which lack intrinsic or common characteristics, yet one gives rise to attachment toward them, thinking, "It is thus," or "It is not otherwise.

This is called the characteristic of establishing a characteristic where none exists. (The phrases "it is thus" and "it is not otherwise" point out the nature of their stubborn adherence; because they cling to it without wavering, it is said, "it is thus" and "it is not otherwise. This is not...
The conceptualization of establishing signs arises from the faults of beginningless falsehood and the attachment to various habitual tendencies (this points out the false cause).

Mahāmati, the establishment of signs based on the view of non-existence refers to the establishment of views regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), sentient beings (*sattva*), life-span (*jīva*), nourisher (*poṣa*), and individual (*puruṣa*).
This is called the establishment of signs based on the view of non-existence. (Nourisher and individual...)

The Wei translation renders this as "the agent and the recipient. [Terms such as] self, person, sentient being, and life-span are views postulated by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Since these various views are fundamentally non-existent and arise from deluded thoughts, they are said to be "the establishment of views that do not exist. The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* (Jingang shu) states:

Grasping at its own essence as "self," one conceives of the self as transmigrating through various realms of existence; this is the view of a "person" (pudgala). One conceives of the self as a continuity of flourishing and decline, of change and transformation; this is the view of a "sentient being" (sattva). One conceives of the self as abiding with its single karmic retribution and life-force uninterrupted;

this is the view of a "life-span" (jīva) and a "nourished man" (poṣa/puruṣa) [as noted in the preceding commentary]. Mahāmati, that which is established as having no cause refers to the initial consciousness arising without a cause, which is subsequently unreal like a magical illusion and fundamentally unarisen.

The elements of the eye, form, light, and attention—having arisen from preceding births, though real at the moment of arising, they return to destruction. This is called [the characteristic of being established without a cause].

It is not a characteristic established by having a cause. (The eye, form, light, and the element of space; the Wei translation reads "eye, form, emptiness, light, and mindfulness. Regarding the claim that "initial consciousness arises without a cause":

"consciousness" (*vijñāna*) means the act of discerning. "Initial" refers to the beginning of arising. This means that when discerning all phenomena, they initially arise fundamentally without a cause. Because they are fundamentally without a cause, although they arise later, their cognition is unreal, like an illusion. "Later" refers to the end of arising. "Fundamentally unarisen" concludes the two preceding phrases, meaning that from the very beginning, a characteristic of arising cannot be found.

"Eye, form, light, and the element of space" demonstrates that visual consciousness arises from four conditions: namely, due to space, due to light, due to the mind, and due to the eye. "Element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of space. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) has the meaning of the mind. [This concludes] the prior arising.

[The text] continues: "Based on the preceding eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), mental consciousness arises. Although the preceding thought-moment arises, once it has arisen it is real; yet having been real, it perishes again. This is called 'establishment based on what is non-existent. This uses the example of eye-consciousness to illustrate that all other phenomena are likewise unreal.

"Mahāmati, the characteristic of establishment based on the nature of non-existence refers to the conceptual attachment to the nature of space, cessation, and parinirvāṇa as being unconditioned. This [establishment] is devoid of both existence and non-existence;
all phenomena are like the horns of a rabbit or a horse, or like the appearance of falling hairs [to one with an eye disease]. Devoid [of such characteristics].

"Existence and non-existence" is called the characteristic of establishing the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-vyavasthāna-lakṣaṇa*). (The passage "Regarding the void... refutes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), [showing they] are free from being and non-being.

The passage "All... refutes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), [showing they] are free from being and non-being. Therefore, the establishment of a [fixed] nature is erroneous. The New Commentary states: "It is said that the non-Buddhists establish the existence of a nature within the three unconditioned phenomena and unconditioned dharmas. The Buddha says these three dharmas are free from being and non-being;

by analogy, this clarifies that all dharmas are free from existence and non-existence, just as the floating hair or falling hairs seen by one with cataracts, or the horns of a rabbit or a horse, which are fundamentally non-existent. Establishment and denial—these are the delusions of the ignorant.
Now, false conceptualization consists in not skillfully observing that which is the manifestation of one's own mind; it does not belong to the wise or the noble.

Therefore, one should practice and study so as to remain free from the evil views of superimposition and denial. (This concludes the discussion of the two views to clarify that the foolish do not know that things are the manifestation of their own minds, and thus falsely give rise to the two characteristics of superimposition and denial, which are not the affairs of the wise or the noble.

"Therefore" and below, he exhorts them to abandon the denial of these two views. Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully knows the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness.
One recognizes the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two kinds of selflessness, proceeding toward the ultimate.

For the sake of establishing sentient beings, one manifests various types of forms, just as the imagined nature depends upon the dependent origination. (This summarizes the preceding sutra’s discussion of mind, thought, and consciousness, further clarifying the benefits of self-benefit and benefiting others.)

As with the preceding discussion on delusion, this is illustrated by way of analogy to clarify the point. That is to say, just as the nature of false conceptualization arises in dependence upon dependent origination, so too do the manifested images of Bodhisattvas exist in dependence upon sentient beings. This example illustrates how these manifestations arise based on living beings; below, another metaphor is provided to clarify that these manifestations are not identical [to the source].

For example, it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel of various colors that universally manifests all Buddha-fields and the great assemblies of all Tathāgatas, wherein they all listen to and receive the Dharma teachings. That is to say: "All phenomena are like illusions."

Like a dream, a shadow, or the moon reflected in water, they are free from arising and ceasing, and from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, as well as the dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

(The passage beginning with "For example" below illustrates how Bodhisattvas who have thoroughly understood the mind, consciousness, and mental factors manifest forms according to the capacities of sentient beings to teach and transform them. The passage beginning with "Universally manifesting" below clarifies that they appear in bodies throughout the dust-motes of all lands to hear and receive the Dharma.

The passage beginning with "That which is called" below indicates the meaning of the Dharma they receive. The passage beginning with "In one moment" below clarifies their freedom from the dharmas of non-Buddhists and the Two Vehicles. They attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis, even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas...
By means of the samādhi of others, having attained this samādhi, they travel to various buddha-fields, make offerings to the Buddhas, and are born in the palaces of the devas.
There they proclaim the Triple Gem and manifest the body of a Buddha, surrounded by great assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.

Through the manifestation of their own minds, they deliver sentient beings and analytically expound upon the non-existence of external natures, causing all to remain far removed from extremes such as existence and non-existence.

"Beholds. (The phrase "obtains a hundred" [is placed below] to indicate the multitude of samādhis attained by Bodhisattvas who have well understood mind, consciousness, and so forth. "Obtains three" [is placed below] to clarify that this Bodhisattva, having already attained right concentration, travels through lands to make offerings to Buddhas. As for "born in celestial palaces," it refers to those born in the heavenly mansions.)

"Showing this" refers to the places where these bodhisattvas are born. "Proclaiming the Three Jewels" clarifies their intent to praise [the Buddhas] without forgetfulness. "Manifesting" and below clarify their manifestation of forms to preach the Dharma, while the three vehicles surround them to listen.

"By means of self" and below clarify that they teach and transform sentient beings through the Dharma of Mind-Only. "Discriminating" and below clarify that external natures are not real, leading [beings] to leave behind all faults). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

The world is the measure of the mind; the Son of the Buddha observes it. Regarding the body of various types, he is free from conditioned activity, having attained power and supernormal faculties, and is accomplished in mastery.

(The phrase "the world is the measure of the mind" is a reversal of word order; that is, the mind, intellect, and consciousness constitute the world as the measure of the mind. The Son of the Buddha observes the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and thoroughly understands their falsity.

As for "the body of various types," the meaning of the verse can be understood accordingly. "Free from conditioned activity" means that this Bodhisattva has attained power, supernormal faculties, and mastery, which are accomplished through the wondrous power of non-action, because he is free from conditioned activity).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain for us the emptiness of all dharmas, their non-arising, their non-duality, and their freedom from the characteristics of self-nature. (Mahāmati, having heard that all dharmas are empty, unarisen, and so forth, was concerned that practitioners might [misunderstand]...)

Because they again give rise to conceptual attachment toward such states as emptiness and non-arising, [the text] repeats [the inquiry] in order to shatter the attachments of sentient beings. All dharmas are governed by the three subsequent phrases—namely, that all dharmas are empty, all dharmas are unarisen, all dharmas are non-dual, and all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature.

Having awakened to these characteristics of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of intrinsic nature, we and the other bodhisattvas shall abandon the false imaginings of existence and non-existence, and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Bodhi. (This is Mahāmati’s own statement regarding the benefit of his inquiry). At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:

Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well. I shall now explain it to you in detail. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “As for ‘emptiness of emptiness’ (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), it refers to the locus of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

[Note: In the Wei and Tang translations, one instance of the character ‘empty’ is omitted; here, ‘emptiness of emptiness’ conveys the sense of both the subject that empties and the object that is emptied. Regarding ‘the locus of the imagined nature,’ it means that the imagined nature is without reality.”
The intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty (emptiness is the locus of intrinsic nature).

Mahāmati, for those who cling to the imagined nature, one speaks of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of the characteristics of intrinsic nature (this means that because the ignorant cling to false imaginings, one says that all dharmas are empty, unarisen, and so forth; if false imagining did not arise, then terms such as "empty" and "unarisen" would both be redundant;

therefore, the preceding text states: "Emptiness of emptiness is the locus of false imagining"). Mahāmati, there is a brief explanation of seven kinds of emptiness: namely, the emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of things (*svabhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*)...

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*): the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression (*sarvadharma-nirabhilāpya-śūnyatā*), the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom (*paramārtha-āryajñāna-mahāśūnyatā*), and mutual emptiness (*itaretara-śūnyatā*).

(These seven kinds of emptiness present both the subtle and the coarse, as well as the false and the correct, in order to clarify the characteristics of the breadth and narrowness of what is realized. This is the general heading; below follows the specific explanation. What is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?

It refers to the fact that all natures are empty of both self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because one observes them as a successive accumulation [of parts] and finds that they lack an inherent nature when analyzed.

Self-characteristics and common characteristics do not arise, because there is no intrinsic nature in their arising from self, other, or both. Characteristics do not abide; therefore, it is said that all natures and characteristics are empty.

This is called the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). (The phrase "First, below" indicates the essence of the emptiness of characteristics. The passage "Observing the unfolding, below" explains the cause for establishing the emptiness of characteristics.

It means that all characteristics, when observed in terms of their causes, are produced through a succession of conditions and are accumulations of marks. They arise through the convergence of conditions and perish when conditions disperse; hence they are called empty. When various characteristics are analyzed, they are fundamentally without intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, self-characteristics and common characteristics do not arise. Self, other, and...)

"Nature and non-nature" refers to the refutation of the four types of nature: (1) "Self" refers to the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*); (2) "Other" refers to that which arises from other causes such as a supreme being (*īśvara*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), or a creator (*kartṛ*), which constitutes the nature of other-dependence (*parabhāva*); (3) "Both" refers to the common nature of both self and other; and (4) "No cause" is mentioned briefly.

Because one observes that all characteristics are without characteristic, it is said that "all characteristics are empty. What is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of things (*bhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

It means that the intrinsic nature of things does not arise from itself; this is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Therefore, it is said to be the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of things. ("The nature of things" refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.)
This refers to all phenomena (*dharma*), each of which is unarisen by its own intrinsic nature; being unarisen, they are empty. What is the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)?

It means that the aggregates (*skandha*) are devoid of "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*). They are produced through causes, the results of past actions, and the application of skillful means; this is called the emptiness of formations. (In the Wei and Tang translations, "aggregates" is rendered as *zhuyin* [all aggregates]. Regarding "emptiness of formations": "formations" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

By citing the emptiness of one aggregate, it follows that all aggregates are likewise so. This is because they are devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self. Furthermore, these aggregates are formed by causes and conditions, are the results of karma performed in the past, and are produced through the conjunction of skillful means. Since they lack an inherent nature apart from these conditions, they are empty.)

Mahāmati, this very emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*), which arises through successive dependent origination and is devoid of intrinsic nature, is called the emptiness of non-formations (*asaṃskāra-śūnyatā*).

(The Collected Commentaries state: "Previously, the absence of the nature of 'I' and 'mine' was defined as the emptiness of formations; here, because the nature of the emptiness of formations is itself without nature, it is defined as the emptiness of non-formations.

What is the emptiness of all dharmas being beyond verbal expression? It means that because the self-nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is inexpressible, all dharmas are beyond verbal expression. This is called...

All phenomena are empty of being beyond verbal expression. (That all phenomena are beyond verbal expression means that all phenomena arise from false conceptualization; because they arise from false conceptualization, their intrinsic nature is empty.

Because their intrinsic nature is empty, there is no verbal expression that can express them; therefore, they are called "all phenomena empty of being beyond verbal expression. What is the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom regarding all phenomena?
This refers to the attainment of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), wherein all views and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are seen to be empty.

This is called the "Great Emptiness of the Noble Wisdom of the Ultimate Meaning of All Dharmas" (this emptiness is termed "great" because, among the seven types of emptiness, it is the essence, the correct, the extensive, and the most supreme and subtle). What is mutual emptiness (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)?

This means that when something is absent from a certain place, that place is empty of that thing; this is called "emptiness of this in that" (itaretara-śūnyatā). (Regarding "when something is absent from a certain place": for example, when the "that" belonging to A is absent from the "that" belonging to B, it is the "that" of B.)

Because that [place] lacks [those things], it is said that "that is empty of those. The *Jizhu* (Comprehensive Commentary) states: "In that there is no this; in this there is no that; as they are mutually and successively empty. O Mahāmati, it is like the house of Mṛgāramātṛ:
although it lacks elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth, it is not devoid of the community of bhikṣus. Thus one speaks of its being empty [of those animals].

It is not that the nature of the house itself is empty, nor is it that the nature of the bhikṣus themselves is empty. It is not that elephants and horses do not exist elsewhere. (By citing the house of Mṛgāramātṛ, he provides an illustration to clarify that.)

"That is empty. This refers to the house of Migāramātā; because it lacks elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, it is said to be "empty of that. "That" points to the oxen, sheep, and so forth. It is not that there are no bhikṣus in the house, nor is it that the nature of the house is empty, nor is it that the nature of the bhikṣus is empty.

Rather, it is said to be "empty of that" simply because elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep are uniquely absent from within the house. This does not mean that elephants and horses are absent elsewhere. However, since there are no bhikṣus in other places, those places are also called "empty of that"; thus, it is termed "emptiness of this and that" (itaretara-śūnyatā). The New Commentary states:

Mṛgāra is a personal name. His mother was the female lay follower (upāsikā) Viśākhā, who deeply revered the Triple Gem. She constructed a vihāra and settled bhikṣus within it. In that place, she did not keep elephants, horses, or the like; because elephants and horses were absent, it was said to be "empty. Yet the dwelling and the bhikṣus were not called empty.

Even if elephants and horses were present elsewhere, one would still not say that those elephants and horses were empty. This is what is meant by the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena: that in a given thing, that which does not exist therein is absent from it.

This is called "emptiness of this and that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). (That [A] is absent in that [B], as explained in the commentary on the first passage). This is called the seven kinds of emptiness (the summary may be understood accordingly). As for the emptiness of this and that, it is the coarsest form of emptiness;
you should distance yourself from it. (The emptiness of this and that is erroneous, coarse, and narrow; it is the conceptualization of non-Buddhists, and therefore should be abandoned).

Mahāmati, [things] do not arise from themselves, yet they are not non-arising—except when abiding in samādhi. This is called "non-arising. Being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is precisely this.

Non-arising. Freedom from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The manifestation of momentary continuity, flux, and diversity. All natures are devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, all natures are devoid of intrinsic nature.

(The section beginning with "not" does not explain non-arising. It means that intrinsic nature does not arise; it is not merely non-arising, for this prevents falling into the nihilism of non-existence. Only those dwelling in the concentration on emptiness perceive all things as empty;

therefore, excluding those dwelling in the concentration on emptiness, it is said that they are not non-arising. The section beginning with "freedom from" explains freedom from intrinsic nature. The meaning of the text is clear). What is meant by "non-..."?

2. This refers to all phenomena being like "shade" and "heat," like "long" and "short," or like "black" and "white. (The Tang translation states: "What is meant by the absence of dual characteristics? Mahāmati, it is like light and shadow, like long and short, like black and white;

these are all established in mutual dependence. Taken alone, they do not exist. [Regarding 'shade' and 'heat': 'Shade' is spoken of in contrast to 'heat,' thus 'shade' carries the meaning of 'cool. Just as the Tang translation uses 'light' in contrast to 'shadow,' so 'shadow' carries the meaning of 'darkness.

This is based on two phenomena to demonstrate the absence of duality. They constitute a duality through mutual dependence, for taken alone, they are not established. As it is said: because of cool there is heat; because of short there is long; because of black there is white. If one were separated from heat, there would be no cool; if separated from long, there would be no short; if separated from black, there would be no..."

[The opponent] says: Both are false; since they are established only through mutual dependence, there are no two. The *Jizhu* (Commentary on the Collected Teachings) uses the substance of the sun as an analogy for the lack of duality between the sun and its shadows or heat, stating that although shadows and so forth differ, the substance of the sun remains unchanged. However, the current text establishes six types [of non-duality] to discuss their lack of duality.
How can you conflate this with the "substance of the sun"? This is not the intent of the sutra. Furthermore, it contradicts the Tang translation. Mahāmati, all dharmas are non-dual.

It is not that within nirvāṇa there is saṃsāra, nor that within saṃsāra there is nirvāṇa. (The word "that" (*bi*) here has the sense of "separate," meaning: it is not that outside of nirvāṇa there is a separate saṃsāra, nor that within saṃsāra...)

Externally, there is a separate nirvana. Since the two natures of nirvana and saṃsāra cannot be apprehended, it is said that they are non-dual. As for their distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*), because they exist as having a nature, this is called non-duality.
Just as with nirvana and saṃsāra, all dharmas are likewise so. (Regarding "because they exist as having a nature": this explains the delusion of the distinct characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvana.

It means that while the two aspects of nirvana and saṃsāra appear distinct, because one can know that these two aspects lack a nature, they are termed non-dual. As for "just as with nirvana," this uses the two aspects as an analogy to show that all dharmas are likewise non-dual. This concludes the section on emptiness and non-arising asked by Mahāmati previously.)

"Non-duality, being free from self-nature (*svabhāva*), and so forth—these are merely the locus where deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) arises. Therefore, the Buddha first replied: 'Emptiness and the like are precisely the locus of the self-nature of deluded conceptualization. If one is free from emptiness and the like, then deluded conceptualization naturally ceases.

For this reason, one should practice and study the characteristics of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and freedom from self-nature. (This summarizes the four meanings and exhorts all practitioners.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:"

I constantly teach the Dharma of emptiness, which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence. Birth and death are like illusions and dreams, yet karma remains indestructible (as the *Zongjing* says:
"Because its nature is empty, the path of karma is not destroyed; cause and effect remain distinct and clear"). This is likewise true for space and nirvāṇa—the cessation of these two is also thus.

Fools engage in false conceptualization; the noble ones are free from existence and non-existence. (Regarding the three unconditioned phenomena, each is explained in relation to a corresponding conditioned phenomenon:

emptiness is contrasted with existence, cessation with birth, and nirvana with saṃsāra. In all cases, two phenomena are used in contrast to reveal their non-duality; thus it is said that "emptiness and nirvana likewise extinguish duality. This is the constructed false conceptualization of fools; the noble ones, however, realize them to be like illusions.)
Therefore, by departing from existence and non-existence, one cuts off all faults.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:

"Mahāmati, emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the departure from the characteristics of self-nature—these universally enter into all the sūtras of the Buddhas. Whatever sūtras there may be, they all expound these."

This meaning [is as follows]: *Sūtra* (translated as "Scripture of Accordance" (*kī-āgama*)—the new explanation states that it refers to meanings such as emptiness, which universally enter all scriptures, such that there is not a single dharma that does not contain this principle).

All *sūtras* are taught by way of differentiation in accordance with the inclinations and desires of sentient beings to reveal their meanings; however, they do not truly exist within the words themselves.
It is like the mirage of a thirsty deer, which deceives a herd of deer; the deer, regarding those signs, falsely clings to them as being water.

There is no water there. (*Āśā* means desire or longing; that is to say, all that is taught arises according to the desires and inclinations of sentient beings. For their sake, one analytically reveals meanings such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in order to cause them to abandon their attachments.

However, meanings such as emptiness do not truly exist within the words themselves. As in the example of the deer below, the analogy is used to clarify the Dharma: it is like a herd of deer, driven by thirst, who see a mirage and perceive it as water. That mirage is not actually water.

This serves as an illustration for sentient beings who cling to words as being the meaning of emptiness and so forth; yet those words are not in reality emptiness itself. This chapter warns against grasping the meaning while forgetting the words, so that one may first attain access to noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). Thus it is in all these *sūtras*.)* Thus, in all these *sūtras*...
The various dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of inspiring joy in the foolish;

they do not constitute the actual noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), which lies beyond verbal expression. Therefore, one should rely upon the meaning (*artha*) and not cling to the words. (To "inspire joy" means to teach according to the capacities of beings so that they may attain the joy of the Dharma and give rise to goodness.

Regarding the phrase "not the actual," etc.: verbal expressions are like a finger pointing at the moon; noble wisdom is like the moon being pointed out. Only by letting go of the finger does one recognize the substance of the moon; by clinging to the words, one cannot attain noble wisdom. The preceding [teachings] on emptiness, non-arising, and so forth, are precisely the intended meaning of noble wisdom.)
Therefore, the practitioner should rely on the meaning and not cling to the words.

*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* Annotated Commentary, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra during the Liu Song dynasty;
revised by the later scholar Śramaṇa Guangmo of Huxing under the Imperial Ming;
and verified by Yuan Huang of Xiali, Grand Officer of the Summer Ministry.
The First Chapter of the "Essence of the Buddha’s Words," Part Two.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has stated in the sūtras that the Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature;
it possesses the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings."
It is like a precious jewel of great value wrapped in a soiled garment;

the Tathāgata-garbha is likewise eternally abiding and unchanging, yet it is enveloped by the soiled garments of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, and defiled by the dust and toil of unreal conceptualization, greed, hatred, and delusion.

"This is what all Buddhas have proclaimed. (Mahāmati follows upon the preceding statement that all sūtras should teach emptiness, non-duality, and the absence of self-nature, etc., and thus raises his objection.

As in the passage below, he cites a simile to clarify that the *tathāgatagarbha* within the bodies of sentient beings is eternally abiding. The application of this principle to the Dharma can be understood accordingly. This is the citation; below follows the formal objection.

"How is it, World-Honored One, that you speak of a *tathāgatagarbha* in the same way as the non-Buddhists speak of a 'self' (*ātman*)? World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of an eternal agent who is free from..."

"World-Honored One, regarding the *guṇas*, they are all-pervasive and imperishable; thus, he asserts that there is a self (*ātman*). (The *Fuxing* [Sub-commentary] translates *guṇa* as 'relying on the truths,' while the new commentary states: This objection is as follows:

if the Tathāgata were to speak of the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it would contradict the aforementioned principle that 'all sūtras should teach emptiness,' and would become identical to the non-Buddhists' assertion of a divine self. Now, that conception of a self has three aspects: first, its essence is eternal and it is called the 'agent';

second, although it exists within the five aggregates, it is distinct from the *guṇas*; third, it traverses all realms of existence, yet is truly subject neither to birth nor extinction. How is it that the meaning of the 'garbha' now being taught does not coincide with the self of the non-Buddhists? The Buddha told him:
"Mahāmati, what I call the Tathāgatagarbha is not the same as the 'self' (ātman) propounded by the non-Buddhists.

Mahāmati, at times I speak of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), nirvāṇa, being free from intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing, primordial quiescence, and natural nirvāṇa.
Having spoken of the Tathāgatagarbha through such terms, the Tathāgata..."

The Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in order to sever the fear of fools regarding the phrase "non-self," has taught the gateway of the Tathāgatagarbha—a realm free from false conceptualization and devoid of [inherent] existence.
Mahāmati, future and present Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should not form attachments based on the view of a self.

(The passage beginning with "I say" indicates that the World-Honored One speaks according to the capacities of beings; his skillful means are not uniform, and he differs from the "self" taught by non-Buddhists. The passage beginning with "At times" clarifies how he responds to those capacities.)

The meaning of non-identity is as follows: Having revealed the *tathāgatagarbha* through such phrases as "sometimes it is said to be empty," up to "naturally in a state of nirvāṇa," the Tathāgata further fears that if foolish people hear of this emptiness, signlessness, and so forth, they will conclude that there is no self at all.

Furthermore, fear arises again. To sever this doubt, it is further taught that within the realm of non-existence, which is free from conceptual construction, there exists the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. This very non-existence serves as the gateway for entering the *garbha*-nature, preventing one from falling into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, practitioners must not, regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, harbor attachments based on the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*). It is like a potter who, from a single lump of clay, uses human effort, water, wood, a wheel, and rope as skillful means to produce various vessels.

In the same way, the Tathāgata likewise, from the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) which is free from all marks of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), employs various forms of wisdom and skillful means to sometimes speak of the *tathāgatagarbha* and sometimes [to speak of...]
There is no self. For these reasons, the Tathāgatagarbha is taught; it is not the same as the "self" (ātman) spoken of by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

This is called teaching the Tathāgatagarbha in order to attract and guide those non-Buddhists who cling to a self, so that they may abandon the false conceptualization of the view of self and enter the realm of the three gates of liberation.
(The passage beginning with "Just as" below is the analogy; "The Tathāgata" below is the application to the Dharma. "Tao-jia" [potter]—the sound is *yáo*—is the potter, which serves as the metaphor.)

The Tathāgata is like a lump of clay; the "store-nature" (*tathāgatagarbha*) is the metaphor for this. The human artisan, the wooden wheel, and so forth, are metaphors for the various wisdoms and skillful means (*upāya*). The making of various vessels is a metaphor for either speaking of the store-nature or speaking of names such as "non-self.

From "By this... below, the intention of differentiating [this] from non-Buddhists is concluded. From "This is called... below, the intention of the World-Honored One’s skillful means is concluded. Regarding the "three liberations": these are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Because these three can liberate the mind, intellect, and consciousness, they are metaphors for "gates," which signify exiting and entering.

Regarding the meaning: Yang Yanguo’s compilation states that the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says that when a Bodhisattva contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and realizes the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), they attain the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*). When they contemplate the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as being extinguished by their own nature, they attain the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*).

Entering into emptiness and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), yet acting solely for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they attain the liberation of wishlessness; hence it is called the "three liberations. The phrase "hopes to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" refers to the perspective of the Buddha:

it means the Buddha hopes that sentient beings will quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and thus he speaks of the various gates of the treasury of nature (*dhātu-gotra*). For this reason, the Tathāgata...
He makes offerings to the Perfectly Awakened One and speaks thus of the Tathāgata-garbha. Were it not so, he would be no different from the non-Buddhists.
Therefore, Mahāmati, in order to avoid the views of the non-Buddhists, one should rely upon the selflessness of the Tathāgata-garbha. (The passage beginning with "Therefore" follows here.)

This concludes the preceding intent, clarifying that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma in accordance with [the capacities of beings] is free from the fault of external views. Next, from the words "Therefore" onwards, the text exhorts all bodhisattvas to abandon external views and instead rely upon this storehouse nature of non-self.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The person (*pudgala*), the continuity (*saṃtāna*), the aggregates (*skandha*), conditions (*pratyaya*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), the supreme (*īśvara*), and the creator (*kartṛ*)—these are merely the deluded imaginings of the mind (*cittamātra-vikalpa*).

(Non-Buddhists calculate that nine things produce the world: first, time; second, space; third, atoms; fourth, emptiness; fifth, the great elements (*mahābhūta*); sixth, the self (*ātman*); seventh, the supreme spirit (*viśeṣa*); eighth, the Lord God (*īśvara*); and ninth, the Great Brahmā.

Now, regarding the first [point], "person" is a synonym for the "self," referring to the *ātman*. The "aggregates" are that which is produced, while the person, atoms, the supreme, the Lord, and so forth, are that which produces. "Creator" refers to the agent; it means that the person and others create the various phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.)
[The mind] abides in a continuous succession. This is to reveal the nine kinds of agents asserted by non-Buddhists; [it is merely] the mental construction of the deluded mind).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, observing future sentient beings, again requested of the World-Honored One:
"I only pray that you will explain the uninterrupted practice, such as the great skillful means of those who practice, like the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas. (Mahāmati)

Previously, the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* was raised as an objection; now that the World-Honored One has resolved those doubts, it is known that the nature of the *garbha* is the essence realized through practice. Therefore, he now asks again about the sequence of practice so that future students may find its gateway. Regarding the phrase "uninterrupted practice" (*anantara-pratipatti*):

it means that while practices have degrees of depth, the Way is fundamentally equal, just as the hundred rivers flow into the sea and share the same salty taste; hence it is called "uninterrupted. Furthermore, this shares the same meaning as the "non-interruption of the five natures" (*pañca-gotra-anantara*) mentioned in the preceding sutra. As for the passage beginning with "Just as all... [and so forth].

Although Mahāmati’s question encompasses both the sudden and gradual approaches, its primary intent lies specifically in the Mahāyāna; thus, he employs the skillful means (*upāya*) of the bodhisattvas as his pretext. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain the great skillful means of the practitioner. What are these four? They are: (1) skillfully discerning that which is manifested by one's own mind;

(2) contemplating that external natures have no intrinsic reality; (3) being free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing; and (4) attaining the excellence of the noble wisdom of self-realization."
Joy. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of four dharmas, by which one attains the great skillful means of the practitioner.

(The section beginning with "accomplishment" below indicates the dharmas; the section beginning with "how" below provides the names; the subsequent text explains their meaning). How does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully discern what is manifested by one's own mind?
It means to contemplate in this way that the triple world is merely the extent of the mind, free from "I" and "mine," unmoving, devoid of coming and going, and non-existent.

Initially, one is perfumed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of falsehood and delusion, bound by the various forms and activities of the three realms, and established with a body and possessions. Thus, through the entry of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), these things appear.

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of what is manifested from one's own mind. [The phrase] "How so? [below] interrogates the name; [the passage] beginning with "As follows" (謂如下) is the formal explanation of the meaning.

Regarding the contemplation that the three realms are mind-only: this means there are no phenomena external to the mind; they are the manifestations of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Because all is consciousness-only, regarding all phenomena, one is detached from "I" and "mine," there is no creator, and one is free from the characteristics of coming and going.

Because they have been permeated by beginningless falsehood, there arise various forms and appearances, bound by various mental activities. The "body" refers to the sense-faculties; "wealth" refers to the objects for sustaining life. Whether as the environment or as the internal faculties, all are manifestations of deluded thought.
This is called the "lower fetter. What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful contemplation of the non-existence of external natures?
It refers to all natures such as mirages, dreams, and so forth, which have their cause in the habitual tendencies of beginningless, false conceptualization.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the intrinsic nature of all natures in this way; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful contemplation of the non-existence of external [natures].

"Nature and non-nature. (The phrase "How so? below interrogates the name. The passage beginning with "That which is like a mirage... is the formal explanation of the meaning. Regarding "external nature and non-nature": "external nature" refers to phenomena existing apart from consciousness. Since its nature is not real, it is called "non-nature," as in the case of mirages, illusions, dreams, and the like, because they do not truly exist.

They arise from the causal conditions of habitual tendencies of beginningless false conceptualization. Because Bodhisattvas can observe these causes, they know that external nature is non-nature. This concludes the section on the name).
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully abandon views of arising, abiding, and ceasing? It means that all natures are like illusions and dreams, [arising] from self, other, or both.

The nature of things is unborn. By entering into the limits of one's own mind, one sees that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent; one sees that consciousness is unborn and that conditions do not accumulate.
One sees that they arise through the conditions of false discrimination, and thus finds all phenomena—whether within or without the three realms—to be unattainable.

Seeing that [phenomena] are devoid of intrinsic nature, all views of arising are completely extinguished. Knowing that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is like an illusion and so forth, one attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, one is free from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing;

this is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who skillfully discriminates and is free from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. (The phrase "How is it? below interrogates the name; the phrase "It is as follows" below correctly explains the meaning. It means that because one skillfully contemplates that the nature of all things—whether existent or non-existent—is like an illusion, a dream, and so forth... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "self-". The translation above reflects the full available context.]

The nature of self, the nature of other, and the nature of both are not produced. Because all natures are unproduced, one enters the realm of one’s own mind according to what is realized—namely, that the triple world is mind-only (*cittamātra*).

"Limit" (*pramāṇa*) has the meaning of "objective sphere. Because one sees that external natures are non-existent, internal consciousness does not arise. Because internal consciousness does not arise, external conditions do not aggregate. Because one sees that they are produced through the conditions of false discrimination (*vikalpa*), when seeking all phenomena within and without the triple world, none are to be found.

"Seeing that which is devoid of intrinsic nature" means that the seeing which performs the observation is itself also devoid of intrinsic nature. "The production of views is entirely extinguished" means that both the external production of conditions and the internal capacity for seeing are extinguished. Because one knows that all natures are like illusions, one accordingly attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Having attained this patience, [one realizes the truth].

Thus, one is able to remain far removed from all views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. This is called "the lower" (concluding the section). What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s attainment of the sublime bliss of the noble self-realized wisdom?

It refers to attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), dwelling in the eighth Bodhisattva stage, and attaining liberation from mind, thought, mentation, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two forms of selflessness, thereby obtaining the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).

(The phrase "What is... poses the question regarding the name; the phrase "It refers to attaining... provides the formal explanation of the meaning. Attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena...)

Regarding the eighth stage, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Eighth Stage, states: "The Bodhisattva, having skillfully cultivated the wisdom of skillful means throughout the seventh stage, enters into all phenomena as being fundamentally unborn, unarisen, signless, unformed, indestructible, inexhaustible, non-evolving, and having non-nature as their nature.

Free from all conceptualizations of mind, thought, and consciousness, and devoid of any grasping or attachment, they are like space. Entering into all phenomena as having the nature of space—this is called attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). As for 'patience' (*kṣānti'), it means..."

To silently realize non-arising and to accept it within the mind—such that one desires to cease [effort] but is unable to do so—is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). When a bodhisattva accomplishes this patience, they immediately enter the eighth stage, the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*); this is the same as in the present sutra. Regarding the attainment of the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*):

The *Avataṃsaka* further states: "This bodhisattva, according to the various differences in the faith, understanding, and mental dispositions of sentient beings, manifests his body within the assemblies of those buddha-fields; he even manifests in the form of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha as may be required."

To those who are to be liberated by the body of a Bodhisattva or the body of a Tathāgata, he manifests them all; this is called the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body). It is so called because it arises according to the mind’s intention, being without obstruction.

“World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions does the *manomaya-kāya* arise? The Buddha told Mahāmati: “The *manomaya-kāya* is like the movement of the mind: it is swift and unobstructed; therefore, it is called ‘mind-made.
Just as the mind moves without obstruction through stone walls, it reaches immeasurable *yojanas* in distant lands.”
Recalling what was previously seen without forgetting, the flow of one’s own mind continues uninterrupted, and there arises within the body a state free from obstruction.

Mahāmati, such a mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) arises simultaneously; the mind-made body of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva—adorned with the power of the illusion-like samādhi, sovereign supernormal faculties (abhijñā), and wondrous marks—is born all at once as a body of the noble lineage, just like [the reflection in] a mirror.
It arises according to one’s will, without obstruction, and in accordance with the spheres of one’s original vows as they are recalled.

For the sake of maturing sentient beings, one attains the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization. (Mahāmati asks this question because, although he has heard the name "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), he does not yet understand its meaning.

The Buddha’s reply begins with a brief explanation by means of a simile, followed by a detailed explanation of that simile’s significance. Finally, Mahāmati applies the teaching to the dharma to clarify how the three types of mind-made bodies are simultaneously manifested. As for the three types of bodies: first, the mind-made body of the meditative absorption in the bliss of *samādhi*; second, the [body] that realizes the Dharma...)

The *svābhāvika-nirmāṇakāya* (nature-born mind-made body) and the three types of *sahaja-anabhisamskāra-nirmāṇakāya* (spontaneously born, effortless mind-made bodies)—although these are treated briefly in the present text, their meanings must necessarily be included together. They can be understood by correlating the text as follows: first, the previous metaphors are reiterated and combined for clarification; then, from "obtaining the self-" [onward], the conclusion is reached.
In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and dwells in the eighth bodhisattva stage.
He completely abandons the body of the mind, intellect, and consciousness, as well as the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the two forms of selflessness;

he further attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and realizes the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-awakening. (The phrase "in this way" below clarifies the station of the mind-made body. The phrase "completely abandons" below demonstrates the departure from the delusions of conditioned practice. The phrase "further attains" below clarifies the realization of the truth of non-action. He attains...

From here below, the names of the four dharmas are again summarized. These four dharmas proceed in a sequence of ever-deeper penetration, serving as the great skillful means for practitioners. First, it concerns internal contemplation; therefore, it says, "discriminating one's own mind. Second, it concerns external contemplation; therefore, it says, "contemplating that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent.

Third, it concerns the subject and object; therefore, it says, "seeing external natures and seeing their non-arising. Fourth, it concerns effortlessness, by which the three preceding methods are stilled; therefore, it says, "attaining the patience of non-arising," which is to be free from mind, thought, and consciousness.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishing the four dharmas and attaining the great skillful means of the practitioner. It should be understood in this way.
Study. (A summary of the four dharmas, exhorting those who should study. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the World-Honored One:
"I pray only that you will explain the characteristics of the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) of all dharmas.

By awakening to the characteristics of these causal conditions, I and the other Bodhisattvas shall be free from the false views of existence and non-existence regarding all natures, and shall be free from the views of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) concerning gradual or simultaneous arising. (The term *pratyaya-hetu* [causal condition] appears in both the Wei and Tang translations.)

[He] forms the causal conditions. ○ Mahāmati’s intention in questioning arises from the previously mentioned internal and external natures. These various internal and external natures are phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-dharma*). Therefore, he now asks: what constitutes the cause, and what constitutes the condition? This is because he seeks to realize the characteristics of conditions and causes.
One is able to leave behind all false views regarding the existence or non-existence of all natures. Because one leaves behind false views, there is neither gradual nor simultaneous arising.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All phenomena have two kinds of causal conditions: namely, external and internal. As for external conditions, they refer to such instrumental causes as a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, water, wood, and human effort;

from these various instrumental conditions, a jar arises. It is like a clay jar, or threads and wool [making cloth], or grass mats, or seeds and sprouts, or curd and butter—these are all instrumental conditions."

Birth is also like this; this is called external conditions (*bāhya-pratyaya*). [The phrase] "before and after" refers to successive arising. (All that follows below first indicates the number of conditions; the section beginning with "external" below next lists the internal and external.)

Regarding "external conditions" below: this is a separate explanation of the meaning of external conditions. "External" refers to external assistance to the cause. The lump of clay, the wheel, and so forth are cited as examples to clarify that all phenomena arise through the conditions of skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding "arising through successive transformation": "previously,"...

This refers to the preliminary conditions (*pūrvapratyaya*). For example, in the making of a vessel such as a jar, one first prepares the wheel, the cord, and so forth; this is the "prior" [condition]. The subsequent [conditions] refer to the fuel, the heat, the application of force, and so on;

because each preceding stage successively gives rise to each succeeding stage, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The lump of clay is the cause, while water, the staff, and so forth are the conditions, resulting in the jar as the effect. Just as it is with the cause and effect of the clay jar, the same principle applies to the other four cases—thread, wool, seed, and curd—as well. Thread, grass, seeds, and curd serve as the causes, while woven cloth, mats, sprouts, and butter serve as the effects. The meaning of the conditions is to be understood accordingly.

This is called the phenomenon of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein cause must necessarily precede effect, arising through successive stages. That which directly produces is the cause; that which indirectly assists is the condition. What are the internal conditions? They are as follows:

Dharmas such as ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and karma receive the name "conditions" (*pratyaya*). The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) that arise from them receive the name "that which is arisen from conditions.

These are without distinction, yet they are falsely conceptualized by the ignorant; this is called the "internal conditioned dharma" (this is a specific explanation of the meaning of internal conditions).

Regarding "ignorance, craving, and karma": these cite two of the twelve links of dependent origination. "Ignorance" refers to the delusion of afflictions since beginningless time. A single moment of non-awakening causes clarity to turn into turbidity and the True to become the false, shrouding the original nature so that there is no wondrous enlightened clarity; therefore it is so called.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of the past. "Craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) refers to the greed for various excellent and wonderful requisites, as well as for objects such as sexual desire; this is called craving and is the cause of the present. By briefly citing the causes of the past and present, the future is implied by extension;

thus, one should know that the twelve links of dependent origination are termed "internal dependent phenomena. Since these are the causes of the past and present, why are they called "conditions" (*pratyaya*) in this text? It is because the twelve links function as causes to one another and also function as conditions to one another; therefore, they receive the name "conditions."

"Those things arisen with the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana) as conditions" refers to all dharmas such as the aggregates, because they all arise in dependence upon the twelve [links]. Furthermore, within the twelve links of dependent origination, ignorance (avidyā) and craving (tṛṣṇā) are the root of birth; for this reason, these two are mentioned together to reveal the essential nature of dependent origination.

"That which is without distinction" means that both ignorance, craving, and so forth, as well as those things arisen from conditions, are both devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), and thus there is no distinction between them. As for "distinction," it is merely a conceptual construction of the deluded and ignorant.

This concludes the explanation of conditions (*pratyaya*); the following text explains causes (*hetu*). "Mahāmati, those causes are of six kinds: namely, the cause of what is to be (bhaviṣyaddhetu), the cause of continuity (saṃtānahetu), and the cause of characteristics (lakṣaṇahetu)."

The producing cause (*kāraka-hetu*), the manifesting cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*), and the dependent cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) (these are the headings; the following explains their meanings). Regarding the "cause of what is to be" (*bhaviṣyat-hetu*): once the producing cause has functioned, internal and external phenomena arise.

(The "cause of what is to be" refers to a present producing cause that will bring about a result in the future; because it is non-existent now but is to exist later, it is called the "cause of what is to be"). Regarding the "causal continuity" (*saṃtati-hetu*): once the object-condition (*ālambana*) has been grasped...

Internal and external phenomena arise from the seeds of the aggregates and so forth. Regarding the cause of continuity (*saṃtati-hetu*): because consciousness takes internal and external aggregates as its object, the seeds and their manifestations proceed without interruption;

this is called the cause of continuity. "Internal" refers to mental phenomena (*nāma-dharma*), and "external" refers to material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). Regarding the cause of manifestation (*lakṣaṇa-hetu*): it produces uninterrupted manifestation, which is continuous arising. "Manifestation" refers to the state of being uninterrupted. "Uninterrupted" means that once the preceding moment has ceased, [the subsequent moment arises].

The subsequent thought arises in succession; because there is no interval between the preceding and the succeeding, it is termed the "characteristic of immediacy" (*ānantarya-lakṣaṇa*). These two aforementioned causes belong to the "condition as immediate antecedent" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) among the four conditions. Because the succession is uninterrupted, it constitutes continuity.

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, that which is successive is called the "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The treatise states: "That is to say, the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (caitta), the preceding group [of moments] in relation to the subsequent, open up and guide their own respective classes without interval;

this is termed 'equal and immediate'. The commentary on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses states: "As for 'equal and immediate,' it refers to the preceding moment of each consciousness having already ceased, thereby opening up a space to induce the subsequent moment to arise. That there is no gap in between is its characteristic. The "immediacy" in the present text precisely refers to this meaning. As for "acting as a cause," it acts as a predominant...

Regarding the phrase "the matter above" (*śreṣṭha-vastu*): it is like a *cakravartin* (wheel-turning king). "Action" (*kāra*) refers to functional activity. When the various consciousnesses undergo transformation and possess sovereign power (*adhipati-bala*), such that they cause all phenomena to arise without obstruction, this is called the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

This belongs to the category of the four conditions (*pratyaya*) as the "sovereign condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The sovereign condition refers to a phenomenon that possesses superior power and function, which is able to manifest the specific conditions for other phenomena; this is named the sovereign condition. The present term "matter" (*vastu*) refers to what that text calls "matters" such as arising, abiding, accomplishing, and attaining.

The "wheel-turning king" serves as the analogy. A wheel-turning king is the most preeminent among humans and possesses sovereign power and function; likewise, this condition possesses superior power and function among the four conditions. Thus, the dharma and the analogy correspond.

[This is] merely an illustration). Regarding "manifesting the cause": once the phenomena of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) have arisen, the characteristics of the agent and the acted-upon appear, just as a lamp illuminates forms and so forth.

"Manifesting" (*pradarśana*) refers to the appearance of the characteristics of the subject and object; because they are visible to the eye and possess resistance (*sapratigha*), they are called "manifest. "Phenomena of false conceptualization" means that due to false conceptualization, the produced phenomena arise. Once these phenomena have arisen, the characteristics of the agent and the acted-upon appear.

The agent is like a lamp; the acted-upon is like form. The agent consists of the various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); the acted-upon consists of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), such as form. The mind can illuminate its objects just as a lamp illuminates form. Because the agent manifests the acted-upon, it is said to "produce the acted-upon."

This belongs to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) among the four conditions. The details of these four conditions are as explained in that treatise. According to both the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, internal form (*rūpa*) alone serves as the object-condition; external substance is not taken [as such].

Therefore, regarding the observation of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is said: "Internal form appears as if external; it serves as the object-condition for consciousness. It is accepted that its aspect (*nimitta*) resides within consciousness, and because it is capable of producing consciousness. The present statement, "acting as the agent and the acted upon," precisely intends to refer to internal form.

However, the scriptural text is too concise, making it difficult for people to understand clearly (as detailed in that treatise). Regarding the "conditioned cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*): it acts at the time of cessation; when the continuity is severed, the nature of non-delusive conceptualization arises. (Conditioned cause.)

The Wei translation renders this as the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). This contingent cause should be linked with the "manifesting cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*), and both belong to the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Why? Because when the characteristic of the produced (*kārya-lakṣaṇa*) manifests, the contingent cause is subsumed therein.

As it is said: "At the time of ceasing, it again acts; at the time of acting, it again ceases. How could this not be contingent? Although the texts of these three translations of the present sutra differ slightly regarding these six causes, their meaning is largely the same. Yet, various commentaries do not explain them in detail; even if they were explained, there would be no basis for verification. Following what, then, should scholars proceed? Therefore, I have examined [the matter] according to my own judgment.

Commentary and Supplement: May those who come seek this out with care. The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "It is said that when all dharmas cease, they arise again; when they arise, they cease again. The continuity of the nature of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is severed, and the nature of non-delusion arises once more. Because they depend upon one another in succession, it is called 'dependent cause' (*pratītya-hetu*).

"Mahāmati, those deluded commoners (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) regarding the marks of their own deluded conceptualization do not perceive that these arise gradually, nor do they perceive that they arise simultaneously.

(The Wei translation says: "Mahāmati, such dharmas are the false discriminations of the commoners' own minds. Mahāmati, these dharmas do not arise in sequence, nor do they arise at once. [This clarifies that the aforementioned characteristics of causes and conditions are merely the products of the deluded conceptualizations of commoners; in reality, they do not exist.]

As for substantial entities, whether they arise successively or simultaneously, they cannot be found upon investigation; therefore, in all cases, it is said "no. Why is this so? If they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no distinction between the agent and the action, and thus the characteristic of a cause could not be established.
If they were to arise successively, the characteristic of a self (ātman) could not be established. Successive arising is non-arising; it is like having no father when a son has not been born.

(The term *xiang-wo* [characteristic-self] is translated as *shen-xiang* [body-characteristic] in the Wei version and *ti-xiang* [substantial-characteristic] in the Tang version; according to this, it refers to the substance of the causal characteristic.)

"○ This 'simultaneous arising of the subtle and the luminous' is also a duality; it is not so. If, as stated below, they were to arise simultaneously, then subject and object would not be distinct and there would be nothing to differentiate. In that case, the characteristic of the cause could not be established, and thus it would not be simultaneous arising.

If, as stated below, they were to arise gradually, then since the self-substance of the causal characteristic could not be attained, how could there be gradual arising? Therefore, it is said that 'gradual arising does not arise. Furthermore, he cites an analogy to clarify this: the causal characteristic is the cause, and gradual arising is the fruit. If the fruit does not arise, the cause has no name by which to be designated (just as if a son were not born, from what source would the name 'father' emerge?).
Mahāmati, the expedient means of the continuity of gradual arising is not so; it is merely a product of false discrimination. It arises from clinging to objects."

Because [the cause] successively acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and so forth for that which is produced. (The Tang translation states: "Various speculative thinkers say: 'By means of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and so forth...')"

The produced and the producer are mutually dependent. The foolish, through their deluded calculations regarding the means of continuity, imagine that there is a gradual arising; the Buddha refutes this, saying it is not so, for it is merely a product of false discrimination. (This refers to the passage below on "clinging to causes," which further clarifies the cause of gradual arising:

namely, that all foolish people, due to the four conditions, give rise to what is produced. Mahāmati, whether there is gradual arising or no arising, it is because of clinging to the characteristics of the falsely discriminated self-nature.

(The Tang translation states: "The principle of successive arising cannot be established, for all are merely attachments to appearances based on deluded sentiments. Regarding 'not arising successively,' this means knowing that [phenomena] exist only through false conceptualization and clinging; because they are known as such, they do not arise.")

Gradually and simultaneously, they do not arise, because they are the manifestation of one’s own mind as experience. Regarding self-characteristics and common characteristics, external natures are non-natures. (The Tang translation says:

"Gradually and suddenly, both are entirely non-arising, for they are merely the body, requisites, and so forth manifested by one's own mind. [Regarding 'gradually and simultaneously non-arising': it means that one realizes the body and the requisites of life are manifestations of one's own mind;

because of this realization, both are non-arising. 'Experience' refers to the requisites of life. When one realizes they are manifestations of one's own mind, then self-characteristics, common characteristics, and natures are themselves non-natures. Mahāmati, gradually and simultaneously, they do not arise, except..."

The appearance of marks arises from the deluded conceptualization that fails to realize that [all things] are manifestations of one's own mind. (Regarding the statement that they do not arise either gradually or simultaneously: this is because one has realized the falsity of these two modes of arising;

it is only when one does not exclude the failure to realize that they are manifestations of one's own mind that one perceives the arising of marks. Therefore, regarding the marks of causes, conditions, activities, and skillful means, one should abandon the views of gradual and simultaneous [arising].

(This concludes the preceding section on the four conditions and their expedient means. Since all are unawakened to the characteristics of delusive thoughts, I urge all practitioners to abandon views of both gradual and simultaneous [attainment]).
