At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
All things are without arising, nor do they cease through causes and conditions. Within that arising and ceasing, one gives rise to the notion of causes and conditions (meaning:

although all phenomena are fundamentally without arising or ceasing, how could there be [such things]? Yet foolish ordinary people, amidst illusory arising and ceasing, give rise to the notion of the four conditions). This is not to deny cessation followed by rebirth arising from the continuity of causes and conditions;
it is solely for the purpose of severing the delusive, false conceptualizations of foolish ordinary people. (The Tang translation says: "It is not to deny the convergence of various conditions. Thus.

Ceasing and then arising again—this merely halts the attachments of the deluded thoughts of ordinary fools. The Buddha said that he does not negate the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) which continue through the succession of arising and ceasing. Why is this? Because one realizes that all phenomena are, in their very essence, empty and tranquil.

It is due to ordinary fools that they give rise to false grasping and attachment; if one simply cuts off the mind of grasping, what phenomena could there be? Whether it be the existence or non-existence of dependently originated phenomena, they are all without arising.

They revolve through the delusion of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and from this, the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) manifest. In reality, there is no arising of conditions, nor is there any cessation. Thus one contemplates.
All conditioned phenomena are like flowers in the sky (the meaning of this verse is clear).

That which grasps and that which is grasped—abandoning the deluded views [regarding them]—are neither already arisen nor yet to arise, nor do they possess causes and conditions. All things are non-existent; these are all merely verbal designations.

(Grasping is consciousness; that which is grasped is the object. The wise should abandon the various deluded views. Since all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent and do not fall within the three periods of time, it is said that they are neither already arisen nor yet to arise.)

Since the three periods of time do not exist, how can causes and conditions exist? Therefore, it is said that "all things are non-existent. Whether as the agent or the object, whether as cause or condition—those who fall into the discourse of the three periods of time speak nothing but conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will expound for us the *Sūtra on the Mind as the Appearance of Verbal Conceptualization*. (The term 'Sūtra' is rendered as 'Dharma-gate of the Mind' in the Wei and Tang translations. This question arises from the two preceding themes of 'verbal expression' and 'conceptualization' in the verses.
World-Honored One, if I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas thoroughly understand this *Sūtra on the Mind as the Appearance of Verbal Conceptualization*, then..."
One who is able to penetrate the two kinds of meanings—the expressive speech and that which is expressed—will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By means of these two approaches of expressive speech and that which is expressed, one purifies all sentient beings. (Note: "Expressive speech" is translated as "the speaker" in the Tang version.

This is Mahāmati’s own statement of his intention for questioning; he says that because there are such benefits, he ought to inquire. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect upon it well. When [he had spoken thus]...
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are four kinds of conceptual proliferation regarding the characteristics of speech: namely, speech based on signs (*nimitta*), dream-like speech, speech based on attachment to past conceptual proliferations, and speech based on beginningless conceptual proliferation" (these are the headings;
the following explains their meanings). Regarding speech based on signs: it arises from one's own conceptualization of form (*rūpa*).

The attachment to marks (*nimitta*) arises. "Marks" refers to blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth; "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to high and low, curved and straight, and so forth. These marks are originally not marks; they arise from one's own false conceptualization and attachment. This explains the origin of verbal discourse regarding marks.
As for "discourse regarding dreams," it arises following the recollection of objects previously experienced.

After waking, these objects are found to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). (The Wei translation renders "objects are without intrinsic nature" as "arising from unreal, false objects. Regarding "objects previously experienced": this refers to realms encountered in the past. Following such recollection, dreams arise. Once the dream has ended...)

Upon awakening, the speech uttered within a dream, or the speech that arises following a dream, is all false. It is said that the reason speech arises upon emerging from a dream is that it fundamentally arises from the realm of non-substantiality (the "non-substantial" refers to the dream-realm, which possesses appearances despite lacking substantiality).
Regarding speech arising from the attachment to deluded conceptualization:

this refers to speech produced by recollecting past deeds committed against an enemy (the "faults" are the evils, namely various harsh and violent words; these arise now through recollection of deeds committed against an enemy at a previous time). Regarding speech arising from beginningless deluded conceptualization:

This beginningless false attachment arises from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of one's own seeds. (The Wei translation states: "Beginningless discourse" means that, since time immemorial, it arises from the perfuming of the seeds of afflictions through adherence to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Regarding "arising from the seeds of transgressions": this refers to the self-seeds of transgression. Transgressions differ according to greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; each has both seeds and manifestations, which mutually perfume one another to give rise to discourse.)
These are called the four kinds of characteristics of the conceptualization of verbal expression (the conclusion of the names may be understood).

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested the World-Honored One regarding this same meaning: "I pray that you will further explain the objects manifested by the conceptualization of verbal expression."

(The previous question concerned the cause from which verbal expression arises; this question concerns the objects manifested by verbal expression. "World-Honored One, in what place, for what reason, in what manner, and by what cause do the deluded verbal expressions of sentient beings arise?

(The Wei translation says: "I pray that you will again explain for me the four kinds of characteristics of false attachment to language. From where does the language of sentient beings emerge? How does it emerge? By what cause does it emerge?

[In the present text, the four 'whats' are all interrogative particles. They are unified by the single term 'verbal expression,' meaning: in what place does verbal expression arise? For what reason does verbal expression arise? etc., as can be seen in the Wei translation]. Buddha...
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Head, chest, throat, nose, lips, tongue, gums, and teeth—through their combination, sound is produced. (This clarifies the locations from which speech arises.

*Yin* [gums] is pronounced as *yú-jīn*; it refers to the flesh at the base of the teeth. The Tang translation renders it as *è*, meaning the palate beside the teeth. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, are speech and conceptualization different, or are they not different? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Speech and conceptualization are neither different nor not different. Why is this so?"

Why? It is because those [dharmas] arise from the characteristics of causes. (The "because" below; the Wei translation says: "For what reason? Because speech arises from the characteristics of those false dharmas. [The "cause" refers to deluded thought (*vikalpa*). The characteristics arising from that cause are speech.
They are neither identical nor separate, as both lack substantial reality; thus it is said they are "neither different nor not different," as will be explained in detail below.
Mahāmati, if speech were different from deluded thought, then deluded thought would not be its cause. If they were not different, then words would not manifest meaning. And yet...

It is revealed. Therefore, it is neither different nor not different. (This follows the preceding text, which uses verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) to distinguish between difference and non-difference in relation to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

The ancient commentary states: "If verbal expression were different from conceptual construction, it would not arise based upon conceptual construction. If verbal expression were not different from conceptual construction, then verbal expression could not reveal its meaning.

It is not that they are not different. Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is verbal expression itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), or is that which is expressed the ultimate truth?"
[Regarding] the meaning: The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Neither is speech the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), nor is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth.

(If speech were taken as the ultimate truth, it would not point toward the moon; if that which is expressed were taken as the ultimate truth, then dharmas would become conditioned, because they exist in dependence [upon causes]. This [passage] simultaneously eliminates the two faults of the subject and the object. Why is this so? Because the ultimate truth is the noble bliss of the sages;
it is the ultimate truth as that which is entered via speech, yet it is not speech itself."

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). (Words are like a door; the practitioner enters by means of the door of words. To ascend to the hall and enter the inner chamber is the ultimate truth; it is not the door itself, but rather the hall and the chamber.

As for the ultimate truth, it is that which is attained through the self-awakening of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); it is not a realm perceived through the conceptualization of words. (That which is "attained through self-awakening" refers to the attainment wherein the object and mind are one, and principle and wisdom are both quiescent.

It cannot be communicated through verbal explanations or intellectual understanding; therefore, it is said to be "not a realm of conceptualization through words. For this reason, conceptualization through words does not manifest [it].
It reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Verbal expression is subject to arising and ceasing, and is characterized by fluctuation; it arises through a succession of causes and conditions.

If something arises through a succession of causes and conditions, it does not reveal the ultimate truth. Mahāmati, because self and other are devoid of intrinsic nature, the characteristics of verbal expression do not reveal the ultimate truth.

(For the ultimate truth is without sound and without odor; it is quiescent and without trace. Verbal expression, however, is subject to arising and ceasing and is characterized by fluctuation, arising from a succession of causes and conditions.)

Therefore, verbal expression cannot reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Regarding the absence of self-nature in terms of self and other: that which speaks is considered the "self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), and that which is spoken is considered the "other-characteristic" (*paralakṣaṇa*); since both self and other are false, verbal expression cannot reveal the ultimate truth.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, because various characteristics arise according to the measure of what appears to one's own mind, external natures—whether existent or non-existent—are merely verbal conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) that do not reveal the ultimate truth.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should abandon all verbal conceptualizations.

Regarding "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa). [The Tang translation states: "The primary meaning (paramārtha) is that there is only one's own mind; all various external characteristics are entirely non-existent. They cannot be manifested through verbal discrimination. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should remain far removed from verbal discrimination.

This means that by entering into accordance with everything as being merely the manifestation of one's own mind, one knows that the various external characteristics are neither existence nor non-existence. The realm of Mind-only transcends all speech; therefore, the primary meaning cannot be manifested.

Thus, [the text] below exhorts the bodhisattvas to depart from both words and the characteristics of false conceptualization. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
All natures lack intrinsic nature, and they are likewise beyond verbal expression. The profound meaning of emptiness within emptiness cannot be understood by the foolish.

(Regarding "all natures": these are the natures of false conceptualization. Since natures themselves lack nature, how could there be verbal expression? Hence it is said, "they are likewise beyond verbal expression. As for "emptiness within emptiness," this follows from the preceding two lines, referring to the emptiness of all natures and the emptiness of verbal expression.)

The realm of emptiness within emptiness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, the foolish are unable to comprehend it. All natures and self-natures are like shadows in the discourse on the Dharma;

this is what I have taught as the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) for the sons of the noble ones who possess the wisdom of self-realization. (The first two lines employ a metaphor to clarify that both all natures and verbal expressions are like shadows, meaning they are unreal.

The latter two lines follow from the preceding two to state the intended meaning: the World-Honored One has spoken of the reality-limit of all natures and verbal expressions solely for the sake of those sons who have attained the wisdom of self-realization.)
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us that which is free from existence and non-existence, oneness and difference, bothness and not-bothness, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence—that which is not traversed by any externalists, but is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization;
that which is free from the self-characteristics and common characteristics of false conceptualization, and enters into the supreme reality."

The meaning of this is as follows: the continuous succession of the various stages (*bhūmi*), the gradual and progressive marks of increasing purity, and the entry into the marks of the Tathāgata stage;
the manifestation of original vows without effortful cultivation; and the marks of the various divisions of the realms appearing within one's own mind—these are all the phenomena of all dharmas.
(From "I pray that you will explain" up to this point, it is all the sense of requesting an explanation. The two characters "yǐwèi shuō" [for the purpose of explaining] constitute the conclusion.)

This directly leads to the final sentence. It means: "I pray that you will explain that which is free from characteristics such as existence and non-existence—that which is not practiced by outsiders but is practiced by noble wisdom; furthermore, explain that which is free from self-characteristics and common characteristics and enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);

and further, explain the continuity of the stages up to the stage of the Tathāgata, the infinite characteristics and practices, and all dharmas which are the manifestations of the divisions of mind-only.

Because Mahāmati has heard of the ultimate truth as a realm beyond verbal expression, he asks this question with the intent to further clarify that the various views reckoned by all outsiders cannot function within the ultimate truth, and that what can be practiced therein is solely the noble wisdom of self-realization. I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas...

“Sā. By departing from such views of the self-nature and the individual and common characteristics of imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with and filled with all peace and happiness. (This is Mahāmati’s own statement of his intention in asking the question;

that is to say, if one hears the aforementioned meanings, one can distance oneself from such views of the individual and common characteristics of imagined nature and swiftly attain *anuttara-bodhi*. Since this is so for one's own benefit, one is likewise able to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed and filled [with these qualities].)
"May all beings be at peace and happy. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent!

That you are able to question me on such a matter as this will bring great peace and happiness, and provide great benefit, out of compassion for all gods and people of the world. (The World-Honored One, about to answer the meaning of the question, first praises the inquiry.)
[This is] the fulfillment of the benefit of both self-interest and the interest of others). The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Ignorant ordinary beings, not knowing the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), grasp at internal and external natures based on [the notions of] identity, difference, both, or neither."
Existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, and impermanence—these are conceptualizations based on attachment to intrinsic nature and habitual causes.

(The World-Honored One, about to answer this question, first reveals the cause of delusion to define the fundamental basis upon which ordinary people and fools rely. The *Xin shuo* states: It refers to the foolishness of ordinary beings who do not know that phenomena are manifestations of their own mind; taking deluded habits as the cause, they manifest various forms and cling to internal and external dharmas as being either existent or non-existent, giving rise to views such as the four propositions.

By means of twelve metaphors, he illustrates how these dharmas—existence, non-existence, identity, difference, and so forth—are all unreal and should be abandoned. For example, it is like a herd of deer driven by thirst.
Driven by this, they see the shimmering heat of springtime and conceive the thought that it is water; deluded and distracted, they rush toward it, unaware that it is not water (this is the metaphor).
In this same way, foolish people, conditioned by false conceptualizations from beginningless time, have their minds scorched by the three poisons and take pleasure in the realm of forms.

They perceive arising, abiding, and ceasing; they grasp at internal and external natures; they fall into the conceptualizations of oneness, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence, being ensnared by false views.
(This refers to the Dharma. The herd of deer represents foolish people. Being oppressed by thirst represents being perfumed by beginningless false habit-energies.

The mirage represents the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. The perception of water represents the attachments of the non-Buddhists. Wandering about in confusion represents falling into views such as oneness and difference. Not knowing it is not water represents being ensnared by false views). It is like the city of the Gandharvas.
City. The ignorant and foolish, lacking wisdom, give rise to the perception of a city. Due to beginningless habitual tendencies, the manifestation of signs is clung to as real.

That city neither exists nor does it not exist (this is the analogy). "That city neither exists nor does it not exist" means that although what appears resembles a city, being manifested by sea mist, it is in reality not a city; yet the illusory appearance is not non-existent, for it manifests due to causes and conditions.
Thus it is with the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Due to their attachment to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless falsehood, they rely on views of identity, difference, both, or neither;

existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence; and permanence or impermanence. They are unable to realize that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). (The "Dharma" refers to this. The "city" is a metaphor for the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

The "conception of a city" is a metaphor for the habitual tendencies of the non-Buddhists' attachments. The "appearance of attached signs" is a metaphor for the arising of views such as identity and difference based on delusive habits. "Neither a city nor not a city" is a metaphor for their inability to realize that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds.)
[This refers to] the false arising of conceptualizations such as existence and non-existence.

For example, suppose there is a person who, in a dream, sees men and women, elephants and horses, chariots and infantry, cities, gardens, mountains, rivers, and bathing pools, all variously adorned. He enters into them, and upon waking, he remembers them.
Mahāmati, what do you think? Is this man wise to continue remembering and not relinquish what was seen in his previous dream? Mahāmati.
He said to the Buddha, "No, World-Honored One. (This is a simile. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "In this same way, ordinary people are bitten by evil views."
The wisdom of the non-Buddhists does not understand that all things are manifestations of one's own mind, which is like a dream;

they rely on views of identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and permanence and impermanence. (This is the Dharma. A dream does not come from outside; it arises from the manifestation of one's own mind. Since the aggregates and so forth are like dreams, why further discriminate between identity and difference and the like?)

This is because those non-Buddhists do not understand that all things are the manifestation of their own minds; they cling to various views, which is the same as those who do not relinquish memories of dream-objects.
It is like a painted image that is neither high nor low, yet foolish commoners perceive it as being high or low (this is the analogy).

In the same way, future non-Buddhists will be filled with the habitual tendencies of evil views, relying on the views of oneness and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence, as well as the views of permanence and impermanence. Their own...

They destroy and cause others to destroy. Other [teachings] that are free from the discourse of existence and non-existence and the doctrine of non-arising also say "it does not exist" (referring to phenomena). It is not that the painting itself has height or depth; height and depth arise from the mind.

Just as those dharmas are fundamentally and naturally equal, yet in the future, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) will fill the world with false views of identity and difference. Others who propound a discourse on the departure from existence and non-existence and the absence of arising claim this to be the Tathāgata’s correct doctrine; they contemplate the non-arising of dharmas as being free from existence and non-existence.

Yet these non-Buddhists likewise calculate that there is "non-existence," thereby destroying themselves and others—a fault that is most extreme. Holding such views that slander cause and effect, they uproot the roots of goodness and destroy the causes of purity.
Those seeking excellence should distance themselves from them. Such people fall into the views of both self and other, as well as existence and non-existence.

Having engaged in such false conceptualization, one falls into the extremes of reification and denial. Due to these evil views, one shall fall into hell. (The following section on "denying the cause" sets forth the fault of repudiating [the existence of causes].)

[The section] "Seeking the Supreme" below exhorts those who practice correctly to abandon these evils and apply the following remedies; this is the method of distancing oneself [from them]. For example, it is like one with cataracts seeing hanging hairs and saying to others, "You all should look at these.
Yet these hanging hairs are ultimately neither existent by nature nor non-existent by nature, because they are seen by some and not seen by others.

(The term "hanging hairs" is rendered as "tufts of hair" [mao-lun] in the Wei and Tang translations. This is a metaphor. A "tuft of hair" refers to the circular shadow seen upon a lamp; "hanging hairs" refers to the hair covering the face seen by one with cataracts. The phrase "yet these" below clarifies the nature of the hanging hairs.)

This is delusion. It is like a person with cataracts seeing floating hairs before their eyes, yet not knowing that these floating hairs neither exist nor do not exist. Because they are seen by one with cataracts, they are not non-existent; because they are not seen by those with clear vision, they are not existent. Both existence and non-existence are false perceptions.

In this same way, these outsiders harbor false views and expectations based on the notions of identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence, as well as the views of permanence and annihilation.

They slander the True Dharma, thereby sinking themselves and leading others to sink as well. (The term "Dharma" refers to the teaching. The metaphor of cataracts and floating hairs illustrates the false perceptions of the various outsiders.)

Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—the passage beginning with "denigrating" below reveals the fault of such evil views). It is like a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*), which is not a wheel, yet the foolish conceive it as a wheel;

this is not the perception of the wise (this is a simile. A fire-brand wheel is a whirling firebrand; fundamentally there is no wheel, yet the foolish falsely form the conception of a wheel; this is not the vision of the wise).

In this way, the evil views and aspirations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) rely on conceptions of unity or difference, both or neither, existence or non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence or impermanence—all of these.

The arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). [This refers to] phenomena (*dharma*). The fire-wheel has no intrinsic nature; it is falsely conceptualized as existing. This is like how all phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet one forms notions of oneness, difference, and so forth regarding external objects;

thus, there is the arising of all intrinsic natures. For example, a water bubble resembles a *maṇi* jewel; a foolish person lacking wisdom perceives it as a *maṇi*, becomes attached to it, and pursues it, yet that water bubble—

It is not a *maṇi* jewel, nor is it not a *maṇi* jewel, because it is neither grasped nor not grasped (this is the analogy). The wise do not grasp it, hence it is not a *maṇi*; the ignorant and small-minded pursue it, hence it is not "not a *maṇi*" (the simile).

Likewise, those of external paths (*tīrthika*), perfumed by the habitual tendencies of evil views and false imaginings, speak of the arising of conditions where there is nothing at all, and say that what exists is extinguished (this is the dharma).

In the analogy, the "ignorant and small-minded" refers to the ignorant, who are the externalists, and the "small," who are the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). In the dharma, saying that there is no existence yet speaking of existence means reckoning that a distinct nature (*svabhāva*) can give rise to phenomena.

Furthermore, some say "extinction" (referring to the nihilistic views of non-Buddhists). Moreover, Mahāmati, having established the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*), one attains the self-realization of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-svasaṃvedana*).
Yet, one still clings to the false conceptualization of existence regarding phenomena that are free from the two natures (*svabhāva*).

(The New Exposition states: Regarding the mention of the "three types of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*): first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); second, inference (*anumāna*); and third, authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*). "Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is a term for definitive measurement; it is like using measures such as pecks or bushels to measure objects. As for "direct perception," "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifest; it refers to the clear and distinct realization of an object.)

It is not associated with verbal designations (*nāma-pada*), nor does it involve a mind of deliberation; one directly attains the essence of the Dharma and is free from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), yet it is not erroneous. Regarding inference (*anumāna*): "inference" means to infer by analogy; that is, because one comes to know through the measurement of analogical comparison based on reasons and examples.

Regarding authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*): this refers to taking the holy teachings of the Tathāgata as the standard. Regarding the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*): first, the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); and fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*). The three members—thesis, reason, and example—are also called the "three-limbed inference" (*tri-avayava-anumāna*); the application and conclusion merely serve to establish [the proof].

For example, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) falsely conceptualize and cling to sound as being permanent. Within the science of grammar (śabdavidyā), they formulate a syllogism (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is necessarily permanent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because it is a product" is the reason (*hetu*); "like space" is the similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*).

However, since space is not a product, the reason does not apply to the subject; thus, the example is inconsistent, and the establishment of sound as permanent is not proven. In the Buddha’s teaching, however, sound is impermanent; therefore, one formulates a syllogism as follows: "Sound" is the subject; "it is necessarily impermanent" is the thesis; "because it is a product" is the reason.

Because of their nature. A common analogy is like a jar or a basin. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Sounds mixed with speech merely rely on names, phrases, and meanings; how could they be permanent? By what means, then, can non-Buddhists abandon their attachments? The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "The Tathāgata established three kinds of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

The Fivefold Argument. Having distinguished and clarified the false and the correct, one causes [the practitioner] to leave behind the two kinds of self-nature arising from dependent origination and conceptual construction, thereby attaining the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). Yet, foolish people still reckon that there is a nature of existence and give rise to conceptual discrimination.

Mahāmati, for those practitioners who cultivate the noble wisdom of self-realization on the stage of the Tathāgata, the mind, intellect, and consciousness undergo a transformation, and all conceptual constructions regarding the grasped and the grasper—which are manifestations of one's own mind—are severed.
They do not form notions of "existence" or "non-existence" regarding those [phenomena]. (That is to say, the true practitioner severs...)

Because of the various false imaginings of mind, intellect, and consciousness as subject and object, one attains a superior transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) within one's own body and mind, rather than forming notions of existence or non-existence regarding the grasped and the grasper, or the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Furthermore, if a practitioner...
Regarding those for whom the perception of grasping arises toward such objects as being either existent or non-existent: they grasp at what is nourished and grasp at a self and a person.

(That is to say, when practitioners incorrectly adhere to such objects of grasping and that which is grasped, reckoning them as having existence or non-existence, the perception of grasping arises; they then fall into views such as the nourishment of a self and a person, and lose right reception.)

Mahāmati, if one speaks of the self-nature of those [dharmas] and their individual and common characteristics, all such things are spoken by the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (transformation buddha), not by the *dharma-buddha* (dharma-body buddha).

(That is to say, the self-nature and so forth are the provisional teachings of the *nirmāṇa-buddha*, not the teachings on the ultimate truth of the *dharma-buddha*). Furthermore, all verbal expressions arise from the longing views of the ignorant;
they do not establish a separate path for the dharma of self-nature, nor do they lead to the attainment of the self-realized wisdom of the noble ones.

Regarding those who dwell in the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi-sukha-vihāra*), [the Buddha] makes a distinction and reveals: (That is to say, the speech of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas arises entirely in accordance with the inclinations and perceptions of foolish people;

it does not establish for them the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the self-nature of the realms. Why is this? Because the dharma of self-nature is revealed through the distinctions made for those who have attained the blissful dwelling of the samādhi of self-realized noble wisdom.

It is, for example, like the reflection of a tree appearing in water: it is neither a shadow nor not a shadow, neither the form of a tree nor not the form of a tree. (This is the analogy. Such is the case with the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Habitual tendencies from past learning perfume the mind, leading to false conceptualizations and attachments based on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither;

existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence; permanence or impermanence. Thus, one fails to realize that these are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind. (Regarding the two phrases "neither phenomenon nor reflection": it means that apart from the tree there is no shadow;

the shadow actually exists within the tree, therefore it is not a [separate] reflection. That which appears is only water, yet because of the tree it forms a shadow, therefore it is not a non-reflection. Water originally has no tree; it is only what is manifested by the water, therefore it is not the tree. Apart from the tree there is no shadow; the entire shadow is the tree itself, therefore it is not...)

It is not a tree. This is used as an analogy for the manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*), which transcends being and non-being. The ignorant outsiders (*tīrthika*) falsely speculate on such things as identity and difference.

It is like a bright mirror that, according to conditions, manifests all forms and images, yet remains free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). That mirror is neither an image nor a non-image, yet it appears as both image and non-image;

only the deluded fool perceives it as an image and forms a conception of it. (This is the analogy: just as a mirror manifests various images according to external conditions while the mirror itself has no preference or aversion—thus transcending being and non-being—"neither image nor non-image" is the same as the previous example of the tree.)

"O shadows! All these foolish people falsely perceive these images as being either images or non-images, and thus form conceptions of them as such. In this way, the evil views of the outsiders manifest as images within their own minds;
they are attached to false imaginings based on the views of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence, and permanence or impermanence.

(The Dharma is like the mirror, which is the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind; the images are like the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. This means that the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases have no separate nature apart from what is manifested by one's own mind, for just as an image has no separate existence apart from the mirror, so it is. Yet, these outsiders do not understand their own minds...")"

[This refers to] false conceptualizations of identity, difference, both, or neither, and so forth. It is like wind and water: when they combine, sound arises; yet that sound is neither an intrinsic nature nor a non-nature (the Tang translation says:

"It is like an echo, which arises from the combination of wind, water, human voices, and so forth; it is neither existent nor non-existent. [This is the analogy. The phrase "neither an intrinsic nature" is as explained previously regarding the reflected image).

In this same way, the evil views and false imaginings of the outsiders depend upon notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence.

(The application of the principle may be understood). For example, in a place upon the great earth where there is no grass or wood, there appear shimmering mirages that flow like rivers and surge with waves like clouds.

These are neither of the nature [of water] nor of a non-nature, because they involve both craving and the absence of craving. (This is the analogy. That the rivers and waves surge is the appearance of the movement of the shimmering mirage.

Regarding "craving and the absence of craving," this explains the meaning of "neither of the nature nor of a non-nature": because thirsty deer pursue them, they are craved; thus, it is said they are not of a non-nature. Because people know these are but mirages, they do not crave them; thus, it is said they are not of the nature). In this same way, the foolish person lacks...
Initially, they are permeated by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of falsehood and attachment through deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

They rely upon [the notions of] arising, abiding, and ceasing; unity and difference; bothness and not-bothness; existence and non-existence; neither-existence-nor-non-existence; and permanence and impermanence. Taking as their object the door of their own inherent phenomena, they are likewise like those mirages and waves. (This refers to the *dharmas*.

The place on the great earth where there are no plants or trees is a metaphor for the non-characteristic state of True Suchness (*tathatā*); the mirages and so forth are metaphors for the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. This means that these non-Buddhists, being permeated by the habitual tendencies of falsehood from beginningless time, falsely rely upon arising...)

Abiding in the characteristics of cessation, identity, difference, and so forth, one relies upon the gateway of the objects of noble wisdom (*āryajñānavastu*). This is likewise like those views of identity, difference, and so on; therefore it is said, "it is also like that shimmering mirage and waves.

For example, it is like a person who, through incantations and mechanical devices, conjures by skillful means a *piśāca* spirit—which is not a sentient being—to move, act, and perform various functions.

Ordinary, ignorant people, through their deluded thoughts, cling to the notion of coming and going. (The Wei translation says: "For example, suppose there is a person who, by the power of incantations, causes a corpse or a wooden automaton to rise;

though they lack the substance of a sentient being, they perform acts of going and coming by relying on the power of a piśāca or the power of a magician. [This is a metaphor. "Those not included among the category of sentient beings" refers to human forms fashioned from woven or carved wood and grass, which are brought together through skillful means—either by incantations or by relying on the power of a piśāca ghost—and are set in motion from within by a mechanism to move and act.

However, because these woven and carved forms of wood and grass are fundamentally not sentient, they are said to be "not included among the category of sentient beings. *Piśāca* is translated as "eater of vital essence. Thus, externally...
The path of evil views consists of hope based on the views of identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence; permanence or impermanence.

It is a proliferation of conceptual play, a clinging to mental constructs, and an unreal establishment. Mahāmati, therefore, one who wishes to attain the reality of the noble wisdom of self-realization should abandon birth, abiding, and cessation;
identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence; and permanence or impermanence.

[This refers to] false views and delusive imaginings. (The Dharma. The wooden man is a metaphor for True Suchness (*tathatā*) being without self. The incantations, mechanical devices, and *piśāca* demons are metaphors for the hopes of false views.

The coming and going is a metaphor for giving rise to views such as birth, abiding, and extinction, or identity and difference, based on the dharmas of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). Therefore, [the passage] below concludes by exhorting those who have attained self-awakening to abandon [views of] identity and difference).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Like an illusion, a dream, the moon’s reflection in water, a tree’s shadow, a mass of hair, or a mirage in the heat—thus one should contemplate the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). By contemplating through these analogies, one attains ultimate liberation.

Just as the thirsty deer, with a flickering and deluded mind, perceives a mirage as water while in reality no water exists, so too does consciousness (*vijñāna*), through its seeds, flicker and perceive [objects].
Objects of perception arise from the deluded imaginings of fools. Like being obscured by a cataract, they have, throughout beginningless birth and death, clung to and grasped at the nature of things.
Just as one drives out a wedge with another wedge, one must abandon the grasping of craving. (With movement, there is arising and ceasing;

this realm of arising and ceasing arises from the deluded imaginings of fools. The *Jiuzhu* (Collected Commentaries) says: "Sentient beings, because of their clinging and grasping, are like those struck by a wedge and unable to escape. The Tathāgata, out of compassion, uses various metaphors for unreality as wedges to strike against [and remove] it."

It is like driving out a wedge to cause it to emerge, so that one is no longer obstructed by evil views, false conceptualizations, or the nature of grasping. Like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, or flashes of lightning—by contemplating these, one attains liberation and forever severs the three continuities.

(The examples of floating clouds and lightning flashes, which do not persist for long, serve as secondary metaphors. The "three continuities" refers to: 1. The continuity of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃtati*). 2. The continuity of karma (*karma-saṃtati*). 3. The continuity of birth (*janman-saṃtati*). By realizing that all phenomena are like illusions, spells, and the like, one transcends these three modes of continuity. Thus, one is liberated from the cycle of existence.
(See the third fascicle). In that [state], there is no agent; it is like a mirage in the sky. When one knows all phenomena in this way, then there is nothing to be known.
(The phrase "mirage in the sky" is rendered in the Tang translation as "like a mirage in the air. This means that all phenomena are fundamentally without an agent, like a mirage in the air;

knowing them thus, the object of knowledge is found to lack reality. Verbal teachings are merely provisional names, and they too possess no marks. To give rise to deluded conceptualization regarding them is like the aggregates and formations [in the air].

"Like hanging hair. (The "able-to-be-illustrated" refers to the verbal teachings; the "that which is illustrated" refers to the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth. By correlating the verbal teachings with the aggregates and so forth, one realizes that both the subject and object are without marks; hence it is said, "they too are without marks.

To give rise to deluded conceptualization regarding that subject and object is the flux of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Relying on delusion to produce further delusion is like the hanging hair that is not real). It is like painted hanging hair, a magical illusion, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas.

The fire-wheel and the heat-mirage appear to sentient beings though they do not exist. (The final phrase; the Tang translation reads: "truly non-existent yet appearing as existent. This means that all delusions are fundamentally non-existent, yet when they manifest, they seem to exist. Though non-existent, their various marks constantly appear.

The word "sentient beings" in the final phrase refers to these various marks. This verse illustrates the meaning of the metaphor. Regarding permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, being both and neither—these are likewise so.
The succession of faults from beginningless time is the foolish person’s deluded conceptualization. (This verse illustrates the meaning of the Dharma. A clear mirror, water, and a pure eye...
Just as various colors appear within a wondrous mani-jewel, yet in reality nothing exists there; so too do all natures manifest.
Like a shimmering mirage in the heat of the day, various colors appear, yet like a dream, they are non-existent.
(The repetition of these similes within the verse serves to repeatedly illustrate through analogy that all phenomena are unreal, exhorting practitioners to strive to remain far removed from them.)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from these four positions: namely, identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence;

it is free from the extremes of affirmation and denial regarding existence and non-existence. (This follows the preceding chapter to clarify that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from these various faults.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma consists of the analysis and compilation of the Truths, Dependent Origination, the Path and Cessation, and Liberation.

This is the foremost (the *tattva* [reality], namely *pratītyasamutpāda* [dependent origination]; and *mārga-nirodha* [the Path and Cessation], two of the Four Truths, which are the supramundane cause and effect; these implicitly include the mundane cause and effect of *duḥkha-samudaya* [Suffering and Origin];

and *vimukti*, which is *nirvāṇa*). The Tathāgata’s method of transformation divides [the teaching] into three parts; because he first taught the Two Vehicles, it is said that "this is the foremost. He teaches the Dharma [stating that it arises] not from a primal nature (*svabhāva*), not from a Lord (*īśvara*), not without cause, not from atoms (*paramāṇu*), not from time (*kāla*), and not from the continuity of self-nature (*svabhāva-saṃtati*).
(This is a refutation of errors; it means that the Tathāgata teaches all things by means of correct causes and conditions.)

The Dharma is not like the conceptualizations of those non-Buddhists who speak of such things as "Nature" (prakṛti) or "Īśvara. Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is for the sake of purifying the obstacles of afflictions and cognitive obscurations.

It is like a caravan leader who, in successive order, establishes the hundred and eight propositions of non-existence, skillfully discerning the characteristics of the various vehicles and the stages (*bhūmi*).

(The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "The Tathāgata establishes the meaning of the hundred and eight propositions and discerns the characteristics of the vehicles and stages, causing all sentient beings to purify and eliminate the two obstacles and sever all delusions;

this is just as a caravan leader guides a multitude of merchants directly to the place of jewels, employing various skillful means at dangerous and obstructed places to ensure they all pass through them. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are they?
There are four types: namely, the dhyāna practiced by fools; the dhyāna of examining meanings; the dhyāna of taking suchness as its object;
and the Tathāgata-dhyāna. (These are the headings; the following explains their meanings. What is the dhyāna practiced by fools?

It refers to practitioners among Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who take as their primary focus the contemplation of the selflessness of persons, the specific and general characteristics [of phenomena], the skeleton, and the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and impurity, while remaining attached to them.

To have such characteristics, to observe them without variation, and to progress further and further while not yet eliminating these mental images—this is called the "dhyāna practiced by fools" (the contemplation of white bones, which is the *śrāvaka* practice of the Lesser Vehicle).

Regarding the phrase "to observe such characteristics without variation": "such characteristics" refers to the non-self of persons and so forth; "observing without variation" means observing that the intrinsic nature of all characteristics is empty and quiescent, and thus they do not differ. As the ancient commentary states:

"The two vehicles contemplate the emptiness of persons, and furthermore contemplate the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, performing the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and impurity. In this way, the characteristics and the observations of specific and general characteristics, as well as the modes of observation such as impermanence, though [different],..."
There is superior progress, yet it does not transcend [conceptual] marks; this is called the dhyāna practiced by fools. What is the dhyāna that investigates meaning?

It refers to the realization that the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) lack intrinsic nature—whether from oneself, another, or both—and having done so, one observes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

As the meaning of the marks of those stages gradually advances, this is called the dhyāna that investigates meaning. (Below the word "meaning" (*artha*), the character "observe" (*guan*) should be added for the sense to be complete. This "observing the two vehicles" refers to the meaning of the two vehicles; "below 'non-Buddhists'" refers to the meaning of the non-Buddhists. One observes phenomena...)

"Lower. This refers to the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). "Both self and other are without nature" means that there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), no extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), no nature consisting of both self and other, and no nature at all—meaning the absence of causality. These four are the doctrines imagined by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); since all vehicles contemplate these, it is called the "contemplative meaning meditation" (*vipaśyanārtha-dhyāna*).
What is the "meditation on the object-condition of suchness" (*tathatālambana-dhyāna*)? (The Wei and Tang translations insert the character "true" [zhen] before "suchness" [ru]).

This means that regarding the two kinds of false discrimination—the false discrimination of self and the false discrimination of phenomena—one does not give rise to false discrimination within the state of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*). This is called the meditation on the object-condition of suchness. (Regarding "object-condition of suchness": this refers to the Bodhisattva vehicle.)

A person takes wisdom as the condition for suchness (*tathatā*). Since the characteristics of the principle of wisdom are quiescent, this is called "the dhyāna of taking suchness as its object. Regarding the phrase "delusive thought (*vikalpa*) and the two kinds of selflessness": the first instance of the word "delusive thought" refers to the wisdom that takes [suchness] as its object.

Wisdom is called "delusive thought" because its essence is like an illusion; thus it is also termed *vikalpa*. The second instance of the word "delusive thought" points to the two kinds of selflessness. These two selflessnesses are the objects of cognition and, being merely categories of phenomena (*dharma-saṃkhyā*), they are also termed *vikalpa*. In the state of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*), there is no further delusive thought;

therefore, it is said that "in the state of reality as it is, delusive thought does not arise. (This concludes the definition). What is the Tathāgata-dhyāna? It is said to be entering the stage of the Tathāgata and attaining the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Abiding in the three kinds of bliss through these marks, he accomplishes inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the Tathāgata-dhyāna (meaning, as the Wei translation states: because one enters the stage of the Tathāgata as it truly is;

because one enters the three kinds of blissful practices within the three emptinesses of internal-body noble wisdom; and because one is able to accomplish the inconceivable tasks performed for sentient beings—this is called the contemplation of the Tathāgata-dhyāna.

Regarding the "three kinds of bliss of noble wisdom," these are the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti; thus, the Wei translation refers to the three emptinesses of the internal body to signify the three virtues). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate...
He proclaimed this meaning and spoke in verse:
"The dhyāna practiced by the foolish, the dhyāna that contemplates the characteristics of objects, the dhyāna that takes reality as its object, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.

(These verses list the names; the following verses explain their meanings. "It is like the reflection of the sun each day, like the deep and treacherous *padma* lotus pond, and like the fire in the sky."

Ashes. The practitioner observes [this]. (In Sanskrit, *padma*; translated as "red lotus flower. A new explanation states: this clarifies the characteristics of the meditative cultivation of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

It is said that non-Buddhists, clinging to a self-soul (*ātman*), when practicing meditative contemplation, see forms like the sun and moon, bright, pure, and radiant; or they see what resembles a red lotus flower beneath deep precipices. The Two Vehicles take the individual and common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) to be substantially real;

they reduce the body to ashes and extinguish cognition, becoming like empty space. Like fire being extinguished when the fuel is exhausted, they consider this to be ultimate *nirvāṇa*). Such various signs belong to the common meditations of the paths of non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, they fall into the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas (the "paths of meditation" refers here to the meditations practiced by non-Buddhists).
Abandoning all of those is "non-existence" (abandoning all marks and entering the *tathatā*-meditation; non-existence is precisely *tathatā*).
All Buddhas of all lands, with inconceivable hands, simultaneously stroke their crowns, causing them to enter accordantly into the mark of suchness (this verse describes the *tathāgata-dhyāna*).
The first three lines of the verse accomplish inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings; the final line concludes by entering the *tathatā-lakṣaṇa* (the characteristic of suchness).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding 'parinirvāṇa,' what dharma do you teach when you speak of it as nirvāṇa?

(This question arises from the preceding discussion of the three kinds of bliss in the Tathāgata-dhyāna. Nirvāṇa is the essence, while the three kinds [of bliss] are its qualities. Mahāmati asks this because he has heard of these qualities.)

This is a question concerning the essence [of nirvāṇa]. The *Xin shuo* (New Exposition) states: "Non-Buddhists regard the perception of a self-soul (*ātman*) as nirvāṇa; the followers of the Two Vehicles regard the extinction of body and consciousness—like the extinguishing of fire when the fuel is spent—as nirvāṇa. Therefore, he asks: 'What kind of dharma does the Tathāgata teach that is called nirvāṇa?'"

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The transformation of all self-natures, habitual tendencies, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the mental organ (*manas*), and the active consciousnesses (*vijñānas*), as well as the habitual tendencies of views, is called *nirvāṇa*.

The *nirvāṇa* of all Buddhas and myself is the sphere of the reality of the emptiness of self-nature. (This clarifies that the transformation of the mind, intellect, and consciousness, along with all views and habitual tendencies, is termed Great *Nirvāṇa*.

The passage beginning with "All Buddhas" clarifies that their bodies, lands, Dharma-transformations, teachings, realizations, causes, and fruits constitute the sphere of the reality of the emptiness of self-nature, which is *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, it can be interpreted that the emptiness of self-nature is the very essence of *nirvāṇa*, while the "sphere of reality" refers to...)

The mastery of powers and supernormal knowledges, and the three kinds of mind-made bodies—these are the functions of nirvāṇa. The *Compendium of Notes* states: "As for the objective realm of phenomena, it is like the *Avataṃsaka*’s dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. Furthermore, Mahāmati:
Nirvāṇa is the realm of self-realization through noble wisdom; it is free from the false imaginings of annihilation and permanence, and its nature is neither existence nor non-existence.

(This follows the preceding text to explain the meaning of nirvāṇa in detail. Why is it not permanent? Because the false imaginings of specific and general characteristics have been severed, it is not permanent.
Why is it not annihilated? Because all noble ones—of the past, future, and present—attain self-realization, it is not annihilated. (The commentary on the text is clear. Mahāmati, Nirvāṇa...
Nirvāṇa is indestructible and deathless. If nirvāṇa were subject to death, it would necessarily undergo the continuity of rebirth.

If it were subject to destruction, it would fall under the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, nirvāṇa is free from destruction and free from death; thus, it is the refuge for practitioners. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Nir" means non-arising; "vāṇa" means non-extinction. Non-arising and non-extinction is called Great Nirvāṇa. What is here termed "destruction" refers to the characteristic of change (*anyathātva*) among the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. This is because [nirvāṇa] is... [Nirvāṇa].

It is eternally free from the four characteristics; therefore, it is said to be "neither decaying nor dying. The New Commentary states: Because one no longer undergoes the continuity of birth, Nirvāṇa is not dying; because it is not a conditioned phenomenon subject to arising, abiding, and ceasing, Nirvāṇa does not decay.

Because it neither decays nor dies, it is that to which practitioners take refuge. Furthermore, Mahāmati, Nirvāṇa is neither abandonment nor attainment, neither annihilation nor permanence, neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings;

this is called Nirvāṇa. (The New Commentary states: In Nirvāṇa there are no afflictions to be abandoned and no Bodhi to be attained; therefore, it is neither annihilation nor permanence, nor a single [meaning].)
It is different; it is merely the realization of correspondence. This is called the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas consists in awakening to their own-characteristics and common-characteristics, and not associating with sense objects (not associating with sense objects means, according to the Tang translation, "forsaking clamor and bustle"). They possess non-perverted views.

Conceptual construction does not arise. Those [beings] perceive that state as being nirvāṇa. (Regarding "non-perverted," etc.: this means that because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not conceive of a self (*ātman*) and so forth, their view is non-perverted.

Because it is non-perverted, conceptual construction does not arise; they then form the notion of nirvāṇa regarding that very state where there is no arising. This intent is to distinguish them from those who have not yet exhausted the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of nirvāṇa).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). What are the two? They are: attachment to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression, and the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of things.

Attachment to the characteristics of intrinsic nature. Attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression arises from attachment to the false habitual tendencies of beginningless verbal expression.
Attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things arises from the failure to realize that they are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.

(This passage may be understood as follows). Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata establishes the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas through two kinds of spiritual powers (*adhiṣṭhāna*), so that they may prostrate before the Buddhas and listen to and receive the exposition of the meaning of the teachings. What are these two kinds of spiritual powers by which they are established? They are:

the spiritual power of manifesting all bodies, faces, and speech through the meditative absorption of *samādhi*; and the spiritual power of the hand-consecration (*abhiṣeka*). (These two kinds of spiritual powers refer to practice...)

When one is in the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*), there is the Buddha’s power of manifesting his body, face, and speech, as well as the power of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Mahāmati, at the first bodhisattva stage, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides by the Buddha’s power;
that is to say, they enter the bodhisattva Great Vehicle Illumination Samādhi (*bodhisattva-mahāyāna-avabhāsa-samādhi*).
Having entered this samādhi, all Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions, through their supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), manifest to them all their bodies, faces, and speech.
It is said: "Such as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have likewise accomplished such marks and virtues.

(Those who have accomplished such marks and virtues refers to Bodhisattvas who have accomplished two kinds of supernormal powers. The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "Such as the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra.")

When dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*), they receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power (and the same applies to other bodhisattvas). Mahāmati, this is called the first bodhisattva stage for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Having attained the spiritual power of the bodhisattva’s samādhi and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), it is accomplished through the cultivation of roots of goodness over hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

They successively master the stages, penetrating to the ultimate limit of the characteristics of both the remedies and that which is to be remedied. (This concludes the first [section on] the spiritual power of verbal expression. Next...)
The third stage: This refers to the period from the first bhūmi through the ninth bhūmi, wherein one is empowered by the accomplishment of merit through the power of verbal expression.

Upon reaching the Dharma-Cloud bhūmi (Dharmameghā), one dwells in a subtle and wondrous palace of great lotuses, seated upon a great lotus jewel lion-throne, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of similar kind.
Their bodies are adorned with various precious necklaces and ornaments, like golden campaka flowers, and [radiant] as the light of the sun and moon. All...
O Son of the Most Victorious One, bodhisattvas come from the ten directions and confer the empowerment upon the crown of his head while he sits upon a lion throne within a great lotus palace.
It is like the empowerment conferred upon a sovereign wheel-turning monarch or the crown prince of Śakra, Lord of Devas. This is called the "bodhisattva’s power of hand-consecration.

(The Wei translation states: "Upon reaching the Stage of Dharma-Cloud, he dwells in a palace of a great jewel lotus king, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a retinue of similar bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.")

Adorned with crowns and necklaces, his body was like Jāmbūnada gold or the Campaka flower; his radiance surpassed that of the sun, moon, and the color of lotuses. At that time, all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions each extended their hands and stroked from afar the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva upon the Lotus King throne.

It was like the consecration of a crown prince by Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, or a Wheel-Turning King, who bestows the position upon him. Mahāmati, because those consecrated Bodhisattvas and their retinue of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have their heads stroked by the hands of the Tathāgatas, they attain bliss throughout their entire bodies.

Therefore, it is said that the power of sustaining [the Bodhisattva] comes from the hands stroking the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head. (Note: According to the two translations by Wei and Tang, as well as the heading of the present sutra, all state that "the Tathāgata’s hand sprinkles the crown of the Bodhisattva. Only the current text [differs].)

It says: "The Sons of the Most Victorious Ones [then] conferred the empowerment upon him at that very seat. Regarding the metaphors and the designations, there appears to be a contradiction in meaning; this must be an error by the chief translator or the scribe. Therefore, I have recorded the Wei translation as above; one should rely upon its meaning.

In some versions, the character for "son" (子) in "Son of the Most Victorious One" (最勝子子) is written as "hand" (手). This would imply that the hands of all the Most Victorious Ones come from the ten directions to consecrate his crown. According to this interpretation, the meaning is consistent with the passage beginning "For example, at the outset... which clarifies the significance of the conferral of office. The section beginning "This is called...
concludes the second [section on] the spiritual power of consecration. Mahāmati, this is what is meant by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in two kinds of spiritual power.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in these two kinds of spiritual power, he beholds the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, face to face. If it were not so, then [he would not].

[He] is able to see. (This concludes the preceding section; it may be understood accordingly. The passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva... clarifies the benefits of abiding in the two powers. The passage beginning with "If not... reveals the fault of non-abiding).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, all the various practices of dharmas—such as the differentiations of samādhi and the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*)—performed by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, all of these [are as follows].

All abide by the two kinds of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata. (The two powers previously mentioned were those by which the Buddha empowers the bodhisattvas for their own self-benefit. The present text refers to how the bodhisattvas so empowered further rely on these two powers to discern the practice of all dharmas and benefit sentient beings;

this constitutes their practice for the benefit of others. Since both self-benefit and the benefit of others are empowered by these two kinds of supernatural power, it is said: "All these abide entirely by the two kinds of supernatural power of the Tathāgata").
Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were able to expound and analyze [the teachings] apart from the supernatural power of the Buddha, then all...
Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) should also be able to speak [the Dharma]. Why is this? It is because they do not abide in the power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhibala*).

(This means that those who can preach the Dharma must rely on the spiritual powers of all Buddhas; apart from these two powers of the Buddha, their eloquence would be stunted and their teaching of the Dharma would be obstructed. [The following section] interrogates and explains the reason why ordinary worldlings cannot speak [the Dharma]: it is because they do not abide in these two powers, and therefore cannot speak.
Mahāmati, mountains, stones, trees, various musical instruments, city walls, and palaces [resound] through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata’s entry into a city.

By the power [of the Tathāgata], musical sounds spontaneously emerge from all things; how much more so for those with consciousness? Those who are deaf, blind, mute, or afflicted by immeasurable sufferings all attain liberation.
The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable spiritual powers as these to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings.

(If even insentient objects like wood and stone can produce sounds, and within those sounds there are inevitably verses praising the Buddha’s virtues—just as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the jeweled nets upon the cloud-platforms all contain verses extolling the Buddha—how much more so should sentient beings offer praise and hymns? This reveals...)

When the Tathāgata enters the city, he possesses such great supernormal power and such profound benefit that he clearly manifests two powers to empower the practitioner; this is surely inevitable. Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas [possess these qualities]?"
When dwelling in the meditative absorption of samādhi, as well as at the time of consecration upon the stage of supreme advancement, he bestows his supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

(Regarding this, Mahāmati again asks for the reason behind the bestowal of supernatural power. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is for the sake of abandoning the karmas of Māra and afflictions; for the sake of not falling into the dhyānas of the Śrāvaka stage;
for the sake of attaining the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization; and for the sake of further increasing the dharmas already attained. (Because there are such causes and conditions...)
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas will certainly receive its benefit, and all Buddhas will certainly be graced by its merit.
For this reason, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all establish the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through their supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

If they were not established by supernatural power, they would fall into the evil views, delusions, and expectations of the various Śrāvakas and Māras, and would fail to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[They attain] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, universally employ their spiritual powers to sustain and receive all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

(The phrase "For this reason" below concludes the basis for being sustained. The phrase "If not" below clarifies the fault of not receiving such support. The phrase "For this" below reiterates the basis for being sustained, thereby clarifying that the intensity with which the Buddhas sustain them lies herein.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The One Honored Among Men, by his supernormal powers, has completely purified his great vows. Through the empowerment of samādhi, he attains the first stage and the tenth stage.

(Samādhi is also called samāpatti. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: 'All meditative concentrations that collect the mind are termed samādhi. It is translated as 'the locus of right mental activity. This mind, from time immemorial, has been constantly crooked and not upright; having attained [samādhi],...")"

This is the sphere of practice for rectifying the mind; thus, the mind becomes upright and straight. It is like a snake that always moves in a curve, yet becomes straight when entering a bamboo tube. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Mingyi ji*) further translates this as *samādhi*. "Equanimity" (*sama*) refers to being free from dullness and agitation; "concentration" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to causing the mind to remain one-pointed.
The second is called "common usage" (therefore, the long prose version says "samādhi").
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Buddha speaks of dependent origination, he is speaking of causes and conditions;

he does not speak of a path established by itself" (the Wei translation says: "The Tathāgata also speaks of all dharmas arising in dependence upon causes and conditions, yet he does not speak of dharmas established by themselves").
This objection [suggests] that there is a fault in the causal conditions taught by the Tathāgata, as it would be identical to what is taught by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of causal conditions, asserting that all things arise from the Primal Nature (prakṛti), Īśvara, Time, or atoms; that is, they claim all such natures arise [from these].

However, the discourse of the World-Honored One regarding the arising of all natures through causal conditions involves both the *siddhānta* with intervals and the *siddhānta* without intervals. (That is to say, the World-Honored One...)

[The interlocutor] says: "If all dharmas likewise arise from causes and conditions, then is there a distinction between what the Buddha and the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) teach, or is there none? If there is a distinction, then there is a different meaning; if there is no distinction, then [the Buddha's teaching] is the same as the *siddhānta* of the non-Buddhists (as explained in the preceding note).
World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also say that existence arises from non-existence. The World-Honored One also says that there is no arising, and that once arisen, there is cessation.

(The Tang translation states: "The non-Buddhists also say that because of an agent, existence arises from non-existence. The World-Honored One also says that because of causes and conditions, all dharmas originally do not exist but arise, and having arisen, they return to cessation. [This concludes the prior objection.]

The term "conditioned origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is precisely what makes the meaning of "conditioned origination" difficult to grasp. Regarding the phrase "arising from existence or non-existence": this means that [some claim] there is arising from non-existence. As the Blessed One has said:

"With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations," and so on, up to "old age and death. This is a teaching by the Blessed One that is without cause; it is not a teaching that posits a cause.

The Blessed One established his teaching by saying: "Because this exists, that exists. He did not establish it as a gradual production. (The Tang translation says: "As the Buddha taught, 'with ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations,' and so forth...")

...up to old age and death. This teaching is said to be without cause; it is not said to have a cause. The World-Honored One has said: "Because this exists, that exists. If this were established as occurring simultaneously rather than through sequential dependence, its meaning would not be established.

The intent of Mahāmati’s objection is to draw a parallel between the correct and the false by giving them the same name, "causeless. Therefore, he first says: "The World-Honored One also taught that there is no arising, and that once arisen, things perish. He suspects this implies causelessness. If it were causeless, it would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Thus, he cites what the World-Honored One previously taught as proof, saying:

"As the World-Honored One has taught, 'ignorance conditions volitional formations' and so forth—these arise dependent on others and cannot exist of themselves; therefore, they belong to the category of being causeless, not a teaching of having a cause. Furthermore, the World-Honored One established: "Because this exists, that exists," which refers to gradual arising. If [it were] simultaneous...

If establishment were not dependent upon one another, then gradual succession would be impossible; therefore it is said that there is no "establishment through gradual arising. When observing the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they are superior, yet they are not like those of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? World-Honored One, the causes taught by the non-Buddhists do not arise from conditions, yet something is produced.

World-Honored One, you teach that when one observes the cause, the effect exists; when one observes the effect, the cause exists. In this way, causes and conditions become confused and entangled, revolving in an endless cycle.

[The opponent] challenges the Buddha’s teaching, claiming that it is not superior to that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and that the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the non-Buddhists are, in fact, superior to those of the Buddha.
