This is the skillful means and original vow of one who manifests through expediency; hence it is said, "he preaches various teachings within the realm of deluded thought.

Regarding the phrase "manifesting below," this clarifies the meaning of external manifestation: it means that while harboring great aspirations within, he externally manifests the Lesser Vehicle. Although he has attained the self-manifesting measure of his own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), he does not yet claim to have transcended it. As for "attaining the marks of the fruit," he manifests the Lesser Vehicle...

This is the trace [of the teaching]. This discourse is called the meaning of the provisional manifestation of attaining the fruit. Furthermore, Mahāmati, one who wishes to transcend the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) should abandon the marks of what is manifested by one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).

(The "dhyānas and immeasurables" refer to the four dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds; the formless realms are likewise understood. Since those four dhyānas and four formless realms have not yet abandoned what is manifested by one’s own mind, the practitioner is exhorted to transcend and leave them behind.

The *Jizhu* states: this means to eliminate the previously attained marks of the fruit of what is manifested by one’s own mind. Mahāmati, as for the attainment of cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*), it transcends...

That which is the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind is not so. Why? Because there is the measure of mind (cittamātra). [The meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (nirodhasamāpatti) is the pinnacle of all concentrations of the form and formless realms.]

"Even though one has fully realized this meditative absorption, one is still unable to transcend the mental scope of the Peak of Existence; therefore, it is incorrect to say that this absorption transcends it. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, said:
And he spoke in verse:
"The various dhyānas, the four immeasurables, The formless attainments, and the cessation of all sensation and perception— In the Mind-Only, these do not exist.

(This verse refers to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the cessation of sensation and perception. When these various manifestations of mind are observed through the perspective of true reality, they are entirely unobtainable; therefore, they do not exist. *Srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer).
The fruits—the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat—these states are but the delusions of the mind. (This verse describes what is realized by those in the four fruits;

because their minds are deluded, they falsely perceive nirvāṇa. Within the principle of ultimate truth, nothing exists at all. When the meditator, through meditation and its objects, cuts off [defilements] and realizes the ultimate truth, this is merely the measure of conceptual construction.

If one awakens to this, there is liberation. (The word "and" [及] is rendered as "object" [所] in the Tang translation; the character "know" [知] is rendered as "delusion" [惑]. ○ "Cuts off and knows" means knowing suffering and cutting off the origin.)

The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "The first four lines clarify the dharmas to be practiced; the next four lines clarify the person who realizes them; the current four lines clarify both the subject and object together. All are the measure of the deluded mind (*vikalpa-citta-mātra*).
If one awakens to the unreality of this measure of the deluded mind, one immediately attains ultimate liberation."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening: the awakening of investigation (*vicaya-buddhi*) and the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-parigraha-abhiniveśa-vyavasthāna-buddhi*).

(This is the heading; the following is the explanation. Generally, investigation is considered true and attachment is considered false. Below, the awakening of investigation is explained first. Mahāmati, as for the awakening of investigation:

it refers to the awakening that realizes the self-nature and characteristics of phenomena are, when analyzed, found to be unobtainable because they transcend the four logical positions (*catuṣkoṭi*). This is called the awakening of investigation. (Awakening, according to the Wei and Tang [dynasty] translations...)

Translated as "Wisdom. The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "If the self-nature and characteristics of the nature of awakening are fundamentally empty and quiescent, then among all phenomena, upon selecting and discerning them, not a single phenomenon can be found to be truly real.

When one is free from the four propositions—identity, difference, and so forth—then all phenomena are utterly unobtainable. "Mahāmati, those four propositions refer to: identity and difference; both [identity and difference] and neither;

existence and non-existence; and neither existence nor non-existence; permanence and impermanence. These are called the four propositions. Mahāmati, being free from these four propositions is what is called 'all phenomena'."

(These four phrases are free from the following. The Tang translation reads: "I [take] all dharmas. Being free from these four phrases, it is therefore said that all dharmas are free. These four phrases of freedom are called "all dharmas," meaning that when all dharmas are free from these four phrases, then all dharmas are, in their very essence, True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is what is meant by: "being free from all marks is itself all dharmas"). Mahāmati, this fourfold analysis examines all dharmas.

One should practice and study this. (This exhorts the Bodhisattva to contemplate all phenomena as being free from the faults of the four extremes. Mahāmati, what is the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination?
It refers to the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination—namely, the unreal characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion;
it is the establishment of an unreal foundation by means of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), logical reasons (*hetu*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). This is it.

This is called the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false conceptualization. (The phrase "謂妄" [referring to the "false"]—the Tang translation states:

"It refers to taking up the characteristics of, and becoming attached to, the various great elements (*mahābhūta*) of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion; it is a false discrimination that establishes [these] through propositions, reasons, and examples. This is termed the wisdom of grasping characteristics, discrimination, attachment, and establishment. [This explains the false conceptualization of erroneous wisdom in order to clarify that such establishments are unreal. Solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are the natures of earth, water, fire, and wind, respectively.

Any calculation that regards these unreal great elements as real or permanent is merely erroneous wisdom. Regarding propositions, reasons, and examples: in India, whenever one establishes the principles of dharmas, it is invariably by means of propositions (*pakṣa*), reasons (*hetu*), and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).]

This is the standard of measurement: if there is no fault in these three branches, it is correct; if there is a fault, it is erroneous (as explained in detail in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*). These are called the two characteristics of awakening.

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accomplishes these two characteristics of awakening—the characteristic of the selflessness of persons and phenomena—and thoroughly understands the skillful means of the awakening to non-existence, he observes the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) and attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). He enters one hundred samādhis and attains the various distinct samādhis.
One sees a hundred Buddhas and a hundred Bodhisattvas; one knows the events of a hundred kalpas for both the past and future limits;

light illuminates a hundred lands. (This concludes the two types of awakening. The following section, beginning with "If a bodhisattva," reveals the merit of these two awakenings. Within these two awakenings, that which is true is selected and followed, while that which is false is suppressed and distanced. This process of one adopting and one rejecting is collectively termed "accomplishment.")

"Ultimately below" reveals the characteristics of the first stage (*bhūmi*). "The awakening to non-existence" refers to what is called the "stage of effortlessness" (*anābhoga*) upon ascending to the first stage in the *Tiantai sijiao yi*. Here, "non-existence" is precisely that effortlessness. The *Jizhu* states:

"If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva integrates the true and the false, accomplishes these two aspects of awakening, realizes the emptiness of persons and phenomena, and finds no self to be obtained, then by means of the awakening to non-existence, they skillfully observe at the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), thereby attaining the first stage and entering the Great [Vehicle]."

Riding upon this radiance, it illuminates and shines throughout a hundred buddha-fields. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: When a bodhisattva enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), they realize ten hundred gates of clarity (*vidyā-mukha*). 1. In a single kṣaṇa, they realize one hundred samādhis. 2. With the pure divine eye, they see one hundred buddha-fields. 3.

By the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), they can shake one hundred buddha-worlds. 4. They can travel to one hundred buddha-worlds to teach and transform sentient beings. 5. They can, with a single body, manifest one hundred types of physical forms for sentient beings to behold. 6. They can bring to maturity one hundred types of sentient beings who are to be transformed. 7.

For the sake of benefiting others, they can maintain their presence in the world for a hundred kalpas. 8. They can know the events of one hundred kalpas of the past and future limits. 9. They can, through wisdom, enter the gate of clarity regarding one hundred dharmas, penetrating and comprehending them thoroughly. 10. [The tenth is as follows:]...

He is able to manifest himself in a hundred types of retinues (with each successive stage doubling in excellence). He knows the characteristics of the higher and highest stages, possesses the distinction of great vows, and has mastery over spiritual powers.
At the empowerment of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghābhiṣeka*), one shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.

Skillfully binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases, one matures sentient beings through various transformations, adorned with radiance. One attains the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-awakening (*svayambhū-ārya-sukha-samādhi-samāpatti*).

From the first stage up to the tenth stage, and even unto the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening, there is a progressive and superior advancement, fully endowed with various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and mastery over samādhis. All of this is due to the accomplishment of the two characteristics of awakening; thus, its merit is ultimately revealed.

Such is the virtue [of these vows]. Regarding the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣayapada*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, "Chapter on the Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*), states: "The Bodhisattva of the first stage, the Joyous (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*), makes a vow as vast as the *dharmadhātu*. Because these ten phrases are inexhaustible, my great vow is likewise inexhaustible: 1. the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible;

2. the realm of worlds is inexhaustible; 3. the realm of empty space is inexhaustible; 4. the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is inexhaustible; 5. the realm of *nirvāṇa* is inexhaustible; 6. the realm of the appearance of Buddhas is inexhaustible; 7. the realm of Tathāgata-wisdom is inexhaustible; 8.

the realm of the objects of the mind is inexhaustible; 9. the realm of the objective sphere entered by Buddha-wisdom is inexhaustible; 10. the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom are inexhaustible. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhi...
O Mahāsattva, you should skillfully understand the derived matter of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the derived matter of the four great elements?

Mahāmati, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this realization: "That which is ultimate truth is that the four great elements are unarisen. Regarding the non-arising of those four great elements, he performs such an investigation.
Having investigated, he realizes the limits of the conceptual construction of names and marks as being [the projections of] his own mind.
The manifestation of limits. External natures are neither existent nor non-existent; this is called the manifestation of the limits of mental construction.
That is to say, when observing the nature of the four great elements and the derived matter of the triple world, one transcends the four propositions and attains purity.

Free from "I" and "mine," they abide in their own distinct segments according to their true and specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and their unarisen specific characteristics are established. (Regarding the passage below, the Tang translation says: "How does one come to know? Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should observe those various great elements in this way...")

In reality, there is no arising. This is because the three realms are merely conceptual constructions; they are seen only by the mind, and no external objects exist. When one contemplates in this way, the primary elements and their derivatives are all devoid of intrinsic nature and transcend the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). Being free from self and what belongs to a self, one abides in the state of suchness and achieves the characteristic of non-arising.

The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "Because ultimate truth is eternally quiescent, the four great elements do not arise. Having observed that the four great elements do not arise, one then knows the limits of names and forms; these are the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind, for external natures lack inherent existence."

Therefore, one should skillfully contemplate the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*): they are fundamentally non-existent and free from the four logical extremes (*catuskoṭi*). When free from the four extremes, there is no impurity; when there is no impurity, one is free from "I" and "mine. By thoroughly understanding the dharmas of self-characteristics and temporal divisions, and abiding in the state of suchness (*yathābhūta*), one realizes the non-arising of self-characteristics.
Mahāmati, how do those four great elements give rise to derived form? It is said that the great element of moisture arises from false discrimination (*vikalpa*).

The internal and external water element arises from the delusion of moisture (the moisture is the primary creator; the internal and external water element is the derived). Regarding the statement "arising from delusion": it is because they are manifestations of one's own mind. As for "internal and external": "internal" refers to within the body;

"external" refers to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). (The following cases are to be understood similarly). The great elements arise from the delusion of capability (the Tang translation renders this as "intense heat.

If "capability" is contrasted with the aforementioned "moisture," then translating it as "intense heat" is correct. *Zongjing lu*, fascicle 69, states: "The delusion of capability refers to the calculation of the fire-element, because its nature is capable of maturing all things"). The wind element arises from the delusion of movement.

The conceptualization of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) gives rise to the internal and external wind element (*vāyudhātu*). By severing the conceptualization of form, the great elements give rise to the internal and external earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).

[Regarding "severing form": the Tang translation renders this as "dividing form. "Severing" carries the sense of "dividing. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, fascicle 4, states: "Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation; thus there is the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).

Firm awareness and the jewel [of clarity] combine to form it. Agitated clarity produces wind; when wind and gold rub against each other, the fire-circle arises. The brilliance of the jewel produces moisture; the fire-light steams upward, thus the water-circle arises. Fire ascends and water descends; through the mutual delusion of these, solidity is established, and thus the gold-circle arises. This gold-circle is precisely the earth-element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*); all are produced from deluded clarity.]

These two passages have the same meaning; however, the former is detailed while the latter is concise. "Matter (*rūpa*) and space (*ākāśa*) coexist. [The text] clings to false truths (*mithyā-satya*).

"The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) gather, and the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arises. (Regarding "matter": this refers to the aggregate of form. Regarding "space": this refers to the other four aggregates, such as sensation. "Coexist" means the gathering of the five aggregates. Because the physical body first arises through the gathering of the five aggregates, it is said that "the five aggregates gather.

As for "the derived matter produced by the four great elements arises," "derived matter" here refers to the physical body. Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) establish twenty-five principles (*tattva*) regarding these five aggregates; these are indeed false truths. This is explained in detail in the *Huayan jing shuchao* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra). The preceding passage generally treated both the internal and external, whereas this speaks only of the internal body to clarify [the point].

[This is] merely the cause for the arising of sentient beings). Mahāmati, as for consciousness (*vijñāna*): because it delights in various traces and objective spheres (*viṣaya*), it continues into other realms of existence (*gati*).

(The *Jízhù* [Collected Commentaries] says: "As for 'consciousness,' this refers to the deluded consciousness within the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandha*). Due to being deluded regarding the True Mind, the five aggregates, the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are all traces and spheres of consciousness.

Because the deluded consciousness delights in and clings to these various traces and spheres, it performs karma and undergoes birth, continuing without interruption within other realms of existence). Earth and the other four great elements (*mahābhūta*), as well as derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and so forth, have the four great elements as their conditions.

It is not due to those four great elements (*mahābhūta*). (The Wei translation says: "Mahāmati, the four great elements have causes, namely color, fragrance, taste, and touch. Mahāmati, the four great elements have no causes.

[This follows the preceding discussion on the internal and external great elements to clarify the meaning of the ultimate and conventional truths. The four great elements such as earth refer to the external vessel-world; the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) refers to the internal sense-faculties and body. "Having the conditions of the four great elements" refers to the four subtle particles—color, fragrance, taste, and touch—which serve as the generative conditions for the four great elements;

this is the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Not due to those conditions of the four great elements" clarifies the meaning of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): it means that the nature and characteristics of the four great elements are fundamentally empty, and both subject and object are unreal; therefore, they are not those conditions). Why is this so?
This refers to the characteristics of nature, form, and place; the skillful means of their formation lack inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Mahāmati, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not arise.

Mahāmati, the characteristics of nature, form, and place, along with the skillful means of their formation, arise through combination; they are not formless. (This interrogative-explanatory passage clarifies the two meanings of the ultimate and conventional truths. That is to say, the ultimate truth is quiescent, as it is free from the characteristics of subject, object, causes, and conditions;

therefore, its characteristics of length, shortness, magnitude, and so forth, as well as the skillful means of their combination, are all devoid of inherent nature. Being devoid of inherent nature, the great elements do not arise. From "Mahāmati" onwards, the meaning of the conventional truth is clarified. That is to say, all forms and characteristics...)

The eight factors of subject and object arise through the conjunction of expedient means; they are not non-existent in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-satya*), but are existent in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Therefore, they are not formless.

For this reason, the characteristics of the four great elements and the derived matter are the false conceptualizations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and not mine. (The Wei translation states: "Therefore, Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists falsely discriminate the four great elements and the four objects; such discrimination does not exist within my Dharma.

This concludes the clarification that the aforementioned four great elements and derived matter are the false conceptualizations of non-Buddhists and were not taught by the Tathāgata. "I" refers to the World-Honored One’s own designation). Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Nature and Characteristics. (Previously, it was instructed that a bodhisattva should be well-versed in the four great elements and derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*). Now that derived form has been clarified, one must further be well-versed in the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates (*skandha*). For while the previous section clarified their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), this section clarifies their specific characteristics;

therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of his own accord without being questioned). What are the self-nature and characteristics of the aggregates? They are the five aggregates. What are the five? They are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Among them, the four aggregates are non-material: namely, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Mahāmati, as for form, it consists of the four great elements and derived form.

"Each has its own distinct characteristic, Mahāmati. It is not that there are four numbers for the formless, like space. For example, space transcends numerical characteristics and is free from number, yet through false conceptualization one speaks of 'one space.
[The phrase] 'How so? below interrogates the heading; [the phrase] 'namely, the five' below enumerates the five numbers; [the passage beginning with] 'Mahāmati' below correctly explains the meaning.

The four great elements constitute the vessel-world (the environment), and the derived forms constitute the root-body (the sentient being). Because they differ in their dependent and primary natures and characteristics—such as solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—it is said that each has its own distinct characteristic. This explains the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). As for 'it is not that there are four numbers for the formless': "

That is to say, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are formless (*arūpa*). Since they are formless, how could there be the number "four"? Therefore, it is negated as "not so. If the four aggregates (*skandha*) were not form, they would be like space, transcending all numbers; hence it is said that they "transcend the characteristics of number" (*saṃkhyā-lakṣaṇa-atīta*).

Having transcended number, yet one falsely imagines them to be "one space"—how can space be called one or many? Both "one" and "many" are false. Mahāmati, such aggregates transcend the characteristics of number, are free from number, are free from existence and non-existence, and are free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
These characteristics of number are what is spoken of by the speech of fools; they do not belong to the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

This is the meaning of "wise" (xian). (This clarifies that the aggregates (*skandha*) lack intrinsic nature. It refers to the false conceptualizations of ordinary fools regarding various numerical categories. Since the aggregates fundamentally have no substance, these numerical characteristics are merely applied in vain. They are free from all four logical extremes—existence, non-existence, identity, and difference. These are the false assertions of ordinary fools; how could they apply to the noble sages?)
Mahāmati, the noble ones are like illusions, appearing as various forms and images, free from the conceptual designations of difference or non-difference.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, they are like dreams, reflections, or the bodies of persons, because they are free from difference or non-difference. Mahāmati, the realm of noble wisdom appears as the manifestation of the false imaginings of the aggregates (skandhas). (The Tang translation states:

"The noble ones merely speak of that which is created like an illusion, being nothing but a provisional designation, free from difference or non-difference. Like a dream or a reflection, there is nothing else existing apart from it. Because they do not realize the objective sphere traversed by noble wisdom, they perceive the existence of the aggregates, and discrimination manifests before them. This explains [the nature of the aggregates].

The vision of the sages and holy ones differs from that of the foolish. It is said that the sages perceive those aggregates (skandhas) and their forms as being like illusions, like shadows, and like manifestations in a dream; they are free from the characteristics of difference or non-difference because they are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

Yet, they know that the characteristics of the aggregates are fundamentally empty. In what way are they different? When provisional names appear before them, how can they be called non-different? Since the characteristics of difference and non-difference are both unattainable, it is said that they are "free from difference and non-difference. Regarding the phrase "the wisdom of the sages" and below: this refers to those who have entered the wisdom of the sages.

They likewise perceive the five aggregates as ordinary people do in their direct experience, yet there is a difference between delusion and awakening. As stated previously regarding "confused phenomena": these are manifested even by the sages, yet they are not inverted. This is identical to the meaning here. This is called the characteristic of the self-nature of the aggregates. You—
One should eliminate them. Once they have been eliminated, one teaches the Dharma of tranquility and severs all heterodox views regarding the Buddha-fields.

(This refers to the false nature of the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandhas*); one is exhorted to eliminate them so that their reality may be realized. "Once they have been eliminated" and below means that once the aggregates have ceased, the tranquil True Mind is taught, causing one to sever all worldly heterodox views.

Mahāmati, when teaching this tranquility, the view of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is purified, and one enters the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). Having entered the Immovable Stage, [one attains] the immeasurable...
They attain mastery over samādhi and the body of wondrous transformation (nirmāṇakāya). They attain the illusory-like samādhi and achieve ultimate mastery over power and clarity.
They rescue, protect, and benefit all sentient beings, just as the great earth supports and nurtures all living things.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s universal salvation of sentient beings is likewise so. (This reveals the merit of tranquility, culminating in the virtues of the fruition. "Power" refers to the ten powers; "clarity" refers to the three [clairvoyances].)

[The remainder of the text is easily understood]. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa according to the non-Buddhists (the new commentary states: the preceding section clarified awakening and wisdom to manifest the superiority or inferiority of their realized virtues;

this section clarifies nirvāṇa to distinguish the correctness or deviance of those manifested virtues. This refers to the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)—namely, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*).

What are the four? They are: 1) the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of things being neither existence nor non-existence; 2) the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of various characteristics being neither existence nor non-existence; 3) the nirvāṇa of the realization that the self-nature of specific characteristics is neither existence nor non-existence... [and so forth].
Nirvāṇa. The cessation of the continuous flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called nirvāṇa.

These are the four kinds of nirvāṇa taught by the various non-Buddhists; they are not the teaching I proclaim. (Translated from the Tang version: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa. What are the four? They are:

the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of all phenomena being without nature; the nirvāṇa of the various characteristics and natures being without nature; the nirvāṇa of awakening to the self-characteristics and natures being without nature; and the nirvāṇa of severing the continuous flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates. Mahāmati, these four nirvāṇas belong to the doctrines of the non-Buddhists; they are not what I teach.)

Regarding these four types of nirvana: the first refers to the fact that the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is non-existent as a nature; this is nirvana. The second refers to the fact that the nature of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is non-existent as a nature;

this is nirvana. The former is explained in terms of nature, while the latter is explained in terms of characteristics. Both of these constitute nirvana by realizing the state where the nature and characteristics of the observed phenomena are non-existent. The third further realizes that the observing awareness itself also lacks an existent nature; this is called nirvana. However, the wording in the text is inverted and not very clear. It should be understood that the word "awareness" (*jñāna*) ought to be placed above the two characters for "non-nature"; then it will be clear.

The fourth is the observation of the point where the flow of the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) is severed; this is called nirvana. This is similar to the perspective of the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), yet it belongs to the outsiders (*tīrthika*), not to the Two Vehicles. This is because...

Because the heterodox and the orthodox are distinct, the new interpretation takes the fourth [type of nirvana] to be that of the two vehicles; however, this is not the intended meaning of the present text. Why? Because the sutra explicitly states that there are four kinds of nirvana for non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). If one were to claim these refer to the two vehicles, then the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox would be lost.

Regarding the *Jijiu* (Collected Commentaries) citing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s "five appearances of nirvāṇa" as proof, the intent is somewhat similar; however, the citation is not precise. Why? Because the "five appearances of nirvāṇa" in the *Śūraṅgama* refers to the five locations—the desire realm and the four dhyānas—which are peaceful, secure, and pure bases of reliance, and thus are termed the "five appearances of nirvāṇa.

That text does not address the individual or common characteristics (*sva-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates (*skandha*). This refers to the meaning of their constant flux. Consciousness functions through the causal conditions of its modes of activity (*ākāra*). (Alternatively, if one interprets this as referring to the seventh consciousness, it would contradict the subsequent verse and the meaning of the Wei and Tang translations. The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) arises together with the manas, conditioned by the conceptualization and attachment to "I" and "mine.

these arise in mutual succession. (This follows the preceding text to clarify the mutual causal arising of the mind, intellect, and consciousness. "Condition. Because it is only through this that birth first occurs. "Not destroyed" and so forth clarifies the cause for the arising of the eighth consciousness. [End of section. (This concludes the intent of the inquiry. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The Awakened Sage. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) generally proceed toward the "Good Vision" (Sudarśana), wherein they sever the grasping and the grasped within their deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

This refers to what was previously stated in the sutra regarding the manifestation of practice (the text is omitted here; the reader may understand it by applying their own insight). Mahāmati, what is the common characteristic of the discrimination of the self-nature of false imagination?
It refers to: the false imagination of verbal expression, the false imagination of the objects expressed, the false imagination of marks, and the false imagination of distinctions.

The delusion of intrinsic nature, the delusion of causes, the delusion of views, the delusion of accomplishment, the delusion of arising, the delusion of non-arising, the delusion of continuity, and the delusion of bondage and non-bondage—these are called the general characteristics of the discrimination of the delusion of intrinsic nature (this is a summary enumeration;
the following is a detailed explanation). Mahāmati, what is the delusion of verbal expression? It refers to various wonderful sounds, songs, and melodies. Beautiful...
Attachment to pleasure is called the conceptualization of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*). Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of the object expressed (*abhidheya-vastu-vikalpa*)?

Marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are also manifold. Yet those various marks are false and unreal. This is called the conceptualization of marks (*lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*). Mahāmati, [this is so].
What is the discrimination of benefit? It refers to delighting in various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels;

(Taking one’s own seeds as the cause and external assistance as the condition, if one discriminates existence, then the marks of causes and conditions arise; if one discriminates non-existence, then they arise spontaneously.

Since both causes and conditions and spontaneity each have their own cause, it is called the discrimination of cause. Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of views? It refers to the evil views of existence and non-existence, identity and difference, conjunction and non-conjunction.

The false imaginings of non-Buddhists and their attachment to such imaginings are called the "imagination of views" (this term comprehensively subsumes all views of non-Buddhists, which do not exceed four categories;

This is called "accomplishing deluded conceptualization" (vikalpa). This is called the false conceptualization of bondage and non-bondage. (Bondage is named "binding," and non-bondage is named "releasing"; because false conceptualization is entangled and difficult to escape from, it is called the false conceptualization of bondage and non-bondage.)

For example, due to various cataracts, a multitude of colors appear through false conceptualization. The cataract itself is neither color nor non-color; yet, through dependent origination, it is not realized as such. (The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: This analogy refutes the reliance on causes and conditions.)

It is also of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Just as when the eyes are afflicted by various cataracts, due to the discrimination of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one perceives the manifestation of colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white; yet the cataracts themselves have neither color nor non-color. Dependent origination is like this:

because of clinging to [false appearances], it is called "non-awakening" (*abodha*). It is like refining pure gold, which becomes free from all impurities, or like the sky, which is without clouds or cataracts.

The purity of false conceptualization is likewise so. (In this passage there are two metaphors that clarify the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* [perfected nature]. That is, false conceptualization is like defiled clouds and mists, while the *pariniṣpanna* is like pure gold and empty space.

However, regarding these metaphors for the *pariniṣpanna*, one should further analyze their respective meanings. For the metaphor of empty space represents the "perfected" (*pari*), and the metaphor of pure gold represents the "nature" (*niṣpanna*). The *Jizhu* states: "This one metaphor serves to sever the falsity of that false conceptualization and the defects of dependent origination;
thus the nature of the perfected is like pure gold free from defilement, and like empty space devoid of clouds and mists. There is no nature of false conceptualization, yet there exists that...

Dependent origination, establishment, and denial—all are destroyed by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). (The *Jizhu* states: This means that the nature of false conceptualization and dependent origination is fundamentally non-existent.

If one conceives of what is not existent as existent, or conceives of what is not non-existent as non-existent, these constitute establishment and denial; both are entirely due to false conceptualization, which destroys the vision of reality. If false conceptualization were without intrinsic nature, [how could there be such errors?]
Yet there is the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). From non-nature there is nature; from the presence and absence of nature, birth occurs.

Depending upon the cause of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one attains that dependent origination. Sign and name are constantly associated, giving rise to various false conceptualizations. Ultimately unestablished, they then transcend all false conceptualizations.

(This follows the preceding verse, providing a detailed analysis of how both false conceptualization and dependent origination are necessarily without intrinsic nature. Regarding the line "false conceptualization" [and below]: it means that within the non-nature of false conceptualization...)

As for that which possesses the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there would be no capacity to produce the nature of existence. If a natureless state could produce a state of existence, then the nature of existence would arise from a natureless state. Regarding the attainment of that dependent origination by relying upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*):

following the aforementioned principle of production from the natureless, it means that dependent origination arises based on conceptual construction; only then does the characteristic of dependent origination come to be. The characteristic of dependent origination and the name "conceptual construction" constantly revolve together, giving rise to various perceptions.

If one is able to ultimately realize its true reality, then both dependent origination and conceptual construction are not established as dualities. Since these two are not established, one transcends all perceptions. Thereafter, wisdom becomes pure; this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

There are twelve kinds of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and six kinds of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). One who has personally realized suchness (*tathatā*) perceives that these possess no differentiation.

(The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "Having transcended all false conceptualizations, one achieves pure wisdom. One thoroughly understands that the twelve false conceptualizations and the six kinds of dependent origination exist merely as names and have no reality. Furthermore, within the noble realm of self-realization...")

One thoroughly understands that these flames of wisdom and the obstructions to knowledge, along with those deluded conceptualizations and dependent origination, are entirely empty and signless, without any distinction. Therefore, the subsequent text establishes the five dharmas and so forth as reality. Regarding the six factors of dependent origination, they are precisely the six kinds of causes within the aforementioned conditions and causes.
As for the five dharmas as reality, there are three kinds of self-nature; by practicing the discernment of these, one does not transcend suchness (*tathatā*). (The *Zongjing lu* says:

"By being deluded regarding the principle of suchness, names and forms are established and deluded conceptualization arises. By awakening to the suchness that is the basis of names and forms, delusion is termed wisdom; thus, there are no longer names, forms, or deluded conceptualization.")

It is solely the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*). Wisdom is established by reason of suchness, yet the essence of wisdom is also empty. Suchness relies upon wisdom for its manifestation; they have been eternally quiescent from the beginning, and thus both are empty. Now, regarding those who practice: although they may be able to distinguish between the true and the false within the five dharmas and the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), [they must realize that these too are empty].

Because they have not yet been able to empty the essence of their cognition, it is said that they do not transcend *tathatā* (suchness). The various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—these are called the arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Those various characteristics of false conceptualization arise from that dependent origination. (The "various characteristics" are the characteristics of the spreading vines of dependent origination; the "names" are the names established by false conceptualization.

Dependent origination and false conceptualization are mutually integrated through name and form, yet both arise from false conceptualization, and those various false conceptualizations, in turn, arise from conditions. Thus, the preceding text states: "Characteristics and names always follow one another, giving rise to all false conceptualizations"—this is precisely that meaning. Awakening...

Wisdom observes well; there is no object-condition and no deluded thought. Once perfected, there is no inherent nature. How can there be the awakening of deluded thought? (Awakening-wisdom is the wisdom of original enlightenment.

By means of the wisdom of original enlightenment, one skillfully observes that both the conditionally arisen and the deluded thought are devoid of the two natures. Since these two natures are absent, the nature of perfect reality is established.

Yet, although it is established, one does not form the notion of its establishment; therefore, it is said that "once perfected, there is no inherent nature. If even perfection is not posited, how could there again be the awakening of deluded thought? That self-nature of deluded thought establishes two [natures].

Intrinsic nature manifests as various forms through deluded thought; it is the realm of the pure sages. (Within deluded thought, one establishes the two natures of dependent origination and deluded thought.

If deluded thought is not eliminated, then within dependent origination, various manifestations appear; yet these are not true manifestations, for they are seen by means of deluded thought. If all deluded thoughts are purified, this constitutes the realm of the sages.

Deluded thought is like painted colors; dependent origination is reckoned as deluded thought. (The Collected Commentary states: Deluded thought is like a painting; although various forms and images exist with distinctions, they lack substantial reality. Sentient beings cling to dependent origination...)

It arises and produces false conceptualization (vikalpa) in exactly the same way. If it were distinct from false conceptualization, it would rely upon the treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). [The New Translation states:

"This clarifies that in the Buddha-dharma, one knows that the dependent origination of birth and death arises from the mind of one's own false conceptualization. If one calculates that the phenomena of birth and death—whether existent or non-existent—are distinct from false conceptualization and arise from atoms (*paramāṇu*), the principle of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), or a sovereign lord (*īśvara*), this is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists.

False conceptualization speaks of what is conceived; it arises due to the conjunction of views. [The Wei translation says: "False conceptualization speaks of false conceptualization; it arises due to the conjunction of views. This means that by means of the subject that conceives, one speaks of the object that is conceived.]

All arise from the conjunction of cognition and its object (*jñāna* and *jñeya*). To be free from these two types of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is what constitutes perfection. (Regarding "to be free from the two types of false conceptualization": this refers to the preceding duality of subject and object.

Once one is free from these two conceptions, that is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). This is because the two conceptions of subject and object are precisely the dependent origination (*paratantra*) and the imagined (*parikalpita*) natures.)
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) and the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

If I and the other bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle, we shall not rely on others to penetrate the Buddha-dharma. (This was the intent of Mahāmati’s question, following the preceding ten [verses].)

In the second chapter on "Discrimination," there is the departure from discrimination and the arrival at the meaning of the noble self-realization (*pratyātma-ārya-artha*), which has not yet been explained in detail. Therefore, I now again request an exposition of the meaning of noble self-realization. The meaning of noble self-realization is the principle (*tattva*), while the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the teaching (*śāsana*); thus, this is a request concerning both the subject and the object.

From here below, Mahāmati describes the benefit of his repeated request, stating that one attains mastery over the Buddha-dharma not through another. What is called the Buddha-dharma is precisely self-realization. Because of skillful self-realization, one penetrates the Buddha-dharma;

apart from realization there is no Buddha, and apart from mind there is no dharma. Hence it is said: "one attains mastery over the Buddha-dharma not through another. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect upon this well."
"I shall explain this for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your teaching. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"That which was known by the former sages has been transmitted from one to another. It is the absence of intrinsic nature in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in a solitary and quiet place, observes through self-awakening and does not rely on others, he becomes free from the conceptual constructions of views; ascending higher and higher, he enters the stage of the Tathāgata. This is called..."

The Characteristics of the Noble Wisdom of Self-Awareness. (From "Next, the Buddha told... onwards; the Wei translation says: "The Buddha told Mahāmati: 'Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, free from the conceptualized characteristics of dharmas as taught by various masters who rely on the names and words of the Āgamas, should dwell in a quiet place, sitting alone and contemplating with their own internal wisdom.

They observe all dharmas without following the teachings of others, remaining free from the false characteristics of various views, and should diligently practice to enter the stage of the Tathāgata and attain the progressively higher realized wisdom.

Mahāmati, this is called the characteristic of the practice of noble wisdom realized within one's own body. ○ Previously, Mahāmati asked about self-awareness. Self-awareness has no other; it is the absence of intrinsic nature in delusive thought (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the Buddhas transmit [the teaching] regarding delusive thought through that which is known by themselves."* *Note: The original Chinese text contains a commentary on the preceding section regarding Mahāmati’s inquiry into self-awareness and the nature of delusive thought.*

The Bodhisattva Asvabhāva causes them to take self-awakening as their object of cognition; it is not an external seeking. However, that which was known by the former sages is likewise only self-awakening. If bodhisattvas wish to know this self-awakening, they should employ skillful means. What are these skillful means? They are: to distance oneself from bustle and clamor, to dwell alone in a quiet room, and to observe based on one's own mind.

By abandoning all false imaginings and comprehending a portion of delusive sentiment, one realizes a portion of self-awakening. Advancing higher and higher, one enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata, where the noble wisdom of self-awakening is perfected and consummated.

This is what is called the bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-awakening. (This was the prior answer regarding the characteristics of self-awakening. Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of the One Vehicle? It is said that one attains—
The awakening to the path of the One Vehicle: I speak of the One Vehicle. What is meant by attaining the awakening to the path of the One Vehicle?

It refers to the non-arising of deluded thoughts regarding the state of reality as it truly is—that is, regarding the grasping subject and the grasped object. This is called the awakening of the One Vehicle. (The preceding passage clarifies self-awakening; next, the One Vehicle awakening is explained.

Self-awakening refers to original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Awakening within the One Vehicle, proceeding from partial severance and partial realization to ultimate perfection, refers to initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). Thus, within the path of the One Vehicle, when one awakens to the reality of those deluded thoughts concerning the grasping subject and the grasped object, then initial and original awakening are non-dual.)

Both subject and object are empty; therefore, one does not give rise to deluded thoughts. From the beginning to the end, nothing is apart from the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Hence it is called the "Awakening to the Path of the One Vehicle. This is the answer regarding the characteristics of the One Vehicle.

Mahāmati, this awakening to the One Vehicle cannot be attained by any others—neither non-Buddhists, nor Śrāvakas, nor Pratyekabuddhas, nor even by the Brahmā kings—with the sole exception of the Tathāgata.

For this reason, it is designated as the "One Vehicle. (The awakening to the One Vehicle is not shared with the various vehicles; the One Vehicle can encompass all vehicles, whereas the various vehicles do not include the One Vehicle.)

For this reason, those of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cannot attain it. Now, the Way is not distant from people; rather, people distance themselves from it. If one can set their will solely upon the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), who would not realize and witness it?

These words were spoken by the World-Honored One to urge on those of the two vehicles and the various non-Buddhist devas and others, in order to manifest the excellence of the One Vehicle. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak of the two vehicles and not the One Vehicle? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because they lack the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa by themselves, I do not speak of all Śrāvakas [as being of the One Vehicle]."

They hear of the One Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. Regarding the phrase "because they do not possess the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa by themselves": this means that the Tathāgata universally delivers sentient beings through the path of the One Vehicle, causing them all to attain extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.

Within the One Vehicle, there is no dharma for entering nirvāṇa by oneself; whereas those of the two vehicles seek nirvāṇa exclusively for themselves and do not deliver sentient beings. Therefore, O World-Honored One, among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the One Vehicle is not spoken of.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain liberation because they are tamed by the Tathāgata and granted the skillful means of tranquility, rather than by their own power.

Because of this power, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is not taught [to them]. Since those of the two vehicles loathe existence and cling to emptiness, and they cherish the three [vehicles] while fearing the one, the Tathāgata employs the skillful means (*upāya*) of tranquility to subdue and ripen them;

only thereafter does he lead them back to the place of treasure. That those who have now attained liberation through tranquility do so by means of the Tathāgata’s skillful means rather than by their own intellectual power—therefore, the One Vehicle is not immediately taught to them.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and karma have not been severed, the One Vehicle is not taught to all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. (The preceding text [deals with] them...)

Regarding what has been cultivated, the reason for not mentioning "intention" (*āśaya*) was explained previously; now, it is further clarified that [the Buddha] does not mention intention because of the obstacles associated with those [cultivations]. As for "the habit-energies of karma being unsevered," this refers to the śrāvakas, who sever only the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). Although the pratyekabuddhas attenuate the habit-energies, they still remain intoxicated by their meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).

For this reason, he did not immediately teach the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Because they do not realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and have not yet transcended death in discrete segments (*paricchedamaraṇa*), he taught the Three Vehicles. (This reveals the fault of shallow realization, clarifying the reason for teaching the Three Vehicles.

That is to say, although those of the Two Vehicles have attained the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), they do not realize the selflessness of phenomena and have not yet escaped death through transformation (*pariṇāmikamaraṇa*); for these reasons, he provisionally taught the Three Vehicles and did not discourse on the meaning of the One. As for "death in discrete segments,"...)

The translations by the Wei and Tang dynasties render this as "death through transformation" (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*). This is because those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) only realize the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and thus only transcend "death in segments" (*bhājana-maraṇa*). The current reading, "not transcending death in segments," is likely a scribal error from the translation hall.

Mahāmati, when all those [bodhisattvas] have severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the faults arising from afflictions (*kleśa*), and have realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), they sever all habitual tendencies of the faults arising from afflictions.

However, their attachment to the flavor of the bliss of samādhi prevents them from realizing the non-substantiality of the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). Having failed to realize it, they enter back into [the cycle].
In the supramundane, most excellent, untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), where all requisites are fulfilled, one shall attain the inconceivable and sovereign *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the phrase "arising from afflictions and speech": "arising" (*qi*) carries the meaning of movement, as well as the meaning of birth and cessation; it pertains to the two delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*). Because these cause the mind to undergo birth, cessation, and fluctuation, they are called "arising. The passage beginning with "That one...

means that once those Śrāvakas have severed the afflictions of views and thought along with their residual habits (*vāsanā*), they attain the blissful dwelling of *samādhi*. Having already given rise to untainted awakening-wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) within the realm of the partial truth of non-nature, and having attained this awakening, they are further able to ascend and progress upward, entering that untainted awakening of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The Way. Having fulfilled the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one shall attain the inconceivable Dharma-body of a Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The vehicle of the devas and Brahmā, the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—I have taught these various vehicles as long as the mind continues to turn.
These vehicles are not ultimate; when that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor one who rides it, and no establishment of vehicles.
I teach this as the One Vehicle. (This is a reiterative verse summarizing the meaning of the One Vehicle and the various vehicles. The prose says "only...")

Except for the Tathāgata, all others are not ultimate. Now, the verse further states that even this Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), if there is a turning of the mind, is likewise not ultimate; this is merely to eliminate the traces of the "three and one.

If that mind of three and one is forgotten, and the vehicles of subject and object cease, then there is no vehicle to be established and nothing dependent to be forgotten. That which is not "one" in contrast to "three" is the true One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). "Vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the dharma being traversed, while the "traveler" (*yāyin*) refers to the person who traverses it.

Because they guide sentient beings, various vehicles are explained through differentiation. There are three kinds of liberation, as well as the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and [the selflessness of] afflictions (*kleśa*).

Through wisdom and so forth, liberation is attained through detachment. (This is the reason for the threefold repetition in verse. The first two lines are easily understood. As for the three kinds of liberation, they are emptiness, signlessness, [and wishlessness].)

There is no aspiration. The phrase "the selflessness of phenomena" (*dharmanairātmya*) should include the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*). "Afflictions and wisdom" refers to the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). The word "etc. encompasses the five dharmas, the eight consciousnesses, and the three natures. The final line follows from the preceding three:

it means that upon attaining liberation, all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) naturally depart. It is like a piece of wood floating on the ocean, which constantly turns with the waves; so too is the ignorance of the śrāvaka.
Swept away by the wind of marks (*nimitta*), their active afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished, yet the delusion of residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) remains.

(The floating wood is a metaphor for the delusion of the Śrāvaka; the waves, for the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); the wind of marks, for the characteristics of phenomena [*dharmalakṣaṇa*]. "Marks" refers to the phenomena themselves, while "wind" is a metaphor. This means that for the deluded Śrāvakas who follow the teachings, what they know has not been severed and the waves of consciousness have not been stilled. They are tossed about by the wind of phenomenal marks; thus, although their active afflictions are extinguished, the delusion of residual habit-energy is not yet severed.

This reveals that although the afflictions within the realm [of desire, form, and formlessness] have been severed, the ignorance beyond the realm has not yet been subdued. Therefore, the ancient commentary states: "Because the Śrāvakas sever the afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), it is said that 'active afflictions arise and are extinguished'").

Furthermore, because they have not yet severed ignorance, they are said to possess "the delusion of residual habit-energies. They relish the bliss of samādhi and dwell securely within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
Having no ultimate destination, yet likewise not retreating, they attain bodies of various samādhis and remain thus for as long as an eon without awakening.

(This verse describes the fault of dwelling in the bliss of samādhi; it refers to those of the Two Vehicles who dwell within the untainted realm of partial truth attained through samādhi. Consequently, they lack the resolve to advance toward the ultimate goal. Nevertheless, they do not return to the realms of birth-and-death, becoming so enamored with these bodies of samādhi that they remain as such.)

"Like a fish caught in ice, even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they still do not realize the fault of clinging to the small [vehicle]. This is the World-Honored One’s ultimate expression regarding the folly of those stagnating in quiescence, intended to rouse them toward the Great Vehicle.
"Just as a person who is intoxicated awakens only after the wine has worn off, so too is the awakening to the Dharma: one attains the unsurpassed body of a Buddha.

(This verse describes how, having awakened from that attachment, one enters again into the supreme, non-outflow state and attains the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas. "Wine" is a metaphor for the samādhi of partial truth; "the intoxicated person" is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles who indulge in the bliss of samādhi without awakening. It means awakening from that intoxication.)
It is said that when the wine has been digested, one turns the mind toward the Great [Vehicle] and advances to attain the Dharma-body).
*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ṭīkā-saṃskṛta* Scroll Four; *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ṭīkā-saṃskṛta* Scroll Five.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra during the Liu Song dynasty;
revised by the later scholar Śramaṇa Guangmo of Huxing under the Imperial Ming;
and verified by Yuan Huang of Xiali, Grand Officer of the Summer Ministry.
The First Chapter of the "Essence of All Buddha-Speech," Part Three.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "I shall explain the characteristics of the various types of mind-made bodies."

I shall now explain. (At the end of the second fascicle, regarding the characteristics of the One Vehicle: it means that when a bodhisattva enters the supramundane, most excellent, untainted realm, they shall attain the Tathāgata’s sovereign Dharma-body, which is the present mind-made body.)

This is precisely what is possessed within the Dharmakāya. As Bodhisattvas practice and progress through each stage up to the stage of the Tathāgata, they successively attain the three kinds of mind-made bodies; therefore, I shall now explain this. Listen attentively, listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three? They are: the mind-made body produced by the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi;
the mind-made body produced by the realization of the self-nature of dharmas; and the mind-made body produced spontaneously according to its kind, which is without effortful activity. Thus he spoke.

The practitioner clearly understands the characteristics of progressive advancement from the first stage upward and attains three kinds of bodies. Regarding the "three kinds of mind-made bodies," the subsequent text states: from the first stage to the fifth stage, one attains the body of the bliss of samādhi;

at the eighth stage, one attains the body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas. As for the "body born simultaneously with its kind," this refers to realizing the joy of the Dharma realized by the Buddha’s own self-authentication; it should be attained somewhere between the stages of *sābhisaṃskāra-anābhoga* and *anabhisaṃskāra-anābhoga*.

Regarding these three kinds of bodies, the three translations of the present sutra consistently speak of attaining them "vertically" (through successive stages) and do not mention possessing them "horizontally" (simultaneously). Upon careful examination of the stages from the first upward, each stage manifests bodies belonging to the ten realms to skillfully deliver sentient beings, and each also mutually possesses the ten *pāramitās* and other dharmas. How could this be...?

Regarding the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), one should understand that they are possessed simultaneously rather than sequentially; this is established by principle, though the present sutra omits it for brevity. Furthermore, at the beginning of the second sutra, the mind-made body was briefly explained without yet revealing its universal characteristics; now, however, they are distinguished as being of three kinds.
Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi? It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages (*bhūmi*).

This is because of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi. (Regarding "the bliss of samādhi": the Sanskrit term *samādhi* is translated as "correct concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*) and also as "correct reception" (*samyak-saṃprajanya*). Correct concentration...)

"... clarifies the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Right reception" (*samyak-pratigraha*) specifies the object received within concentration. Since the current text already mentions *samādhi* and then repeats the term "right reception," it means that the practitioner delights in right reception within *samādhi*; alternatively, it may be a case of citing both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms together.

As for "mind-born" (*manomaya*), it means arriving immediately according to one's will and cannot be detained by external things; thus it is named "mind-born. Various [states] of one’s own mind become tranquil, abiding steadily in the ocean of the mind.

The arising of the marks of the wave-consciousness does not occur. Knowing that the nature of the objective realm manifested by one’s own mind is neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the "mind-made body born of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi.

(Regarding the phrase "the various [objects] are stilled within one's own mind": this refers to the object of the bliss of samādhi. "Various" refers to all sensory objects. "Stilled within one's own mind" means that all objects are manifested by one's own mind and do not flow outward;

thus they attain stillness. Abiding in the ocean of the mind, the waves of consciousness do not arise. Because one knows that external things manifested by one's own mind lack inherent nature, one attains concentration therein; the object does not obstruct the mind, which is termed the "bliss of samādhi").
Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas?
It refers to the eighth stage, wherein one observes and realizes that all dharmas, such as illusions and the like, are entirely non-existent.

Thereupon, the body and mind undergo a transformation, and one attains the illusion-like samādhi as well as other gateways of samādhi, along with immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and clarities, adorned as if with exquisite flowers, swift as one wishes, just like—
Like illusions, dreams, the moon reflected in water, or images in a mirror, they are neither created nor derived from creation;

yet, like all forms consisting of primary and derivative elements, they are fully adorned with various limbs and features, entering all buddha-fields and assemblies because they have realized the nature of phenomena.

This is called the mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas (*dharmasvabhāva*). Regarding "realization of the self-nature of dharmas": "dharmas" refers to all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane. The first instance of the word "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the essential nature of these dharmas;

the second instance of the word "nature" (*bhāva*) refers to the meaning of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). This means to fully awaken to the reality of the essential nature of all dharmas. The reality of the essential nature is the absence of any marks; this markless mark is the true mark of all dharmas.

When Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage realize the true mark of all dharmas, they are able to transform the bodies of the five aggregates and the minds of the eight consciousnesses, thereby accomplishing the body and mind of the reality-limit of the self-nature of dharmas. "Attaining the illusion-like samādhi" means that they have awakened to the fact that all dharmas are like illusions.

In every thought-moment, one accords with the illusory-like [nature], thereby attaining this samādhi. Furthermore, because there are immeasurable gateways to samādhi, it says "and others. Regarding "immeasurable marks, powers, and so forth": "marks" refers to the primary and secondary marks; "powers" refers to supernormal powers; and "clarity" refers to the radiance of the body.

This means that the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) has its form adorned by the primary and secondary marks and luminosity, like exquisite celestial flowers, thereby manifesting the excellence of these marks. Regarding "like illusions, dreams, and so forth," it means that the manifested bodies leave no trace of obstruction. It is not something produced by fabrication.

Regarding "creation" and so forth: this refers to the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). Although it is not composed of the eight factors of primary and derivative matter, it arises according to the will, possessing all forms, limbs, and members, fully adorned with the characteristics of both primary and derivative matter.

Bodhisattvas, mounting upon this bodily form, proceed everywhere without obstruction, entering universally into the great assemblies of all Buddha-fields to transform beings without ceasing. Such merits arise entirely from the thorough penetration of the self-nature of phenomena; this is called the "mind-made body arising from the realization of the self-nature of dharmas.
Mahāmati, what is the "mind-made body arising spontaneously by birth and without effort"? It refers to the realization of all Buddha-dharmas.

Taking as its object the characteristic of the bliss spontaneously attained—this is called the "body born of mental attention that arises simultaneously with one's kind and is without deliberate effort" (*jāti-sahaja-anabhisamskāra-manasikāra-nirmita-kāya*).

Regarding "arising simultaneously with one's kind" (*jāti-sahaja*): from the Buddhas above down to the multitudes of sentient beings below, manifesting universally according to their respective types is what is meant by "arising simultaneously. Regarding "without deliberate effort" (*anabhisamskāra*): this refers to the flourishing of diverse kinds and the universal assembly of myriad forms; acting while there is no acting, and acting while there is no action. It is like spring arriving in the human world, where the ten thousand sprouts all burst forth together;

yet what does spring do? This is precisely what is meant by "without deliberate effort. The *Jízhù* (Collected Annotations) states: "It means awakening to and comprehending all the dharmas realized by the Buddhas. Taking as its object the characteristic of the bliss spontaneously attained, the bodies of a thousand kinds and ten thousand types [manifest] within the state of non-action."

They function through activity; they act without volitional effort, arising simultaneously, like the unimpeded manifestation of a wish-fulfilling gem. Mahāmati, you should observe, realize, and train yourself in those three types of bodily manifestations.

The birth-body (*janma-kāya*). (This phrase [simultaneously] praises the two bodies—the body of the intrinsic nature of awakening and the body born of its kind; since the brief text subsumes these two meanings, it says "various").
Adorned with flowers of mastery (*vaśitā-puṣpa-vyūha*). (The meaning of this praise is clear).

The Sūtra states: Regarding the five Avīci hells (Uninterrupted Hells), there are: first, the uninterruptedness of proceeding toward the fruit; second, the uninterruptedness of suffering; third, the uninterruptedness of time; fourth, the uninterruptedness of life; and fifth, the uninterruptedness of form. This means that those within the hells experience these five conditions such that there is no interval between them.

The *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) states: "The World-Honored One once said that those who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karman*) enter the Avīci Hell immediately; yet he also said that those who perform the five deeds of immediate retribution do not enter the Avīci Hell.
Therefore, this question was raised. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect upon it well. I shall explain it for you.

Hell is retribution; this means that by committing these five karmas, one is moved to experience the retribution of the hells. Now, those who give birth to us are our parents. How could it be anything less than a singular transgression? Furthermore, how can one who commits slaughter not be committing an act of rebellion? Their kindness toward me exceeds that of my own parents; how much more so, then, for one who commits slaughter against them—not to commit an act of rebellion would be impossible. It is only natural that such a person falls into the Avīci Hell. The Saṃgha, through the supreme precepts of the three groups (*tripiṭaka*) and the practice of communal harmony, is the most honored among humans and devas.

"We should take refuge in him; he is our protector and reliance. How much more so, then, to shed his blood with an evil mind? This is the height of treachery; it is only natural that one who does so will fall into the Avīci Hell. However, shedding the Buddha’s blood can lead to either a wholesome or an unwholesome path. For example, when Jīvaka applied acupuncture to draw blood, the Buddha’s illness was swiftly cured."

Drawing blood with a wholesome mind does not constitute a *ānantarya* (heinous) offense; therefore, it is distinguished by the two characters "evil mind. it concerns those who do not enter hell despite committing the five *ānantarya* acts, based on the principle that performing the *ānantaryas* in a forward direction serves as an analogy for those who perform them in a reverse direction. Mahāmati, what is the mother of sentient beings?

It is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) which leads to further rebirth, accompanied by greed and delight, established just as one relies upon a mother. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and delight (*nandī*) rely upon one another and continue through the three periods of time, just as a child depends on its mother to achieve existence. Ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the father, giving birth to the village of the sense bases (*āyatana*). To sever these two roots is called "killing father and mother.

Ignorance is the source of successive births and possesses the quality of yang and masculinity; therefore, it is metaphorically called the father. Delusion and craving are the beginning of sustaining life and possess the quality of yin and femininity; therefore, they are metaphorically called the mother. "Person" refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*);

"bases" refers to the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*); and "village" is a metaphor for that which ignorance relies upon. ...the mother). Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not manifest; they are like the poison of a rat that erupts. To definitively sever those is called "killing an Arhat" (The *Jizhu* [Collected Notes] states:

This constitutes the schism of the Saṃgha. (The *Jizhu* says: "Dissimilar characteristics" refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. (The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: This refers to failing to realize that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), whether their specific or general characteristics, are manifestations of one’s own mind and are unreal. To now take this body as a Buddha—since the seven consciousnesses are the objects of deluded awakening—one gives rise to defilement based upon them. Defilement is termed "blood.

By means of the three untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one cuts off that defiled deluded awakening of the seven consciousnesses; this is called "maliciously shedding the blood from a Buddha's body").

this refers to the fact that phenomena and principle are without interval [uninterrupted], being entirely equal. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are external immediate transgressions which I shall now explain.

This refers to what was previously described as "immediate" (*ānantarya*).
