Apart from these, there are other manifestations of transformative power (*nirmāṇa-rddhi*) that manifest immediate realization; namely, the transformative power of Śrāvakas, the transformative power of Bodhisattvas, and the transformative power of Tathāgatas.

By means of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), for the sake of those who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), he manifests such acts as the immediate transgressions through supernatural transformation in order to eliminate their doubts and regrets, and to encourage them toward awakening.
(Excluding these refers to excluding the actual commission of the five external *ānantarya* acts. "The remaining transformations" refers to the noble ones of the three vehicles;

The noble ones of the Three Vehicles all possess supernatural powers and manifest such deeds as the immediate realization of the Truth (ānantarya-samāpatti); there is only a distinction between their breadth and narrowness. (The Wei translation says: "If one commits the five kinds of *ānantarya* crimes, one will ultimately never attain realization of the factors conducive to the human path. Except for those who realize that all is the manifestation of their own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*), who are free from the delusions regarding the body and wealth, and who are free from the grasping of "I" and "mine," or who at some time encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Craving is called the mother; ignorance is the father. Awareness of objects is the Buddha; the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) are the Arhats.

one does not enter the Avīci Hell. (The *Jízhù* states: "The preceding passage was intended to reveal the five internal immediate transgressions for the purpose of realizing the true Dharma. anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, stinginess, deception, guile, arrogance, harmfulness, lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, incorrect awareness, regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra. This refers to those afflictions that follow and do not abandon their objects—whether favorable or adverse—of such a kind; these are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). As explained in detail in that treatise, the present text states that to be aware of these dharmas without being obscured by them is called the "awakening of a Buddha.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who realize this dharma are also called Buddhas. For these reasons, I teach the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

(That is to say, those of the two vehicles who are able to attain this dharma of being free from hindrances are called Buddhas. However, it is not only those of the two vehicles who are Buddhas; even sentient beings of the six realms who are able to attain this dharma are also called Buddhas. For example, the dragon girl deeply penetrated the nature of sin and merit.)

Suddenly awakening to the Buddha-vehicle, in a mere instant they attain perfect enlightenment. This is what is meant by saying that the Way is not distant from people; it is only through the realization or non-realization [of this truth] that distance or proximity is established.

these and other hundreds of thousands of births are taught in the sūtras. (King Mandhātṛ is rendered as King Śīrṣajanman in the Wei and Tang translations. The seer Sunetra is rendered as the seer Vināśa in the Wei translation.)

Wisdom. Because of these four equalities, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words amidst the great assembly:

[Voice]. Because they share the same gate of the One Vehicle, the same true essence, and even the same mind, the same wisdom, the same awakening, and the same path.

Equality of names (nāma-samatā). [The Tang translation says: "It means that my name is 'Buddha,' and all Tathāgatas are also named 'Buddha. There is no distinction in the name 'Buddha'; this is called equality of names. What is equality of speech (vāk-samatā)?

It refers to the fact that both I and those Buddhas have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). Because they are supple, faith and the others become faculties (*indriya*); when these faculties increase, they become powers (*bala*). The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are distinguished, and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is the correct practice. These are collectively illustrated by analogy: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like the earth; the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are like seeds; right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) is the planting; the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are like the emerging sprouts;

the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are like the taking root; the five powers (*pañcabala*) are like the growth of stems and leaves; the seven factors of enlightenment are the blossoming flowers; and the eightfold noble path is the ripening fruit. That which is realized by all Buddhas is no different;

this is called the equality of dharmas (*dharmasamatā*). Briefly stated, the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha-dharma is called the four equalities. Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, amidst the great assembly...

He uttered these words therein (concluding the preceding fourfold equality to clarify the intent of his proclamation). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and I—these four are equal. For these reasons, I have taught this for my disciples.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has said: 'From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment...'"
"Up until the night he entered parinirvāṇa, during that interval, not even a single word was spoken; nor was anything already said or yet to be said.

It is not the case that this is what the Buddha taught. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, say that this is not what the Buddha taught?

(The phrase 'attaining perfect enlightenment on such-and-such a night and entering nirvāṇa' refers to the World-Honored One’s demonstration of the two matters of the beginning and the end of his life.)"

This is because it encompasses all within it. The term "someone" (*mò*) is a generalizing expression. The traces of the World-Honored One’s birth, attainment of the Way, and entry into *nirvāṇa* are detailed in such scriptures as the *Ruiying jing* (Sūtra of Auspicious Responses) and the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra), as well as in the *Zhou shu yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou) and the *Kaifu sanbao lu* (Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era).

Regarding the discrepancies in the dates recorded therein, I dare not presume which is correct; those who seek the ultimate truth should examine them for themselves. Now, our Buddha manifested his birth for eighty years, during which he preached the Dharma in various ways. Why, then, is it said that he did not speak a single word? It is because the *prajñā* is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of written words.

If there were anything spoken, it would constitute slandering the Buddha. As it is said: "There is no dharma that can be spoken; this is called the Buddha's teaching. Thus, Mahāmati has heard throughout that the One Vehicle is neither speech nor letters; therefore, it is described by means of non-speaking.
(This is stated as a question). The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is because of two dharmas that I speak thus. What are the two dharmas?

They are the dharma of self-attainment (*pratyātma-adhigama*) and the dharma of primordial abiding (*pūrvasthita-dharma*). These are called the two dharmas. It is because of these two dharmas that I speak thus.

(The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "That which is realized without depending on another is called 'self-attainment'; that which is understood as having no point of origin is called 'primordial abiding'). What is the dharma of self-attainment? If that Tathāgata..."

What has been attained by him, I too have attained; there is neither increase nor decrease. It is the ultimate realm of the Dharma realized through self-attainment, free from verbal conceptualization and free from the two paths of letters.

(Regarding "condition" [pratyaya]: it is to accord with it through the mind. "Dharma realized through self-attainment" means to attain it silently within the mind such that it cannot be expressed in words.

As a Chan practitioner says: "It is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself. This is called the Dharma realized through self-attainment. To accord with principle through the mind, so that principle and wisdom merge, and contemplation and speech unite in the conditionless condition—only then can it be called a "condition. The phrase "If he... refers to the fact that the Dharma realized through self-attainment does not come from another.)

It can be attained. Yet, one cannot bestow it upon me. For this reason, the Buddhas can be attained and I too can be attained; for there is no increase in the Buddha and no decrease in me. Because one personally realizes the ultimate realm, which is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, and wherein both the speaker and the spoken characteristics cannot enter, it is said that "one is detached from the two courses.
What is the primordially abiding dharma? It refers to the path of the ancient sages, like the nature of gold, silver, and so forth—the *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding.

(The passage beginning with "it refers to the ancient" is translated in the Wei version as: "The primordial path is level and smooth, just as gold, silver, pearls, and other treasures exist in that place. Mahāmati, this is called the original nature of dharmas.")

The Abode. ○ The "ancient path of the sages" refers to the meaning of the "original path" as described in the Wei translation; it signifies the path traversed by ancient sages that is inherently and eternally present. This is the true principle of the *dharmadhātu*, which neither increases nor decreases, and neither shifts nor changes.

It is like the nature of gold or silver: it does not diminish while within the ore, nor does it increase once extracted from the ore. From antiquity until the present, this path remains eternally present without any alteration; thus it is called the "primordially abiding dharma" (*pūrvasthita-dharma*).

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the *dharmadhātu* remains eternally present, like the road leading to that city. (That is to say, the eternally abiding path of the *dharmadhātu* exists whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or not.)

What is called "unchanging" is like the nature of gold and silver. It is primordially and eternally present; whether it is extracted from the ore or not extracted from the ore, its nature does not shift. It is like one who travels toward a city along a path: the road is as it has always been, and it is not subject to increase or decrease based on whether one walks upon it or not.
For example, suppose a man traveling through a vast wilderness sees a level, direct road leading to an ancient city;
he then follows it into the city and experiences bliss according to his wishes. Mahāmati, what do you think? Did that man create this path and the various things within the city?
"Is it pleasant? He replied, "No. (Regarding the phrase "In your opinion," the Wei translation says: "Does that person first create this path, or first create the various adornments?

The man traveling through the wilderness is a metaphor for all sentient beings traveling through the wilderness of birth and death. The comparison of birth and death to a wilderness is because birth and death are vast and boundless, like traveling through a wilderness where fear often arises. Seeing the level, direct road leading toward the ancient city is a metaphor for awakening to the principle of the eternally abiding *dharmadhātu*.

Immediately entering the city is a metaphor for advancing toward *nirvāṇa*. Experiencing wish-fulfilling bliss is a metaphor for realizing the bliss that accords with the nature of reality. However, that path and bliss of the *dharmadhātu* are originally...)
Nevertheless, it exists (for it is not something produced for the first time by a practitioner). The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I and all the Buddhas of the past—the Dharma-realm is eternally abiding—and it is likewise so" (as explained in the preceding note). Therefore, it is said:

"From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I entered parinirvāṇa, in the interval between those two, I have not uttered a single word; nor have I spoken, nor shall I speak."
(Explaining the reason for not speaking, as previously mentioned). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa, during this interval in between, I have not spoken anything at all.
(This reiterates the reason for not speaking). Because the Dharma realized by myself abides, I have made this statement. That Buddha and...

I am entirely without distinction. (Regarding the first phrase, the character "abiding" [住] refers to the primordial abiding [本住]. The single character "Dharma" encompasses both the meanings of self-attained and primordial abiding.
The latter two phrases mean that the dharmas attained by all Buddhas and by Śākyamuni are entirely equal.)
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the World-Honored One:

"I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may be free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

(The mental measure of the world mostly falls into two views; therefore, Mahāmati requests the two characteristics of existence and non-existence so that he and others may leave behind these two afflictions and realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.)"
[...Bodhi]. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There are two kinds of reliance in this world: namely, reliance on existence and reliance on non-existence. These fall into the categories of 'nature' and 'non-nature,' and their views do not depart from the characteristic of departure. [Falling into nature is existence; falling into non-]"
The nature [of things] is non-existent. These two views are both not free from desire, yet they perceive the appearance of being free from desire.

Mahāmati, how does the world rely on existence? It means that the world arises from causes and conditions; it is not non-existent. From existence there is arising, not from non-existence. (This expresses the view of existence. That is to say, their view is:

"The world arises through the combination of causes and conditions to produce all phenomena; it is not non-existent," meaning it is not nothingness. Furthermore, it reiterates the preceding phrase: "All phenomena arise from existence; they do not arise from non-existence. Mahāmati, they speak in this manner.

This refers to what is called the "causeless world" (the Buddha’s judgment is that such a view falls into the error of causeless arising. This means that if one seeks the nature of existence from the very beginning and finds it unobtainable, then there is fundamentally no cause;
because there is fundamentally no cause, there is likewise no cause at the end, and thus one falls into the view of causelessness). Mahāmati, what is meant by the world depending on non-existence?

It means that after having experienced the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, one subsequently engages in false conceptualization and attachment regarding whether the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion exists or does not exist. (This expresses the calculation of non-existence; that is to say, after one has experienced the nature of greed and so forth...)

When one seeks greed and the like, they are unfindable; thus they are reckoned as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Mahāmati, if one does not grasp at the existence of an intrinsic nature, then the characteristics of that nature are quiescent.

Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas do not grasp at the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent. (This means that because those [fools] hold a view of non-existence, they fail to grasp at the existence of the nature of greed and so forth; thus, the nature of greed and the rest is quiescent in its characteristics.

Because it is quiescent, they then compare the Buddhas and the followers of the two vehicles to themselves and conclude that these also do not grasp at the nature of greed and the rest, and thus reckon them to be non-existent. This is what is called the speech of those with overweening pride.)

[The Buddha] said: "Now, regarding whether [the objects of grasping] exist or do not exist, the heretics privately claim that the Buddha and those of the Two Vehicles do not grasp at the existence or non-existence of greed and so forth. That which they do not grasp is likewise categorized as non-existent. Thus, it is known that by relying on this 'non-existence,' the heretics possess overweening pride;

their harm is no small matter. For this reason, the subsequent passage denounces them as 'destroyers'. "Mahāmati, among these, who is the destroyer? (Here, "among these" refers to the two views of existence and non-existence mentioned above.

The Buddha asks which of these two is the destroyer. A "destroyer" is like a scorched seed or a broken jar; because they have no further utility, they are called destroyers. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if they grasp at greed..."

[Regarding] the nature of hatred and delusion, one does not subsequently grasp them again. (The Tang translation states: "Mahāmati said: 'If there is a nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, and one subsequently grasps at their non-existence, this is called a nihilist.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent! You understand it thus. Mahāmati, it is not only the nature or non-nature of greed, hatred, and delusion that constitutes a nihilist;

even with respect to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, one who [denies them] is likewise a nihilist. (This is the Buddha responding in accordance with Mahāmati's intent to clarify that the outsider [heretic] relies upon...)

This refers to the fault of falling into nihilism. To claim that those who rely on the nihilistic views of non-Buddhist outsiders are not only reckoning greed and other afflictions as being without intrinsic nature, but are also equating the Buddha and the followers of the Two Vehicles with those outsiders in their reckoning—this is to say that they too are "destroyers" (badheya).

This is an extreme statement emphasizing the gravity of the fault of falling into nihilism. However, the Buddha uses a single phrase to clarify two meanings simultaneously: first, to refute the errors of non-Buddhist reckonings; second, to distinguish the Buddha and the followers of the Two Vehicles from those who are "destroyers," showing they are different from mere nihilists.

Therefore, the subsequent text briefly explains the meaning of "destruction" to clarify that the Buddha and the followers of the Two Vehicles are not destroyers. Why is this so? Because both the internal and external are unobtainable, and the nature of the afflictions is distinct [from such nihilism].

Because they are distinct. (This inquiry clarifies the reason why the Buddha and the followers of the two vehicles [śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas] undergo disintegration. It means that the nature of greed and so forth cannot be apprehended internally or externally; therefore, it is termed "disintegration. Since afflictions are neither different nor non-different [from their nature], they are not a substantial nature and thus appear as if non-existent.)

For this reason, they propose that [the self] is non-existent like themselves. Although the name "destruction" is the same, the reasons for that destruction differ. Mahāmati, greed, anger, and delusion—whether internal or external—cannot be apprehended, because the nature of greed, anger, and delusion has no body.
It is not the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas who are the destroyers; for the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are liberated by their very nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*).
This is because both bondage and the cause of bondage lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). (Regarding "bondage and the cause of bondage," the Wei translation reads "that which binds.")

The cause of bondage and that which is bound. This clarifies that greed and the like lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), thereby distinguishing the Buddha and the followers of the Two Vehicles from those who, like non-Buddhist proponents, fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and act as destroyers. "Mahāmati" and below correctly argue against such destruction. "The Buddha and the voice-hearers" and below state the reason why they do not destroy [the teachings]:

it is because the Buddha and the followers of the Two Vehicles do not conceptualize the existence or non-existence of greed and the like; they contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions, and thus their self-nature is liberated. Since both bondage and its cause lack intrinsic nature, this is not the same as the "non-existence" asserted by non-Buddhist proponents. "Bondage" refers to the entity of bondage.

That is to say, the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are the causes of bondage; these refer to greed, hatred, and delusion. Since all matters of bondage arise because of greed and the other afflictions, and because the Buddhas and those of the two vehicles have realized that their nature is empty and thereby attained liberation, they are not called "destroyers."

Mahāmati, if there were a binder, there would necessarily be that which is bound, because it is the cause of binding. (The Wei translation states: "If there is a binder, there must be that which is bound;

if there is that which is bound, there must be a binder. [Note: "The binder" refers to that which binds, namely the object of bondage. "The cause of binding" refers to that which performs the binding, namely greed, hatred, and delusion. This is because the object of bondage arises due to greed and the other afflictions. Mahāmati, ...
To speak thus of "destruction" is called the characteristic of non-existence. (This concludes the meaning of destruction as held by the Buddha and the two vehicles; this is what is called correct.

It serves as a contrast to the meaning of destruction held by the non-Buddhists, which is of the nature of annihilationism. Therefore, the text below says: "I would rather embrace the view of a self as large as Mount Sumeru than give rise to the view of emptiness based on the arrogance of 'nothingness'"). For this reason, Mahāmati:
I say that it would be better to hold a view of a self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness based on the overweening pride of thinking "nothing exists.

(The Wei translation says: "Based on this meaning, I have stated in other sutras: 'It is better to give rise to a view of a self as large as Mount Sumeru'—one does not say that all phenomena are empty and non-existent. As for the phrase 'for this reason,' it refers back to the preceding text; because non-Buddhists fall into overweening pride by relying on 'non-existence,' they do not adopt [this view].

It is better to hold a view of a self because, though such a person clings to existence, they can still be transformed; whereas those with the view of emptiness based on overweening pride cannot be transformed, as their error is truly profound. This is a warning to practitioners of the correct path: do not rely on 'non-existence'. )

It is indeed so. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "To deny the two truths is the nihilistic view of emptiness; the Buddhas declare such persons to be incurable. Mahāmati, this refers to those who possess the pride of thinking that nothing exists.

This is called "destruction. It refers to falling into the longing for views of self-characteristics and common characteristics. (The Tang translation states: "If one gives rise to such a view, it is called 'destruction,' meaning one falls into the longing for views of self and common [characteristics]. 'Longing' (*āśā*) has the sense of 'desire' (*chanda*).

This means that those with the view of emptiness based on overweening pride fall into the longing for views of self and common [characteristics]. This is because, relying on the distinctions of existence and non-existence regarding self and common characteristics, they long for emptiness; therefore, they are called 'destroyers.

In the subsequent section on the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness, it is stated that even those of the two vehicles fall into the longing for views of self and common [characteristics]. One must understand that although the view of emptiness held by the two vehicles and that of the non-Buddhists are the same, they differ in being heterodox or orthodox. This is because the two vehicles attain the Way by contemplating the emptiness of nature.)

[This is] correct. Because the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) form their understanding by means of negation, they are [therefore] heterodox. Not knowing that [all things] are the manifestation of one's own mind, they perceive external natures as impermanent, undergoing moment-to-moment destruction.
They see the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) as a continuous flow that undergoes transformation and cessation.

To be free from the conceptualization of verbal signs is what is called "the destroyer. (This passage points out the error of those who rely on the notion of non-destruction. The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "Not knowing that [all things] are the manifestation of one's own mind, they perceive external phenomena as impermanent; within a single moment, they undergo successive change and destruction, as well as the continuous flow of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases...")

[They] comment on transformation and extinction, asserting that all things ultimately return to non-existence; that is, having already abandoned the characteristics of words and conceptual discrimination, they nonetheless fall into the nihilistic view of emptiness (*abhāva-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). These are called "the destroyers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Existence and non-existence are the two extremes, extending even to the realm of the mind.

Purifying that realm, the mind of equanimity is quiescent. (The first two lines repeat the existence/non-existence and the realm of one's own mind; the latter two lines repeat the Buddha’s true principle. The ancient commentary states: "Purify the realms of existence/non-existence and the deluded mind; the mind of equanimity is naturally quiescent.
Without grasping at the nature of the realm, extinction is not a state of nothingness. All phenomena are entirely suchness, as with the worthy ones.
The Sphere of the Sages. (The Ancient Commentary states: To know that the nature of the sphere of craving is illusory and devoid of anything graspable is itself the quiescence of essential nature;

it is not a state where nothing else exists. This is true quiescence. To contemplate all phenomena as entirely equal and non-dual is the sphere of the noble ones. Without seed yet there is birth; having been born, it perishes again. Conditioned by causes and conditions, it is both existent and non-existent; it does not abide within my teaching.
(That "there is birth without seed" means that existence arises from non-existence. That which is reckoned as *pradhāna* [the primal nature] and so forth is without seed; thus, once born...)

"Furthermore, 'annihilation' refers to the doctrine of nihilism (*ucchedavāda*). To calculate that there are no causes and conditions is to fail to abide within the teaching of the Tathāgata. It is neither from outsiders nor from the Buddha; it is neither from me nor from anyone else.
Since things arise through the gathering of causes and conditions, how could they be non-existent? Who gathers the causes and conditions for existence, yet then speaks of non-existence?

This is the production of dharmas through false views and the deluded conceptualization of existence and non-existence. (The Ancient Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'the production of dharmas,' it means these are not created by outsiders.")

Furthermore, it is not created by a Buddha, nor by a divine self (*ātman*), nor by others such as atoms or the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). This is because it arises solely from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Since it only comes into being through the gathering of causes and conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

this clarifies that there is no such thing as a "produced phenomenon. If produced phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, what need is there to further negate them? A new teaching states: within the four great elements and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), each lacks a master. Who, then, gathers them together? Yet it is still said that production occurs through causes and conditions. If production does not exist, [how can there be gathering?]

How could one further claim that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are destroyed? This is taught to clarify the false views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who speak of the arising of dharmas because of their deluded imaginings (*parikalpa*) and thus reckon them as existent or non-existent.

If one knows that there is nothing produced and likewise nothing extinguished, and observes that all is entirely empty and quiescent, one is free from both existence and non-existence. (This verse expresses the true meaning of the Tathāgata.)
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle (*tathatā-prativedha-lakṣaṇa*). If the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle are skillfully distinguished, I and all bodhisattvas shall thoroughly understand these characteristics;
having understood these characteristics, we shall swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and not follow after discursive perceptions."
[Including] the various Māras and non-Buddhists. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon this well. I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"Yes, we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas have two kinds of pervasive characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa):

namely, the penetration of the fundamental principle (siddhānta-prativedha) and the penetration of the teaching (deśanā-prativedha). [The reason why all three vehicles possess these two kinds of penetration is that they both possess self-cultivation and the transformation of others]."

Therefore, the "penetration of the principle" (*zōngtōng*) pertains to one's own practice, while the "penetration of the teaching" (*shuōtōng*) pertains to transforming others. The *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "This generally refers to what is realized and taught by both the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas, establishing the characteristics of the shared principle and teaching of the three vehicles. The *Zōngjìng* (Mirror of the Source) says:

"Internally realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of one’s own mind, abiding in the stage of self-awakening, and entering the gate of noble wisdom—being in accord with this is called the characteristic of the penetration of the principle. This is the time of practice, not the time of understanding. Because practice is perfected through understanding, once practice is perfected, understanding ceases; then the path of words and speech is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. It further states: "The penetration of the principle is for bodhisattvas; the penetration of the teaching is for the ignorant.
Mahāmati, as for the penetration of the principle, it refers to the characteristic of supreme progress attained through personal realization, which is far removed from words.

This refers to the conceptualization of words and letters. It is the realm of the outflow-free (anāsrava-dhātu), the stage of self-realization, wherein one’s own characteristics are free from all false and deluded perceptions.
It subdues all external paths and the hosts of Māras; it takes the path of self-realization as its object, and its radiance shines forth brilliantly.

This is called the characteristic of the penetration of the ultimate principle (*siddhānta-naya*). (Regarding "objectively attained by oneself," see the preceding commentary. Regarding the "characteristic of superior progress," this refers to the characteristic of progressing toward ever-increasing excellence at each successive stage. This is the realm of the superior progress attained by oneself, which is far removed from verbal expression and written characters.)

Second is the characteristic of *saṃjñā* (conception). It refers to proceeding toward the increasingly superior realm of outflowlessness (*anāsrava-dhātu*), reaching the stage of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana-bhūmi*), and completely distancing oneself from all false conceptualizations regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, this characteristic of self-awakening is a direct realization of the essential nature; it cannot be expressed or demonstrated through words. If one attempts to deliberate upon it using conventional language, one will move further and further away from it.

Because it is called "self-awakening," by awakening to one's own inner radiance, which eclipses all else, one is able to subdue demonic adversaries and destroy their deep-seated darkness. This is called the characteristic of the penetration of the essence (*zongtong-xiang*). What is the characteristic of the penetration of the teaching (*shetong-xiang*)?

It refers to the exposition of the various teachings of the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*), which is free from the characteristics of difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence, and so forth.
By means of skillful expedients, he accords with sentient beings and teaches the Dharma as is appropriate, causing them to attain liberation.

This is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching (*deśanā-prativedha*). Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this. (The meaning of the penetration of teaching is thus known; below, Mahāmati, [the Buddha] exhorts the bodhisattvas that they should study the two penetrations.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The fundamental tenets (*siddhānta*) and the communication through teaching (*deśanā-praveśa*) take as their objects both the self-nature [of phenomena] and the teachings [themselves]. (Regarding "self-nature," this refers to the *siddhānta-praveśa*; regarding "teachings," this refers to the *deśanā-praveśa*).

One who clearly perceives and correctly discriminates these does not follow various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*). (This means that one who skillfully distinguishes these two modes of penetration does not follow deluded thoughts, discursive reflection, or investigation).

There is no real nature [to external objects], yet they appear as the false imaginings of fools. (The Wei translation says: "In reality there are no external dharmas, just as ordinary people discriminate them"). How do such false imaginings arise? [One understands that] non-existence is the true nature.

Liberation. (This follows the sense that there is no true reality, intended to refute the notion of non-existence. It means: since all phenomena are not real, how can one give rise to various deluded thoughts? How could one take the absence of nature to be liberation? Since phenomena are not real, both existence and non-existence are delusions.

To transcend these is wisdom.

The "cause" is what is termed wisdom (*jñāna*). This distinguishes it from the non-wisdom of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). Furthermore, below this, regarding the characteristic of "nurturing": "nurturing" means the sense of continuous, uninterrupted arising. This refers to the cause of arising as conceived by the non-Buddhists;

it is the consciousness of erroneous understanding, not the wisdom of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom: namely, knowing arising and ceasing, knowing specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing.

(Although the essence of wisdom is fundamentally one, the reason there are three distinct modes of knowing is that, from the perspective of the person who knows, there are differences in breadth and narrowness, as well as in being erroneous or correct. That which is erroneous, though it be "wisdom," is still merely "consciousness.")

[This is] the ear. Now, that which knows arising and ceasing is the wisdom of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). That which knows specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is the wisdom of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). That which knows the unborn and unceasing is the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom;

the various obstructed characteristics of objects are consciousness (*vijñāna*). (This distinguishes between the obstructed and the non-obstructed to clarify the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness.

Furthermore, when the three factors [root, object, and consciousness] come together, the arising of the characteristic of expedient means (*upāya*) is consciousness; the characteristic of the self-nature of expedient means without objective entities is wisdom. (Root, object, and consciousness—)

The conjunction of name and object arising together is called the characteristic of expedient means (*upāya*). That which arises from these three factors is consciousness (*vijñāna*). That which is without objects or expedient means, whose intrinsic nature is luminous clarity, and which is not characterized by arising or ceasing, is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, that which perceives characteristics is consciousness; that which does not perceive characteristics is wisdom. "Perceiving characteristics" refers to the non-forgetting of the mind and its objects—this is consciousness. That which is able to forget both is wisdom.

(The above is a detailed discernment of the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness, intended to cause all Bodhisattvas to rely upon wisdom and not upon consciousness. Having personally attained the realm of noble wisdom, one neither goes out nor enters, and is therefore like [a reflection] in water.

The Moon. (Having attained sagely wisdom, one does not emerge when among the ordinary, nor does one enter when among the sages. From the Buddhas above to the myriad beings below, it neither increases nor decreases; it neither departs nor arrives. This is called Immovable Wisdom. As for the moon in the water:

the water is a metaphor for the mind, and the moon is a metaphor for wisdom. When the water is clear, the moon appears; yet the moon has nowhere from which it comes. When the water is turbid, the moon vanishes; yet the moon has nowhere to which it goes. This is called the realm of sagely wisdom—without emerging and without entering).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Gathering [objects] is consciousness (*vijñāna*); not gathering is wisdom (*jñāna*). (To "gather" means to grasp and maintain. Consciousness is able to grasp and maintain the seeds of good and evil;

this is explained in detail in the first commentary. The essence of wisdom is the extinction of self. Its spiritual discernment is how could it be partial? Like a mirror reflecting objects, beauty and ugliness do not contend. What gathering could there be? Therefore, it is called wisdom.
To observe all phenomena and penetrate their non-existence, thereby attaining the power of mastery—this is what is called prajñā. It is bound to its object.
The mind is that which acts; the arising of discernment (*saṃjñā*) constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*). When there is nothing [to grasp] and that which is supreme, insight (*prajñā*) arises from this.

(Discernment refers to awakening-illumination. Because it arises from awakening, it is called wisdom; for it is not bound by objects. Master Sengzhao said: "The mind’s engagement in discrimination is called insight; the definitive examination of principles is called wisdom. Thus, insight lies in the cause, while wisdom lies in the fruit.

In the present text, it says that the arising of discernment constitutes wisdom, while that which arises from "nothingness" and the "supreme" constitutes insight. Thus, wisdom lies in the cause, while insight lies in the fruit. The *Zongjing* further states: "Prajñā is wisdom.")

*Jñāna* (knowledge) is knowing; *prajñā* (wisdom) is seeing. Thus, knowledge and vision belong to the cause, while wisdom is designated as the fruit. Indeed, wisdom consists of both cause and fruit and cannot be discussed as being fixed to one alone; these two must mutually interpenetrate as cause and fruit. As the ancient commentary states:

"That which is bound by the objects of affliction is the mind of delusive thought (*vikalpa-citta*). To realize that the objects of affliction arise from delusive thought is knowledge (*jñāna*). This is the state of non-existence, the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). "Victory" is the Buddha-stage.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are far removed from conceptualization and ideation; having attained the dharma of non-ideation, such a one is a Son of the Buddha, not a Śrāvaka.

(This verse concerns the wisdom of self-attainment that is neither born nor extinguished. It means that by remaining far removed from the conceptualizations of the arising and ceasing of mind, intellect, and consciousness, one attains the dharma of non-arising, non-ceasing, and thoughtlessness;

this is the wisdom of a Bodhisattva, not that of a Śrāvaka. The patience of tranquil and supreme progress, the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom, arises from the excellent ultimate truth; all spheres of activity are utterly transcended. (The *Jízhù* states:

The *Renwáng jīng* speaks of five types of patience—namely, subduing (*fú*), faith (*xìn*), compliance (*shùn*), non-arising (*wúshēng*), and cessation (*jìmìng*). Each has lower, middle, and superior grades. Prior to the [Bodhisattva] stages, one only attains the three grades of subduing patience.)

In this chapter, the nine stages (*bhūmi*) are respectively assigned to the first three types of patience (*kṣānti*). The tenth stage, Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and Buddhahood attain the Patience of Quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*); hence it is called the "Patience of Supreme Progress toward Quiescence. This is the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata.
It clarifies that the Buddha’s pure wisdom of patience arises from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and is entirely free from the spheres of activity of the deluded mind and consciousness.

"I possess three kinds of wisdom through which the Sage reveals the reality. (The ancient commentary states: 'The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings; thus there are three kinds of wisdom. These three kinds of wisdom are spoken of precisely because he wishes to awaken sentient beings, enabling them to attain the reality that transcends words and speech. Regarding those perceptions..."
Contemplation thoroughly encompasses all natures; it does not correspond with the wisdom of the two vehicles.
Wisdom is detached from all that exists, yet [those who] cling to self-nature give rise to the various Śrāvakas. Transcending all mental measures, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure. (Jisheng says:

"To give rise to contemplation regarding those deluded thoughts and to encompass all natures of arising and ceasing—this is worldly wisdom. The wisdom of the two vehicles can detach from all that exists and does not correspond with arising and ceasing; however, they still cling to self- and common-nature.")

Regarding their characteristics: that which arises from the Śrāvaka is supramundane wisdom. That which transcends the various mental measures (*cittamātra*)—both mundane and supramundane—of ordinary fools and the two vehicles, thereby attaining the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata, is the supreme-supramundane wisdom.
(This is a summary verse for the two aforementioned sets of three types of wisdom.)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of theories of transformation among the non-Buddhists, from which the views of transformation among the non-Buddhists arise.

They are: transformation of shape and location, transformation of characteristics, transformation of cause, transformation of accomplishment, transformation of view, transformation of nature, transformation of the clarity of conditions, transformation of the clarity of what is produced, and transformation of things. Mahāmati, these are called the nine kinds of transformation.

Transformation-observation (*pariṇāma-darśana*). All non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) give rise to theories of existence and non-existence based on this, and thus produce the doctrine of transformation. (The fourth is "transformation through accomplishment"; the Wei translation renders it as "corresponding transformation. The sixth is "substance producing phenomena";

the ninth is "phenomena producing birth. [The Ancient Commentary states: The differing forms of the six paths of humans and devas are called "transformation of form and place" (*ākṛti-sthāna-pariṇāma*). The characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—which do not abide for even a single moment, are called "transformation of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*).

The cessation of the cause and the arising of the fruit is called "transformation of cause" (*hetu-pariṇāma*). The destruction of the phenomena accomplished by the cause is called "transformation of accomplishment" (*siddhi-pariṇāma*). Seeing a single phenomenon as correct at first and later seeing it as incorrect is called "transformation of view" (*darśana-pariṇāma*). The transformation of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all things is called... [text ends]... transformation.

The transformation of nature; the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination without abiding is called the "distinctive transformation of conditions. The destruction of the fruits produced by conditions is called the "distinctive transformation of what is produced. The cessation of conditioned phenomena is called the "transformation of things. Based on these, the various non-Buddhists [propose their views].

There are nine kinds of transformation that give rise to views of existence and non-existence, producing the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma-vāda*). What is meant by "transformation of form and location"? It refers to the perception of differences in form and location.

For example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, diverse forms and locations appear; yet it is not the nature of the gold itself that changes. The same applies to the transformation of all natures.

[The distinctions between] the three realms and six paths, whether horizontal or vertical, are called "perceiving differences in form and location. It is like gold being fashioned into vessels, where there are differences such as jars, basins, hairpins, and bracelets; yet the nature of the gold remains as it was, and does not change according to the vessel.

"Transformation. All transformations refer to the other eight types of transformation. Since they are all like the nature of gold, it is said, "it is likewise so. Non-Buddhists rely on these transformations to construct various treatises.

There may be non-Buddhists who harbor such false imaginings, even to the point of imagining the transformation of phenomena; yet those [phenomena] are neither identical nor different, because they are based on false imagination. (The Wei translation says:

"Mahāmati, there are further non-Buddhists who discriminate that all dharmas depend on causes for their transformation. Mahāmati, those dharmas are neither thus, nor are they not thus, because they rely on discrimination. [There is another group of non-Buddhists who do not understand the preceding nine... )

This is false. Yet, within this, one should thoroughly investigate its cause; for that reason, the Buddha refutes it as being neither identical nor different, stating that it is merely a single deluded perception (as can be understood from the Wei translation).

In this way, regarding the transformation of all natures, one should know it to be like the ripening of milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth. This is the "transformation-delusion" of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); yet in reality, there is no such transformation.

Whether existent or non-existent, these are manifestations of one's own mind; external natures have no intrinsic nature. (The New Commentary states: "The non-Buddhists' false conceptualization that all natures undergo transformation is not...")

They are neither identical nor different, just as when milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth undergo transformation. One obtains curd from milk; it cannot be said to be different, yet because their flavor and aroma differ, it cannot be said to be identical.

In reality, there is no such thing as a non-existent dharma that undergoes transformation. To speak of existence or non-existence is but the false manifestation of one's own mind, for external natures have no reality. Mahāmati, in this way, ordinary and ignorant beings arise from the habitual cultivation of their own妄想 (vikalpa).

Mahāmati, there is no dharma that is born or extinguished, just as one perceives the arising of forms in a magical illusion or a dream. (The Tang translation states: "All these are deluded ordinary beings arising from their own minds...")

They arise from the habitual tendencies of discrimination; in reality, there is not a single dharma that either arises or ceases, just like the various forms seen in illusions and dreams, or like speaking of birth and death regarding the son of a barren woman. This section concludes by clarifying that these nine transformations arise from false imagination (*vikalpa*).

To say they "arise from the cultivation of false imagination" means that these nine transformations are all produced by the perfuming of erroneous habits; in truth, there is not a single dharma that either arises or ceases. One should contemplate all dharmas as being like the forms in illusions, dreams, and so forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The transformation of shape, location, and time, the four great elements, and the sense organs—these arise gradually in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Such conceptual constructions are not the wisdom of the enlightened. (The New Commentary states: The non-Buddhists claim that shape, location, time, and the four great elements act as seeds, whereby the sense organs undergo transformation. Those of the Two Vehicles reckon that there is an intermediate state through which the aggregates of the subsequent birth gradually continue.

All such views are merely conceptual constructions. Regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Most Victorious One is not like those conceptual constructions; yet worldly dependent origination is like a city of the Gandharvas.

"Most Victorious" (Sugata) is the Buddha’s self-designation. It means that regarding the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Buddha is free from all conceptual discrimination; he is not like those non-Buddhists who give rise to various false imaginings concerning the law of dependent origination.
Rather, he knows that the dependent origination of the world is like a city of the Gandharvas—neither an intrinsic nature nor a lack of nature.
Annotated Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Five;
Annotated Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra of the Liu Song Dynasty.

Part Three of the First Chapter: "The Essential Heart of All Buddha-Speech."

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the meaning of the continuity of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation.

If you skillfully distinguish between the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, I and the other bodhisattvas will thoroughly understand the skillful means regarding all continuities, so as not to fall into attachment to the literal meaning of what has been taught."

Continuity. (In the question, there are two meanings. Continuity is understandable. Regarding the meaning of liberation: it refers to what is stated later—that all phenomena have neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity, because they attain tranquility. That very tranquility is what is called the meaning of liberation.

"Not falling below" means being skillful in the expedient means of understanding continuity; thus, one does not fall into the sickness of clinging to the meaning of words, lest one's own mind become attached to continuity.

Being skilled in the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all phenomena, as well as in the awakening that is free from the deluded thoughts of verbal expressions and letters, one wanders through all [realms].
In all Buddha-fields, there are the seals of the power, mastery, supernormal knowledges, and dhāraṇīs of immeasurable assemblies;
they manifest various transformations and radiate brilliant light. Their awakened wisdom skillfully enters the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣayamukha*).

Their practice of non-expedient means is like the sun, the moon, the maṇi jewel, and the four great elements. (The *Jizhu* commentary states: "The illumination of the sun and moon, the reflection of colors by the maṇi, and the pervasive presence of earth, water, fire, and wind are all without deliberate action. The bodhisattva’s practice of non-expedient means is likewise.")
In all stages, one leaves behind the marks of one's own deluded conceptualizations and views;

seeing all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth, one enters the body of the Buddha-ground and, throughout the realms of all sentient beings, teaches the Dharma according to their needs and guides them.

He causes all beings to dwell securely in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and so forth—free from the categories of existence and non-existence, as well as the deluded conceptualizations of arising and ceasing.

This is distinct from the meaning of verbal expressions; his body becomes increasingly superior. (The above is Mahāmati’s own description of the benefits of his inquiry. "Distinct from the meaning of verbal expressions" means being distinct from both views and verbal expressions.

A bodhisattva skilled in the two meanings manifests forms to deliver sentient beings, causing them to leave behind various heterodox views, so that their bodies attain a superior transformation of the basis. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive the teaching.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Regarding the infinite and all-encompassing dharmas, there is a continuous attachment to their expressed meanings. That is to say:

the continuity of attachment to marks (*nimitta*), the continuity of attachment to conditions (*pratyaya*), the continuity of attachment to existence and non-existence (*bhāva-abhāva*), and the continuity of attachment to birth..."
The continuity of conceptual attachment to birth; the continuity of conceptual attachment to cessation and non-cessation; the continuity of conceptual attachment to vehicles and non-vehicles;
the continuity of conceptual attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned; the continuity of conceptual attachment to the specific characteristics of each stage;
the continuity of conceptual attachment to self-conceptualization and uninterrupted conceptualization; and the external categories of existence and non-existence.
The Path depends upon the continuity of conceptualization and attachment; the three vehicles and the one vehicle likewise depend upon the continuity of uninterrupted conceptualization and attachment.

(This answers Mahāmati’s concern regarding the attachment to the continuity of grasping at meanings according to words. While there are immeasurable aspects, they may be summarized as eleven kinds. The following lists the names of these eleven kinds of continuity of conceptual attachment. First, regarding the term "characteristic" [lakṣaṇa]:)

This refers to the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*). "Conditions" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). One should understand that regarding nature and non-nature, arising and non-arising, and so forth, they are likewise to be known. Regarding "vehicles" (*yāna*) and "non-vehicles": the vehicle is the trace of the three and one, while the non-vehicle is the essence of the three and one.

For anyone who calculates the three and one in terms of essence and trace and fails to forget them, this too constitutes a clinging to deluded conceptualization (*parikalpita-vikalpa*). Regarding "deluded conceptualization of the self-characteristics of each stage": from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), each stage possesses its own objective realm; these characteristics are not non-existent.

However, if one calculates them and does not relinquish them, this too constitutes a clinging to deluded conceptualization. Regarding "deluded conceptualization of the self and uninterrupted deluded conceptualization": this means that based on one's own mind and relying on the uninterrupted dharma, various deluded conceptualizations arise. Although the paths of teaching for the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle differ, they are identical in realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore—

It is said that there is no interval; yet to reckon these three as being without interval is itself a continuity of deluded conceptualization and attachment. Furthermore, Mahāmati, this and other ordinary, ignorant beings continue in their own deluded conceptualizations.

Because of this continuity, the deluded conceptualizations of the ordinary and ignorant are like a silkworm making a cocoon, binding themselves and others with the threads of their own conceptualization, and becoming attached to the characteristics of the continuity of existence and non-existence.
(The phrase "this and others" refers to the eleven aforementioned forms of attachment.)

This refers to these eleven forms of attachment, as well as the immeasurable characteristics of other attachments held by ordinary, ignorant people, which cannot be fully described; hence the phrase "and others. From this point downward, the text concludes by revealing the fault of the continuity of such attachments, likening it to a silkworm spinning its cocoon.

"Delusive thought is like thread; it is said to be dense and interwoven, binding oneself by its own nature. Furthermore, one uses this same method to delusively teach others, thereby binding them as well. However, all such attachments do not transcend the two categories of existence and non-existence;

therefore, the conclusion states: 'the continuous attachment to existence and non-existence. (The above clarifies the meaning of continuity; below, the meaning of liberation is clarified). Furthermore, Mahāmati, within that [state], there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.
One perceives all phenomena as quiescent, and thus delusive thought does not arise. Therefore, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive the One...

All phenomena are quiescent. (In this context, "within them" refers to the aforementioned eleven continuities. To say that the point where these continuities cease is itself liberation means: because one is able to see the quiescence of phenomena, one thoroughly understands that all phenomena possess neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity;

this is the meaning of liberation). Furthermore, Mahāmati, having realized that external natures are not-natures and that the manifestations of one's own mind are non-existent, one should conformingly contemplate the presence or absence of all natures as they appear within the measure of one's own mind, seeing them as being without characteristics.

The continuity [of the mind] is stilled; therefore, regarding all phenomena, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity. (This means that one realizes external objects have no intrinsic nature, and the internal mind is without characteristics.

By observing in accordance with this, one sees that the existence or non-existence of the nature of what is manifested by one's own mind is entirely devoid of characteristics. Thus, the continuity [of the mind] is stilled. Because it is stilled, regarding all phenomena, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity;
this is called the meaning of liberation). Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither bondage nor liberation. Others fall into error because they do not realize things as they truly are.

There is bondage and there is liberation. (In this context, "therein" refers to the state of tranquility. Within the meaning of tranquility, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Other non-Buddhists do not know that tranquility as it truly is;

therefore, they have the bondage of continuity and the liberation of non-continuity. Why is this so? It is because among all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—a sentient being cannot be apprehended.

(The Tang translation says: "Whether all phenomena exist or do not exist, their essential nature cannot be found. In the present text, the character *zhòng* [sentient] carries the meaning of "essential nature"; this may be understood by consulting the Tang translation. Furthermore:
Mahāmati, there are three continuities for the foolish: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as craving.

This is accompanied by joy regarding future existence. (The Master Le explains: greed, hatred, and delusion are the causes of continuity; the five destinies are the fruits of continuity. From past causes, present fruits are produced; from present causes, one again invites future retribution.

Regarding the "three continuities," this refers to the cyclic progression of the three periods of time, continuing without interruption. Greed, craving, and joy are assigned to these respectively. Because of this continuity, there is the continuity of the destinies; that is continuity.

[This refers to] that which continues through the five destinies. (The Wei translation says: "Because they continue by means of this, there is rebirth in future lives. Mahāmati, sentient beings continue and are born into the five paths. [Master Le’s commentary says: "By means of the continuity of these three poisons..."]

Therefore, there is the revolving of the various realms of existence (*gati*). As for what is called "realms," these are the six paths; however, because the *asuras* are included throughout the five paths, they are simply referred to as the "five realms. Mahāmati, regarding the severance of continuity:

there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity (meaning that when the three continuities of greed and so forth are severed, then the characteristics of continuity and non-continuity no longer exist; thus, both the meanings of continuity and liberation are empty).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, through the conjunction of the three conditions, one forms attachments as a skillful means;

thus, the continuity of consciousness arises without interruption (meaning that when one forms attachments by means of the conjunction of the conditions of the sense organs, objects, and consciousness, the various consciousnesses arise in succession for long kalpas without interval). Where there is attachment to skillful means, there is continuity;

when the consciousness arising from the conjunction of the three conditions is severed, one perceives the three liberations, and all continuity ceases to arise. (Where there is attachment to skillful means...)

There is a continuity. When consciousness is severed through three conditions, one perceives the three liberations. Having perceived liberation, no further continuity arises. This verse clarifies the causes for both the meanings of continuity and liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Unreal conceptualization is said to be the characteristic of continuity. If one knows that reality, the web of continuity is severed.

(Because of attachment to unreal conceptualization, there is continuity; if one knows its true nature, the web of continuity is severed. The analogy of continuity to a web is used because continuity is immeasurable and mutually interwoven.)

Like being caught in a net or a snare, it is difficult to escape; this verse explains the two meanings of "succession" (*saṃtati*) and "liberation" (*vimukti*). Regarding all natures, there is ignorance, and one is grasped by verbal designations.

Just as that silkworm spins a web and entangles itself, so too are the deluded ones bound by their own false imaginings, continuing in this state without discernment (due to a lack of awareness regarding the nature of all phenomena).

Following the meaning of what has been taught, they persistently cling to it—just as a silkworm makes a cocoon and entangles itself within it. So it is with ordinary, foolish beings who are bound by false imaginings;
thus, they lack the wisdom to discern the continuity [of existence].
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has taught: 'By means of this or that conceptualization, one conceptualizes this or that nature;

yet those natures do not possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), for they are merely the nature of conceptualization itself. (The Wei translation conveys the same meaning. [This is Mahāmati citing the Buddha’s previous words as a question.

"Those various natures" refers to all phenomena. By means of this or that conceptualization, one conceptualizes these various phenomena; however, those phenomena do not possess an intrinsic nature, being nothing other than the single nature of conceptualization. Mahāmati said:

The Buddha said, "World-Honored One, if it is merely the self-nature of false imagination and not a nature that exists through mutual dependence, would this not be a fault in the World-Honored One’s teaching regarding the non-substantiality of afflictions and purification? For all dharmas are of the nature of the self-nature of false imagination and lack substantiality.

(The Wei translation states: "World-Honored One, if it is only the discrimination of one's own mind and not the characteristic of those dharmas, then according to what the World-Honored One has taught, all dharmas should be without defilement or purity. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has said that all... )

The Dharma is seen through false conceptualization, for it lacks substantial reality. ○ In the preceding passage, Mahāmati first cited the Buddha’s words as evidence; here he formally restates the objection:

"If it were merely the nature of false conceptualization, and not the case that all natures exist in mutual dependence upon one another, would this not mean that the World-Honored One would fall into the error of asserting that turbidity and purity are without intrinsic nature? Why? Because all dharmas are not [inherently] existent natures, but are merely the nature of false conceptualization. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is so, it is so. It is as you have said, Mahāmati. It is not like the imagined reality of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of fools.

(Mahāmati raised an objection based on the absence of intrinsic nature, yet he did not understand the intent of that objection; thus, his words accorded with the correct principle. Therefore, the World-Honored One, following that objection, immediately testified, saying: "It is so, it is as you have said. One must know that both defilement and purity are without intrinsic nature.)"

These two dharmas are unobtainable; they are not like the foolish who, by means of their own-nature (*svabhāva*), reckon them to be real. This imagined self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not possess the characteristic of a real self-nature (the Tang translation says:
"This is merely false attachment; there is no nature or characteristic"). [This restates the preceding point that the imagined self-nature lacks the characteristic of an external self-nature.

However, Mahāmati, as for the self-nature that exists through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*)—known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, and perceived by the noble eye of wisdom—it is in this way that the self-nature is known (the Tang translation says: "However, the various noble ones...").

Previously, it was clarified that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are merely a single deluded thought; now, it is revealed that noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) possesses its own essential nature. That which is the "noble knowledge and vision" is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: a knowing without knowing and a seeing without seeing, which constitutes true knowledge and vision. Regarding the "noble eye of wisdom" (*prajñācakṣus*), it refers to penetrating the reality of all phenomena and comprehending the delusion of all sentient beings.

The first fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Discrimination is called wisdom (*prajñā*), and illuminating observation is termed the 'eye' (*cakṣus*). It further states: "Among the five eyes, the eye of wisdom contemplates principle (*li*). Principle has no diverse flavors."

The eye of wisdom observes phenomena; there is nothing it does not see, and this is called the noble eye of wisdom (*ārya-prajñā-cakṣus*). However, the nature of the noble ones is not empty [of reality], whereas false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is without substance. One must not take prior false conceptualization as a precedent. (The character "ran" at the beginning of the passage was divided and attached to the preceding sentence in the old commentary;
however, according to the Tang translation, it should be connected to this one, serving as a particle to introduce a change in the narrative. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"If it is as the noble ones do—with noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom, which is neither the divine eye nor the fleshly eye—and they know the self-nature of things in this way, rather than like foolish commoners..."

"Conceptual construction, World-Honored One. (This, Mahāmati, restates the meaning of the preceding passage to raise a subsequent objection. It means: if one were like a sage, who knows and perceives the nature and self-nature through sagely knowledge, such knowing would be real and not false;

it is not comparable to the conceptual constructions of the divine eye or the fleshly eye of ordinary people. World-Honored One, how can foolish people be free from these conceptual constructions? It is because they do not realize the reality of the sagely nature."

(The Tang translation says: "How can ordinary fools be free from discrimination? Because they cannot awaken to the dharmas of the noble ones. The meaning of Mahāmati’s question is: How can ordinary fools be free from such false conceptualization (*vikalpa*)?
And why is it that those who do not leave false conceptualization behind fail to realize the nature of the noble state? "World-Honored One, they are neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this?

It is because they do not awaken to the self-nature of the reality of the noble state, and they do not perceive the departure from the marks of existence and non-existence. (The Wei translation says: "World-Honored One, those deluded ordinary fools are...")

It is a perverted view; it is not a non-perverted view. Why? Because they are unable to see the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) within the realm of the noble ones as it truly is, and because they perceive the marks of existence and non-existence through transformation.

According to the Wei translation, Mahāmati states that those foolish commoners are not non-perverted because they do not awaken to the self-nature of the noble nature, yet they are not perverted either because they perceive the marks of existence and non-existence through transformation. In the current text, the final character "not" (*bù*) is absent, whereas the Wei translation uses the character "because" (*yǐ*) and the character "separated from" (*lí*).

The Wei translation renders this as "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). "Departure" (*li*) carries the same meaning as "transformation. In the current text, the character "not" (*bu*) should follow the Wei translation and be read as "by means of" (*yi*).

Considering the intent of Mahāmati, it is meant that those deluded ordinary beings (*bāla*) also possess a certain kind of non-inverted view that can be grasped, whereas the noble ones (*ārya*) may also possess a certain kind of view like that of false imagination (*vikalpa*) which cannot be grasped; hence there is the objection in the following passage. This is because [the opponent] suspects that the noble ones would incur the fault of self-contradiction in their own words.

The two preceding sections used the objection that there is a difference between ordinary beings and noble ones regarding awakening and non-awakening, thereby lamenting that ordinary beings possess the defects of both inverted and non-inverted views. "Bhagavān, the noble ones do not see things in such a way, as one falsely imagines them to be. By means of...

"Because they take the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) realm as their object. (The Tang translation says: "Even the noble ones do not attain things in the manner of conceptual construction as ordinary people do; because it is not a characteristic of the realm traversed by themselves. [The intent of this objection is:

Even the noble ones should not perceive such things as the *tathatā*-nature (*tathatā-dhātu*) in the same way that foolish commoners are attached to and conceptually construct worldly phenomena. Why? Because a Tathāgata should not take the self-characteristic realm as an object. Therefore, even for the noble ones, there is a kind of perception resembling conceptual construction that is ungraspable.
"World-Honored One, that too is the characteristic of the nature of intrinsic-being (*svabhāva-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*); such is the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."

[The Buddha] manifests [dharmas], yet does not speak of them as having causes or being causeless. This is because they would fall into the view of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇadṛṣṭi*). (The Wei translation states:

"Those noble ones perceive the substance of dharmas and discriminate their characteristics. Why is this? Because the World-Honored One neither speaks of them as having causes nor as being causeless. For what reason? Because it would entail falling into the view of the characteristics of existing dharmas. This is Mahāmati’s presentation of the Buddha’s correct view, raised as a subsequent objection.

That is to say, those noble ones also perceive the nature and self-nature of all dharmas as they appear through the nature of false imagination; however, they do not speak of them as having causes or being causeless. Why? If one were to speak of causes or the absence of causes, one would fall into the view of the characteristics of nature. This implies that although the noble ones perceive all dharmas, they appear in the same manner as to ordinary beings.)

Because one can realize that things are like illusions, one does not speak of existence or non-existence, and thus does not fall into views of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). As stated in the second sutra: "That delusion appears even to the noble ones (*ārya*), yet it is not an inversion"—this is identical to the meaning of the present text—[it is] a distinct realm of experience.
"It is not as it is for those others; thus there would be the fault of infinite regress. World-Honored One, this is because they do not perceive the self-nature and characteristics of phenomena.

(The Wei translation says: 'When other people perceive objects, they do not see them in this way. World-Honored One, if you speak thus, there is the fault of infinite regress. Why? Because they do not realize that the characteristics of all dharmas lack intrinsic nature and characteristics. [The phrase] 'perceiving objects differently than those others' means...")"

According to the Wei translation, "others" refers to other persons; "other persons" refers to sentient beings. "They" refers to the aforementioned noble ones (*ārya*). This means that the objects perceived by other sentient beings are not as they are perceived by those noble ones.

If this were so, it would result in the fault of infinite regress. The passage beginning with "The World-Honored One" clarifies the meaning of "not as they are. It means that because other sentient beings do not realize that the characteristics of the self-nature of phenomena lack substantial reality, the nature of the noble ones exists while the realm of ordinary beings does not.

How could this be anything other than a fault? Furthermore, O World-Honored One, it is not the case that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is the cause of the self-nature of characteristics. If that were so, how could that which is imagined not be non-imagined?

"One knows false discrimination as it truly is. (The Tang translation says: "World-Honored One, the nature and characteristics of all dharmas do not arise because of discrimination. Why, then, do you say that because of discrimination there are all dharmas? Mahāmati’s intention is this:
