The nature and characteristics of self-nature (*svabhāva*) do not exist because of the existence of the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). How is it that those noble ones (*ārya*), by means of noble-natured false discrimination, claim it is not false discrimination, yet say they know the nature and characteristics of self-nature as they truly are?

Is it merely a single instance of false discrimination? This objection challenges the incorrectness of the preceding passage’s statement that "it is merely the nature of false discrimination. (This can be understood by consulting the Tang translation). "World-Honored One, false discrimination is distinct; the nature and characteristics [of self-nature] are distinct. World-Honored One..."
The cause is dissimilar to the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

How is it that the noble ones do not engage in such imagination regarding each [of these], while the foolish do not know them as they truly are? (The "difference in imagination" refers to the mind that takes objects, which has various distinctions; the "difference in characteristics" refers to the objects themselves, which also have various distinctions.

Thus, the subject that perceives and the object perceived have dissimilar causes. How is it that those noble ones do not engage in imagination regarding the characteristic of the imagined nature, and how is it that the foolish do not know that non-conceptualized state as it truly is?)

However, for the sake of sentient beings, in order to cause them to abandon false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is said that things exist as they appear in false conceptualization, yet do not exist in accordance with reality.

(This, Mahāmati, is because the mind falsely speculates; it is the reason for the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*). That is to say, because sentient beings must abandon false conceptualization, the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*) is said to exist. Because it exists [in this sense], it is said to "exist as it appears in false conceptualization. Yet, because it is said to exist only as a skillful means, what exists is necessarily not existent; therefore, it is said to "not exist in accordance with reality").

World-Honored One, why do you negate sentient beings' views of existence and non-existence, and their attachment to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things? Why [do you speak of] the noble ones...?

[The objection: "They are attached to the sphere of activity of wisdom and thus fall into the view of existence (*bhavadarśana*). You teach that the dharmas of emptiness lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), yet you speak of the self-nature of the reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-svabhāva-vastu*) [Tang translation:

'World-Honored One, for what reason do you cause sentient beings to leave behind the attachments of the views of existence and non-existence regarding grasped dharmas, yet again become attached to the sphere of noble wisdom and fall into the view of existence?

Why is this? Because you do not speak of the quiescent dharmas of emptiness and non-existence, but instead speak of the self-nature of the reality of noble wisdom. This objection constitutes a contradiction with the Tathāgata's own words; it means: 'For what reason does the World-Honored One negate the views of existence and non-existence in sentient beings, while the World-Honored One himself again becomes attached [to them]'?"]

"Regarding the noble knowledge and vision, etc., [you] fall into the view of existence (*bhavadarśana*) by teaching that sentient beings and phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), yet you also teach that there exists the reality of noble wisdom within one's own sphere of experience.

Is this not a contradiction of your own words? The preceding section, from 'If it were as the noble ones... up to this point, consists of ten sections. Examining the intent of these ten sections in detail: The first section has Mahāmati cite the matter of the noble nature (*āryatva*), subsequently presenting nine points to construct a complex objection. He concludes by summarizing that teaching emptiness results in falling into existence. Thus, we know that 'teaching emptiness and falling into existence' is the foundation of the objection raised.

Therefore, in the World-Honored One’s response below, he specifically highlights the concluding words of the objection to demonstrate that the noble nature is real. Why must one separately list the names of the objections and elaborate on redundant phrasing? For this reason, I have merely provided a brief summary at the points where the flow of the argument shifts."

I have clarified their essential points so that those who come to study this text may clearly understand the meaning of the words; this is sufficient. Therefore, I shall not further incorporate the interpretations of previous commentators [into this work]. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that I teach that dharmas are empty and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Nor do I fall into the view of existence when speaking of the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). Rather, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon phrases that provoke terror.

(This passage refutes what Mahāmati has raised as an objection, thereby clarifying the reason for teaching the reality of the noble ones. That is to say, regarding the reality of noble wisdom spoken of by the Buddha, it is because he speaks of all dharmas lacking intrinsic nature; when sentient beings hear this, they give rise to...)

Because it eliminates fear, it is said that apart from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there exists the reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). This is taught in order to cause one to abandon such fear. However, the previous difficult questions were answered by cutting through them with five new points of refutation.

Upon examining these five refutations, some are correct and others are not; therefore, they are not accepted here. Now, following the intended meaning of Mahāmati’s speech, I have explained it as above. Observing the World-Honored One’s response, it appears he merely addressed the debate concerning falling into existence based on the teaching of emptiness.

Since this [previous] discourse constitutes the root of the objection, he raised its essentials and answered them collectively, because by attaining suchness-emptiness (*yathābhūtaśūnyatā*), the nature of the noble ones (*āryagotra*) is thereby revealed. Such is the general purport of the answer. Sentient beings, since beginningless time, have been attached to the characteristics of self-nature (*svabhāva*).

The attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom is called the teaching of emptiness. (The Buddha taught emptiness because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been attached to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things and to the objects of noble wisdom, perceiving them all as having real marks;

it is for this reason that he spoke of emptiness. Emptiness is taught in opposition to existence; emptiness is not a substantial dharma. Mahāmati, I do not speak of the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things. (The Wei translation says: "Mahāmati, I do not say that the essence of dharmas exists or does not exist.

[In the preceding passage, emptiness was taught because sentient beings were attached to existence; in this passage, he further clarifies that regarding the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things, I do not speak of either existence or non-existence, thereby simultaneously negating both existence and non-existence.]

(The current text lacks the characters "you" and "wu"; they can be understood by referring to the Wei dynasty translation. Mahāmati, I abide in the dharma of self-attained suchness-emptiness (the term "suchness-emptiness" refers to the dharma of the true, eternal Middle Way;

it is not the emptiness previously described in contrast to existence. It is non-attachment to both existence and non-existence, yet it is not a state of total oblivion; therefore, it is called suchness-emptiness). One sees [reality] by departing from delusive confusion, and one sees by departing from views regarding the existence or non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind.
Thus one attains the three liberations, which are sealed with the seal of suchness, regarding the intrinsic nature of things.

One attains the dwelling of self-realized contemplation based on conditions, free from the views and signs of existence and non-existence. (This clarifies the virtuous characteristics of emptiness as it truly is.

Within emptiness as it truly is, one is fundamentally free from the confusion of delusion and the views regarding the nature and signs of existence and non-existence that appear to the mind; thus, one attains the three gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. All realized dharmas and practices are sealed by the seal of emptiness as it truly is. It is said that all phenomena are free from signs and views, merging into the Middle Way.

By relying on the noble wisdom of self-realization to contemplate the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things, all natures and signs do not depart from their original state, for they are eternally abiding. Therefore, the dharma of emptiness as it truly is is free from existence and non-existence.)
[This refers to the view of phenomenal characteristics]. Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva should not establish the thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen.

(That is, the thesis of non-arising is what is conceptualized by the outsiders; those who rely on the Buddha for practice should not establish this thesis. This is the thesis that all phenomena are non-arisen. Why is this?

Because the thesis [asserts] that all natures are neither-nature nor non-nature, and because it relies on the characteristic of arising as its cause to proclaim the thesis that all dharmas are unarisen. That thesis...

Then it is destroyed. (This refers to the fault in the thesis that "subtle luminosity does not arise. It means that those non-Buddhists take "non-existence" as their thesis; they claim that all natures exist yet are not existent, and thus speak of "non-arising.

However, that non-arising depends upon arising for its existence and possesses its own characteristics. To explain briefly: this follows the preceding inquiry to clarify that the thesis of non-arising is subject to destruction.

That thesis holds that all phenomena do not arise; yet that thesis is destroyed because the thesis itself arises dependently. (This clarifies the reason why the thesis of non-arising is destroyed. It means that they establish "non-arising" by depending on "arising"; because there is something upon which it depends...)

That which is unarisen cannot exist independently; therefore, it is negated. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent. This is indeed true.

Furthermore, their thesis of non-arising would be included among all phenomena (the ancient commentary states: "Moreover, that thesis of non-arising would fall within the category of all phenomena. 'All phenomena' refers to such things as arising and non-arising, identity and difference, permanence and impermanence, etc. To say that if one establishes the thesis of non-arising, it falls into this category of all phenomena, and therefore one cannot establish the thesis of non-arising).
Since the characteristic of being unnegated is non-arising, those who establish the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen [contradict themselves].

That teaching would then be undermined. (Yang Yanguo’s compilation states: "The true nature is not undermined; it is inherently unborn. Now, by establishing this doctrine and entering into all phenomena, how could that establishment not be undermined?")
Mahāmati, there is the thesis that existence and non-existence are not produced. That thesis enters into all natures because the characteristics of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.

(Previously, the thesis of non-production was established solely with respect to existent dharmas; here, the thesis of non-production is established by taking both existence and non-existence together; hence it is said that "existence and non-existence are not produced. The *Jizhu* states: "If one establishes the thesis of non-production upon the basis of existence and non-existence, then one enters into the nature of all that exists and does not exist.

Since the characteristics of the natures of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended, where, then, could one establish the thesis that existence and non-existence are not produced? Mahāmati, if that thesis were not produced, then all...

If you establish a thesis based on the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that very thesis is undermined. Since neither existence nor non-existence possesses the characteristic of arising, a thesis should not be established.

(That is to say, if one were to establish a thesis by relying on the non-arising of existence or non-existence, since no intrinsic nature whatsoever arises, with respect to what further phenomenon would one discuss "non-arising"? Thus, it is known that the thesis must be refuted. Why?

Because neither existence nor non-existence possesses the characteristic of arising, a thesis should not be established. Furthermore, because the five-membered syllogism contains many fallacies, and because its successive reasons possess differing characteristics, and...

Because it is for the sake of establishing [a proof], one should not posit the *pakṣa* (the thesis). (This clarifies that the two types of theses in the preceding text contain many fallacies. Regarding the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vāda*), see the previous note. As for using the five members to eliminate fallacies, there are thirty-three kinds of such fallacies, as explained in detail in the *Nyāyapraveśa*. The *Jizhu* states:

"The five-membered syllogism is said to have many fallacies because they successively depend on contradictions, unestablished reasons (*asiddha*), inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika*), non-exclusion (*avyāvṛtta*), and so forth; these are distinct characteristics, as well as the presence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and the act of performing a formal operation (*kriyā*).")

Therefore, one should not establish these as formal propositions (*pakṣa*). That is to say: "All phenomena are unarisen," "In this way all phenomena are empty," and "In this way all phenomena lack intrinsic nature"—one should not establish these as propositions.

[The phrase] "unarisen" cites the names of the two preceding propositions; [the words] "in this way" and so forth subsume the remaining established doctrines, such as emptiness and the absence of intrinsic nature.

"Mahāmati, none of my disciples who practice correctly should establish a thesis (*pakṣa*) regarding this. However, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva speaks of all phenomena as being like illusions and dreams, because they possess the characteristics of appearing and not appearing, and because of the faults of views and cognition.
(The above admonishes the practitioner that they should not establish various false theses; this teaches them to speak according to the Dharma by means of the correct principle.

That is to say, one should teach that phenomena are like illusions and like dreams, because they lack the two characteristics of appearance and non-appearance. Regarding 'the faults of views and cognition,' this refers to all the aforementioned false theses, which all arise from the defects of deluded views and cognitions. The Bodhisattva is able to demonstrate this to them.)"

[This is] a fault. [He is] called one who skillfully teaches the Dharma. One should explain that all phenomena have the nature of illusions and dreams. (Building upon the previous point regarding the faults of perceiving cognition as real, this exhorts the Bodhisattva to teach the Dharma as being like illusions and dreams.)

Except for the case of speaking for the sake of removing the fear of fools. (Fools may fall into the interval between the fears of existence and non-existence; therefore, one uses skillful means to speak of existence and non-existence to cause them to leave behind such fear.

This does not apply to those who speak through skillful means [for other purposes], which is why it says "except for"). Mahāmati, do not let fools fall into the views of existence and non-existence, lest they become terrified.

"To distance oneself from the Mahāyāna" (this admonishes the Bodhisattva teaching the Dharma: one should observe the faculties of others and skillfully preach for them; without being dogmatic or self-attached, one should not cause them to be startled or terrified—this is what it means to distance oneself from the meaning of the Mahāyāna).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

There is no intrinsic nature and no verbal expression; there is no entity and no continuity. These are the false imaginings of the foolish, like a corpse and evil perceptions (the *Jizhu* commentary states:

"It is said that all dharmas originally have no intrinsic nature and are free from the characteristics of verbal expression; furthermore, there is no substantial dharma that constitutes a continuity. The foolish falsely give rise to evil perceptions, and their conceptual attachments are like a corpse;

therefore, the Tang translation says, 'evil perceptions are like a corpse'). All dharmas are unarisen; this is not the tenet of those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Ultimately, nothing whatsoever is produced.

All phenomena are accomplished through conditions. (The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "The Buddha taught that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn; this is not a tenet falsely imagined by those non-Buddhists.
All phenomena ultimately have no arising, because all natures are accomplished through conditions. All phenomena are unborn; the wise do not form conceptions of them.

Because their tenets arise from the notion of birth, the awakened ones completely eliminate them. (The *Guzhu* [Ancient Commentary] states: "The wise know that the essence of all phenomena is unborn, and therefore they do not form the conception of 'unborn. That tenet of 'unborn' is established based on the characteristic of birth.")
Therefore, the awakened ones completely eliminate them. For example, it is like one with cataracts seeing the appearance of falling hair;

the nature of conceptual attachment is likewise such that the foolish have false and deluded imaginings (this is a metaphor for those who establish the thesis of non-arising: this conceptual attachment is like the vision of falling hair by one with cataracts). Thus, they designate the three realms of existence.

There is no intrinsic nature in phenomena; it is only through the provisional designation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena that conceptualization arises. Based on these marks and phenomena, verbal teachings are established.

When the mind is distracted and violently agitated, the Son of the Buddha is able to transcend them and remain far removed from all conceptualizations—meaning that the dharmas of the three realms of existence in the world are merely provisional designations, and all causes, effects, and activities lack intrinsic nature.

Due to the false reflections of sentient beings, various deluded thoughts arise; the various non-Buddhists cling to the notions of individual and common characteristics, establishing them as verbal teachings.

The teachings cause the mind to become utterly deluded, trembling, and agitated. A son of the Buddha can transcend such verbal instructions and remain free from all conceptualizations; this is called a true practitioner. One does not experience the perception of water where there is no water.

This arises from craving; thus are the delusions of the foolish. For the noble vision, it is not so. (That is to say, the activities of the three realms of existence are fundamentally devoid of self-nature.

Yet, due to ignorance and craving, all ordinary fools falsely give rise to the notion of a self-nature within that which lacks nature. It is like a deer’s thirst: seeing a mirage, though it is originally not water, they perceive it as water.

The deluded confusion of worldly fools is thus; the knowledge and vision of the Buddha, however, is not so. The noble ones see purity; the three liberations and samādhis arise, far removed [from defilement].
Regarding arising and ceasing, they wander in non-existence and practice non-existence;

there is neither nature nor non-nature, for nature and non-nature are equal. From this, the fruits of the noble ones arise. (The phrase "wandering in non-existence" is rendered as "attaining unobstructed tranquility" in the Wei translation.

[This follows upon the preceding meaning that the noble vision is not so, thereby clarifying the noble practice. It means that because the noble one’s knowledge and vision are pure, the three liberations and right concentration arise from them, and all practices of arising and ceasing are likewise abandoned through them. In the realm of non-existence, moment by moment...

Correspondingly, since there is neither the characteristic of existence nor non-existence, all is tranquil and equal. From this equality, the various fruits of the sages arise. What is meant by existence and non-existence? What is meant by equality?
It is said that when that mind does not know and is utterly tossed about within and without, if one can destroy that [state], the mind will see with equanimity.

(This interrogates the mind regarding gain and loss, thereby clarifying the source of delusion and awakening. That is to say, what is existence and non-existence? Because the mind has no knowledge and is drifting and agitated within and without, there is "existence.")

It is not a characteristic of inherent nature. If one can destroy that ignorance, then both the internal and external will be tranquil. Because of this tranquility, the mind becomes equanimous, and one attains right view.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, just as one cannot obtain wisdom by grasping at objects of perception (ālambana-vastu), so too—[as the Wei translation states]—wisdom, when observing, cannot perceive the phenomena of the external objects before it. [Regarding the phrase 'like grasping at objects of perception': 'like' (yathā) refers to *tathatā* (suchness)."

That is to say, based on the object as it appears, it belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*). It does not apprehend the prior object; for the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is able to contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena, and thus it does not apprehend [an inherent object].

This is a mere conventional designation (*prajñapti-mātra*). It is established by convention, and that which is grasped is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); even the act of grasping is without intrinsic nature. Because there is no grasping, cognition (*jñāna*) does not arise;

it is merely a conventional name (meaning that the grasper and the grasped are merely provisionally established; since both the grasper and the grasped are absent, cognition does not arise, hence it is said "merely a conventional name"). What is the world?

World-Honored One, is it because the nature of non-perception is neither different nor non-different from its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that cognition does not apprehend it?
Or is it because the various natures and intrinsic characteristics of the own-characteristic and common-characteristic are obscured that cognition does not apprehend it?

Or is it because of obstructions such as mountains, cliffs, stone walls, earth, water, fire, and wind that cognition does not apprehend it? Or is it because of extreme distance or extreme proximity that cognition does not apprehend it?

"Is it because they are old, young, blind, ignorant, or lack the full sensory faculties that wisdom cannot be attained? (This establishes five general points to give rise to doubt; below, the specific points follow these to form a formal objection.

World-Honored One, if wisdom cannot be attained because one does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or not different, then one should not speak of 'wisdom,' but rather of 'non-wisdom,' since there is an object that is not attained.
(This follows the first point to distinguish between wisdom and non-wisdom. The intent of the objection is that if one says [self-]...)

Regarding the difference between the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): since the specific characteristic is not a cause, how could there be a general characteristic? Therefore, they are not different. If one says they are not different, then there would be no distinction between the specific and the general; yet, in reality, they are distinct. Thus, they are not non-different. Not realizing this cannot be called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); it should rather be called "non-knowledge.

Why then is it called "knowledge," and why do you say it is "not attained"? Furthermore, because the various natures of specific and general characteristics mutually obscure their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), [they are not perceived].
"O Bhagavān, that which is not attained by wisdom is itself without wisdom; it is not wisdom. Because there is such an object (*ālambana*), wisdom arises;

it is not that wisdom is produced through the encounter with a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Therefore, it is called wisdom. (This follows the second point to clarify that wisdom is non-wisdom. Regarding 'various self-characteristics and common characteristics':

this means that all phenomena each have their own self-characteristics and common characteristics, and each has its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). 'Concealed' means obstructed—just as the light of the sun and moon is obstructed by clouds and smoke, or as the vast expanse of space is hindered by mountain peaks. If wisdom attains this [the unobstructed] but does not attain that [the obstructed], it would likewise not be wisdom. O Bhagavān... [text continues].

Venerable One, Mahāmati explains the meaning of the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*). "Object" (*artha*) refers to that which is known; that which is known is the object, and that which knows is knowledge. When the object is present before one, the knower arises. It is not that the knower lacks an essence such that it could encounter the object.
Only when knowledge and the object are conjoined is it called "knowledge. This is Mahāmati’s erroneous explanation of the essence of knowledge, intended to clarify the fault of its non-attainment.

If knowledge cannot be attained due to mountains, cliffs, stone walls, earth, water, fire, wind, or because of being extremely distant or near, or due to old age, childhood, blindness, ignorance, or the impairment of the sense faculties—this too would not be knowledge. It should rather be...

It is non-cognition, because there are objects that cannot be apprehended. (This follows upon the third, fourth, and fifth points to collectively demonstrate that such states are not cognition. That is to say:

if obstructed by mountain crags, rocky walls, or the like, or separated by earth, water, fire, or wind, then even extremely distant objects cannot be apprehended; or if one is old, young, blind, or otherwise lacks the sensory faculties, then even extremely proximate objects cannot be apprehended. How can these be called cognition?)

"It would be non-intelligence, because although such matters as these exist, intelligence cannot be apprehended. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not thus that it is non-intelligence; rather, it should be understood as intelligence."
It is not non-knowledge. I do not speak of the concealment of objects of perception in such a way that wisdom would be unattainable;

rather, this is established as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-mātra*). (The Buddha means that one should not thus propound a theory of ignorance. As for what is called "unattainable," it should be understood as knowledge, not non-knowledge. Why? Because it is not by concealing the objects of perception in such a manner that wisdom is said to be unattainable;

rather, it means realizing that the preceding objects are not real, being merely conventional designations and provisional constructs. One awakens to the fact that the measure of reality is the manifestation of one's own mind, and that external natures—whether existent or non-existent—do not exist.

It is not that the nature is known, but rather that the phenomenon cannot be apprehended. Because it cannot be apprehended, cognition does not arise toward such an appearance; this accords with the three gates of liberation. Cognition, too, cannot be apprehended.

(This is because one knows that the preceding object is merely a provisional designation, realizing that it is what appears within the internal mind. One knows that external objects, though seemingly existent, are in fact non-existent. Their nature is thus non-nature. Since the phenomenon cannot be apprehended, and because it cannot be apprehended...)

Wisdom does not arise toward that which is known; rather, it accords with the three liberations. Yet, even while acceding to the sphere of wisdom, it is likewise unattainable. That which is not false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) refers to the beginningless habituated wisdom regarding existence and non-existence, which is deceptive by nature.

To produce such a cognition is to know that [the object] is unknown [by that cognition]. (This follows from the fact that noble wisdom is not something that can be known by the ignorant who engage in false conceptualization.

For those ignorant ones who rely on the habituated wisdom of beginningless existence, non-existence, and deception are unable to comprehend such a Buddha-knowledge and vision; therefore it is said, "this knowledge is unknown by them," meaning that their wisdom does not penetrate it. Therefore...
Regarding external objects and locations, their characteristics and the absence of intrinsic nature, the deluded imagination (*vikalpa*) is not severed.

Based on the manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), they establish and speak of the characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to self" (*ātman-ātmīya*). They grasp at and become attached to them (meaning that because ordinary fools lack penetrating wisdom, regarding all characteristics within external perceived objects, their deluded imagination regarding the existence or non-existence of their essential nature is not severed;

thus, based on the manifestation of their own mind, they speak of the characteristics of self and what belongs to self, firmly grasping and giving rise to various attachments). Failing to realize the manifestation of their own mind, they [remain] with respect to wisdom...
"O Jvālin, one gives rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Because of false conceptualization, external natures—whether existent or non-existent—cannot be apprehended through investigation;

thus, one relies upon the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). (This is because, failing to realize that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to various false conceptualizations regarding the knower and the known. Due to this false conceptualization, when investigating external natures, existence and non-existence cannot be found.

Because they cannot be found, one relies upon the view of annihilation. The distinctions regarding the point where knowledge finds no object are as follows. A practitioner of correct cultivation must distinguish these well. A slight deviation results in being separated by a thousand *li*; how can one not be cautious? At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to...
To reiterate this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"When there are objects of attachment, wisdom does not observe them. This is called 'non-wisdom,' not true wisdom; so say those who harbor false imaginings.

(The first two lines describe what Mahāmati doubted: that wisdom does not apprehend various objects of attachment. The latter two lines take up this point and state: To claim that wisdom does not apprehend due to the presence of objects of attachment is merely a term for 'non-wisdom' [a lack of realization].)

This is not true wisdom; it is merely the speech of those who harbor false conceptions. When wisdom does not observe the nature of non-differentiation, and when there are obstructions, or notions of distance and proximity, this is called false wisdom.
In the case of the elderly or the young whose faculties are dull and whose wisdom does not arise, yet for whom such appearances (nimitta) actually exist, this too is said to be false wisdom.

(The first two lines praise the Buddha’s correct wisdom, meaning that since characteristics and nature are not real, wisdom does not observe them. The next two lines describe various [forms of ignorance].)
Concealment is that which is reckoned by false imagination; therefore, it is designated as "erroneous knowledge" (the latter four phrases may be understood accordingly).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings are turned around by the beginningless, false, evil, and erroneous imaginings [of their own minds].

At the time of turning back, they do not properly understand the thorough realization of one's own school (*svapratyātmagatigocara*) and the communication through teaching (*deśanā*). (This follows from the preceding text regarding the point where wisdom does not find [its object]. That is to say, the various ordinary, ignorant people...)

Driven by evil, false, and deluded imaginings, they fail to properly understand both the fundamental principle (*siddhānta*) and its exposition (*deśanā*). Because they cling to the external characteristics of natures manifested by their own minds, they cling to expedient teachings and fail to correctly discern the pure, universal characteristics of the fourfold logic within their own fundamental doctrine.
(The *Jizhu* states: "This means that they adhere to the literal text while neglecting the underlying intent; they have not yet attained the meaning through the forgetting of words.

By fixating on natures and characteristics and clinging to expedient verbal expressions, they fail to correctly discern the Dharma of the fundamental doctrine which transcends the four extremes. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "It is truly as [you have said]..."
"Venerable Teaching! I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, explain in detail the *sūtra-vehicle* (the teaching) and the *principle-vehicle* (the realization).

By this, I and other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may become proficient in these two vehicles, so that in future ages ordinary people, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas shall not be able to find any deficiency in us. (The *Jizhu* notes:

"When both the principle and the teaching are thoroughly understood, understanding and practice correspond, and there are no further faults; thus, when ordinary people or those of the two vehicles seek for flaws or openings, they cannot find them. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "So be it;

we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharma-passages: namely, the passage of teaching (*deśanā-prativedha*) and the passage of one's own realization (*svapratyātma-gotra-prativedha*).
As for the passage of teaching, it refers to the expounding of various skillful means according to what is appropriate to the minds of sentient beings."

The Sūtras are called the "Exposition of the Teaching" (*deśanā-pravṛtti*). (Regarding "the various collections": this refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Because these sūtras contain diverse names—such as *upadeśa*, *geya*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *jātaka*, and *itivṛttaka*—it is said they are "the various collections.

As for the "Mastery of One's Own School" (*svaprakriyā-gati*), it means that practitioners, having detached from the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own minds, do not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither.
They transcend all mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*) and realize the noble realm of self-awakening, which is free from [all conceptualization].

It is because they have not yet transcended the characteristics of views produced by causes. (As for "the ultimate tenet" (*zong*): it means the primary, the goal. It signifies that one's practice has a primary focus, thereby attaining the correct direction. The "ultimate tenet" belongs to practice, while the "teaching" (*shuo*) belongs to understanding.

Since practice relies on self-awakening and does not seek outwardly, it is called the "ultimate tenet. To transcend the characteristics of views produced by causes means to attain self-awakening and remain far removed from the views and characteristics produced by causes and conditions.

This is something that all heterodox teachers, *śrāvakas*, and *pratyekabuddhas* who fall into the two extremes cannot know. (That is to say, the "ultimate tenet" is the meaning of the Mahāyāna; the various ordinary and small-vehicle practitioners, falling into the two extremes of existence and non-existence, cannot understand this. I...

This is called the Dharma of the self-school’s ultimate realization (*sva-siddhānta-paramārtha*). (This concludes the characteristics of the ultimate realization. Mahāmati, these are the characteristics of the self-school’s ultimate realization and the teaching of the doctrine (*deśanā-pāṭha*).
You and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study them. (The section beginning with "Mahāmati" below summarizes the two types of penetration.

The section beginning with "You and" encourages their practice and study. The *Jízhù* states: "The two penetrations of the school and the doctrine were already clarified in the preceding text. That they are stated again now is for a specific reason. Previously, regarding the Two Vehicles, the school was mentioned first and the doctrine second; here, regarding the One Vehicle, the doctrine is mentioned first and the school second. This difference arises from the distinct capacities of the audience; it is not a mere repetition.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"I speak of two kinds of penetration: the penetration of the principle and the penetration of verbal expression. The verbal expression is for the sake of instructing the ignorant; the principle is for those who practice cultivation.
(The 'ignorant' refers to the śrāvakas, who have not yet opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; the 'practitioners' refers to the bodhisattvas, who are able to cultivate the practice of reality.)"
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has at one time said:

'Regarding the various treatises of the world and their manifold arguments and explanations, you must be careful not to study or associate with them. (The term 'worldly treatises' is rendered as *Lokāyata* in the Wei and Tang translations.

[Collected Commentary] states: *Lokāyata* translates as 'left-of-the-world' or 'evil treatise'; it refers to the treatises of the non-Buddhists. If one studies or associates with them, one will embrace desire and fail to embrace the Dharma. (If a person...)

To study and become intimate with worldly treatises is to embrace fame, profit, and all forms of craving—just as those in the world today who labor over textual passages and burn or cook yellow and white [substances] are engaged in matters of craving, not in supramundane dharmas.
"World-Honored One, why do you speak thus? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Worldly discourse employs various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and parables, collecting and adorning them to entice and delude foolish ordinary people; it does not enter into the reality of self-..."
[They] do not realize that all phenomena are false conceptualizations and inversions, falling into the two extremes. Being ordinary, foolish, and deluded, they destroy themselves;

their succession through the various realms of existence continues, and they fail to attain liberation. (The Tang translation says: "The discourses of the Lokāyata merely adorn words and phrases to deceive and delude the ordinary and foolish.

They follow worldly, false speech; they do not accord with reality, nor do they conform to principle. They cannot enter the realm of true reality, nor can they awaken to and understand all phenomena. They constantly fall into the two extremes, losing the right path for themselves and likewise leading others astray.")

Human beings transmigrate through the various realms of existence and never escape from them. Failing to realize that all is but the manifestation of one’s own mind, they do not depart from external natures and intrinsic essences, remaining attached to false conceptualizations.
For this reason, the various discursive explanations of worldly treatises do not free one from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction;
they only deceive and delude. (The above clarifies the harm of associating with worldly treatises; the following shows that worldly treatises are not to be relied upon. Mahāmati, Śakra—
Indra, who extensively expounded various treatises, composed a work on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*) himself.

A disciple of that proponent of worldly doctrines (*lokāyatika*), assuming the form of a dragon, went to the palace of Śakra-devendra to establish his own philosophical tenets. He vowed that he would break Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel;
should he be defeated, he would sever one head for each spoke as an atonement for his submission. Having made this vow, he proceeded to use the methods of Śakra to subdue [his opponents].

Śakra, having fallen into a position of defeat, immediately destroyed his chariot and returned to the human realm. (In Sanskrit, Śakra-devānām-indra; translated as "The Heavenly Lord Capable [of Victory].

Those who assume the form of a dragon are said to adorn themselves with the dragon's shape in order to enhance their majesty. As for those who sever each head one by one, these are the teachers of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and their followers. Non-Buddhists take the severing of the head as their primary requirement when establishing their doctrines.

Just as they would establish a thesis in debate against the Buddha—whether asserting existence, non-existence, speech, or silence—they likewise use the severing of the head to express their submission when defeated. The Buddha did not permit this. Now, the Buddha cites the discourse of Śakra-devānām-indra to further clarify that worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*) are not to be relied upon. Why is this? Śakra...)

The celestial realms transcend the human world; their wisdom surpasses that which lies beyond the heavens. Even their treatises can be refuted, let alone those of the other devas and humans. This citation of the superior serves as a warning against those who fall short;
hence it is said: "Be careful not to study or associate with worldly treatises. Thus, Mahāmati, worldly discourse is adorned with causes and analogies;

even animals can, through various phrases and expressions, delude the various devas and asuras, causing them to become attached to views of arising and ceasing—how much more so for humans? (This refers to all worldly [treatises]).

Various different types of beings, even down to animals, are capable of composing various discourses, adorning them with causes and analogies in diverse phrases and expressions. They refute the delusions of gods, asuras, and others who are attached to views of arising and ceasing; how much more so, then, would they not destroy [the views of] humans?
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should distance oneself from worldly discourse, for it can bring about the causes for the arising of suffering.

Be careful not to study or associate with it. (This concludes by manifesting the faults of worldly treatises and admonishing practitioners to be careful not to study or associate with them. Mahāmati, those who propound worldly treatises speak only of the body.

It is merely the awakening to objects of perception. (This clarifies the meaning of worldly discourse (*lokāyata*) to demonstrate its superficiality. Those who speak of the body take the essence, energy, and spirit as fundamental; they practice the circulation of *kan* and *li*, ingesting and exhaling, desiring to seek longevity—such are their kind.

Those who speak of awakening hold that primordial darkness gives birth to awakening, and awakening gives birth to the great elements, taking the divine self (*puruṣa*) as the awakener—such are their kind.

These two are what is called the study of nature and destiny; they are close to this [superficiality]). Mahāmati, those proponents of worldly discourse number in the hundreds of thousands. (This indicates the manifold varieties of worldly discourse. However, in later times, during the final five hundred years...

In this year, when the destruction of the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*) occurs, it will be because evil views have flourished due to the causes of false awakening, and wicked disciples will accept them. (The Buddha prophesied that the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma each last five hundred years.

Now, it is said to be the latter five hundred years; this is precisely the beginning of the Final Dharma. At that time, strife will become entrenched, and heterodox doctrines will arise extensively. They will destroy one another, yet all these are views arising from the causes of false awakening and divergent factors.

These flourish in the world through the influence of demonic energy and the eruption of their own inherent evils, acting as such disciples. Thus, Mahāmati, the worldly treatises (*lokāyata*) destroy the communal recitation with various phrases and expressions.
"Adorned with causes and similes" refers to the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). They are attached to their own causal conditions and lack any self-attained realization.

(What is taught by the worldly treatises adorned with causes and similes does not transcend the categories of existence and non-existence, identity and difference, nor such matters as the *pradhāna* (Primal Nature) and atoms; being attached to their own false types of causal conditions, they are not within the scope of the Tathāgata’s self-attained realization. Mahāmati!

Those various non-Buddhists have no system of their own; regarding other worldly treatises, they extensively expound immeasurable hundreds of thousands of categories of phenomena, yet they possess no self-attained realization, nor do they recognize that these are merely foolish worldly treatises (meaning that although these worldly treatises extensively expound immeasurable hundreds of thousands of categories of phenomena, they never contain the meaning of the Tathāgata’s self-attained realization;
furthermore, while those non-Buddhists each claim to have perfected the unsurpassed path, they do not realize that their own discourse is a foolish one). At that time, Mahāmati addressed the Buddha:

He said: "World-Honored One, if the worldly discourses of the non-Buddhists—adorned with various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies, yet lacking any self-attained realization and characterized by attachment to their own affairs—are also spoken of by the World-Honored One as 'worldly discourse' for the sake of the various assemblies gathered from different regions?"
"Devas, humans, and asuras extensively expound immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions; are these not also their own realizations?
Are they not also included within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhists? (Mahāmati raises this objection based on the preceding passage, saying:

"If the hundreds of thousands of doctrinal gates of the non-Buddhists do not constitute their own realizations, then the World-Honored One has also extensively expounded various phrases and expressions for the immeasurable multitudes gathered from other regions—such as devas, humans, and asuras—and these are identical to what the non-Buddhists teach. Are they not also [merely] their own realizations? Are they not also included within the wisdom of the non-Buddhists?")
[Is this] the enumeration of verbal discourse? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not speak of worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*), nor is there coming and going;

I speak only of neither-coming-nor-going. Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to gathering and arising; 'going' refers to dispersal and destruction. Neither-coming-nor-going is the root of the True Dharma (*saddharma*);

coming and going are the traces of the gathering and dispersing of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). That which neither comes nor goes is non-arising and non-ceasing; this is the meaning I have taught, which does not fall into the world."

In the discourse on the enumeration of false conceptions (*vikalpa*), [it is stated that] one does not fall into the categories of worldly treatises (continuing from the preceding meaning to clarify why one does not fall into the categories of worldly treatises). For worldly treatises are dharmas of arising and ceasing, whereas the Buddha’s teaching alone transcends them;
therefore, one does not fall into their categories. Why is this so? It is because one does not cling to external existence or non-existence.

Within the realm of what is manifested by one's own mind, one cannot be turned by the false conceptions of the two extremes. (The "two extremes" refers to the two sides of external existence and non-existence, as well as the internal realm of mental manifestation. The Buddha, having integrated the Middle Way, is able to master things and is not swayed by the false conceptions of the two extremes.)
The objects of characteristics are not real entities. When one realizes that these are manifestations of one's own mind, then the delusions manifested by one's own mind cease to arise.

When delusions do not arise, this is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); one enters the three gates of liberation, which is called emancipation. (Realizing that objects characterized as existent or non-existent are all manifestations of one's own mind, they are therefore not real entities.

Once one has realized the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind, then the delusions manifested by one's own mind cease to arise. Because internal and external delusions no longer arise, there are the three gates of liberation—emptiness of persons, signlessness, and wishlessness—which is called the Tathāgata’s true emancipation.)
"Mahāmati, I recall that once, while I was dwelling in a certain place, a world-theorist (*lokāyatika*) brāhmaṇa came to where I was.

He did not ask for an interval [of silence]. (To 'not ask for an interval' means that he wished to ask a question and requested the Buddha to answer at once, rather than halting him with an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) response.

'Interval' refers here to the intent of halting him with an indeterminate answer. It is incorrect for the old commentaries to interpret 'interval' as 'selflessness. As the *Jizhu* states: 'Brāhmaṇa' is fully called *brāhmaṇa-māna*, translated as 'Pure Lineage. They claim their ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā; thus they follow the Brahmanical clan. In various sūtras...")"

"Brahmin," [the Buddha] replied, "this is precisely their name; it exists only in the five regions of India and not in other countries. Furthermore, they are called 'those with external intentions' (*bāhirattha*). Their lineage possesses its own distinct scriptures, which they inherit as their profession. Whether living as householders or having left the home-life, they rely on their arts and are arrogant;

they are also called 'those of pure conduct' (*brahmacarin*). He then asked me: 'Gautama, is everything created? I then replied to him: 'Brahmin, everything is created. This was the first worldly doctrine (*lokāyata*).

(That he addressed the Buddha as 'Gautama' rather than by his title is the speech of an outsider who is arrogant and disrespectful. Yet the Buddha was able to tolerate this and still provided an answer.)"

That which is "produced" is reckoned as existing. Among the hundreds of thousands of worldly treatises (*lokavāda*), the reckoning of existence is the most superficial; therefore, it was explained first). He asked again: "Is everything not produced?"
I replied again, saying: "All things are uncreated. This is the second worldly doctrine. (That which is "uncreated" is a calculation of non-existence. Non-existence is more profound than existence.)
Therefore, it follows next). He asked again: "Are all things eternal? Are all things impermanent? Are all things born? Are all things unborn? I replied to him:
"These are the six worldly doctrines (ṣaḍ-laukika-vāda). Because they increase sequentially from the preceding ones, they are called the six worldly doctrines. O Mahāmati!
He further asked me: "Is everything one? Is everything different? Is everything both? Is everything neither?
Does everything manifest through birth based on various causes? I then replied to him: "These are the eleven types of worldly theorists."

(The views held by the non-Buddhists do not go beyond the four positions, as stated in the text. Regarding "arising and manifesting from various causes": the non-Buddhists reckon that all phenomena arise and manifest from the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth.

The eleven points of superiority are as before. Mahāmati, they further ask: Are all things indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Are all things determinate (*vyākṛta*)? Is there a self (*ātman*)? Or is there no self?
Is there this world? Is there no this world? Is there another world? Is there no other world?
Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Are all things momentary? Are all things non-momentary? Is there space? Is there cessation through non-calculation?
Is there nirvana? Gautama, is there action? Is there non-action? Is there an intermediate state (antarābhava)? Is there no intermediate state?
“Mahāmati, I then replied to the brāhmaṇa: ‘Such statements as these are all merely worldly discourses (*lokavāda*); they are not what I teach. These are your worldly discourses.

[This refers to] non-analytical cessation (in the Tang translation, *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). [Regarding the categories: ‘the created and the uncreated,’ ‘the agent and the non-agent’—the former was stated from the perspective of the object created, while the latter is now stated from the perspective of the agent.

As for the ‘indeterminate’ (*avyākṛta*), it means that all things lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, they cannot be defined. The ‘determinate’ (*vyākṛta*) is the opposite of this. The same applies to ‘self and no-self,’ ‘world and non-world,’ ‘momentary and non-momentary. As for the three [elements] beginning with space (*ākāśa*), they are as follows:”

This is the third of the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "That which is not due to the power of deliberation, but is pure by its own nature, or is manifested by the absence of conditions, is therefore called cessation not through deliberation. Regarding the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*): it refers to the body of the intermediate aggregates that exists when this life has already ended but that future birth has not yet been established;

hence it is named the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*). The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Because it arises between two existences (*bhava*) and proceeds toward various destinies (*gati*). From the beginning of the *Lokāyata* treatise up to this point, all are the calculations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Those who brought these questions to the Buddha were answered by the Buddha with worldly discourse (*lokāyata*); it was said: "This is not what I teach.
I only teach the various evils of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), which are beginningless, false, and habitual tendencies of delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa-vāsanā*)."

This is the cause. Failing to realize that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, they give rise to false conceptualization and grasp at external natures, as in the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who claim that cognition arises from the conjunction of the self, the sense organs, and their objects.
I do not hold such a view. (The passage following "as in the non-Buddhists" is translated by the Wei version as: "O Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists say...")

“Brahmin, the union of the three—the self (*ātman*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*)—is able to produce cognition. Brahmin, I do not say this. (The *Táng* translation says: ‘As the non-Buddhists claim that the self, the faculties, and the objects, these three, unite to produce [cognition], I do not say this.

This can be understood by comparing the two translations). Brahmin, the word ‘self’ refers to the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) as conceived by the non-Buddhists. Brahmin, I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no cause;

I speak only of the nature of the grasped and the grasper within false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the designation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is not for you, nor for others who fall into the continuity of the notion of a self.”

It can be realized by those capable of such awakening. (The phrase "not yours" in the Tang translation means: it cannot be fathomed by you or others who are attached to a self. [In the present text, "receiving the continuity of the self" carries the meaning of clinging to a divine self and not relinquishing it].
Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and cessation are not of three kinds; there are only three enumerations. (Cessation is translated as "non-analytical cessation" in the Tang version).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time, the Lokāyata Brahmin again asked me: "Ignorance, craving, and karma are the causes."

"Therefore, do the three realms of existence exist? Or are they without cause? I then replied: "These two views are also merely worldly discourse (loka-vāda)—namely, the distinction between existence with a cause and existence without a cause.

I replied once more: "This too is worldly discourse, O Brahmin. Even up to the flow of the mind, the false conceptualization of external objects is entirely [worldly discourse]."

Worldly Discourse. (The phrase "down to" [乃至]—as the Tang translation notes: "Even a slight movement of consciousness that discriminates external objects is all worldly discourse"—indicates that he did not exhaustively describe all non-Buddhist views, but rather surpassed them; hence the use of "down to").
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Brahmin of Worldly Discourse again asked me: "Is there anything that is not worldly discourse?
I am the master of all non-Buddhists, and I speak of various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and parables.
“Adorned. I replied again, “Brahmin, there is that which belongs to me, yet does not belong to you; it is neither a non-doctrine, nor is it something that is neither spoken nor unspoken.

It is adorned with various phrases and expressions, and is not without causes or analogies. (When the Brahmin heard the Buddha’s response regarding the faults of worldly discourse, he was struck with alarm by those words and asked in turn, “Is there anything that is not worldly discourse?

The Buddha replied again, “There is, but that which belongs to him does not belong to you. The Brahmin spoke further, “I am one who is honored as the preeminent teacher among all the heterodox paths, capable of creating—”)

"Is there anyone capable of composing a treatise that is likewise adorned with various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies? The Buddha replied, "There is. However, whatever they possess—both their tenets (*siddhānta*) and their expositions (*deśanā*)—are all correct principles.

They do not constitute non-tenets. Yet, it is neither a case of non-exposition nor non-non-exposition. Their various phrases and expressions are fully adorned; what they say accords with reality, and thus they are free from the fault of deluded conceptual attachment. Therefore, this is not yours.

The Brahmin asked, "What is it that is not worldly discourse (*lokavāda*), yet is not a non-tenet, and is not a non-exposition? [The Brahmin] repeated the previous words as a question. I then replied to the Brahmin: "There is."

It is not a worldly doctrine (*lokavāda*). It is that which you various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are unable to know, because you cling to false imaginings and delusions regarding external natures as being real.

(The World-Honored One answers only that it is "not a worldly doctrine" without explicitly identifying the person; this is because the Buddha acknowledges it himself, yet he also implicitly points toward those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

This is because the supramundane path they practice consists of the Dharma realized within themselves and cannot be compared to the false imaginings of non-Buddhists. Furthermore, because that path is profound and far-reaching, it is not known by non-Buddhists. This is because of attachment to unreal conceptualizations. It means that conceptualization does not arise when one realizes that existence and non-existence are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.

When conceptualization does not arise, one does not receive external objects, and conceptualization is forever stilled; this is called the "Non-Worldly Discourse" (*alokāyatika*). This is my teaching, not yours. (Regarding the Non-Worldly Discourse:

it is the complete wisdom that realizes the nature and characteristics of existence and non-existence as being the manifestations of one's own mind. Therefore, conceptualization does not arise. Because conceptualization does not arise, one does not receive external objects, and conceptualization is forever stilled.)
It ceases. This is called the path of those who do not engage in worldly discourse. The Dharma taught by the Buddha does not belong to the non-Buddhists (this repeats the previous phrase:

"it does not belong to you," O Brahmin). Briefly stated, O Brahmin, that consciousness—whether coming or going, dying or being born, pleasure or pain, sinking or seeing, touching or clinging to various signs, whether in combination or continuity, or through craving and attachment to causes—is thus, O Brahmin.

"This [comparison] belongs to your worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*); it is not mine. The characteristics conceptualized by deluded consciousness all belong to worldly treatises; they do not exist within the Dharma of the Tathāgata. Therefore, I say they are not mine.

(The above is the Buddha citing past instances of refuting external doctrines to prove that practitioners must not associate with them. This serves as a response to Mahāmati’s question, intending to lead practitioners to enter deeply into their own school, to teach according to the capacities of beings, to be fully endowed with the two types of supernatural knowledge (*abhijñā*), and to remain far removed from all faults.
Thus, he extensively clarifies the errors of worldly treatises. "Mahāmati, a Brahmin of worldly treatises asked me this:"
He answered thus. The other remained silent and withdrew without taking his leave, reflecting on the point of his own understanding and thinking to himself:

"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have strayed outside of direct realization; they preach non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, [merely] awakening to the manifestations of their own deluded imaginings."

"False conceptualization does not arise. (The Brahmin withdrew and reflected upon the domain he himself had mastered. He began to suspect that the Śramaṇa was speaking of meanings such as "non-arising" that lay outside his own mastery.

His mind remained unenlightened, and thus he continued to harbor this doubt. "Mahāmati, this is precisely what you asked me just now: 'For what reason do you say that those who study worldly treatises engage in various forms of sophistry, which embrace greed and do not embrace the Dharma?

"What is the meaning of the phrases regarding the acceptance of sensual desire and the Dharma? (Mahāmati asked: "What is the harm in accepting sensual desire as taught by the worldly philosophers? And what is the benefit for a śramaṇa who accepts the Dharma?

You are able, for the sake of future sentient beings, to contemplate and inquire about such meanings. (While Mahāmati was certainly clear regarding the points of harm and benefit, he posed this question for the sake of sentient beings in the final age. Because of this, the Buddha..."

Master and disciples shared in compassion, responding to one another in harmony; they have bestowed great kindness and virtue upon us—how could anyone repay them? Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
What is called craving: whether grasping or rejecting, whether touching or tasting, one becomes fettered and attached to external objects and falls into the views of the two extremes.

This arises from associating with and following worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*) and those who propound such treatises. I and all the Buddhas declare this to be "greed. This is called "embracing greed while not embracing the Dharma. What is meant by greed?

It refers to grasping at what is agreeable to one's mind and rejecting what is contrary to one's feelings—namely, the contact of the body with smooth textures and the taste of the tongue for sweet flavors;

these are the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-bāhyaviṣaya*). Furthermore, one may advance to speculate on existence or non-existence, falling into the views of the two extremes. One is born and then dies; having died, one is born again. Through birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress, one revolves in saṃsāra.

It does not cease. Such afflictions as these all arise from craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving is the source of birth and death, yet people do not know how to avoid it. This is truly because they do not realize the non-arising (*anutpāda*) of phenomena; they habitually frequent worldly treatises (*lokavāda*), and those who rely on such worldly treatises act as their teachers and friends, mutually leading one another astray.

The Buddha said that such people are called "those of greedy desire. For example, in the world today, some sages may aspire to longevity and indulge in the practice of ingesting elixirs; others may be skilled in literary compositions and seek fame and achievement; or like Liezi, who rode upon the wind, or Tao Zhu, who attained great wealth—these are such cases.

All these are the cravings of worldly desire; they are the restings of saṃsāra. Furthermore, some fools may practice the delusory and extravagant teachings of Luo Qing, falsely claiming in their speech that all is empty. Or they may deceive themselves regarding the true cultivation of the First Patriarch, hoping to attain Buddhahood instantly. They sit cross-legged in silence within dark rooms, practicing a "single transmission" in vain.

There is no distinction between male and female; one need not be restricted in food and drink. These are all the harms of worldly discourse, by which one falls oneself and causes others to fall as well; even after exhausting kalpas in hell, one will still not reach the end. It means to skillfully awaken to and know the manifestation of one’s own mind, to perceive the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), so that false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise.

It is to skillfully know the successive higher stages (*bhūmi*), to be free from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*), and to receive the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of the wisdom of all Buddhas.

This refers to not falling into any views, any falsehoods, any delusive thoughts, or any...

Nature. All dualistic extremes (this refers to the True Dharma, which does not fall into such views). Mahāmati, there are many foolish outsiders who fall into the two extremes of either permanence or annihilation;

The mind-only is invisible; one does not examine the two minds. Subject and object are without intrinsic nature; it is free from both extremes of annihilation and permanence.
"Even unto the movement of the mind—this is the worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). For one whose false imaginings (*vikalpa*) do not move, that person perceives their own mind.

(The first four lines are as previously understood. [Such as] permanence and impermanence, the created and the uncreated, this world and the other world, and so forth.
All of these are common worldly theories (the meaning of the verse can be understood).

"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it for you. As for the various non-Buddhists who falsely conceptualize nirvāṇa, that which they conceptually construct does not accord with true nirvāṇa.

When all aggregates of sensation are exhausted—like the extinguishing of a lamp’s flame or the destruction of a seed—delusive thoughts no longer arise.

Those who perceive this state conceive of it as nirvāṇa. However, Mahāmati, it is not by the destruction of what is seen that one calls it nirvāṇa. (The Buddha refutes the preceding view, stating that nirvāṇa is not defined by the cessation and destruction of perceived phenomena;

[Regarding the phrase] "from direction to direction": this refers to those non-Buddhists who speculate about directions. It means that if there were no other destinies...

Then the perceptions of self and other, and of objective realms, are extinguished, like the ceasing of the wind; this is called Nirvana. If objective realms were not extinguished, self and other would exist in relation to one another, moving from here to there just as the wind blows; therefore, the cessation of the wind is used as a metaphor for the extinction of perception.

"Death. Thus, my own mind-nature is called 'permanent,' while that which undergoes birth and extinction is truly of an impermanent nature; such is this view.

One then develops a deep attachment to this state, conceiving it to be *nirvāṇa*. (Since the perception of marks contains all forms of craving, it becomes the cause for the suffering of future rebirth. For this reason, one denies existence...)
They see nothing; they develop a deep attachment to the object of signlessness and, right there, conceive the notion that it is nirvāṇa.

Or, they perceive that all internal and external phenomena—whether characterized by specific or general traits, and whether past, future, or present—possess an indestructible nature, and they conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa (meaning they reckon that the nature of the internal mind, external objects, specific and general characteristics, and the three times is indestructible).

Based on this view of permanence, they conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*. Or, they claim that the self (*ātman*), the person (*pudgala*), sentient beings (*sattva*), life-span (*jīva*), and all phenomena (*dharma*) are destroyed, and thus conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*.

(The former is the calculation of permanence; this is the calculation of annihilation). Alternatively, those whose wisdom has been scorched by the evil of non-Buddhists perceive primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*).

They hold that there is an interval between these two, and that which is produced by the spirit is called primordial nature, similar to the analogy of the "dark origin" (*tamas*). [They further maintain] the transformation of the qualities (*guṇa*), and the qualities...

This is the agent (*kartṛ*). It conceives of itself as *nirvāṇa*. "Self-nature" (*svabhāva*) refers here to the self-nature of the atoms (*paramāṇu*). "Person" (*puruṣa*) is a name for the agent. "The existence of those two" refers back to the aforementioned self-nature and the person;

Some claim it is wisdom; others see Īśvara as the true creator of saṃsāra, conceiving of him as nirvāṇa (Īśvara refers to Maheśvara.

Non-Buddhists collectively hold that this deity is the cause of all things. The *Huayan Chao* states that this deity possesses four attributes: first, unity; second, omnipresence; third, permanence; and fourth, the capacity to give rise to all dharmas.

Therefore, they cling to this deity as being permanent and unitary, the cause of all things, and the cause of nirvāṇa). Others claim that beings arise through a continuous succession, and that there is no other cause for saṃsāra. As...
This is precisely attachment to a cause, yet those who are ignorant are unable to perceive it;

because they do not know it, they conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*. Section. These six treatises contain the meaning of *Rāṣṭrapāla*. ...due to false conceptualization (vikalpa), it is not established). Mahāmati, all such cases fall into the two extremes and are conceived as *nirvāṇa*.

Existence, non-existence, identity, difference, both, neither, permanence, and impermanence—all are included within the discourse of the two extremes. "Such as these" and so forth further clarify the falsity of the non-Buddhist *nirvāṇa*, stating that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of their *nirvāṇa* cannot be found; how then could [it exist]?)*
(The marks of arising and ceasing). Mahāmati, regarding the nirvāṇa of each of those non-Buddhists, when examined with wisdom according to their own treatises, nothing at all is established.

(That is to say, those non-Buddhists have composed their treatises based on their own delusions; when observed with wisdom, they are all collectively a mere falsehood and nothing is established therein.
