They lose what they have postulated, and for this reason, [the non-Buddhists] are terrified.)
At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse: (The following two rounds of question and answer are combined into a single verse in the Wei and Tang translations.
"What is it? What is its cause? By what reason does it arise? In what place do they combine to form the doctrine of non-causality?

(Mahāmati follows up on the previous discussion of the blazing doctrine of non-causality to pose this question; his intention is to ask: 'What is meant by non-causality? If there is no cause, then what is it caused by? For what reason do those non-Buddhists come into existence? Since they belong to [the category of] non-causality...')"
"By what cause, and through the conjunction of what further factors, does birth occur? (Thus he asked four times by way of repetition).
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
Contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*): they do not arise without cause, nor do they arise from a cause. Thus, the views of those proponents of arising and ceasing are extinguished.

(The *Jizhu* [Compendium of Notes] states: The Buddha said that one should contemplate all conditioned phenomena; they do not arise without cause, nor do they arise from a cause. Therefore, it is said they are "unborn. Consequently, the theories regarding arising and ceasing held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are thereby destroyed.)
At that time, Mahāmati spoke in verse, asking:
"What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature? Or is it because one observes all conditions that a phenomenon is called 'non-arising'?

A name should not be without meaning; pray explain this for my sake through analysis. [Note on "observes" (顧視): According to the Tang translation, this means "to depend upon" (待). The Tang translation reads: "Is it because of non-existence that there is no arising? ]

"Is it because of dependence upon various conditions? Or is it that the name exists while the meaning is absent? I pray that you will explain this for me. Mahāmati asked: 'What is meant by "non-arising"? Is it that the absence of intrinsic nature is called non-arising? Or is there a distinct dharma, dependent upon various conditions, which is named non-arising?
Since the name "non-arising" already exists, its meaning cannot be non-existent. If both name and meaning are not absent, one falls into the view of existence. What, then, is meant by non-arising?'"
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered in verse:
"It is not that there is no nature and thus no arising, nor is it that one merely looks toward conditions. It is not that there is a nature which is then named, nor is the name without meaning.
This is not the domain of any of the non-Buddhists, the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, or those in the seventh stage; this is called 'non-existence'."

The Characteristic of Arising. (Answer: It is not that non-existence is called "non-arising," nor is it a distinct dharma that exists dependent upon conditions. Since it is named "non-arising," how could it be said to have no meaning? How great is non-arising! It is beyond the reach of the Two Vehicles;

for all outsiders, it is not within the scope of their knowledge or vision. Thus, while the Two Vehicles merely exhaust arising and ceasing, this is not true non-arising. To attain even a portion of the seven natures is not ultimate. Only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood does one first realize the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of non-arising).

Far removed from all causes and conditions, and also detached from all phenomena, there remains only the abiding of the subtle mind. Both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned. As for its body...

"Following transformation, I say this is non-arising. (The term *míxīn* [subtle mind]—in the Wei and Tang translations it is *wéixīn* [mind-only]. Since the character *wéi* appears above in the current text, it has been changed to *mí*; it likewise carries the meaning of *wéi*.
Although the *Jízhu* interprets it as 'subtle mind,' which accords with the sense, when examining the intent of the original verse, it simply carries the meaning of *wéi*).
Without external nature, without the absence of nature, and without the mind’s grasping, having severed all views—I say this is non-arising. Thus, there is no self-nature, emptiness, and so forth."

This should be analyzed. It is not because it is empty that it is called "empty," but because it is unarisen that it is called "empty. (As for this "unarisen": externally there is neither nature nor non-nature; internally there is no grasping mind; all divergent views are severed—this the Buddha calls "unarisen.

Thus, below, one should analyze by way of the meanings of "lack of self-nature," "emptiness," and so forth. That is to say, emptiness is not a nihilistic emptiness; it is skillfully taught according to the capacity of the audience.

Therefore, though it is not empty, it is spoken of as empty. Emptiness is itself the unarisen, and the unarisen is itself emptiness; thus it is called empty. As for the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes other names, namely: *tathatā* (suchness), *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature), *vimukti* (liberation), and so on. [End of] Section on Causes.

Through the conjunction of the conditions of the causal chain (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is arising and ceasing. Apart from these conditions of the causal chain, there is no separate arising or ceasing. (The Ancient Commentary states:

"Because there is the transformation of the sequence of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is termed 'arising and ceasing. Apart from this sequence, there is no further dharma that arises. Apart from the conditions of the causal chain, there is no other distinct nature.
To speak of identity or difference is the false conceptualization of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Neither existence nor non-existence as a nature gives rise to anything.

It is neither existent nor non-existent; apart from the transformation of these enumerations, none of this can be apprehended. (The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "If one is separated from delusive conditions, there is no further nature of arising.

Apart from the transformation of the twelve enumerations, the four positions—existence, non-existence, both, and neither—regarding the nature of arising are all unapprehendable. There are merely conventional enumerations that link together like a chain;

apart from those chains of causes and conditions, the meaning of "arising" cannot be found. (The *Jizhu* states: "The various conventional enumerations refer to the twelve links of dependent origination. This is the new explanation.")

It is said: Ordinary beings cannot comprehend that all things arise from delusive conditions; therefore, throughout long kalpas, they are caught in a hook-and-chain, an unbroken succession of links. Thus, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is termed "hook-and-chain. If one is free from delusive conditions, there is no separate dharma of birth.

Since birth lacks intrinsic nature, it does not arise; thus, one avoids the errors of the various non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*). I speak only of the hook-and-chain of conditions, yet the ignorant and foolish cannot comprehend this. (The *Jizhu* [Collected Notes] states: "Birth has no self-nature; therefore, though it arises, it is non-arising.

'Arising' is synonymous with 'birth. Therefore, the Tang translation says: 'Because birth is non-existent, there is no arising. Because there is no arising, one avoids the error of the non-Buddhists' doctrine of a dharma of birth. I merely speak of dependent origination as a hook-and-chain.")

...the hook and chain. Yet the foolish man cannot know that within conditions there is no arising. If, apart from the hook and chain of conditions, there were a separate nature of arising, this would be the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), which destroys the meaning of the hook and chain.
(That is to say, if one claims there is a separate nature of arising apart from the causal conditions of the hook and chain, this nature has no basis;

it is falsely taken as a cause, and thus the Buddha judges it to be the doctrine of causelessness. The outsiders reckon that this cause can produce all phenomena, yet the phenomena themselves cannot arise of themselves. Is this not a fault that destroys the principle of the causal hook and chain? It is like a lamp revealing [objects].

If the manifestation of various forms through the chain of causes were like this, then apart from the chain of causes, there would have to exist other inherent natures (*svabhāva*). (This follows the previous analogy to clarify that the nature of arising is without cause.

The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) speculate that it is because of an inherent nature of arising that the chain of causes can manifest. If this were so, it would be like a lamp being able to reveal forms; the lamp is the metaphor for the nature of arising, and the various forms are the metaphor for the phenomena of the chain of causes.)

It is like various forms in the dark that become manifest due to a lamp; by analogy, all phenomena (*dharmas*) arise through their causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). If this were so, there would be distinct natures (*svabhāva*) existing apart from the chain of causality.

Consider the lamp: it can only manifest, but it cannot produce. To claim that it can produce the various forms is incorrect. Why? Because each form has its own substance; how could a lamp produce it? Therefore, the Buddha’s judgment that there is no [independent] cause is indeed well-founded.

Where there is no nature, there is no arising, just like the self-nature of empty space. If one is separated from the chain of causality, wisdom has nothing to differentiate. (The Wei translation says: "Arising...")

The Dharma is fundamentally without substance; its self-nature is like empty space. To seek the Dharma apart from the hook and the chain is for the ignorant to remain without knowledge. ○ That which is without nature and without birth means that the nature of birth is not real, and is therefore without nature. Being without nature, there is nothing capable of producing.

If the self-nature capable of producing [phenomena] does not exist, then it is identical to empty space and cannot produce things. If one is separated from the "hook and chain" (the causal nexus), the nature of production is like space;

even if one possesses wisdom, what could there be to differentiate? Furthermore, there is another non-arising, which is the dharma attained by the worthy and noble ones. That which is produced yet is non-arising is precisely the "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). (This follows the previous meaning of being separated from the "hook and chain" to correctly clarify non-arising.

It means that apart from the "hook and chain," there is inherently non-arising, which is the dharma attained by the worthy and noble ones of the Three Vehicles. Since that which is produced through causes and conditions is itself non-arising, this constitutes the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.)

If all people in the world were to observe the meaning of the "hook and drill" (gōu-zuǒ), they would realize that all phenomena are fundamentally free from the hook and drill; from this, they would attain samādhi.
Ignorance, craving, and various karmas—these are the internal hook and drill. The fire-drill, the clay lump, the potter’s wheel, seeds, and so forth are called external. (Ignorance, [Wei...])

The two translations from the Tang dynasty render this as "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Ignorance is one of the two causes among the past links; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is one of the three causes among the present links. Within the twelve links of dependent origination, these two causes—the past and the present—are cited briefly to encompass the remaining ten, collectively forming the "inner chain.

The fire-drill, the lump of clay, and the potter’s wheel serve as examples of the "outer chain," which applies analogously to all phenomena. The fire-drill is the tool by which people obtain fire; the lump of clay and the wheel are the conditions for a potter to fashion vessels.

The seed is the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), while water and soil are the auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). All internal and external phenomena share this principle of being like a chain. By citing these three factors as examples of such chained causal conditions, it is shown that they exist through a combination of factors. It is because of this...

The internal and external are interlocked; this is because all worldly phenomena achieve accomplishment [through this]. If there were another nature that arose from causes and conditions, it would not possess the meaning of being "interlocked," and thus it would not be accomplished.
(The Wei translation says: "If there were further other dharmas arising from causes and conditions, they would be devoid of the meaning of being interlocked;

they would not abide in the Holy Teaching. This states that outside of causes and conditions there are no separate dharmas, thereby clarifying the principle of successive mutual production. If, outside of causes and conditions, there were a separate other-nature that arose from those causes and conditions, that would be a causeless nature; it would not be this [dependent origination]).

[The meaning of] "hook and chain" cannot be established). If arising has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for whom would there be hook and chain? Because they arise in a continuous succession, one should know that this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

(The first two lines refute the non-reality of the nature of arising according to the non-Buddhists; they cannot serve as the causal basis for hook and chain. This means that if the productive causal nature is not real, how could it act as the cause for hook and chain?

Since that nature is empty, for whom would there be hook and chain? The next two lines clarify the Tathāgata’s correct teaching: one should know that it is necessarily through ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, and so forth, up to old age and death, that they arise in a continuous succession; this is the "hook" of the Tathāgata.)
(Regarding the causes and conditions of the "lock"): The dharmas of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—of these, the ignorant give rise to delusive conceptions (*vikalpa*).

Apart from these enumerations, there is no distinct dharma; this is what is meant by "the absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*). (All dharmas do not depart from the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion. Within these dharmas, the ignorant cling to them as being substantially real, and thus give rise to various delusive conceptions.

However, apart from the names and categories of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, no separate dharma can be found. Therefore, all dharmas are said to be without intrinsic nature). It is like a physician treating various illnesses; there is no [fixed] plurality [of methods].
Treatise: Because there are differences in illnesses, various remedies are prescribed. For those sentient beings, I destroy their various afflictions;

knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I preach the gates of liberation for them. (The first four lines are the analogy; the latter four lines are the Dharma. The analogy may be understood accordingly.)

The final passage of the *Dharmaparyāya* refers to the "gates of deliverance," which means the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). "Deliverance" carries the sense of transcending the mundane and entering the sacred; therefore, it is metaphorically called a "gate. There are three distinct types—mundane, supramundane, and the supreme supramundane—which are taught according to the superior or inferior capacities of sentient beings.
It is not that there are various dharmas due to differences in the roots of affliction; rather, by teaching only the Single Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna-dharma*), this constitutes the Mahāyāna.

(This clarifies the intention of establishing provisional means for the sake of the ultimate reality. The Buddha is able to teach the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings, provisionally deploying the three vehicles. Once they have emerged from the burning house, he bestows the white ox-cart and so forth; it is not that [the afflictions]...)

The afflictions differ, and thus the teachings given are also different. Excellent, World-Honored One! You have provisionally administered remedies according to the illness; once the illness has subsided, they are discarded. The teaching that returns one to the source is singular and alone. Therefore it is said: "I preach only the One Vehicle."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence.
World-Honored One, you also say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and are subject to the law of arising and ceasing.

What is the meaning of this? Is it erroneous or correct? And how many kinds of impermanence are there? (Mahāmati had previously heard from the Buddha that non-arising and non-ceasing constitute the meaning of permanence; now, based on that permanence, he asks.)
"Impermanence distinguishes the heterodox from the orthodox. However, how many kinds of 'impermanence' are there? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain seven kinds of impermanence; these do not belong to my teaching. What are the seven? Some say that after something has been produced, it is abandoned—this is called impermanence.
Some say that the destruction of form and location is impermanence. Some say that form itself is impermanence. Some say that form..."

The interval of transformation is called impermanence; it is the immediate disintegration of itself. Just as the interval of transformation in milk, curd, and so forth is invisible, so too is the destruction of impermanence.
All natures undergo transformation. Some say that nature itself is impermanent; some say that the nature of non-nature is impermanent;
some say that the non-arising of all phenomena is impermanence, which enters into all phenomena. (The Tang translation says: "What...")

These constitute seven [types]. Some say that the very moment of initial arising is abandonment; this is called impermanence, because once produced, it does not arise again due to its impermanent nature. Others say that the transformation and decay of form and location is called impermanence. Others say that form itself is impermanent. Others say that the alteration of form is called impermanence.

All phenomena continue in an uninterrupted succession, yet they are capable of undergoing transformation and naturally return to extinction. Just as with milk and curd, although their gradual transformation from beginning to end cannot be seen, it nonetheless exists within the phenomena themselves, destroying all dharmas.

Some say that things are impermanent; some say that both things and non-things are impermanent; some say that non-arising is impermanence. It dwells pervasively within all dharmas. [The Uighur translation lists eight kinds of impermanence, which do not correspond to this sutra, and thus they are not recorded here.

Wherever there are points among them that can be understood, I have also taken those to explain. Now, in the text following "some say," seven names of impermanence are listed. Master Le’s commentary states: "These seven kinds of impermanence are all externalist calculations; first they are listed, and then explained. [The listing follows.]

The middle section concerns only the impermanence of the transformation of form (*rūpa*). To briefly explain the meaning: "form" refers to the derivative matter produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). "Transformation" refers to arising, abiding, change, and cessation; "continuously and spontaneously disintegrating" means that while the stream [of existence] is uninterrupted, it is capable of undergoing alteration and naturally returns to extinction.

This is like the transformation of milk into curd; although it is invisible, within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), all dharmas naturally undergo transformation and decay. The remainder is fully explained in the text below. Within the commentary, some passages combine refutation of misconceptions with the explanation of the meaning, while others provide only the explanation of the meaning.

It is still not sequential; it does not emerge from the nature of form (*rūpa-dhātu*). Mahāmati, as for "impermanence of existence and non-existence," this refers to the destruction of the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*).

The self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements cannot be apprehended, for they are unarisen. (The Tang translation states: "As for the impermanence of things and non-things, it means that the characteristics of the primary and derivative elements perish and are destroyed.")

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is fundamentally without arising. This refutes the sixth [view]: that there is neither nature nor lack of nature, and that they are impermanent. "Nature" (*xing*)—translated as "substance" (*wu*) in the Tang version—is the essential body of all things.

Since all things constitute their own substantial form through the four great elements, both as the creators and the created, their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are unreal and ultimately perish. Once these characteristics have perished, their intrinsic nature cannot be found. Because it cannot be found, it is said to be "unborn. Since the nature of things has no substance, it is called "nature-less nature. This is merely applying the name "impermanence" to that which is unborn.

Here, the text presents the opponent's position in its entirety without explicitly stating the words of the refutation; this is the Buddha’s intended method of refutation. It means that since the opponent perceives "non-arising," they are establishing their view based on non-existence, which belongs to the doctrine of nihilism (*ucchedavāda*). This error is easily revealed, even though...

[This is] explained in detail (it is as clear as looking at one’s own palm). Regarding that "unborn impermanence": it is not the case that all phenomena, whether permanent or impermanent, existent or non-existent, arise.
Even when analyzed down to the level of atoms, they cannot be perceived; this is the meaning of "unborn. It is not arising. This is called the characteristic of unborn impermanence.
If one does not realize this, one falls into the doctrine of the various non-Buddhists regarding the impermanence of arising. (The Tang translation states: "Regarding unborn impermanence...")

This refers to all such phenomena as permanence and impermanence, existence and non-existence, and so forth; none of them have any arising. Even when analyzed down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), nothing at all can be perceived. Because they do not arise, they are called "unborn" (*anutpāda*). This is the characteristic of the impermanence of non-arising.

If one does not understand this, one falls into the non-Buddhist (Tīrthika) view of the impermanence of arising. This refutes the seventh [type of] impermanence, the "impermanence of non-arising. This is the calculation of those outsiders: they perceive that those phenomena of permanence, impermanence, existence, and non-existence are fundamentally unborn. Why? Because even when analyzed down to the level of atoms, they can ultimately never be seen.

Since they cannot be seen, they are non-arising rather than arising. Based on this non-arising, the name "impermanence" is established. This is the characteristic of the impermanence of non-arising. Their intended meaning is as follows: *(Note: The original Chinese text contains a section marker "○" indicating the end of a specific argument or section.)*

If one does not realize this and fails to give rise to the mind [of such realization], one falls into the view of other non-Buddhists who hold that the meaning of impermanence (*anityatā*) pertains to "arising. This is because they do not see that arising is non-arising;

for those non-Buddhists reckon the extreme of non-arising when discussing the meaning of impermanence, while other non-Buddhists reckon the extreme of arising phenomena when discussing the meaning of impermanence—thus they differ. The preceding heading states that "non-arising impermanence enters into all dharmas. "Entering" means universally entering all arising phenomena and seeing them as non-arising. Because one sees non-arising by means of arising, these stand in mutual dependence;

what is thus established collapses of its own accord. According to the Tang translation, the meaning is directly and clearly understood. The current text’s phrasing—"it is neither permanence nor impermanence"—is somewhat obscure and its meaning is not fully clear. It likely intends to say that non-arising impermanence is not that [dualistic] permanence or impermanence, nor is it any [extreme of] existence or non-existence.

Regarding the categories of dharmas: what is it? Because they are non-arising by their very nature (*svabhāva*), the term "all dharmas" should be placed under the terms "existence" and "non-existence," so that the text follows its proper sequence. As stated in the Tang translation regarding "prior nature" and "absence of nature": the former establishes "non-existence" based on "nature" (*dhātu*), whereas this "non-arising" establishes "non-existence" based on "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).

Although nature and characteristic are distinct, the intent of their refutation is the same as before). Mahāmati, the notion that "nature is impermanent" is a false discrimination of one's own mind; it is not a nature characterized by permanence or impermanence. Why is this?
It is because the self-nature of impermanence is indestructible. Mahāmati, this is the absence of all natures.

The nature of things is impermanent. Apart from impermanence, there is nothing capable of rendering the nature of all phenomena non-existent, just as a staff, a tile, or a stone destroys various objects.

(The Tang translation states: "There are things that are impermanent" refers to the state of being neither permanent nor impermanent, where one gives rise to conceptual discrimination. What is its meaning? That [position] establishes impermanence.)

It does not itself perish, yet it can destroy all phenomena. If there were no impermanence to destroy all phenomena, phenomena would never cease and would become non-existent. It is like a staff, a hammer, a tile, or a stone, which can destroy objects while remaining undestroyed themselves; this case is also like that. This refutes the fifth [view]: the impermanence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding those non-Buddhists who reckon that intrinsic nature is impermanent, the Buddha judged that such a reckoning is merely the false imagination of one’s own mind, and is not the nature of any phenomenon, whether permanent or impermanent. Therefore, he set forth the meaning of this false imagination of impermanence:

since this impermanence does not destroy its own intrinsic nature, how could there be a separate impermanent nature outside of all other natures that remains indestructible? This is simply the nature of false imagination grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The Buddha again addressed Mahāmati, saying: "This impermanence is merely the effect of the non-existence of all natures; it is the phenomenon of the impermanence of all natures. Why? Because all natures take impermanence as their fruit. Below this, [the text] reiterates a false calculation:

namely, that apart from the self-nature of impermanence, there is no other entity capable of rendering all natures non-existent, because impermanence can destroy all natures. As for the analogy: it is like a staff, a tile, or a stone, which can destroy various objects while the staff and so forth themselves are not destroyed;

impermanence is likewise. This calculation holds that the nature of impermanence is permanent, whereas the dharma-nature is impermanent. Yet, we see before our eyes that each is not different; this is the phenomenon of the impermanence of nature, not [the permanence of a separate impermanence]."
There is a distinction between the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object of action (*karma*); this [distinction] is impermanent, and this is the entity (*vastu*).

If there were no difference between the agent and the object of action, then all natures would be eternal and devoid of causality. (The Tang translation says: "O Mahāmati, it is directly perceived that impermanence and all phenomena lack the distinction between agent and object of action.

To say 'this is impermanence' and 'this is the object of action'—because there is no such distinction, both the agent and the object of action should be eternal. One does not see any cause that could bring about the non-existence of all phenomena. This citation uses the directly perceived object of action to prove that there is no impermanence. Each [instance] refers to the individual.)

All phenomena are said to be non-different; that is to say, there is no distinction between the destroyer and the destroyed. However, what is presently perceived is the object destroyed by the nature of impermanence, for one does not perceive a distinct characteristic of agent and action.

Impermanence is taken as the agent, and all phenomena as the action. Within all phenomena, no distinction is seen between agent and action, nor is there a separate nature of impermanence apart from all phenomena. If one were to distinguish between agent and action, clearly pointing out, "This is impermanence" and "This is the phenomenon acted upon," then you would have to admit your own position.

Furthermore, if there is no difference between agent and action, then all natures would be permanent. Why? Because, according to your reckoning, the nature of impermanence itself is permanent. Thus, it is known that according to their reckoning, all [phenomena]...
If impermanence were something existing apart from phenomena themselves, it would be causeless. Mahāmati, all things and non-things have causes; this is not known by the ignorant and foolish.

(This follows the preceding meaning and explains the doubt regarding the absence of a cause. For these non-Buddhists reckon that impermanence can destroy all natures, thereby causing all natures to become non-existent. Thus, they take impermanence as the cause. The Buddha therefore judges:

"All natures do not begin as non-existent due to the cause of impermanence. That which is non-existent possesses its own true cause; it is merely that the ignorant, through their false reckonings, do not recognize this).
They do not arise from causes that are dissimilar. If they were so produced, then all natures would be entirely impermanent; thus, the dissimilar would act as the agent and the acted-upon.

There is no distinction [between cause and effect], yet they are all seen as distinct. (The Tang translation says: "Mahāmati, a distinct cause should not produce a distinct effect. If it could so produce them, then all distinct phenomena would arise simultaneously;

there would be no difference between those phenomena and this phenomenon, or between the producer and the produced. Yet we clearly see that there is a difference. How, then, can a distinct cause produce a distinct effect? This clarifies that a permanent cause cannot produce an impermanent effect.

'Non-cause' and 'non-characteristic' are terms used for negation. 'Dissimilarity' is the meaning of 'distinctness. That is to say, a distinct cause cannot produce a distinct effect. 'Matter' refers to the effect. There must be such a cause to produce such an effect. If cause and effect were dissimilar, the effect would simply not exist)."

This refutes the heterodox view that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternal while their manifested form is impermanent. Regarding the passage beginning with "If [the cause] were not similar" (*yadi na sadṛśaḥ*): this follows from the preceding to demonstrate by contrast that an entity cannot arise from a dissimilar cause.

If a dissimilar cause could produce a dissimilar effect, then all natures would be entirely impermanent. Why? Because whatever is produced arises from a cause; thus, even what is considered eternal would become impermanent. For example, could empty space (*ākāśa*) produce jars and the like? Space is an unconditioned cause (*akṛtaka-hetu*), whereas jars and the like are conditioned effects (*kṛtaka-phala*). Could such a thing be possible? No.

How could that which is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) produce a conditioned fruit? The unconditioned is eternal; the conditioned is impermanent. If empty space were to produce jars and such things, then empty space would also be impermanent.

Extending this logic, all that is eternal and unconditioned would become impermanent and conditioned. Therefore, it is said that "all natures are entirely impermanent. This refers to the fact that these dissimilar phenomena, since they arise from causes, imply that if the agent were eternal, the product would also be eternal;

there would be no distinction between the agent and the product for them to be considered capable of producing. Yet, what we observe in the world is entirely characterized by difference. How then can one speak of "producing"? Thus, we know that a dissimilar cause cannot produce a dissimilar effect. If natures were impermanent...
[This] falls into the nature and characteristics of being a cause of production. If it falls [into this], then all natures are not ultimate. (The Tang translation says:

"If the nature of impermanence is a dharma that exists, it should be identical to that which is produced. This means: if the nature of impermanence exists as a distinct essence apart from all dharmas and is able to destroy all dharmas, then it falls into the nature and characteristics of being a cause of production. If it falls into being something produced, then its own self-nature should perish.

How then could one know whether all natures are destroyed or not? Therefore, it is said that all natures are not ultimate. If all natures fall into the characteristics of being a cause of production, they themselves should be impermanent. They should...
[If you say] it is impermanent: because impermanence is impermanent, all natures (*sarva-bhāva*) would not be impermanent; they ought to be permanent. (The Tang translation says:

"If [impermanence] is itself impermanent, because it is itself impermanent, then all phenomena that are impermanent should all be permanent. [This restates the preceding text as a logical reason to clarify that the thesis is unestablished. That is to say, if one falls into the fallacy of using 'all natures' as the reason for the characteristic of impermanence, then the self-nature of impermanence should itself be impermanent. Why? Because it falls into the characteristic of being a reason. Since its own nature is impermanent, then all those natures which are the objects of negation would not be impermanent; they ought to be permanent. Why?

Because if the self-nature of impermanence has already fallen into the role of a reason, how could it be permanent?"* ) *Note: This passage critiques the opponent's argument by demonstrating that if the property of "impermanence" is applied as a reason (*hetu*) for the nature of all things, it leads to a contradiction where the subject of the reason (impermanence) must itself be impermanent, thereby rendering the objects of negation (all natures) permanent.*

If that were so, then all created natures, although they are causes of creation, would also have to be eternal. If that which is impermanent were included among all natures, it would necessarily fall within the three periods of time.
That past form is accompanied by destruction; the future does not arise because form does not arise. Present form is accompanied by the characteristic of destruction.

As for form, it is a specific accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The four great elements and the derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) do not perish in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because they are free from being either different or non-different.
All non-Buddhists [assert] that all four great elements are indestructible, as are all four great elements within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Furthermore, derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) exists among the objects of knowledge; it undergoes arising and ceasing.

Apart from the derived matter of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), what could all the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) possibly conceive as being impermanent in nature? Since the four great elements are unarisen, their essential nature and characteristics are indestructible. (The Tang translation states:

"Mahāmati, if there were no eternally abiding dharmas, [derived matter] would be identical to those dharmas, falling within the three periods of time: it would have already ceased simultaneously with past form, it would not arise in the future, and it would perish together with the present. All non-Buddhists reckon that the essence and nature of the four great elements are indestructible; as for form...")

This refers to the differentiation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*). Because they are neither different nor non-different, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is likewise not subject to destruction. Mahāmati, within the three realms of existence, there is nothing among the primary elements and the derived matter that does not possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

How could there be any other nature of impermanence that could produce things without itself being extinguished? [Note: According to the Tang translation, this is clearly understandable. The present text refutes [the opponent's view] by stating: "If impermanence were to enter into all phenomena, it would necessarily fall within the three periods of time; thus, the self-nature of impermanence itself would be destroyed. How, then, could it be permanent?

Regarding the passage beginning with "As for form" (*rūpa*), it sets forth the view of all non-Buddhists who maintain that the essence of form exists apart from consciousness. They claim that form is a differentiation of the accumulation of the four great elements; because the nature of the primary and derived elements is indestructible, [they assert that] the agent and the object...

Because the nature of conditioned origination exists through mutual dependence, the characteristics of difference and non-difference are free from conceptual construction. Indeed, all those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) falsely imagine an indestructible [nature], yet they have not attained the true indestructible nature; this is due to their false views. However, these four great elements (mahābhūtas), within the mind of the knowable, all belong to the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Yet what do these non-Buddhists contemplate when they calculate that there is a nature of impermanence, claiming that the four great elements are unarisen and that the self-nature of impermanence is indestructible? This is merely the deluded imagination of one's own mind; it is not a real self-nature of impermanence.

(The refutation of the impermanence of nature is hereby concluded. Regarding the departure from the impermanence of initial creation: it is not that the four great elements are something other than the four great elements.

Each has its own distinct characteristic due to its specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, no differentiation can be found. Since they are without differentiation, these do not further produce [one another].

Because the two conditions (*upāya*) do not act [together], one should know that this is impermanence. (The Tang translation says: "That which is abandoned immediately upon initial production is impermanent" means that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not mutually produce other primary elements because they are distinct;

they do not produce themselves because they are non-different; nor do they produce together because they are dissociated. One should know that this is not impermanence consisting of being produced at the beginning and then abandoned. [This refutes the first type of impermanence: being produced and then abandoned]. Now, the text [proceeds with] the refutation...)

The character "shih" (捨) means "to abandon. This is the calculation of these non-Buddhists, who claim that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the creators that initiate arising; once they have created the derived matter (*bhautika*), the creators themselves are abandoned. Because this state of abandonment is termed "impermanence," one must understand the intent behind this calculation. That intent does not depart from the two characteristics of creator and created.

Therefore, the Buddha established three types of creative characteristics—mutual creation, self-creation, and common creation—to refute it. "Not four" below refutes mutual creation. "Not shih" means "to dispel. The refutation says: if one calculates [the relationship between] creator and created...

Regarding "mutual creation": it is not that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) further create distinct four great elements; rather, because these [elements] act as both the agent and the object of one another, it is called "mutual creation. Since there are no distinct four great elements, mutual creation cannot be established. As for the reason why it is not established, the text says:

"Because the agent and the object are each distinct," meaning that because the causes of this and that are dissimilar, the effect is not established. In the current text, following the phrase "each having distinct characteristics," the character "hence" (*gu*) is missing, which makes it difficult to understand. Following the phrase "own-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*), the refutation of "self-creation" is presented. The refutation states: "If one calculates the four..."

Regarding the great subject and object, each being produced by its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): since a specific characteristic cannot be apprehended as differentiated, the meaning of "producing" is not established. It must be through the conjunction of two dharmas that it is called "production. Since there is no such conjunction, production by itself is not established. [The passage continues: "That which is below... [is non-existent].

This refutes [the notion of] "co-creation. The phrase "there is no distinction" serves as a transition from the preceding to the following argument. The refutation states: If there were no distinction in their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), then these factors—the agent and the object—would be mutually independent in their own natures;

therefore, they do not co-create. The word "moreover" (*geng*) is read in the level tone (*píngshēng*); "moreover" here carries the meaning of "together" (*gòng*). To explain why it is not "non-common": because the two expedients of the agent and the object are mutually independent and do not act upon one another, the three characteristics cannot create. Since all agents and objects of creation are thus empty, how could there be an initial creation that is subsequently abandoned?

Thus, we know that those who calculate an initial creation are deluded. Therefore, the conclusion states: "One should know that 'initially created and then abandoned' is the meaning of impermanence. The Tang translation is direct and easily understood; the present commentary largely follows it. Readers should rely on the Tang translation.

(Read them together; their meaning will become clear). Regarding that impermanence which consists in the destruction of shape and location: this refers to the fact that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) are not destroyed, and ultimately are not destroyed.
Mahāmati, "ultimately" means that even when analyzed down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), the four great elements and the derived matter are observed to be indestructible.

The view that [things] are impermanent because their shape and location are destroyed is untenable. Length and shortness cannot be apprehended; they are not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), nor are the four great elements destroyed.

It is only the shape and location that appear to be destroyed, which falls within the Sāṃkhya school. (The Tang translation states: "Regarding the impermanence of the destruction of shape: this is not the destruction of the primary causes (*bhūta*) or the derivative matter (*bhautika*), but merely the destruction of shape. What is the meaning of this?

It means that when matter is analyzed down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), only the perceptions of shape, such as length and shortness, are extinguished, while the essential substance of the primary causes and derivative matter is not destroyed. This view falls within the Sāṃkhya system. ○ This refutes the second [view]: the impermanence of the destruction of shape and location. They reckon that the four great elements are the primary causes.")

The nature of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) does not perish; only its spatial configuration (*saṃsthāna*) perishes. Therefore, it is said that "the impermanence consists in the destruction of spatial configuration. Regarding the word "ultimately" (*anta*) below: "ultimately" refers back to the character *jìng* (ultimate). This means that as for that which can ultimately be destroyed, one analyzes its spatial configuration down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Upon examination, [form] must perish. Why? Because when one seeks its shape and location within the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), one cannot find it; for instance, one perceives length and shortness, yet these are not obtainable [as inherent]. Thus, it is not that the four great elements themselves perish;

rather, while the four great elements do not perish, the shape and location appear to perish. This distinction between perishing and not perishing falls into the [dualistic] reckoning of the Sāṃkhya school. As for "matter is impermanent," this means that matter itself is impermanent; therein, it is the shape and location that are impermanent, not the four great elements.
If the four great elements were impermanent, it would not be a conventional designation; yet conventional designations are not [ultimately real].

"Nature" (svabhāva) refers to falling into the worldly discourse (*lokavāda*). To see all natures as being merely verbal designations and not seeing their own-characteristic arising—this refutes the third [view], that form itself is impermanent.

This refers to the calculation of non-Buddhists who claim that the matter produced by the four great elements is itself impermanent because it is not "nature. The Buddha judged this, saying: "Those who calculate that the locus of form is impermanent fall into the Sāṃkhya school; it is not that the nature of the four great elements is destroyed, but rather that the locus of form is destroyed.

As for this calculation that the nature of the color-form of the four great elements is impermanent, since "non-nature" belongs to the worldly, it is said that it is not a conventional numerical designation; it is indeed a conventional verbal expression. To reveal the reason why they fall into the worldly, he says: "They see all..."

[This refers to] nature. It is merely a verbal expression, for one does not perceive the characteristic of the arising of form (*rūpa*). Regarding "impermanent transformation," this means that a different nature of form manifests;
it is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is like gold being transformed into an ornament: the manifestation is a transformation, yet the nature of the gold is not destroyed.

It is only the state of the ornament that is destroyed; other transformations of nature are likewise so. (This refutes the fourth [view], the impermanence of transformation in the midst of form. "A different nature of form" means a variation occurring within the interval of form.)

This is its nature. The preceding passage states: "Just as with the transformation of milk into curd and so forth, the intermediate stage is invisible. This means that because milk and curd are not two distinct entities, their essential nature (*dharmatā*) is not destroyed;

rather, it is at the point where the transformation is invisible that the name "impermanence" is established. It is like a person who grows from youth to adulthood, and from adulthood to old age. The transition from youth to adulthood cannot be seen, yet the body naturally returns to extinction; thus, the point of transformation is designated as impermanence. Now, it says: "As gold is fashioned into ornaments..."

The nature of gold is indestructible; it is only the form of the ornament that perishes, which is the same as the case with milk and curd. The nature of all forms (*rūpa*) is likewise so. Such are the various false conceptions of the non-eternalism held by the outsiders (*tīrthika*).

[The Ancient Commentary states: "This summarizes the seven kinds of non-eternalism held by the outsiders. When the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are burned by fire, their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not burned.

If each of their own specific characteristics were to perish, then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced from the four great elements would have to be annihilated. [The New Explanation states: "The outsiders claim that when the four great elements are burned by fire, they cannot burn the self-characteristics of the various great elements..."]

[The opponent] says: "If that which is capable of burning [the fuel] were to exist, then the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) would eventually be severed and extinguished. However, because they are seen not to be severed, one concludes that the nature of the primary elements is eternal.

Mahāmati, the arising of phenomena in my teaching is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? It is because external objects lack determinate reality; I speak only of the subtle mind (*cittamātra*) within the three realms of existence. (The term *wei* [微] is translated as *wei* [唯] in the Tang version.

The Buddha said: "I teach that all dharmas arise from conditions; they are neither eternal nor non-eternal. The reason for this is to clarify why they are neither eternal nor non-eternal: it is because external objects are illusory and lack substantial reality, and thus are indeterminate.)

Concentration is the meaning of non-reality. Since external objects are illusory, upon what further dharma could one discourse regarding permanence or impermanence? One should simply know that the phenomena of the three realms of existence are manifested solely by the mind. The World-Honored One constantly teaches this principle for the sake of sentient beings.

He does not speak of various characteristics, such as arising and ceasing, the distinctions of the combination of the four great elements, or the primary and derived matter of the four great elements.

Through the two kinds of deluded conceptualization—the grasped and the grasper—one knows these two types of conceptualization and becomes free from the two views of external existence and non-existence.

(Continuing from the preceding point regarding the meaning of "only" (*citta-mātra*): it means that the Buddha taught only mind-only (*cittamātra*), and did not teach various marks, arising and ceasing, the combination of the four great elements, derived matter, or the imagined nature of the grasped and the grasper.

However, one knows that these two kinds of imagined natures—the grasped and the grasper—are not real, because they arise from the departure from the two kinds of false views concerning external objects: existence and non-existence. All non-Buddhists fall into a continuous succession of evil views regarding the two extremes because they fail to realize that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind.

These ordinary people lack any fundamental basis; they speak of the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane, yet these arise from the conceptualization of false imagination (*vikalpa*) and are not realized by the ignorant.

"Detached from initial creation, as well as from the alteration of form and location;

the nature and color are impermanent—such are the deluded imaginings of the non-Buddhists (the seven kinds of impermanence mentioned above, which are the deluded views of these non-Buddhists). The various natures do not undergo destruction; the Great Elements abide in their own intrinsic nature.

Yet all of them remain submerged in various views. Those non-Buddhists [claim] that there is neither arising nor ceasing; the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal by their very nature.

Brahmā is the root of the tree, and its branches extend everywhere. Thus I have taught: it is only that.

Mind-only (*cittamātra*). (These two characters refer back to the preceding two lines. The awakening of the wisdom of quiescent extinction (refers to the two vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage who equally realize the bliss of the samādhi of extinction). although they perceive the bliss of the gate of the samādhi of extinction, through their original vows, compassion, and the fulfillment of great pity (*mahākaruṇā*), they know how to distinguish the ten kinds of [non-arising].
