“If one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, this is an explicit prediction (*prakaṭa-vyākaraṇa*), unlike the hidden and secret bestowal of predictions found in the Vaipulya [sūtras]. If we rely on this principle, then both the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* should also contain this; why would it be unique to the *Laṅkāvatāra*? Furthermore, it says:

“One should know, Mahāmati, that this was initiated as a secret teaching. Therefore, he asks about the matter of bestowing predictions. Mahāmati, for this reason, the predictions given to the Śrāvakas are no different from those given to Bodhisattvas. Mahāmati, it is not...
As for the differences: Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have severed the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and their liberation is of a single flavor;

it is not that they have severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Mahāmati, as for the cognitive hindrance, it is the seeing of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is supreme and pure. As for the afflictive hindrance, it is first severed through the practice of seeing the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*);

the seven consciousnesses cease, and there is liberation from the hindrance of phenomena. When the habitual tendencies of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are extinguished, ultimate purity is attained.

"Purity" (this answers the first question). "Because of this" (this cites the three preceding points to initiate the answer). "Not different" and so forth clarify the meaning of difference and non-difference. "Not different" means that the three vehicles equally sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and equally attain the single-flavor liberation; therefore, it is said they are not different.

If they were different, then while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have eternally severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the Śrāvakas would not have severed them. Now, with respect to the severing of the afflictive hindrances, one speaks provisionally of non-difference; it is not [that there is no difference in other respects].

This refers to the severing of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Below, the characteristics of the severance of the two hindrances are clarified. Regarding the severance of the cognitive hindrances: it is the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), the attainment of the principle of the Truths, and the resulting preeminent purity; this is the characteristic of the severance of the cognitive hindrances. Regarding the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*):

once one has previously cultivated and realized the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), the afflictive hindrances are severed and the seven consciousnesses cease. Because the cognitive hindrance is liberated, the habitual causes within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are also extinguished.

Since both hindrances have been extinguished, ultimate purity is attained. Because of the primordially abiding Dharma, there is no intrinsic nature in terms of prior or posterior; because of inexhaustible original vows, the Tathāgata expounds the teaching without deliberation or investigation.

He teaches the Dharma because he is transformed by right knowledge and because his mindfulness is not delusive. He is without vitarka and vicāra because he has severed the habitual tendencies of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance.
He has severed the two obstacles of affliction and has transcended the two kinds of death. He awakens to the selflessness of persons and phenomena.

And the severance of the two obstacles. (This answers the second question. It means that the primordially abiding Dharma is equal throughout the three periods of time; it is the profound stillness of the one mind. Therefore, it is said that "before and after are not its nature. The Tathāgata’s original vow accords with this nature and is all-pervasive.)

Therefore, it is inexhaustible. Because it abides in its original state, there is no deliberation and no investigation. Because his vows are inexhaustible, he expounds the Dharma. That which is transformed by right wisdom is the meaning of the Middle Way; that is to say, he applies the wisdom of the Middle Way to sentient beings, mindful of their liberation from both existence and non-existence.

Therefore, it is not false. What is spoken is non-speaking; delivering sentient beings is identical to emptiness. Thus, it is further called "without deliberation and without examination. This is because the Tathāgata has exhausted all obstacles and is perfectly endowed with the three types of awakening.

Mahāmati, the mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, and the seven [consciousnesses] such as visual consciousness have momentary habitual tendencies as their cause. When they are separated from the category of wholesome outflows, they no longer undergo cyclic existence.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of cyclic existence and nirvāṇa, of suffering and happiness. It is [the object of] those with deluded minds and wisdom who are confused about emptiness.
"O Mahāmati, that which ordinary beings cannot awaken to is merely a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) protected by the Vajrapāṇi;
it is not the true Tathāgata. O Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata is beyond all faculties and measures (pramāṇa).

All the faculties and measures of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists are extinguished therein. Having attained the bliss of the present dharma, one abides in the patience of the knowledge of the uninterrupted dharma."

Therefore, it is not protected by the Vajrapāṇi spirits. (This answers the third question. That is to say, the seven [consciousnesses] such as visual consciousness are the causes of momentary habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). When one cultivates the wholesome and untainted categories, one departs from these seven and no longer undergoes transmigration.

For this reason, they cannot serve as the cause for the suffering and pleasure of birth and death. Only the Tathāgatagarbha, which is eternally abiding and indestructible, can serve as the cause for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

This is not something that ordinary or inferior beings are able to perceive. Regarding "the wisdom of those with distracted minds who are confused about emptiness": "emptiness" refers to the wisdom of the Two Vehicles, while "distracted minds" refers to non-Buddhists. Those protected by the Vajra [spirits] are the hidden traces of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha; they are not the fundamental reality of the *dharmakāya* Buddha. Below the section on the True Tathāgata...)

This restates the fundamental meaning of the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*). It means that the Dharma-Buddha is free from all mental measurements (*cittamātra*); all the limited mental measurements of ordinary and small-minded beings are extinguished. One attains the manifest bliss of the Dharma and abides in the equalizing patience of the Dharma (*samatādharmanidhyānakṣānti*).

Being uninterrupted—translated as "equal" in the Wei version—it is free from subject and object, and cannot be moved by any demons; therefore, it is not something protected by physical strength. All transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*) do not arise from karma. As for transformation-buddhas, they are not [the ultimate] Buddha.
He does not depart from the Buddha. He preaches the Dharma by means of the manifested signs created by sentient beings, such as the potter’s wheel;

he does not preach within the realm of self-attainment that is the domain of self-realization. (This answers the fifth question. That is to say, the transformation Buddha is not the true [Buddha]; he manifests signs according to the capacities of beings, and his preaching of the Dharma is likewise provisional.

Therefore, he is not produced from the karmic activities of self-attainment. Because the transformation Buddha is a provisional manifestation, he is not [the ultimate] Buddha; yet because there is no transformation apart from the Dharma, he does not depart from the Buddha. It is like the moon facing the four seas: the myriad reflections are all identical to the truth. The Buddha responds to the multitudes of beings: all provisional manifestations are ultimately real. By means of the potter’s wheel, he creates signs for sentient beings.)

Regarding the "Teacher of the Dharma": it refers to how all sentient beings revolve through the six realms, ascending and descending alternately like the wheel of a potter. The manifestation of the Tathāgata’s body likewise appears as superior or inferior; this is not the self-communicating Dharma-Buddha, nor is it the state of self-realization that he describes.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, fools give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven consciousnesses. Because they do not awaken to the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of permanence.

Due to their own false imaginings, they do not know the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). When the wisdom of one's own false imaginings is extinguished, there is liberation from the four stages of abiding.

Because the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) are severed, all faults are eliminated. (This answers the fourth question. That is to say, those deluded worldlings give rise to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) based on the seven consciousnesses which perish moment by moment;

they give rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) when they perceive a continuity [of existence] without knowing that it is the essence of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). However, all arising and ceasing arise from one's own false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); because of this false conceptualization, the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is illusory, and thus they do not know it.

If the wisdom that discerns one's own false conceptualization is extinguished, one attains liberation from the primordial limit of birth and death. [The section] "Below the four abidings" clarifies the virtue of severance (*prahāṇaguṇa*) attained through the extinction of false conceptualization and the attainment of liberation). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate...
He proclaimed this meaning and spoke these verses:
"The Three Vehicles are also not vehicles; The Tathāgata is not subject to extinction. That which is spoken by all Buddhas Is said to be free from all faults and evils.

(The Three Vehicles are provisionally established, and thus the vehicles are not [ultimate] vehicles. Although the transformation-buddhas are not real, they do not depart from the Dharma; therefore, they do not undergo extinction. That which is spoken in common by all Buddhas refers to their common teaching that the Buddha is free from all faults.)
For the sake of those with uninterrupted wisdom and for the sake of nirvana without remainder, [the Buddha] entices and encourages those of inferior capacity;
therefore, he spoke with intentional concealment. (This refers to the first three meanings of the verse. The wisdom arising from all Buddhas distinguishes and explains the various vehicles;

yet these vehicles are not truly vehicles, and that which they attain is not true nirvana. (This means that the Buddhas, by means of the wisdom arising from reality as it is, distinguish and explain those various vehicles, but they are not actual vehicles, and the nirvana they obtain is likewise not [true nirvana].)

The realm of desire, the realm of form, the realm of existence, and the realm of views—these are said to be the four abodes. They arise from the mental consciousness; the consciousness is the house and the mind is that which dwells therein.
(The four abodes, such as desire and the rest, arise by means of the mind; the mind takes the storehouse-consciousness as its house and dwells in dependence upon it.

The mind and the visual consciousnesses, etc., are described as being subject to cessation and impermanence, or else they are viewed as nirvāṇa and thus taught to be permanent. (This means that the first seven consciousnesses are momentary and undergo cessation, and are therefore said to be impermanent. Seeing this...)

[If one] clings to permanence, one then becomes attached to annihilation; [if one] views the continuity of the *ālayavijñāna* as nirvāṇa and reckons it to be real, one is then attached to permanence).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked in verse:
Those bodhisattvas who are resolved to seek the Buddha-way ask: "Regarding alcohol, meat, and onions, how should one consume them?
We pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One will compassionately explain this for us. These things to which fools are greedily attached are foul-smelling, impure, and bring ill repute;
they are what tigers and wolves delight to eat. How can they be consumed? To eat them gives rise to various faults; not to eat them..."

To cultivate merit and goodness, I pray that you will explain for me the offenses and blessings regarding eating and abstaining from food [specifically] onions—onions being the general name for the five pungent roots (pañca-gandhaja)—even though they are mentioned here alone.

In truth, the mind encompasses both. Therefore, the subsequent verse says: "All meats, onions, and various leeks and scallions. Regarding the five pungent roots (*pañca-gandhaka*), the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: first, garlic; second, *ge-cong* (which is leek); third, *ci-cong*, which is the formal name for the common onion; fourth, *lan-cong*, which is small garlic;

and fifth, *xingqu* (also called *xingyi*), whose leaves resemble those of the turnip and whose root resembles a radish. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that it is not small garlic, but rather wood-onion, which is the chive. The five pungent roots are: 1. Garlic; 2. *Ge-cong* (leek); 3. *Ci-cong* (onion); 4. *Lan-cong* (small garlic); 5. *Xingqu* (wood-onion). According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, *xingqu* is not small garlic but wood-onion, which is the chive. Its leaves are like those of the turnip and its root is like a radish.
Whether raw or cooked, it smells like garlic. It originates from the kingdom of Khotan; as it does not exist in this region, it is not translated [into Chinese].
After the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had spoken these verses in question, he addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the merits and faults of eating and not eating meat, so that I and the other bodhisattvas, in the present and the future, shall [act accordingly]."
For those various sentient beings who desire to eat meat, he expounds the Dharma with skillful distinctions, causing them to direct their hearts toward one another with loving-kindness.
Having attained this mind of loving-kindness, each shall become pure and clear in their respective stages, swiftly attaining ultimate, unsurpassed Bodhi.
Even the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having brought their own stages to rest, can swiftly attain unsurpassed Bodhi.

If even the various non-Buddhists with evil and heterodox doctrines—who hold the perverted views of annihilationism and eternalism and are attached to such errors—still possess prohibitions against eating meat, how much more so for the Tathāgata, the protector of the world, who has perfected the True Dharma; could he possibly eat meat? The Buddha told Mahā-...
“Mahāmati, excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, “Indeed, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat.
Nevertheless, I shall now explain them for you: all sentient beings, from the very beginning, have been related to one another through a succession of causes and conditions.”
One should not eat meat because it is always [the flesh of] one's own six kin; since they should be regarded as kin, one should not eat meat.
One should not eat meat because the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, and other beasts are sold mixed together by butchers.
One should not eat meat because it grows from impure vapors and elements. When sentient beings smell its odor, they all become terrified, just like when they encounter a *caṇḍāla* or a *tāpasa*.

Because dogs see [meat] with loathing and fear, barking in packs, one should not eat meat. (Caṇḍāla: translated as "the one with the fierce emblem," referring to one who carries a staff and shakes a bell.)

Because one adorns oneself with evil insignia, and because they are called "butchers" (tānava; translated as "those who eat dog meat"), and because they cause compassion not to arise in practitioners, one should not eat meat.
Because it is what the foolish and ignorant crave, because it is foul-smelling, filthy, and impure, and because it brings no good reputation, one should not eat meat.

One should not eat meat because it prevents the success of various incantations and arts. One should not eat meat because those who kill living beings perceive the form and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor.
(For one who eats meat, upon seeing the forms of those birds and beasts, they give rise to perceptions and thoughts, developing a deep attachment to their taste; therefore, one should not eat it.

One should not eat meat because those who eat it are abandoned by the devas. (The *Śūraṅgama* says: "The celestial seers of the ten directions loathe their foul stench and all distance themselves from them.")
Because hungry ghosts and others lick one’s lips and mouth during meals (as they constantly dwell with such beings), one should not eat meat. Because it causes foul breath, one should not eat meat.
Because tigers and wolves will catch scent in secluded forests, one should not eat meat. Because it leads to a lack of moderation in eating and drinking, one should not eat meat.

(As for those who indulge in excess, cooking the five tripods and roasting the eight delicacies—if one lacks moderation in food and drink, what need is there to mention [the consequences]?)* *Note: The final sentence appears to be an incomplete rhetorical question intended to emphasize the point regarding lack of moderation.*
[This applies to] those beyond this [stage]. Because it causes practitioners not to give rise to revulsion and detachment, one should not eat meat.

I have always said that regarding whatever food and drink one consumes, one should conceive of it as the flesh of one's own child and as taking medicine; therefore, one should not eat meat. As for those who permit the eating of meat:

Such a thing is impossible. (The Buddha admonished those who eat meat: "One should conceive of the food as being one's own son's flesh" in order to restrain the mind. Furthermore, he enjoined the bhikṣus: when begging for alms among the people, do not cook food yourself.

In all eating, distinguish not between the refined and the coarse; one eats for the sake of curing hunger, maintaining the thought that it is like taking medicine. Since one seeks food to cure hunger, why must it necessarily be meat?

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasauvarṇa who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually came to eat human flesh. His ministers and subjects could no longer endure this, and they immediately plotted a rebellion.

Their stipends shall be cut off. Because those who eat meat have such faults as these, one should not eat meat. (This indicates the subtle nature of the faults inherent in eating meat. The king was named Siṃhasaudāsa;

the Wei translation renders this as "Siṃhadāsa" (Lion Slave), while the Tang translation renders it as "Siṃhajātaka" (Born of a Lion). Based on the two meanings of "slave" and "born," these appear to be translations of the term Saudāsa.

To examine the origin of his name: the Tang translation states that formerly there was a king who went hunting on horseback. His horse became startled and bolted, fleeing into a mountain wilderness. Having no way to return and being far removed from human habitation, he encountered a female lion with whom he lived and traveled. He subsequently committed lewd acts with her, and [sons] were born...

My son, the eldest was named Pāda-pāṇḍu (Spotted-foot). Later, he became king and ruled over seven hundred million households. He ate meat without ever becoming satiated; first he ate birds and beasts, and later even humans. This is likely the origin of his name.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all those who kill for the sake of profit slaughter and trade in living beings.
Those foolish beings who eat meat use money as a net to capture various meats. As for those who kill, whether by means of wealth or...
With nets and snares, they capture those beings that move through the air, on water, or on land, killing them in various ways to slaughter and sell for profit.
Mahāmati, there is no fish or meat that does not result from instruction, seeking, or conceptualization; for this reason, one should not eat meat.

(This demonstrates the causes for killing. One kills for two reasons: first, for the sake of profit; second, for the sake of craving food. "All those who... refers to those who kill for the sake of profit. "Those various beings... refers to those who kill for the sake of food. "Because of that killing...

means that because of killing, one manufactures various instruments of slaughter. Whether for the sake of food or for the sake of profit, one kills sentient beings. Therefore, one should not eat meat. The *Jizhu* states: "Regarding the meat of this world, there is no meat obtained without killing.

Even if one obtains it without being taught, sought after, or thought of [as coming from a specific animal], it must ultimately derive from killing. Therefore, one should not eat it). Mahāmati, at times I have spoken of prohibiting the five kinds of meat, or I have forbidden them.
There are ten kinds. Now, in this sutra, in every respect and at all times, all expedient allowances are abolished and everything is completely forbidden.

(The *Jizhu* states: "Various sutras prohibit five or ten kinds [of meat] because they cannot suddenly cause sentient beings to cease eating meat; thus, there were still expedient allowances. Now, in this sutra, everything is completely forbidden as the final, pure, and clear instruction.")

The ten types are: human, snake, elephant, horse, dragon, fox, pig, dog, lion, and monkey. The five types are: those not seen, not heard, not suspected [of being killed for food], those that died naturally, and those left by birds.
Mahāmati, even the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has nothing to eat, much less meat or fish; nor does he teach others to do so. (The *Jizhu* states:

"The Tathāgata takes only the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna as his sustenance, and thus has nothing to eat. How much less would he consume pure or impure meat? Would he ever teach others to eat it? Because he is preceded by great compassion, he regards all beings...

Sentient beings are like an only child; therefore, I do not permit the eating of their flesh. (That which is preceded by great compassion means that when the World-Honored One delivers sentient beings, he takes great compassion as his guide.

There is no suffering he does not uproot, and no happiness he does not bestow. He regards all sentient beings equally, as if they were his only child; therefore, he does not permit the eating of meat. The word "child" in "the flesh of a child" carries forward the meaning of the "only child," signifying that one regards all sentient beings with the thought of them being one's own child.
To eat the flesh of sentient beings is thus to eat the flesh of one's own child. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
In the past, [meat] was our own kin; it is base, filthy, and impure. It grows from what is unclean, and its mere scent strikes terror into all.
All types of meat, along with onions, leeks, garlic, and the like, as well as various intoxicating liquors that lead to heedlessness—those who practice the Way must always keep far away from them.

(Regarding intoxicating liquors: liquor can give rise to greed, anger, lust, and evil, leading to the ruin of families and states. Thus, the rites established rules against the calamities born of such things, and the *Book of Documents* records the principles regarding the veneration of drink. If even worldly teachings are thus, how much more so...)

If one cultivates unsurpassed bodhi, how could one not restrain oneself? There is no evil that does not originate from this; therefore, it is called the intoxicant of negligence. For this reason, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* enumerates thirty-five faults, beginning with being destitute in the present life and ending with ignorance in future lives.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* further clarifies thirty-six faults, beginning with being unfilial toward one's parents and disrespectful toward the Triple Gem, and ending with drowning, being consumed by fire, freezing to death, or dying of heat. Such are the transgressions of alcohol; those who cultivate supramundane practices should refrain from it.
Furthermore, one should always avoid sesame oil and beds with perforated slats, for within them dwell minute insects.

It is utterly terrifying. (The *Xinshuo* states: From this point onward, the various verses mostly demonstrate its faults so as to cause one to distance oneself from it entirely. They rarely repeat the prose. Regarding the phrase "leaving off sesame oil":

according to foreign customs, they pound sesame until worms are produced, then press them together to extract a great deal of oil for the sake of increased fatness. How could such things be fit for consumption? Furthermore, there are many cracks and crevices in beds where swarms of insects gather; these are all unfit for sitting or lying upon, because when one sits or lies down, the insects become terrified.)
Food gives rise to negligence; negligence gives rise to discursive thoughts (*vitarka*). From these thoughts arises sensual desire; therefore, one should not eat [such food].
(By "thoughts" is meant evil thoughts. Through eating, sensual desire arises; desire causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated. This delusion and intoxication increase craving and lust.
One will not be liberated from birth and death. To kill sentient beings for profit, or to obtain various meats by means of wealth through a net—both are evil karmas;
after death, one falls into the Raurava (Crying) Hell. If there is no instruction, perception, or seeking, then the three kinds of "pure meat" do not exist.

These do not arise without a cause; therefore, they should not be eaten. (The New Commentary says: Since there is no instruction, perception, or seeking, the three kinds of pure meat do not exist. All meats are obtained by killing living beings. As...)
"What can be eaten? Thinking thus, those practitioners all distance themselves from it. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, all reprove them.
By preying upon one another, they fall after death among the species of tigers and wolves—foul, filthy, and loathsome;
wherever they are born, they are always ignorant and dull-witted. They are mostly born into the castes of *caṇḍālas*, hunters, or *taṃbas*, or perhaps as *ḍākinīs*.
(Dāyinī—translated as "rākṣasī" in the Wei version)—and those of a carnivorous nature, such as rākṣasas, cats, and wildcats, are born everywhere therein.

(This refers to their falling into the category of tigers and wolves after death; this is stated in terms of proximity. All sutras state that one first falls into hell for incalculable kalpas, then enters the realm of hungry ghosts; once the retribution of a hungry ghost is exhausted, one then becomes an animal to repay prior debts.

Only when the repayment of these debts is complete does one finally regain a human body. The severe retributions of the three miserable paths last for aeons as numerous as motes of dust. Seeing this, one should give rise to fear and quickly observe the precepts. Regarding the phrase "those born below": although one has attained a human body, the habit of killing has not been exhausted.)

[The sūtras mention] the Cāṇḍāla and others; the Binding of the Elephant and the Great Cloud; and Aṅgulimāla (the Binding of the Elephant—translated as "the elephant's armpits" in the Wei version and "the elephant's ribs" in the Tang version).
Aṅgulimāla (translated in the *Xiyu ji* as "Finger-Garland"; both are names of sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata) and this Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra—I have completely prohibited the eating of meat in these.
It is censured by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; those who eat it without shame will remain perpetually ignorant and deluded in every birth.

Previously, I taught the three criteria of "seen, heard, and suspected" to prohibit all meat; yet because of their delusive thoughts and lack of realization, they continue to give rise to [this practice].

The Place of Eating Meat. (The *Jizhu* [Collected Commentaries] states: "The Buddha previously taught that meat seen, heard, or suspected to have been killed for one's sake should not be eaten. Yet those foolish people do not understand the Tathāgata’s regulations regarding pure and impure meats;

they have already abandoned all such meats, yet regarding the skillful means of what is permitted or prohibited, they give rise to various deluded thoughts, claiming that the eating of 'pure' meat is allowed.

Just as the fault of lust obstructs noble liberation, so too alcohol, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic are all obstacles to the Noble Path. Sentient beings of future ages will be ignorant regarding meat."
The deluded say: "This is pure and blameless; the Buddha has permitted us to eat. One should eat with the thought that it is like taking medicine, or like eating the flesh of one's own child.
For one who knows contentment, gives rise to renunciation, practices the alms-round, and dwells securely in a mind of loving-kindness—I say that such a person is always detached.
Even tigers, wolves, and all manner of evil beasts may constantly dwell and roam together with them. But as for those who eat various kinds of flesh and blood—

All sentient beings are terrified by this; therefore, the practitioner of cultivation should not eat meat with a compassionate heart. By not eating it, one forever severs enmity and hostility; even with the ferocity of tigers and wolves, one may dwell and travel together with them.

If a person lacks compassion, their murderous intent will prevail excessively; when creatures see such a person, they become afraid—whether flying or fleeing. Not only do they feel fear, but they also harbor resentment. Consequently, packs of dogs howl and chase after them, snapping and biting;

though they may cause no harm to this particular individual, they certainly wound those of its own kind. One who eats meat lacks compassion and wisdom, and forever turns their back on true liberation, as well as violating [the precepts].

The holy manifest signs [of a practitioner] are such that one should not eat [flesh]. (A new commentary states: "Those who turn their backs on right liberation do so because they lack compassion and wisdom, thereby failing to benefit themselves or others, and violating the holy person’s exemplary conduct in protecting living beings.
One will be born into the lineage of Brahmins, or in various places of spiritual practice, or into families of wisdom and prosperity;

this is due to not eating meat. (The preceding section clarified the faults of eating meat; this section demonstrates the merit of abstaining from it. This serves as a comprehensive answer to Mahāmati’s question regarding the virtues and evils of eating or not eating meat. This portion of the great scripture has not yet arrived.)

This land [of the *Buddhatā-hṛdaya-ekadeśa*] consists of but a single chapter of the Buddha’s words. This single chapter of questions and answers speaks exclusively of the one mind (*ekacitta*). Whether this mind is deviant or correct, partial or perfect, is fully revealed throughout the entire sutra. However, once the wondrous mind is clarified and all manner of heterodoxies are refuted, there remains nothing further to be practiced.

Yet, although this mind is clear, if defilements are not eliminated, then compassion and wisdom will not arise; right contemplation will not be pure, and right practice will not be diligent. Consequently, it will be difficult to ultimately reach the realm of its wondrous subtlety. Therefore, the chapter on "Abstaining from Meat" concludes the full significance of the entire work.

This indeed has its reason. It is just as the Śūraṅgama Samādhi establishes three gradual stages: removing auxiliary causes, excising the innate nature, and contravening present karma—all of which are identical in principle.
(Verse upon Setting Down the Brush) At the tip of my brush, not a single word of Laṅkā remains; Floating clouds have dispersed, and the moon shines solitary.
My deep gratitude I wish to repay, yet words fail me; Through kalpas of dust, my tongues shall never wither as I manifest in myriad forms.

I humbly reflect upon the substance of my own mind:
it is ever-quiescent without ceasing its illumination; this is called "wondrous. It is not that one turns away from quiescence...
Constant illumination is called "clarity. It is wondrous yet clear; clear yet wondrous. Body and function revolve into one another, and both the partial and the correct are simultaneously reached.

This cannot be fully exhausted by ordinary human sentiment. Consequently, the various schools of the mundane and heterodox each established their own fundamental tenets to elucidate the intent of the mind.
Yet, none of them attained the correct standard. Why is this? To speak according to their emotional and intellectual capacity, they do not transcend the realm of existence.

This is because of the four propositions regarding the "ineffable" (*anupama*). Therefore, Kāśyapa, [the Buddha] has thoroughly and exhaustively analyzed [this matter], fully exhausting its subtle nuances, so that when the principle reaches its ultimate limit and emotions are forgotten, one awakens spontaneously.
Because of this awakening, one first realizes that one's own mind is inherently sagely;

it is like Yaññadatta regaining his composure after his madness has ceased—the head does not come from outside, for the head was originally there, never having been lost or gained. Such is the original nature of my mind.

The substance is likewise so. Yet, if one turns one’s back on this mind to debate delusion and enlightenment, or if one realizes this mind, then both paths of delusion and enlightenment become mere superfluous words—let alone the sutras and their commentaries.
Now, since this Way is used to awaken the people, every word of this sutra is the mind itself;
how could it be discarded? It is a pity that its phrasing is plain and its meaning is subtle, such that students [struggle to grasp it].
Not yet understanding it, he subsequently annotated and elucidated it; would these annotations not be his own mind?

These annotations are incisive in their phrasing and level in their intent, free from the habits of fragmented or diffuse discourse, and directly clarify the fundamental scripture so that all students may [understand].
Upon seeing it, I understood it at once. Grasping the meaning and internalizing it, I felt as if I had suddenly parted the clouds and mist to behold the clear blue sky; my wish was fulfilled.
As for its enduring fragrance and the bestowing of its benefits, the merit belongs mostly to the donor; what part have I in this?
On the full moon of the eighth month of autumn in the year of Jiyou (1609), the thirty-seventh year of the Wanli era, at Qinting Mountain on West Lake,
the śramaṇa Śākyabhadramoda bows in reverence and respectfully records this.
